View image in fullscreen A voter wearing a Brazil national football team shirt votes during the presidential election at a polling station in Brasilia. Photograph: Igo Estrela/AFP/Getty Images

Perhaps the modern Brazil is particularly sensitive to these questions: dysfunctional and chaotic, captured above all by a sense of endemic decline. By 2030 it will be 28 years since the men’s team won a World Cup. It still has no nationwide academy system or standardised youth development programme. The national federation has had eight leaders since 2012. This is a game that has essentially been broken down into its constituent parts, its players strewn across the globe, an entire country of entrepreneurs and sole traders.

We hear a lot about football’s power to unite a nation. Perhaps we underestimate the extent to which it can also divide; the way it can reflect the very worst of ourselves, our greed and vindictiveness, our lust for feuds and petty entertainment. There is a Women’s World Cup being hosted in Brazil next summer and while Lula has sought to fast-track the professionalisation of women’s football, Bolsonaro’s only public utterances in the field of women’s sport have been to assert his opposition to trans athletes playing it.

Occasionally voices of dissent whisper into the gale. Raphinha has shared posts on workers’ rights and social justice. Richarlison has pledged that if he ever recovers the money he spent on the island, he will donate a portion to the hospital in his home town of Nova Venécia. Former players such as Juninho Pernambucano and Rai have spoken out against the Bolsonaro family. Female footballers such as Carlinha and Tayla Carolina have used their platform to oppose the far-right. Perhaps they, unlike so many of their compatriots, realise that ultimately democracy is like an island retreat: one day it’s gone, and it’s not entirely clear whether you ever had it in the first place.

Sports.title: Pascal Gross: the obsessive runner keeping Brighton ‘one step ahead’ after fast start
Sports.content:
Most footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. Having been part of the Germany squad eliminated in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024, the midfielder entered – and won – a running race.

Gross completed the 8.4km course on Juist, in the East Frisian islands, in 31 minutes and 35 seconds. He is not known as someone who courts attention, and his victory by more than a minute came to light only when a video was posted on social media by a competitor.

Gross was moving from Brighton to Borussia Dortmund after seven years in the Premier League and reported to his boyhood club for pre-season training days later. Running is an obsession for Gross, as it is for his former teammate James Milner, who revealed last month he was training for a marathon after finally hanging up his boots, and that has shown since he returned for a second spell at the Amex in January for a bargain £1.2m.

“I think he’s looking in his free time now: ‘Where can I run a race?’ because he will never stand still,” joked Brighton’s manager, Fabian Hürzeler, after the 35-year-old scored the opening goal in a 3-0 victory over Arsenal last month. “ During the off season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours and do nothing. He always needs to do something.”

Given that Gross has this season racked up an average distance of more than 11.5km per match and has covered the third-most ground of any player in the Premier League, it is no surprise Hürzeler has compared his compatriot to a good wine: “The older the wine gets, the better it gets.”

That analysis is borne out by the rest of his statistics this season as Brighton have emerged as challengers for Champions League qualification, at the very least, before Sunday’s game at Liverpool. Not only has Gross, the Premier League’s player of the month for September, contributed a combined seven goals and assists, he is in the top five for several other metrics such as big chances created (six), chances created from open play (14) and line-breaking passes leading to a goal (three). In a team who have scored the fourth-most goals (23) in Premier League history after seven games, Gross has been the standout performer.

View image in fullscreen Pascal Gross (in white) up against Jablonec's Matej Polidar in the Conference League. The match finished 0-0. Photograph: David W Cerny/Reuters

“Sometimes he’s just one step ahead than his opponent,” said Hürzeler, who is understood to have been instrumental in bringing back Gross. “He might not be the quickest player, but he can be the quickest in the head and sometimes being the quickest in the head is very helpful. No one expected that it would be this good. But it also shows that he still has this capacity in his body.”

At a club where experience is valued despite Hürzeler being the youngest permanent manager in the Premier League’s history, insiders describe Gross as the perfect role model for some of Brighton’s younger players. Charalampos Kostoulas has scored three goals in his past four league matches and the 19-year-old Greece striker is clearly thriving alongside the man who is approaching 300 appearances for the club. Diego Gómez, the dynamic Paraguayan who scored a goal-of-the-season contender against Crystal Palace that will go down in Brighton folklore, the homegrown talent Jack Hinshelwood and the midfield linchpin Yasin Ayari are others benefiting from his vast experience, as is Hürzeler.

Gross managed 75 Brighton goals and assists after joining from Ingolstadt in 2017 in the summer when Brighton were promoted. His departure for Dortmund, a year after his first Germany cap, was to fulfil a boyhood dream but there was always something drawing Gross – who wears a long-sleeve shirt owing to a grass allergy – back to the club where he is known as the Kaiser.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It was really difficult,” Gross said of his Brighton exit. “Only something really special got me out of here. There were a couple of other options [before returning], but Brighton was always the priority. I just stayed in touch with all the lads over the time away. Maybe you watch less of the games or you don’t stay in touch as much any more, it gets less and less. But it never really did.”

Gross retiring from international football after the World Cup has also been to Brighton’s benefit. His status as a club legend was augmented by delivering the free-kick that Palace’s Jaydee Canvot headed into his own net during the 5-0 humiliation on Sunday. That was the third game in a row in which Gross has provided an assist and he has an opportunity to become the oldest player to make it four since Chelsea’s Gianfranco Zola in December 2002.

The trip to Anfield continues a gruelling run of five away fixtures in a row. Brighton drew at the Czech club Jablonec on Thursday in the Conference League and after Sunday they go to Manchester City twice in four days – the first in the Carabao Cup – before heading to Spain to play Getafe. It will test Brighton’s mettle after their spectacular start. Hürzeler can count on Gross – who has started every game in all competitions – to last the course.

Sports.title: Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid
Sports.content:
For the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport.

As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture?

Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga. A Real Madrid victory could be a catalyst for the rest of their season.

Lamine Yamal may be the best player in the world right now, and he could have the Ballon d’Or trophy to prove it by Monday. Kylian Mbappé is up there too. The Clásico doesn’t lack for star power, but the framing of the fixture has changed in recent times. Not so long ago, the world stopped to watch it. Now, the world doesn’t seem so bothered.

Is the Premier League’s dominance a factor?

Unless Manchester City’s financial rule-breaking has a tangible effect on the Premier League’s reputation, the English top flight remains soccer’s dominant league. The league with more fans around the world than any other. A behemoth so omnipresent that even the uninterested are at least aware.

April’s title clash between Manchester City and Arsenal set a new record as the most-watched Premier League match in US TV history, nearly doubling the mark for the most-watched clásico in US TV history set in October 2025. Audience trends point towards the Premier League being European soccer’s most compelling product.

The packaging of the division is possibly part of this. While La Liga has bounced between different broadcasters, the Premier League made a long-term commitment to Sky Sports in the UK and NBC in the USA to properly broadcast and promote matches. Premier League matches are filmed with more cameras. They look better. More vibrant. It also helps that fans know where to consistently find games in their TV guide.

La Liga has tried to broaden its global appeal, setting up an office in New York and even floating the idea of playing a competitive match in Miami. Past clásico encounters have been scheduled for a primetime audience in Asia. The Premier League, however, has the advantage of being an English language-first league which appears to be an advantage in the modern media market.

Are Barcelona and Real Madrid still the best?

At the peak of the clásico’s relevance, there was an unavoidable sense that the fixture was a showcase for the very best that the sport had to offer. That, however, is no longer the case. Barcelona are Europe’s most exhilarating team to watch, but the inherent chaos of their playing style under Hansi Flick comes with problems (primarily their high defensive line) that have prevented them from truly challenging for the Champions League.

It’s been a full decade since Barça last won the Champions League. While Real Madrid have enjoyed continental glory more recently, winning a 14th European Cup in 2024, they are a long way from being the team who dominated Europe under Carlo Ancelotti and Zinedine Zidane.

Real Madrid find themselves behind the curve of the modern game and the appointment of José Mourinho in the summer didn’t change that. If anything, the Special One’s not-so-special return to the Santiago Bernabéu has highlighted the club’s stagnancy. Xabi Alonso dared to introduce new ideas and was hounded out for it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Instead, Paris Saint-Germain are setting the standard at the top of the game – and doing so with a former Barcelona player and manager at the helm. And with a former Barcelona forward performing a false-nine role pioneered by Messi.

Is Mbappé v Yamal the new Messi v Ronaldo?

Lamine Yamal has 20 goal contributions in just 12 games for Barcelona this season. Mbappé has 15 in the same number of games for Real Madrid. Both players represent a new direction for their respective teams and could dominate the clásico as individuals for years in the way Messi and Ronaldo did.

Perhaps Sunday’s encounter will be the first truly memorable clash between the two. Vinícius Júnior is suspended while Raphinha is only just returning to fitness after a minor muscle injury, meaning there will be even more focus on Mbappé and Lamine Yamal.

Messi scored 26 clásico goals, the most of any player in the fixture’s history. Ronaldo had the second most (18), tied with Alfredo Di Stéfano. Mbappé and Lamine Yamal have a long way to go to reach such heights as the two new faces of Spain’s Big Two, but with every meeting their personal rivalry will grow. The narrative will build.

Meaning comes out of history. Shared experience. A consensus that something matters can take time to be reached and while the consensus is that Mbappé and Lamine Yamal are two of the best players in the world, their careers have yet to be intertwined as two rivals whose story can only be told as one. When that happens, the clásico may reclaim its status as soccer’s most meaningful game.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
Sports.content:
1 Glasner needs to fix Forest, fast

After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. Niall McVeigh

Ipswich v Nottingham Forest, Friday 8pm BST

2 New-look Villa host Maresca’s defiant City

It was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too. Their 2-1 victory at the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after their Europa League triumph in Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season. Taha Hashim

Aston Villa v Manchester City, Saturday 12.30pm BST

3 Saka injury may benefit Dowman

Max Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history with his dazzling solo strike against Everton at the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despite scoring twice against Ipswich in the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet the suspected quad muscle injury suffered by Bukayo Saka in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich means Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Everton, Saturday 3pm BST

4 Lampard wants Coventry to toughen up

Coventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularly in the 4-1 rout of Newcastle, but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out. NM

Coventry v Fulham, Saturday 3pm BST

View image in fullscreen Álvaro Arbeloa: still under pressure despite Fulham’s win over Hull. Photograph: Javier García/Shutterstock

5 De Zerbi needs balance for Chelsea challenge

Tottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning there in April 2018. Tottenham finally have a league win – they beat Coventry 3-1 on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance. Jacob Steinberg

Chelsea v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm BST

6 Iraola waiting for Anfield breakthrough

Talk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their unbeaten run to nine matches in all competitions. There have been six clean sheets and 23 goals scored in sequence that featured six wins in a row and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems in the comeback against Villarreal, which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle. Andy Hunter

Liverpool v Brighton, Sunday 2pm GMT

7 Who can rouse Carrick’s rabble?

Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week? Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties – accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus. Jamie Jackson

Manchester United v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm GMT

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth are coming off a 3-0 win against Milan on Thursday. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

8 Disasi must make amends at Palace

It’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension after his reckless red card against Ipswich. The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles were humiliated against Brighton last weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London. EA

Crystal Palace v Newcastle, Sunday 2pm GMT

9 Hull and Brentford thrive off the ball

Something unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball in their 1-1 draw at Leeds. The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.” NM

Hull v Brentford, Sunday 2pm GMT

10 Mukiele issues war cry to Sunderland

Nordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to the Premier League campaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season. Louise Taylor

Sports.title: Asian Football Confederation backs Gianni Infantino in U-turn on Fifa presidency
Sports.content:
The Asian Football Confederation has endorsed Gianni Infantino for another term as Fifa’s president in a turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised the head of football’s world governing body for a breach of trust.

The AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.

“We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”

The AFC has 47 member associations. Even if all the members do not follow the direction of Sheikh Salman, those votes could be a key to guaranteeing another mandate for Infantino. The Fifa election is in March and nominations close on 18 November. So far no one is standing against him.

Addressing his remarks to Infantino, Sheikh Salman indicated not every AFC member would go along with the endorsement but that most will. “My feeling is, I’m sure, the feeling of most of my members,” he said. “And I’ve said that to you.”

This is an abrupt turnaround for Sheikh Salman. In August, the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – in saying that Infantino had committed a “fundamental breach of trust”. They wrote an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

Infantino apologised last week in Zurich to Fifa’s council – which he chairs – for “mistakes” he made in assembling a now-scrapped $4.2bn plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors. Sheikh Salman referenced the differences with Infantino in his speech but glossed over any details.

“Yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past,” he said. “But let’s not relate the two things together. I think the last few [times] we met in Zurich you made it clear that there’s a true understanding between us.”

Even before the AFC endorsement the indications were that Infantino was edging toward a simple majority of the 211 Fifa member federations.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The largest applause came at the end of Sheikh Salman’s address when he repeated his support for Infantino. Fifa’s president took the podium after and acknowledged some errors. “When you do many things, you do – hopefully, as we did, many good things – you do some mistakes as well,” Infantino said.

The largest applause came as he mentioned how, under his leadership, more millions were flowing. “Before I started as Fifa president, each of you, some of you are still [here] and still remember that time … Each of you was receiving $1m every four years. As of the first of January of next year, it will be $25m.”

Sports.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
Sports.content:
This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight.

Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards.

It was certainly an abject return to English soil for Ruben Amorim, who could have been excused in seeing this particular week as the opportunity to prove a point. Amorim may view Bournemouth as kryptonite given they beat his Manchester United side by an identical scoreline at Old Trafford in December 2024. As it happens that is where the Cherries head on Sunday. On this damning evidence the modern version of Milan share more than a few similarities with his former employers.

“A difficult night in every aspect,” Amorim said. It began with a downpour and waves of Bournemouth pressure, an incisive move ending with Justin Kluivert missing his kick and Ben Gannon-Doak’s drive deflecting wide. Milan failed to clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. Kluivert converted the spot kick coolly and the die was firmly cast.

Amorim’s attempt to divide the match into two parts, before and after Maignan’s 27th-minute dismissal, cut no ice. Bournemouth’s tempo had been far too much for Milan before that, Maignan saving untidily from Ryan Christie after Yunus Musah’s pocket had been picked. “We just suffocated them, we didn’t give anything to them,” said a satisfied Marco Rose. “The way they did it today was just brilliant from the first minute until the last.”

View image in fullscreen Tyler Adams hits the deck after Mike Maignan pushes him in the face at a corner, resulting in a red card for the Milan goalkeeper. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Uefa/Getty Images

When Maignan clawed James Hill’s deflected shot wide, everybody on view set up for a left-sided corner. Nobody was prepared for Maignan, who perhaps expected to be manhandling a taller opponent, to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the ball was sent in. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from the captain; the penalty award was inevitable and so, even before confirmation via VAR, was his departure. This time Marcus Tavernier did the honours, beating the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani.

Barely half an hour in, the outcome had been settled. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, in making their “great escape” from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that they might land in such a position against Italian royalty. Past luminaries looked on from the stands, Harry Redknapp among them, while their polished successors turned the screw down below.

The relentless Gannon-Doak, called “a special player” afterwards by Rose, thrilled and frustrated in equal measure; the substitute Rayan almost set up a goal for Christie with a delightful piece of skill. It was Adli, another replacement, who applied a delicate garnish.

Quick Guide Conference League: Salah breaks Hearts and Brighton held by Jablonec Show Injury-hit Hearts produced a spirited display in Turkey but ultimately went down to a 2-0 Conference League defeat at the hands of Mohamed Salah-inspired Trabzonspor. The Scottish side acquitted themselves well amid a hostile atmosphere before going down to Salah’s first-half penalty and a second-half strike from Franculino, laid on by the former Liverpool star (pictured). The defeat leaves Wouter Vrancken’s side with one point from two matches ahead of their trip to Swiss champions Thun in a fortnight. Their visit had started in painful fashion after left-back Harry Milne suffered a suspected anterior cruciate ligament injury during training. Brighton drew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnows Jablonec. The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czechia. Brighton head coach Fabian Hürzeler, in his 100th match in charge, made eight changes from that memorable win with only Bart Verbruggen, Olivier Boscagli and Pascal Gross keeping their places. The visitors squandered a host of chances, the best falling to Jack Hinshelwood, Georginio Rutter and Ibrahim Osman, and Jablonec were looking the likelier to score towards the end. Antonín Rusek almost capitalised on a mistake by Joao Costinha before Verbruggen had to make a spectacular fingertip save to prevent Jiri Slama’s drive from hitting the top corner. Press Association Photograph: Hasan Tascan/Anadolu Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

What a night, then, for a club that knows what it is to gaze into the abyss. “How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer before kick-off, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the Steve Fletcher Stand, but it was worth posing in a different sense too. The sizable elephant in the room was how the Premier League’s 15th-placed team could face down one of Serie A’s most decorated institutions, unbeaten domestically this season, and simply sweep them off the park.

In truth nobody could feign too much surprise; certainly not the bookmakers, who deemed Bournemouth the pre-match favourites. Scoffing at Milan’s inadequacy is, up to a point, simply plucking low-hanging fruit. Football’s ecosystem has arrived in a glum place where outwardly fairytale occasions like this are packaged with caveats: even the English top flight’s relative minnows are, through financial and physical power, playing on a different pitch to representatives of leagues once deemed its equals.

For those understandably immersed in the here and now, Rayan came close to a superb fourth. “I’m happy for our fans especially,” Rose said. It is unlikely to be Bournemouth’s last European gala show.

Sports.title: Europa League: Celtic lose to Celta after leading, Mateta returns in Palace draw
Sports.content:
Celtic suffered more Europa League pain as Spanish side Celta Vigo came from behind to win 2-1 at Parkhead. After defeats by Ferencvaros and Benfica in their first two league phase fixtures, Martin O’Neill’s side struggled to impose themselves on the visitors who were neat and tidy without really testing Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone.

Germany midfielder Mika Baur fired the home side in front just over a minute into the second half to thrill the Celtic fans but Spain defender Javi Rodríguez scored twice in three minutes – a header then an unstoppable drive – to stun the home side who could not find a way back.

It was another damaging Euro night for the Scottish champions, knocked out of the Champions League qualifiers by LASK on a 5-4 aggregate after being 4-0 up at one stage earlier in the season.

Celtic’s ultras group, the Green Brigade, boycotted the game in protest at the running of the club, albeit there appeared to be only a couple of hundred empty seats, while 3,000 raucous Celta Vigo fans helped the noise.

Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day but Crystal Palace could not capitalise on a Besiktas red card to produce a winner in their 2-2 Europa League draw in Istanbul.

Palace were looking to bounce back from Sunday’s humiliating 5-0 defeat at Brighton, and were the superior side before Wilfred Ndidi opened the scoring for the hosts in first-half stoppage time.

Yéremy Pino drew the sides level six minutes after the restart and Mateta – who had a first-half goal chalked off by the video assistant referee – fired Palace to a first-time lead four minutes later.

Junior Olaitan netted a 73rd-minute equaliser, and Palace could not find a winner after Umit Akdag was sent off for a clumsy 77th-minute challenge on Jørgen Strand Larsen, who was subsequently forced off.

Sunderland’s winning start in the Europa League was ended with a 1-1 draw away to Lech Poznan. The point keeps Sunderland unbeaten in Europe this season after back-to-back victories over AZ Alkmaar and Torreense.

In a thrilling opening Sunderland went in front early through Timur Tutierov, who was making only his third competitive start since arriving at Sunderland’s academy in 2023.

The visitors had opportunities to extend their lead when Malick Fofana hit the post and Nordi Mukiele forced a strong save from Mateusz Lis, but Lech responded in the 70th minute through the substitute Leo Bengtsson’s low strike.

Régis Le Bris made six changes from Sunday’s Premier League defeat to Bournemouth, including a first start of the season for Habib Diarra following his return from injury.

Sunderland took the lead in the second minute when Nilson Angulo pounced on a tame pass from Lis, and the winger crossed into Tutierov in the middle of the box to comfortably nod home for his first Sunderland goal.

Robin Roefs was called into action at the opposite end with a double save to deny Patrik Wålemark and palm away Antoni Kozubal’s header before Diarra charged up the pitch and fired into the side netting.

The hosts had two good chances to level when Pablo Rodríguez blasted just past the post and Daniel Håkans was played through in a one-on-one with Roefs but flicked his shot wide.

Sunderland enjoyed a good spell of possession during which the skipper, Granit Xhaka, had a strike parried away by Lis and the rebound fell to Fofana, who rattled the woodwork. Moments later Dayann Méthalie was denied at the near post by Lis as the visitors pushed for a second goal.

View image in fullscreen Timur Tutierov scores his third goal for Sunderland’s first team since joining the academy in 2023. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images

Early in the second half, Fofana cut into the box but could only send his effort over and Poznan looked to strike when Wålemark scuffed a shot wide following a good solo run.

Diarra fired wide for and Angulo’s low strike was scooped up by Lis, who moments later made a great save to tip Mukiele’s shot over the bar.

Bengtsson looked to make an instant impact from the bench when his effort from Wålemark’s cross was sent wide. However, the midfielder made no mistake when next presented with an opportunity as a corner rebounded towards him just inside the area and he fired into the bottom corner with 20 minutes to play.

Poznan almost took the lead moments later when Roefs made a brilliant point-blank stop from Michal Gurgul. Fofana skewed an effort wide as Sunderland looked to restore their advantage and the substitute Chris Rigg’s powerful shot landed on the roof of the net, but the spoils were shared.

Juventus dropped their first points of the Europa League campaign after coming ⁠from behind to draw 2-2 with visitors Rennes.

Zeki Celik gave Juventus a fifth-minute lead, but ⁠the French side ⁠kept their ​composure and were level 10 minutes later when the Jordan international Musa Al-Taamari finished from close range for ⁠his first goal in the competition.

Rennes then stunned the hosts with a Boulaye Dia penalty two minutes before the ⁠break as the Italians struggled to create chances until Nick Woltemade equalised ​from the spot in the 67th ‌minute.

View image in fullscreen Nick Woltemade equalises from the spot for Juventus in their 2-2 draw with Rennes. Photograph: sportinfoto/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

The Germany forward ‌twice went close to scoring again as Luciano Spalletti’s team upped the ‌pressure, and Juve thought they had won it in the 88th minute when Jhon Lucumí found the net from close range, but his effort was ruled out for offside.

The draw at least spared Juventus a second successive defeat following Sunday’s 3-0 home loss to Lazio ‌in Serie A.

Jonas Hofmann made the most of his surprise start for Bayer Leverkusen, scoring twice in three minutes ​to give the Bundesliga side a 2-0 victory at OFI Crete to go top of the table with their third straight win.

Crete, who stunned Hoffenheim 2-0 in their opening league-phase match, were twice caught napping by Hofmann, ⁠who was added to the side following an injury to ​Martin Terrier. Leverkusen have ​nine points and lead Ferencvaros ​on goal difference after the Hungarian side beat Torreense ​4-1.

Sports.title: Julian Nagelsmann is warned NOT to take the Man United job by former Bayern Munich CEO Oliver Kahn because of concerns on his past experience - and 'every manager has failed there'
Sports.content:
Julian Nagelsmann is warned NOT to take the Man United job by former Bayern Munich CEO Oliver Kahn because of concerns on his past experience - and 'every manager has failed there'

A former colleague has warned Julian Nagelsmann against taking over at Manchester United - 'where essentially every manager in recent years has failed sooner or later.'

Nagelsmann, 39, is on a five-man list of managers who have been privately sounded out to replace under-pressure Michael Carrick at Old Trafford.

But Oliver Kahn, the legendary Germany goalkeeper who served as Bayern Munich's CEO during Nagelsmann's period as manager, is warning his countryman a move to Old Trafford may not be a good fit and is an 'enormous risk'.

Carrick's days as manager look numbered after United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League this week - and he could join a graveyard of managers featuring Ruben Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal and David Moyes since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Kahn identifies that history - and Nagelsmann's own past - as reasons not to move to the Premier League. Nagelsmann has managed Hoffenheim, Leipzig, Bayern and Germany but was sacked in his last two jobs amid concerns about his style of communication and approach to training.

Kahn himself said Bayern's squad was playing 'less successfully and less attractively' under Nagelsmann when he sacked him three years ago.

Oliver Kahn has issued a stark warning to ex-colleague Julian Nagelsmann about Man United

Speaking on German television this week, Kahn sent a warning to Nagelsmann saying: 'From his point of view, it's not an easy situation. He isn't someone with a great deal of experience, particularly when it comes to foreign teams.'

On the RTL/Sky Germany show Triple - der Hagedorn Fußballtalk, Kahn went on to add: 'The Premier League and Manchester United have not been known for much continuity in the managerial position in recent years.

'He has to ask himself: What is my next step? Does it have to be the right one? Or do I immediately associate it with an enormous risk like Manchester United, where essentially every manager in recent years has failed sooner or later? You should look very carefully at where you're going.

'Bayern Munich and the national team were already big blows for him. You have to think carefully: Where do my strengths lie? Which club can I really help? I think Julian is someone who can develop a club and a team and take them further. Whether Manchester United are the right next step for that is something only he can know.'

Yesterday, Daily Mail Sport revealed United's director of recruitment Christopher Vivell is pushing hard for Nagelsmann to be the leading candidate, with the ex-Bayern boss out of work following a disastrous World Cup in charge of Germany.

Chelsea assessed Nagelsmann as a potential manager when Vivell was technical director in west London and his admiration remains.

Nagelsmann and Kahn are pictured together with their partners at Oktoberfest in Munich

But sources have suggested that Jason Wilcox, who is Vivell's boss in the chain of command, prefers a Premier League proven manager, with Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte, who have all come up on a shortlist, a tick in that category.

Hurzeler does not have a release clause in his Brighton contract and so would require enormous compensation. There is well-placed scepticism as to whether any move would even be remotely possible, regardless of how well liked he is inside Old Trafford.

Carrick will face the music when he addresses the media today in his pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's game against Bournemouth in which he'll have to address doubts creeping in from players, tensions upstairs among execs and whether he will be able to keep hold of his job.

United are refusing to press the panic button and sack Carrick who is now expected to stay in charge for Sunday's game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at least. United then face Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa before a two-week international break next month.

The fact that Carrick will speak to the media again, less than two days after he tried to explain his team's shocking performance in the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, is the strongest signal yet that United are aiming to stand by Carrick for the time being.

In-fighting at United is rife right now, not least after captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned the tactics of his manager after the abject 4-1 defeat at the hands of Como.

Michael Carrick is under pressure and potential replacements have been sounded out

'It needs to start at the top,' one source close to a first team player said. 'Recruitment guys, manager, the lot need to go.'

Another source said: 'This needs a strong board to make hard decisions fast. They've already wasted too much time.'

United have stressed that Vivell and Wilcox maintain a healthy relationship even in such trying circumstances, but many close to the dressing room are telling a different story.

'At this club, there's too much focus on what's been done in the past, but we're not those people anymore,' Fernandes told Sky Italia after the Como defeat.

'The club and the players need to understand that. Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, but unfortunately that's been very difficult at this club in recent years. That's the situation.'

Sports.title: Backfiring tactics, a rudderless defence and players breaking ranks: how Michael Carrick's reign at Man United is disintegrating just as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's did five years ago
Sports.content:
For now, Michael Carrick keeps his job as Manchester United manager. He's hanging on, just like many of his predecessors did before the dam burst and the trigger was pulled by those upstairs. But more than most the parallels are drawn to how it ended up for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, a fellow club legend who thrived as an interim before it all went south as a permanent boss. By the time Solskjaer was dismissed – he had multiple seasons, rather than the five months Carrick has had to this point – it was Carrick who stepped in to steady the ship for a couple of games as an interim. It was a chastening end for Solskjaer, booed off by supporters in his final game, a 4-1 drubbing away at Watford, and things are unravelling at an alarming rate for Carrick as infighting among players, coaches and executives reaches fever-pitch. Daily Mail Sport compares the end of the Solskjaer tenure to where we are right now with Carrick in the eye of his own storm… Michael Carrick said sorry to fans in Como after overseeing their worst European defeat since 1994 The basic results Solskjaer was pushed out of the door 12 games into the Premier League season following the aberration at Watford, which triggered an emergency meeting that would last several hours. Solskjaer actually started the season well, winning four of the first five and drawing the other, but a 1-0 defeat to Aston Villa triggered a run of one win in seven that cost Solskjaer his job. That run included a 4-2 defeat away to Leicester, a 5-0 drubbing at the hands of Liverpool as well as a 2-0 home defeat to Manchester City. By the time Watford put United to the sword in damning fashion, the writing was on the wall for the club legend. United fell to seventh and while Solskjaer departed with the second-best win record of any post-Sir Alex Ferguson appointment, with 91 wins from 168 games in all competitions, United wanted to arrest an alarming slide and didn't dither after the nadir at Watford. For Carrick, he guided United to third as an interim and after signing a two-year deal, has begun with one win from United's first seven Premier League games, as well as losing at the first hurdle to Brighton in the Carabao Cup and losing two of their first three Champions League games to an aggregate score of 6-1. United's 4-1 drubbing at Watford spelled the end for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer ... who was given his marching orders a day later, with United sitting seventh Where Solskjaer had credit in the bank after two top three league finishes – third in 2019-20 and second place a season later – Carrick doesn't have as much to lean on as results slide. The 1-1 draw at home to Tottenham Hotspur, who finished with ten men, triggered boos from a frequently patient home support, while the 4-1 disaster in Como was extremely alarming, not least because players looked alien to the level, such was the gulf in class. Seven points from a possible 21 in the Premier League is already putting hopes of back-to-back Champions League finishes in doubt. Rudderless defence can't cope By the end of the Solskjaer era the performances were disastrous, with his team so easy to score against. Defensively United looked all at sea and were devoid of any confidence in the approach, shipping so many goals, noting the five against Liverpool and the four that followed at Watford. 'The worst thing is the performances, the team have looked all over the place,' Gary Neville said of Solskjaer's side at the time. '[At Watford] the highlights, some of the goals, the defending is absolutely woeful, the goalkeeper and defenders and that's a back four, five that have played together a number of times. They've looked rudderless on and off the pitch.' Carrick's biggest issue is that the eye test is so bad that both players and supporters have next to no belief that it's going to be turned around. Bruno Fernandes hit out at Carrick's tactics after he was hooked an hour into the Como game In Como, United didn't look capable of competing. They looked too late in the press while they were easy to play through in the middle while the back-line looked as bad as anything we saw under Solskjaer. They aren't running forwards, nor running back, with any sort of intensity and it means United are one of the easiest teams in Europe to come up against right now. Failing to change the style of play Individual mistakes underscored a collapse of performance under Solskjaer with his tenure ending with 11 mistakes leading to shots on goal by full-time at Watford, the joint-worst total in the Premier League at that point in the 2021-22 season. Solskjaer’s United couldn’t keep clean sheets – which is an issue blighting Carrick right now – and both teams give the ball away in costly areas, as Carrick saw away in Como. The signing of Cristiano Ronaldo was hugely problematic for Solskjaer – who didn't want to sign Ronaldo but the club felt they had no choice but to make the move once the Portuguese superstar became available – as it shifted the balance of power in the side. Carrick isn't necessarily facing the problem of managing one specific superstar, but he's trying to shift from a transitional side into a ball-dominant team running a high press and his team simply don't have the physicality capabilities to do so. When Solskjaer’s United lost 5-0 to Liverpool the press was a mess and Carrick’s team don’t look coherent when they press, with Bruno Fernandes running forward alone and turning around to find that he isn’t backed up.

Your browser does not support iframes.

The similarity is that defensively both sides look so incredibly poor and having both played under Sir Alex Ferguson, they would have been well aware that success is built on strong foundations at the back. That hasn’t proven true for Carrick and it certainly wasn’t for Solskjaer at the end. Dressing-room mood Right now with Carrick there is an enormous absence of accountability from the dressing room, which wasn't the case in the final days of Solskjaer. 'It was embarrassing, the way we played today,' goalkeeper David de Gea said post-Watford. 'The first half was very poor - it's not acceptable for this club and the level of players that we have. It's another nightmare. There's been some difficulties but I don't really know what to say.' There was, however, a damning indictment on the level of coaching when De Gea added: 'I have been in difficult moments with this club but we are in a difficult situation - we don't know what to do with the ball, we are conceding a lot of goals. It's a horrible moment.' He added: 'It's hard to be in the dressing room now - we are sad, we are angry. Personally I'm hurt - it's a very difficult moment for the whole club.' Pundits eviscerated the players, just as they are right now. David De Gea admitted United didn't know what to do with the ball after the defeat at Watford - a damning criticism of the coaching staff as well as the players Jamie Carragher said of Solskjaer in 2021: 'So no matter how your manager has set you up or what his tactics are or whatever it may be, whether he has a presence in the dressing room or if those players respect him, who knows? 'But, those players and some of the performances and results they've given this season are an absolute disgrace because that is one of the most expensive squads in world football, one of the highest-paid squads in world football and Watford are pretty awful. 'I've watched them a lot this season and to lose there 4-1 is absolutely disgusting and a disgrace from those players.' Alan Shearer, meanwhile, claimed on Match of the Day: 'It's quite clear from their attitude and their performance that the players don't want the manager. They've stopped running for the manager. They've lost respect for the manager.' That was certainly a debate then: had players downed tools for Solskjaer by the end? He, himself, has since come out to reveal that he asked players at half-time who was up for playing the second half. What Carrick is navigating is that club captain Bruno Fernandes, as well as summer signing Youri Tielemans, publicly questioned the tactics and approach, laying the blame squarely at the manager's door. 'It's a combination of everything: tactical, technical, effort. We need to try do better at everything,' Tielemans said post-Como when asked what's going wrong. Fernandes was much more direct – and cutting. 'It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,' Fernandes said. Youri Tielemans was one of three midfielders signed in the summer but results have not gone to plan Asked if he meant that Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: 'That's on the manager and staff to say, not me.' The mood between players and manager feels much more strained now than it was in the final days of Solskjaer, that much feels obvious. FAN MOOD What isn't disputed is that Solskjaer was booed by a large swathe of supporters at Watford as he went over to supporters that day knowing that his sacking would be imminent. 'Ole can't complain, he's been given three years, he's been backed in the transfer market,' Neville said. 'David Moyes was given eight months and kicked out, so I don't think Ole can complain about the time he's been given and the money he's been afforded.' The general feeling in the fanbase as it unravels for Carrick is one of apathy at how another regime has already hit the rocks, less than six months after Carrick was confirmed as the permanent manager. Much of the anger is being directed at Ineos and those on the football board, not limited to director of football Jason Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada, who many fans feel have badly let down Carrick. Lisandro Martinez publicly criticised Wilcox and there is more anger towards executives in the boardroom right now than there is for Carrick, who many supporters feel has been a sitting duck after not getting enough reinforcements after a third-placed finish.

Sports.title: New York Knicks slammed after staffers are 'denied NBA championship rings in cruel fake email ploy'
Sports.content:
New York Knicks slammed after staffers are 'denied NBA championship rings in cruel fake email ploy'

The New York Knicks ring ceremony on Tuesday night rang hollow for some staff and coaches at Madison Square Garden after the team used the promise of championship jewelry as the backdrop for a cruel phishing test.

According to Joe Vardon of the Athletic, longtime employees at Madison Square Garden - including some that work for the Knicks business operations - will not be receiving rings at all. It's common for most employees of NBA teams to receive rings, however, they are usually not the same quality as the ones received by players and coaches.

But, according to the outlet, those employees discovered this decision at the end of September when the Knicks sent an email to a long list of employees. Recipients of that email got a first glimpse of their would-be championship rings.

'Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,' read the email, obtained by The Athletic. '(Employee name), this one is on the house. MSG is issuing a complimentary employee championship ring. The same jeweler, the same craftsmanship, personalized with your name. No cost to you.

'There are two designs to choose from: Championship Gold and Garden Classic. Reserve the one you want below.'

However, when employees clicked the link at the bottom of the message to choose their ring, they were automatically flagged by the company and forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class.

Some Knicks staffers were fooled by a cruel internal phishing test which falsely promised them championship rings and instead were forced to take cybersecurity courses, per The Athletic

Additionally, the outlet says no assistant coaches received rings - only empty boxes

New York Knicks guard Jose Alvarado looks at his 2025-26 World Champions ring

Sources told The Athletic that this was done to 'satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan's growing cybersecurity concerns.' The Knicks have been widely slammed online for the 'cruel' ploy since the story surfaced.

One fan wrote: 'This is kind of breaking my heart what a cruel thing to do in the face of joy', while another said: 'You have to be a truly terrible person to do this.'

A further post read: 'I get phising emails all the time. Teasing them with rings is just f***ing cruel' and 'All of this is legitimately insane. What an incredibly cruel and humiliating thing to do.'

And even the coaches who rightfully won rings didn't receive them on the night of the ring ceremony, multiple sources told The Athletic.

Team president Leon Rose was the first person to get a ring during the Knicks' on-court ceremony, opening the black box he was given to reveal a sparkling ring specially designed by jeweler Jason of Beverly Hills. But when those same boxes were handed to the Knicks' assistant coaching staff, they were empty.

Two sources told The Athletic that those assistants were informed earlier on Tuesday they wouldn't get their rings that evening. The outlet added that assistants had not been fitted for rings prior to the event.

Those sources 'described assistants' reactions to not getting rings ranging from genuine anger to annoyance.'

Sources told The Athletic that those coaches were told they would receive championship rings eventually.

The outlet also says they received 'conflicting information about whether head coach Mike Brown received his ring on Tuesday and could not immediately verify if he got one.'

When contacted by The Athletic for comment, a spokesperson for MSG Sports said, 'We are not disclosing anything about the rings.'

The Daily Mail has contacted MSG Sports for comment.

Sports.title: Former Scotland rugby star, 39, to go on trial charged with rape, controlling and abusing a woman over a 14-year period
Sports.content:
Former Scotland rugby star, 39, to go on trial charged with rape, controlling and abusing a woman over a 14-year period

Former Scotland rugby international Tim Visser will stand trial in court on charges of raping, controlling and abusing a woman.

The accusations against Visser cover a 14-year period stemming from 2010 to 2024 and are said to have happened in Edinburgh and elsewhere. He has pleaded not guilty.

The trial date has been set for January 12, 2028 in the Scottish capital.

Two of the charges state that Visser raped the woman on multiple occasions - and include claims that he had sex with her after consent had been withdrawn.

Another charge against the 39-year-old alleges that he repeatedly behaved in a threatening and abusive manner towards the woman. He is also accused of taking 'intimate images' of her without her consent and sending one to someone else.

Visser, who won 39 caps for Scotland, was said to have been aggressive, hounded her with calls and texts, demanded to know where she was, controlled her appearance, finances and what she wore and ate.

Former Scotland international rugby star Tim Visser (centre) faces trial, charged with rape

Prosecutors also allege he isolated her from family and friends and that he was physically violent.

A fourth charge states he engaged in a course of abusive behaviour against the woman on various occasions.

In total, there are 26 different claims against Visser. A number are similar to the threatening behaviour allegation but also include a string of sexual matters.

The indictment states the prosecution may lead evidence about other matters dating back to 2004 - which include physical and sexual incidents, threats and controlling behaviour. However, these are not formal charges at this stage.

At the High Court hearing in Glasgow, Ian Duguid, defending, said: 'It is a plea of not guilty to the indictment.'

Visser was born in the Netherlands but represented Scotland over a five-year period between 2012 and 2017, scoring 14 tries for his adopted country.

Visser, who could play on the wing or at full-back, played for Newcastle Falcons - now Newcastle Red Bull - Edinburgh Rugby and Harlequins. He retired from the sport in 2019.

Sports.title: Inside Matthias Jaissle's Newcastle struggles: 'Vertical football' philosophy that led to crisis meeting, fan concern at Ruben Amorim echoes, square pegs in round holes and why he wants to copy Hansi Flick's Barcelona blueprint
Sports.content:
It is a good time to play Crystal Palace. That, at least, is the crumb of comfort being nibbled at on Tyneside this week. The rather more uncomfortable truth is that it is also a good time to play Newcastle United.

Just two months in and, unfairly or otherwise, Matthias Jaissle’s future is being measured by some in days and weeks. Not by those inside St James’ Park, nor inside the PIF towers of Riyadh, and not by those on the outside who make allowance for the difficulty of the situation he inherited in August.

Newcastle sold their best players and replaced them with, to be brutally candid, inferior models. It is hard, of course, to upgrade on stars who leave for Barcelona and Arsenal, and what was billed as a brave new era has, in the short term, looked like a backwards stumble.

But Jaissle’s job, as is that of any manager, is to manage what he has, not lament what has been lost. At present, too many square pegs are being hammered into round holes in the hope that they will fit, which they have not. During Saturday’s 1-0 home defeat by Aston Villa, three players started in a position they would not consider their best.

Among them was £51million marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who arrived on the promise of reinventing himself as a striker. After three starts without a goal, the 21-year-old was shifted to the wing, albeit the opposite flank to where he spent much of his time at previous club Lille.

Meanwhile, at No 10, in the absence of an actual No 10, midfielders and strikers continue to moonlight.

Just two months in and, unfairly or otherwise, Matthias Jaissle’s future as Newcastle manager is being measured by some in days and weeks

In the defeat against Villa, three players started in a position they would not consider their best. Among them was £51million marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo

In the closing stages, centre back Dan Burn was then parachuted in at centre forward. The last time he did that, England were chasing a World Cup semi-final against Argentina.

Jaissle’s ploy was criticised, but the sobering thought for Newcastle, a club who have spent £175m trying to replace Alexander Isak, is that the Hail Mary was their only prayer.

Mitigation for a head coach, however, only extends into so many matches. Another defeat at Selhurst Park – Newcastle have lost three of the last four – and the trauma of summer will be overtaken by the anguish of today. That means more focus on Jaissle and less on the deeper legacy issues as to why his side are struggling.

As opposite number Pierre Sage has found, when there is no easily reachable body of work to use as a shield against scrutiny, judgment can be quick and unforgiving.

Jaissle, at 38 years old and having landed from Saudi Arabia via a successful period with Red Bull Salzburg in Austria, is learning that harsh reality in the harshest of surrounds.

By any reasonable measure, the young German should be afforded time, patience and understanding. He is bright and, increasingly, likeable.

In the Premier League, however, what you deserve you don’t always get. Supporters, especially those amplified by football’s anger-rithm, demand immediate evidence of competence and progress. In other words, results.

Yet the concern when it comes to Jaissle and Newcastle, among those not governed by such outcome-driven emotion, is that the underlying numbers and observations of the eye are more troubling than a far-from-disastrous league position of 11th.

In the closing stages against Villa, centre back Dan Burn was parachuted in at centre forward, a Jaissle ploy that has been criticised

By any reasonable measure, the young German manager should be afforded time, patience and understanding

The manager is not blind to that reality, either. He is aware of his side's critical ball losses and unforced errors ranking too highly in the division. ‘Expected Points’, also, has them in the bottom three.

Jaissle has held meetings with his players over the past fortnight, the first in the wake of last week’s 4-1 defeat by Coventry, when issues over the implementation of his ‘vertical football’ philosophy were addressed. His 4-2-3-1 formation has consistently left them exposed in midfield.

Before that, following another 4-1 loss at Leeds last month, Jaissle determined that the poor performance was not a consequence of his tactical approach.

He felt helpless at Elland Road when his players failed to compete for first balls, never mind second, and were bullied into submission.

Working alongside a dozen analysts in a war room at the club’s training ground, he decided it was no time to abandon his strategy when basic application was more so to blame.

But now that effort is present – few could question Newcastle’s commitment against Villa – the spotlight returns to shape, game-plan and preparation. The basics of a manager, if you like.

‘Expected Points’ has Harvey Barnes and his Newcastle team-mates in the bottom three of the Premier League

That has been the source of debate this week. The doubters have likened the coach to Ruben Amorim or Ange Postecoglou, stubbornly wedded to a style that will likely lead to divorce. Jaissle believes otherwise.

Indeed, he noted a recent interview with Barcelona midfielder Rodri, who spoke of the intensity and physicality with which they train, a level replicated on a matchday. That is Jaissle’s vision.

He looks at what countryman Hansi Flick is achieving at Camp Nou, with a 4-2-3-1 set-up, and he wants that energy and incision at Newcastle. His conviction is to be admired, but there is a fine line between sticking to your principles and being held hostage by them.

Jaissle has the kindest fixture in the calendar this weekend. But if the gift horse bites, patience will be the first thing to bolt.

Sports.title: Widow of Middlesbrough icon Willie Maddren calls for greater protection for footballers over link between headers and fatal MND - which caused Rob Burrow's premature death
Sports.content:
Widow of Middlesbrough icon Willie Maddren calls for greater protection for footballers over link between headers and fatal MND - which caused Rob Burrow's premature death

Long before Rob Burrow's brutal illness and premature death launched Sir Kevin Sinfield on his quest to raise millions for research into motor neurone disease (MND) there was Willie Maddren.

For Teessiders of a certain age, Maddren needs no introduction.

For the benefit of others, he was a local hero at the heart of a glorious era for Middlesbrough, a fearless centre forward converted into a fearless centre half in Jack Charlton's brilliant team promoted as runaway second-tier champions in 1974.

They rattled the elite on their return to the top flight with an unlikely tilt at the title before a late fade to finish seventh.

England recognition came for Maddren at Under-23 level and senior call-ups in the 1974-75 season, but there would be no full cap before knee problems set in and cut short his playing career.

At 26, with 351 Boro appearances behind him, he retired. Later, he returned as physio and manager and, at the age of 44, was diagnosed with MND. He died in 2000 at 49.

After his death at the age of 49, his widow Hilary has become outspoken raising awareness of the connection between the disease and his playing career

Maddren played 351 games for Middlesbrough and was forced to retire aged 26

More than a quarter of a century on, Sinfield is on a mission to beat the disease that killed his team-mate Burrow, raising more than £11million to fund much-needed research.

There is still no sign of a cure. Precious little is known about the causes but as the list of sports stars with MND extends, Maddren's widow Hilary has become increasingly convinced that their athletic pursuits are central to the problem, whether that be the shuddering contact in rugby or heading the ball in football.

'There's got to be a connection,' Hilary tells Daily Mail Sport from her home in North Yorkshire. 'I follow it all closely and it takes me back with a slight sadness to see it happening to such a huge extent.

'It's quite frightening there's so many of them, that's the problem. I realise that you can't just go around bandying these things about, but it feels strange to me nothing is said.

'We know in football, heading the ball is causing neurodegenerative diseases. Years ago, we found out there was a bigger chance of getting lung cancer if you smoked. Not everybody with lung cancer smoked but now we know it is a contributing factor.

'When you see the percentage of rugby players and footballers, this has got to be the same thing with MND. There's nothing definitive, I know nothing is proven but it's got to be.

'I'm not trying to blame anybody. Willie would not want to blame anybody. I'm not on a witch hunt. I don't want to stop anyone playing the game, but I have nine grandchildren and nearly all of them are football mad. It's about education and being aware of heading the ball.'

The Maddrens are one of five families – all connected to Boro – leading a new campaign for clear legal limits to reduce heading in training which they believe will protect future generations from the post-career health problems they have witnessed at close quarters.

It is led by the Head Safe charity founded by Judith Gates, whose husband was a friend and teammate of Maddren's. Bill Gates, who retired before he was 30 suffering serious migraines, died three years ago at the age of 79 after living for years with dementia.

Others at the forefront of the campaign are families of England World Cup hero Nobby Stiles, Gordon McQueen and Hugh McIlmoyle.

Stiles, who died in 2020 aged 78, played for Boro after leaving Manchester United. Scotland legend McQueen, who died in 2023 aged 70, coached at the club for seven years and later worked for them as a scout.

McIlmoyle, 86 years old and diagnosed with Alzheimer's eight years ago, spent two seasons at Ayresome Park during his prolific career as a centre-forward in the 60s and 70s.

Gary Pallister, a former Boro, Manchester United and England defender, is also backing the cause.

When Pallister spoke at the launch of a new petition which the group hopes will force the matter into the House of Commons, he was embarrassed because he could not summon the name of Maddren, the man who had plucked him from the obscurity of non-league Billingham Town.

Former Manchester United star Gary Pallister is among the ex-players to throw their support behind the cause

Hilary teased him afterwards. 'Oh my God, you've got it already,' she said, although acutely aware that behind this light-hearted exchange between friends lurked a serious point.

'Gary and his contemporaries are into their early 60s. They've played their football and headed all those balls. It must be a little bit worrying when they start forgetting things.

'What's ahead? Are they going to suffer dementia? It feels like a ticking time bomb.'

Studies have proved the link between heading the ball and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can lead in later life to different forms of dementia.

MND is slightly different but nevertheless a neurodegenerative condition which damages the nerves sending messages to the muscles. Over time, they stop working and the muscles weaken. It is terminal and often health deteriorates quickly.

Maddren's first sign of the disease was a twitch in a thumb later spreading to an arm, then to the other arm, by which point it had become clear it was not a trapped nerve as he hoped.

In search of reason, he wondered if it was to do with stress from the end of his playing career, and the long hours spent on his business running sports shops and managing Boro in crisis when the club he loved was going into liquidation.

But there seemed no point wasting time searching for answers he could never expect to find, he was determined to spend what limited time he had trying to enjoy life and make a difference.

Middlesbrough held a benefit match and proceeds enabled Maddren to adapt his home and transport to his wheelchair, and he threw himself into raising funds and awareness.

He took part in a clinical trial for riluzole, a drug that is now prescribed in treatment.

Proceeds from his book 'Extra Time' went to the MND Association and funds continued to be raised long after his death, estimated close to £500,000. His family including four children from two marriages, friends, former colleagues and Boro fans joined forces.

His eldest daughter, artist Lucy Pittaway, maintains an active partnership with the charity.

'Willie was convinced if you threw enough money at it, you would find a cause and a cure,' says Hilary, who has continued to campaign tirelessly and worked in volunteer roles for MND charities and others.

'We still don't have a huge amount of hope anybody can be given when they receive the diagnosis. It's not a lot different.

'The incredible amount raised in Rob Burrow's name will make huge inroads.'

Leeds Rhinos legend Burrow died in 2024 at the age of 37. Other international stars from the two codes of rugby include Scotland's Doddie Weir who died in 2022 at 52 and Joost van der Westhuizen of South Africa who died in 2017 at 45.

Lewis Moody, 48, revealed last year he was living with MND. Earlier this month, former Wallabies hooker Nathan Charles, 37, revealed he too had been diagnosed.

The MND Association notes the patterns but notes 'correlation does not prove causation' and that the health benefits of playing sport far outweigh any risks involved.

From football, Marcus Stewart and Stephen Darby are living with MND. Former Rangers favourite Fernando Ricksen died in 2019 at the age of 43. Lenny Johnrose, who played for Bury and Burnley among others, died in 2022 at the age of 52.

'Willie loved his life,' says Hilary. 'He thought he'd had an amazing life and was so lucky to have done the things he wanted to do. He played football for a living. He managed his club, albeit that wasn't brilliant, but he was involved in football, he loved it.

'And if you would have said to him, well this might be the cause of what's going to kill you, would he have done any different? Possibly not. And that's how I feel now. Don't blame anybody, let's draw a line, but we need to learn from it.

'Anybody who has seen the slow-motion footage of a clash of heads or a rugby tackle when you see the head thrown back, it's not a good sign, it's not the way our bodies are meant to work and it's got to be doing something. It's just got to be.'
