World.title: Ebola patient in Nigeria is Swiss, had not visited DRC – Foreign Ministry
World.content:
(FILES) A health official works in the laboratory extraction room of the Institute of Lassa Fever Research and Control in Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital in Irrua, Edo State, midwest Nigeria, on March 6, 2018. The first Ebola case detected in Nigeria is the Bundibugyo strain, which is behind a major DR Congo outbreak, and the patient is a diplomat, an emergency meeting heard on October 21, 2026. The case in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, on October 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said. (Photo by PIUS UTOMI EKPEI / AFP)

The Ebola patient in Nigeria is a Swiss woman and the wife of a staff member at Switzerland’s embassy in Abuja, Bern said Friday.

The couple had recently travelled together to Uganda, but neither of them had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo — the epicentre of the current outbreak, the Swiss foreign ministry said.

On Tuesday, Nigeria announced its first recorded Ebola case, saying it was a woman who arrived in Abuja on a flight from Uganda. A total of 44 contacts have been identified.

On Wednesday, the authorities confirmed that the patient had the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is driving the outbreak in the DRC and for which there are currently no specific vaccines or treatments.

Switzerland’s foreign ministry said Friday she was “the wife of a Swiss member of staff” at Bern’s embassy in the Nigerian capital Abuja.

“The Swiss woman, who is symptomatic, has been hospitalised for about a week at a private clinic in Abuja,” it said in a statement.

“The infection may have occurred during a trip to Uganda approximately two weeks ago,” the Swiss authorities added.

“Her husband is in isolation; he has shown no symptoms. He accompanied his wife on the trip, during which she is believed to have contracted the Ebola virus,” it said.

“Neither individual travelled” to the DRC, it added.

The ministry said that the 25 other embassy staff members — eight Swiss nationals and 17 local employees — “are also doing well”.

Following consultations with the Nigerian health ministry and the World Health Organization (WHO), they do not need to go into isolation, the statement said.

Bern is considering the “potential repatriation of the patient” to Switzerland, it added.

Following the DRC, Uganda and Kenya, Nigeria has become the fourth African country to be affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak.

After flaring up in the northeastern DRC in May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever spread into neighbouring Uganda, where 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths were recorded before the outbreak there was officially over in August.

To date, the epidemic has surpassed 9,700 confirmed cases, including 4,690 deaths, according to WHO figures as of October 20.

AFP

World.title: Kanayo, Kate Henshaw, others mourn late actor Francis Duru
World.content:
Some Nigerian actors have expressed grief over the death of veteran Nollywood actor Francis Duru, describing him as a talented performer whose contributions to the film industry would be remembered.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Duru died on Friday at the age of 57 following a brief illness.

His passing comes just two years after the tragic loss of his 15-year-old son, Ifeanyi, leaving fans and the film industry in deep mourning.

Actor Kanayo O. Kanayo, in a tribute shared on his Instagram page, described Duru as a consummate actor and one of Nigeria’s most versatile and prolific performers.

“A consummate actor has left the stage. One of the most flexible, prolific performers Nigeria ever produced. Rest in peace, my brother,” Kanayo wrote.

Actress Kate Henshaw also mourned Duru, reflecting on the brevity of life and praying for the repose of his soul.

“Like a flame gone out, so are our lives when it all ends,” she wrote, adding a prayer for God to grant Duru eternal rest and comfort his loved ones.

Similarly, actress Mercy Johnson-Okojie expressed her grief, saying she was too overwhelmed by the loss to find the words to describe her feelings.

“Too tired and speechless about this loss,” she wrote.

Actress Stephanie Linus described Duru’s death as tragic and heartbreaking, praying for strength for his family to bear the loss.

“Such a tragic and heartbreaking loss. May God grant his family the strength and fortitude to bear this loss. May his soul rest in peace. RIP Francis Duru,” she wrote.

The tributes reflect the grief of Duru’s colleagues over the loss of a fellow actor whose performances endeared him to audiences.

Duru rose to fame for his role as Ahanna in Amaka Igwe’s classic film Rattlesnake, building a career that spanned more than three decades in the Nigerian film industry.

The actor’s family announced his death in a statement on his official Instagram page in the early hours of Oct. 23, 2026. (NAN)

World.title: When the economy decides what is on your plate
World.content:
By Josephine Agbonkhese

THERE was a time when eating healthily was a conversation many Nigerians could relate to. Parents worried about balanced meals, children were encouraged to eat their vegetables, and eggs, milk, fish and fruits were familiar items on many household shopping lists. Today, for many families, eating healthily is becoming less of a lifestyle choice and more of a financial privilege, as the rising cost of food forces households to rethink what they eat.

Read Also: Why food prices remain high despite FG’s interventions, ongoing harvest

As food prices continue to soar, putting a balanced meal on the table has become a daily struggle for many households, with eggs, milk, fish, meat, chicken, vegetables and even fruits now competing with rent, transport fares, school fees and other household expenses. According to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), the average daily cost of a healthy diet for one adult rose from ₦858 in January 2024 to ₦1,451 in November 2024, reaching approximately ₦1,589 by April 2026. These figures exclude transportation and cooking costs, including cooking gas, which further increase the cost of preparing meals.

For families already struggling to make ends meet, the consequences can be serious. UNICEF’s 2026 mid-year report rated Nigeria as having the second-highest burden of childhood stunting globally, highlighting the difficulties many families face in providing nutritious meals. While the government may point to improvements in economic indicators, many Nigerians are still asking a simpler question: why does the money in their pockets buy so little food?

But with nutritious meals becoming increasingly expensive, how can households eat better without spending beyond their means?

Add Colour to Your Plate

Eating healthily does not necessarily mean buying expensive imported vegetables or fruits. Sometimes, it begins with adding a little colour to the food you already eat.

Ugu, waterleaf, okra, carrots and cabbage can provide essential vitamins and minerals. Rather than buying several varieties at once, choose one or two affordable vegetables and include them in soups, stews, yam dishes or rice.

Seasonal produce is often a more economical choice. Buying from local markets, comparing prices among sellers and purchasing only what your family can consume before it spoils can also help. The goal is to make vegetables a regular part of meals, even when portions are small.

Incorporate More Legumes

Beans deserve a more prominent place in every kitchen right now because they are a valuable source of protein, fibre and other nutrients. They can also help reduce dependence on more expensive animal protein sources. Think bean porridge, moi-moi and akara.

Think beans served with rice, yam or plantain. Groundnuts can serve as an affordable snack, while cowpeas and other locally available legumes offer variety.

For households that find it difficult to afford beans in large quantities, buying smaller amounts regularly may be more manageable. Preparing a pot that provides more than one meal can also save

Prioritise at Least One Intentional Meal Daily

When money is scarce, trying to make every meal perfectly balanced can feel overwhelming. Start with one meal a day that deliberately combines different food groups.

For breakfast, pap could be paired with moi-moi or akara. Rice could be served with beans and vegetables, while yam could accompany an egg-and-vegetable sauce when affordable.

The idea is to look beyond simply filling the stomach. Carbohydrates provide energy, while protein-rich foods and vegetables supply other nutrients the body needs. When eggs, fish or meat are too expensive, beans and other affordable protein sources can help bridge the gap. One intentional meal a day is, however, only a starting point, not a substitute for a nutritious diet throughout the day.

Choose Seasonal and Locally Available Foods

Healthy eating does not have to revolve around expensive cereals, imported fruits or packaged beverages. Nigerian staples such as sweet potatoes, maize, millet and cassava, alongside locally grown fruits, can contribute to a varied diet.

The trick is to buy what is in season, available locally and reasonably priced.

A family can alternate between rice, beans, yam, potatoes and other staples rather than relying on one food item for every meal. It also helps to plan meals around current market prices instead of deciding on a menu only to discover that the ingredients are unaffordable.

Plan, Prepare and Preserve

A little planning can make a difference. Before going to the market, check what is already in the kitchen, prepare a simple weekly menu and make a shopping list. Compare prices and avoid buying perishable foods in quantities your family cannot consume before they spoil.

Cooking beans, soups or stews in batches can reduce repeated spending on cooking gas, provided the food is cooled, stored safely and reheated properly. Leftovers should be refrigerated promptly where possible, while dry staples should be kept in clean, airtight containers.

Vanguard News

World.title: Kaduna rally: ‘Your posters enjoy protection Nigerians can only dream of’ — Atiku tackles Tinubu
World.content:
Collage of Atiku Abubakar and Bola Tinubu

By Ayobami Okerinde

Atiku Abubakar, former vice-president and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), has criticised President Bola Tinubu over reports that security operatives are guarding his campaign billboards in Kaduna State ahead of Saturday’s All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign launch.

In a post on X on Friday, Atiku questioned why Tinubu’s campaign posters were seen protected while Nigerians continued to face attacks by bandits and terrorists.

“Bola, you claim Nigerians love you, yet your billboards in Kaduna require security guards. Bandits raid villages, terrorists attack communities, and families live in fear. Your posters enjoy protection that millions of Nigerians can only dream of,” he wrote.

“What a tragic statement of your government’s priorities. Bola, please protect Nigerians with the same urgency you protect your image!” he added.

Tinubu is expected to attend the inaugural APC presidential campaign rally in Kaduna on Saturday, October 24, alongside other top government officials.

Ahead of the visit, the Kaduna State Police Command announced restrictions on trailers, tankers, lorries and other heavy-duty vehicles in Kaduna metropolis from midnight until 8pm on Saturday.

The Commissioner of Police, Muhammad Rabiu, said the restriction followed consultations between the state security committee and transport unions and was intended to ease traffic congestion and ensure smooth movement during the presidential visit.

Rabiu said the police, military, Department of State Services and other security agencies had put security arrangements in place, including the deployment of tactical teams, explosive ordnance disposal units, traffic officers and crowd-control personnel.

He also warned political parties and their supporters against thuggery, violence, intimidation and the possession of dangerous weapons, urging residents to cooperate with security agencies to ensure a peaceful campaign rally.

World.title: Netanyahu orders West Bank closure as attack wounds Israelis before election
World.content:
EDITORS NOTE: Graphic content / (COMBO) This combination of pictures created on October 23, 2026 shows (top left) an Israeli soldier and an armed Palestinian during a fire exchange, (top right and bottom left) an armed Palestinian reaceting and loading his firearm during the fire exchange, and (bottom right) the bodies of the armed men after the fire exchange with Israeli forces at the northern checkpoint of Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on October 23, 2026. Israeli troops on October 23 shot dead two suspected Palestinian assailants in the West Bank after a shooting that left at least five people wounded, officials said. (Photo by HAZEM BADER / AFP)

Palestinian militants wounded five Israelis in an attack on Friday before being killed in a shootout with soldiers, leading Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order a lockdown in the occupied West Bank days before Israeli elections.

Netanyahu, facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday’s vote, said that Israeli troops prevented what could have been a major attack, with the two assailants allegedly carrying a large quantity of ammunition in their vehicle.

Militant group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised the attack as a “heroic operation” and called for more.

A Hebron-based AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near the Palestinian city, and saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.

Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers, with the AFP journalist seeing their lifeless bodies on the ground next to a petrol station as troops patrolled all around.

The Israeli military said soldiers had rushed to the Judea Junction area after the early-morning shooting and “eliminated two terrorists”.

The attack wounded five people, two of whom were in critical condition, said Magen David Adom, Israel’s emergency medical rescue service.

The service said all five were Israelis in their 20s, including one man in “very serious condition” with gunshot wounds.

With the clock counting down to election day, Netanyahu called for all Likud party political meetings to be cancelled Friday due to the attack.

– ‘Full lockdown’ –

“I salute the courage of our soldiers who acted with determination and prevented what could have been a major attack,” Netanyahu said in a statement.

“I have instructed the IDF (army) and security forces to impose an immediate cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full lockdown of all of Judea and Samaria starting today,” Netanyahu said, using the biblical name for the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

He added that troops were “carrying out stepped-up operations to thwart terrorist activities and are conducting large-scale waves of arrests”.

The military said it had “launched offensive counter-terrorism operations in the Hebron area”, adding that troops were raiding homes of the suspects and others.

Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a fresh military offensive “exactly like in Gaza” in the West Bank.

“There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon,” said Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry.

“In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”

He later said he had “ordered the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.

Israeli National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir, who has been rising in the polls, also called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be “dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely”.

No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian government in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was connected to Friday’s attack.

– Hamas praises attack –

Hamas, which is based in Gaza and carried out the October 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest in Israel’s history, hailed the attack and mourned the two dead assailants.

The attack was a “natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people”, Hamas, the rival of the Palestinian Authority’s ruling Fatah faction, said in a statement.

It called on supporters to “mobilise fully and turn the land into a fire beneath the feet of the invaders”, urging anyone with weapons to carry out more attacks.

Netanyahu in his statement vowed to “pursue Hamas terrorists” everywhere, adding: “You have no place to hide.”

Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, praised the response by troops.

“Like all Israelis, I pray for the complete and quick recovery of the injured,” he said.

The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters, and days ahead of Israeli elections.

According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

AFP

World.title: Tinubu, APC owe Nigerians answers on N10bn Ebola fund — Atiku campaign spokesman
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress, APC, have been challenged to explain the whereabouts of the ₦10 billion the Presidency announced for Ebola preparedness in June, after the ruling party reportedly claimed the fund remained untouched despite a confirmed case in Abuja.

Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication, ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said the claim raised serious questions about the Tinubu administration’s preparedness, accusing the APC of trading political insults instead of accounting for the emergency fund.

In a statement on Friday, Shaibu said the APC’s response to former Vice President Atiku Abubakar’s demand for accountability had focused on the similarity between Tinubu’s name and Ebola rather than the money and the government’s response to the outbreak.

“These aren’t just rhyming words; the effect of Bola’s policies is as deadly as the dreaded Ebola,” Shaibu said.

The statement recalled that the Presidency announced on June 9 that Tinubu had ordered the immediate release of ₦10 billion for Ebola emergency preparedness, questioning why the APC would now describe the money as untouched.

“Was the money released or was it not? If it was released, where is it held, who controls it, and why has it not been used for the preparedness President Tinubu announced in June?” Shaibu asked.

He demanded the release documents, account records and Ebola Task Force expenditure reports, insisting that the controversy could not be settled through attacks on Atiku.

Shaibu also questioned the government’s response timeline, citing the World Health Organisation’s account that the patient developed symptoms on October 7, sought treatment at a private facility on October 11, and received laboratory confirmation on October 20.

“The APC claims surveillance ‘tipped off’ the government. Then publish the timeline. Name the agency that raised the alert, give the date and explain the action taken,” he said.

He asked when Ebola was first suspected, when public health authorities were alerted, when testing was ordered and when contact tracing began.

On the 44 identified contacts, Shaibu said their safety, rather than political point-scoring, should be the priority.

“44 identified contacts are people whose health must be protected. They are not a trophy for an APC press release,” he said.

He said health workers treating the patient and tracing contacts deserved adequate protection, equipment and resources, stressing that scrutiny of the government’s preparedness should not be confused with an attack on those working to contain the outbreak.

Shaibu also urged the Tinubu administration to publish any proposed restrictions on campaigning or voting arising from the health emergency, together with their medical justification and the advice of relevant health authorities.

“Public health guidance must protect people. It must never become a political tool,” he said.

He maintained that the Presidency and the APC must resolve the controversy through documentary evidence, explain the response timeline and demonstrate that the necessary measures were in place to protect Nigerians.

“President Tinubu and the APC owe the country answers, not ‘Bola-Ebola’ tales,” Shaibu said.

World.title: Pope Leo to miss Assisi gathering – Vatican
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV waves to the crowd during the weekly general audience at St Peter’s Square in The Vatican on October 21, 2026. (Photo by Tiziana FABI / AFP)





Pope Leo XIV will not attend a peace gathering at Assisi next week on doctors’ advice as he recovers from lung cancer surgery, the Vatican said Friday.

“To support recovery following last Tuesday’s thoracic surgery, and following the doctors’ advice, Pope Leo XIV will not be able to attend the ‘Disarmed and Disarming Peace’ meeting in Assisi on October 27th,” wrote the Vatican in a note.

The Assisi meeting, on the 40th anniversary of the World Day of Prayer for Peace, will go ahead with Leo sending a message to the event, the Vatican said.

The doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, wrote in a separate note published by the Vatican that although a chest X-ray of the pope showed “excellent progress of the post-operative recovery”, they advised caution for the Assisi trip.

“Considering the short time since the surgery, the attending doctors thought it prudent, as a precaution, to advise against the scheduled helicopter trip on October 27,” they said.

Leo, 71, was discharged on Saturday from Rome’s Gemelli hospital five days after surgery to remove the lower part of his right lung where they had detected a cancerous nodule.

His doctors said Wednesday that no further therapy was required following the successful operation, with the cancer having been found to be “localised”.

On Sunday, the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he would resume his duties “gradually”.

Doctors have said there is no medical reason that the pope cannot go ahead with a long-planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived for two decades, on November 6-17.

Leo last visited Assisi — which celebrates this year the 800th anniversary of St Francis’ death — in August for an event with thousands of young people from across Europe.

The prayer event, held from October Sunday to Tuesday, will bring together 384 representatives of religions, cultures and institutions from 53 countries, according to the Vatican.

The event was started under Pope John Paul II.

World.title: Only 15% of Nigerian Schools Budget for WASH Maintenance, Says LAPO
World.content:
Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

President of the Lift Above Poverty Organisation (LAPO), Faith Negbe Osazuwa-Ojo, has said only 15 per cent of Nigerian schools have budgeted funds for the maintenance of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) facilities, raising concerns over the health, dignity and learning conditions of millions of schoolchildren.

Osazuwa-Ojo disclosed this at the organisation’s 33rd Annual Development Forum in Abuja on Thursday, warning that inadequate access to safe water, decent toilets and handwashing facilities continued to undermine children’s welfare and educational development.

The LAPO president, who spoke at the forum themed ‘Safe Water, Healthy Learning: Advancing WASH in Nigerian Schools,’ said findings from the 2021 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping (WASHNORM) report showed that only 37 per cent of schools had access to basic water supply services.

She added that only 35 per cent had access to basic sanitation services, while 30 per cent provided basic hygiene services, including handwashing facilities, soap and water.

The LAPO president described the figures as more than statistics, saying they reflected the daily struggles of Nigerian children forced to learn in environments where basic necessities were lacking.

“These are far more than statistics. They represent the daily reality and struggles of millions of Nigerian children,” she said.

She painted a picture of pupils arriving at school eager to learn but finding no clean drinking water, decent toilets or facilities to wash their hands, warning that such conditions could encourage the spread of preventable diseases, reduce school attendance and disrupt learning.

Osazuwa-Ojo said every child deserved to learn in a safe, healthy and dignified environment, stressing that access to water, sanitation and hygiene should be treated as a fundamental requirement for quality education.

She called for stronger partnerships, increased investment and sustained action to ensure that Nigerian schools became safe places where children could learn and thrive.

The LAPO president reaffirmed the organisation’s commitment to improving lives, noting that the future of Nigeria depended partly on the choices made today to protect and support its children.

Earlier, the Chairperson of the forum, Dr Oyefemi Obazee, called on government, education authorities and development partners to prioritise investments in school WASH facilities, backed by adequate funding, effective implementation and sustained accountability.

Obazee said Nigeria’s development challenges required collaboration among government, civil society, academia, the private sector and development partners to develop practical and sustainable solutions.

She noted that despite efforts by the Nigerian government and its development partners to improve access to water, sanitation and hygiene through the National WASH Policy, many schools still lacked basic facilities, exposing pupils to conditions that compromised their health, dignity and academic performance.

“At LAPO, we believe that quality education cannot thrive where basic human needs are unmet,” she said, adding that every child deserved an environment that protected their health and enabled them to realise their full potential.

Addressing stakeholders, Obazee urged school proprietors, administrators and teachers to regard WASH as an essential component of quality education and to promote hygiene practices while ensuring that facilities were properly maintained.

She also called on development partners and the private sector to invest in innovative and sustainable solutions for underserved schools, while urging parents, traditional rulers, religious leaders and community stakeholders to support schools and promote good hygiene practices.

Obazee challenged students to become ambassadors of change by practising good hygiene, caring for their environment and encouraging their peers to do the same.

The concerns raised at the forum were reinforced by former Minister of Aviation and Co-Chairman, Chief Osita Chidoka, who was represented by Deputy Corps Marshal Victor Nwokolo (rtd).

He argued that Nigeria had focused too heavily on building infrastructure without ensuring that it continued to function.

Citing the example of a 10-year-old pupil, Hajara, at Sabon Layi Primary and Junior Secondary School in Potiskum, Yobe State, Chidoka said the school had a borehole, but the facility stopped working, forcing the child to carry water from home until it was converted to a solar-powered system.

He said the case illustrated the difference between providing infrastructure and delivering reliable public services.

According to him, government should measure success by the number of facilities that remain functional rather than by the number of projects completed.

Chidoka proposed that every public school should have a clearly designated institution responsible for its water and sanitation services, a funded maintenance arrangement and a publicly accessible record showing whether facilities were operational.

He also called for dedicated maintenance budgets, regular inspections and stronger community participation in monitoring school facilities.

The communiqué issued at the end of the forum identified inadequate funding, poor maintenance, weak institutional accountability and limited community participation as major obstacles to sustainable WASH services in schools.

It recommended gender-sensitive sanitation facilities, adequate menstrual hygiene support for adolescent girls, accessible infrastructure for children with disabilities and stronger coordination among federal, state and local governments.

World.title: Anchor Varsity Marks 10 Years of Growth, Holds Combined Convocation
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Anchor University, Lagos, is set to hold its combined 6th and 7th convocation ceremonies alongside activities marking its 10th anniversary from November 16 to 22, with the Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Samuel Bandele, describing the milestone as an opportunity to reflect on the institution’s growth and achievements.

Bandele, who will be rounding off his tenure early next year, said the celebrations would be particularly significant as they would be his last convocation ceremonies with the university.

He said the institution had recorded considerable progress since its establishment, gaining greater visibility locally and internationally, while its students continued to make breakthroughs in their professional careers.

Speaking ahead of the anniversary and convocation ceremonies, Bandele said the occasion offered the university an opportunity to reflect on its journey and acknowledge what he described as God’s faithfulness.

“There are a lot of activities lined up to commemorate the two events. This occasion gives us a rare opportunity to reflect on where we were coming from and where we are today by the grace of God.

“Looking back, we can confidently say the Lord has been good to us as an institution. The school has grown in leaps and bounds, becoming more visible than ever before. We are making waves within and outside Nigeria,” he stated.

The VC added that the university had made holistic progress as a faith-based institution, noting that increasing parental confidence in the school reflected its growing acceptance.

Bandele also reaffirmed his commitment to the institution, declaring that he would continue to give his best until his last day on campus.

He, however, allayed concerns among some parents over the university’s capacity to accommodate more students, given its current space constraints.

According to him, the new governing council has commenced the process of relocating the institution to its permanent site, while contingency arrangements are being made to accommodate all students in the interim.

The week-long celebration will begin on November 16 with an opening assembly dedicated to praise, worship, prayers and special ministration.

The second day will feature community service, while activities on the third day will include an entrepreneurship and innovation exhibition and a novelty football match on campus.

The fourth day will feature an alumni summit, with activities including reunions, networking, testimonies, drama, spoken-word performances, a music concert and other entertainment.

The fifth day will be dedicated to the decennial and convocation lecture and a book launch.

The anniversary programme will climax with the convocation ceremonies on November 21, at the university campus.

World.title: NUEE Strike: Edo Appeals to Parties to Sustain Constructive Engagement, Reaffirms Commitment to Electricity Workers’ Welfare
World.content:
Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City

Against the backdrop of the current strike by the National Union of Electricity Employees (NUEE), which has put Edo State in total darkness for four days now, the state government has appealed to all parties to sustain constructive engagement, exercise restraint, and prioritise a peaceful resolution that minimises disruption to residents, businesses, healthcare facilities, and other essential services across the state.

The state government also reaffirmed its commitment to the welfare of electricity workers, protection of consumers’ interests, and development of a stable, efficient and sustainable electricity market.

A statement by the state Commissioner for Power, Paul Usenbo, on Thursday, said the state government was aware of the industrial dispute involving members of NUEE and the management of Benin Electricity Distribution Company (BEDC), which culminated in a conciliation meeting convened by the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment in Abuja on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.

The commissioner noted that the meeting addressed critical issues affecting electricity workers, including consequential adjustments, personal protective equipment, staff promotions, staff welfare, salary harmonisation and overtime payments.

According to Usenbo, resolutions reached included the immediate restoration of overtime payments and a three-week timeline for BEDC management to address the remaining issues in consultation with the unions.

“The ministry particularly notes that the industrial action is to be suspended in the affected states, with the exception of Edo State, pending the resolution of issues peculiar to the state. This underscores the need for sustained engagement and a practical resolution of outstanding concerns affecting electricity workers in Edo State,” the statement said.

He stated further that towards this regard, the Commissioner for Labour and Employment, who is presently in Abuja, is actively engaged in efforts to address the labour-related issues and facilitate constructive dialogue towards an amicable resolution.

“The Edo State Ministry of Power will continue to work with the relevant authorities, labour unions, and electricity sector stakeholders to promote industrial harmony and protect the public interest.

“The ministry recognises that electricity workers are indispensable to the effective operation of the power sector. Their welfare, safety, and professional development must remain important considerations in building a functional and sustainable electricity market,” he added.

He maintained that under the leadership of Governor Monday Okpebholo, the Edo State Government remains committed to practical solutions that advance electricity sector reform, encourage investment, protect consumers, and improve electricity service delivery throughout the state.

“The ministry assures the good people of Edo State that it will continue to engage the appropriate authorities and stakeholders towards resolving the outstanding issues in the interest of workers, electricity consumers, and the overall development of the state’s power sector,” Usenbo said.

World.title: Election Security: NPTF Flags Off Training of 10,000 Police Officers Across Nigeria
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Nigeria Police Trust Fund (NPTF) has flagged off the training of 10,000 police officers drawn from police formations across the federation on election security ahead of the 2027 general election.

Speaking at the flag-off ceremony of the 2026 Election Security Training at the Nigeria Police Resource Centre in Jabi, Abuja, the Executive Secretary of the NPTF, Mohammed Sheidu, said the programme demonstrated the Fund’s commitment to strengthening the operational capacity and preparedness of the Nigeria Police Force ahead of the forthcoming elections.

He said the initiative was designed to ensure that officers deployed for election duties were adequately prepared to discharge their responsibilities professionally and effectively.

Sheidu noted that electoral credibility depended not only on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), but also on security agencies’ ability to provide a safe and peaceful environment for citizens to exercise their democratic rights.

He identified proper training, adequate equipment and operational mobility as three critical requirements for effective election security, adding that the programme would strengthen officers’ practical skills in election security management, crowd control, conflict prevention, de-escalation, respect for fundamental human rights and the lawful handling of election-related incidents.

He urged the participating officers to remain disciplined and impartial, stressing that their responsibility was to uphold the law, maintain public order and protect all citizens equally, irrespective of political affiliation.

Declaring the training open, the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu, said the officers were being equipped to make sound decisions under pressure and in accordance with the law.

He acknowledged the likelihood of tension, provocation and misinformation during elections, emphasising that discipline and restraint must guide police conduct.

Disu also stressed the importance of inter-agency collaboration, noting that no single agency could independently secure an election of such magnitude.

He highlighted the need for support from the Armed Forces and intelligence agencies to address security threats and provide timely warnings.

The Chairman of INEC, Professor Joash Ojo Amupitan (SAN), represented by National Commissioner, Rear Admiral Jamila Abubakar-Sadiq (rtd.), said security was paramount to the successful conduct of elections.

He noted that elections were an exercise in public trust, which could not thrive in an environment characterised by fear, physical threats, administrative chaos and security vulnerabilities.

He commended the emphasis on human rights-based and intelligence-led security management, noting that it reflected the police’s recognition of their constitutional role in safeguarding the electoral process.

World.title: NAF Air Mishaps: Of Aircraft Maintenance and Operational Safety
World.content:
The recurring aviation mishaps involving Nigerian Air Force aircraft raise troubling questions about aircraft maintenance, operational safety and accountability, making it imperative to address the underlying causes before more lives are lost, writes Linus Aleke.

Over the past decade, the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has experienced a series of aviation mishaps involving transport aircraft, fighter jets, helicopters, training aircraft and unmanned aerial platforms. Media reports have identified at least 16 incidents during the period under review.

The latest and deadliest incident occurred on 5 October 2026, when an ATR-42 aircraft, designated NAF 931, crashed near the naval base at Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, while undertaking a routine flight from Benin City to Lagos. All 25 people on board, comprising 20 passengers and five crew members, reportedly died. As of 10 October 2026, the cause of the crash had not been officially established, and an investigation had been ordered.

Barely 24 hours later, an NAF helicopter made a precautionary landing in Benue State following an air interdiction mission near the Benue–Enugu boundary. The helicopter subsequently returned safely to base.

Other recent incidents included an Alpha Jet emergency at NAF Base Kainji, Niger State, on 6 December 2025, during which both pilots ejected safely, and the reported loss of a CH-4B unmanned aerial platform in Niger State in January 2026, which did not result in human fatalities.

Earlier incidents included a Super Mushshak trainer aircraft mishap near Kaduna Military Airfield on 7 March 2024, from which both pilots emerged uninjured; the crash of an FT-7NI training aircraft at Makurdi on 14 July 2023, with both pilots reportedly ejecting safely; and the crash of an Mi-171E helicopter at Chukuba, Niger State, on 14 August 2023, during a casualty-evacuation mission. Reports differed on the death toll from the latter incident.

On 1 December 2023, an Mi-35P attack helicopter crashed shortly after take-off at NAF Base Port Harcourt, although all five crew members reportedly survived with minor injuries. In 2022, a Super Mushshak trainer aircraft crashed at NAF Base Kaduna, killing Flight Lieutenant Abubakar Muhammed Alkali and Flight Lieutenant Elijah Haruna Karatu.

The year 2021 witnessed several major incidents. On 21 February, a Beechcraft King Air 350i, designated NAF 201, crashed while returning to Abuja, killing all seven personnel on board. On 31 March, an Alpha Jet disappeared over Borno State, with both pilots presumed dead. The NAF rejected claims that the aircraft had been shot down, stating that a video circulated in connection with the incident did not establish enemy action.

On 21 May 2021, a Beechcraft King Air 350 crashed near Kaduna Civil Airport, killing all 11 occupants, including the then Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Ibrahim Attahiru. A joint investigation by the NAF and Nigeria’s Accident Investigation Bureau subsequently produced an interim report containing 27 initial findings and eight immediate safety recommendations. Another Alpha Jet incident occurred near the Kaduna–Zamfara boundary on 18 July 2021, with the pilot surviving after ejecting.

Earlier accidents included the crash of an Mi-35M helicopter at Damasak, Borno State, on 2 January 2019, with five reported fatalities; an RV-6A Air Beetle trainer aircraft crash in Kaduna State on 17 August 2019, which killed one person; and a training helicopter crash in Enugu State on 14 November 2019, with no reported fatalities. On 28 September 2018, two F-7NI fighter jets collided during rehearsals for Nigeria’s Independence Day celebrations at Katampe Hills, Abuja, resulting in one reported fatality. In July 2017, an Agusta 109 utility helicopter came down in the Borno River following a reported technical problem, without loss of life.

Collectively, these incidents encompass fatal and non-fatal crashes, mid-air collisions, emergency ejections, precautionary landings and the loss of an unmanned platform. They underscore the importance of distinguishing confirmed facts from preliminary reports and awaiting the findings of official investigations before attributing causes.

Although the NAF has institutionalised civilian harm mitigation through intelligence-driven targeting, collateral damage assessments, adherence to international humanitarian law and measures to protect civilians during air operations, concerns persist about the adequacy of its preventive policies and programmes. Public outcry from communities affected by collateral damage, amplified by international human rights organisations such as Amnesty International (AI), has further intensified scrutiny of the service.

Meanwhile, questions about the effectiveness of existing aviation safety safeguards remain. The persistence of mishaps has fuelled public criticism, with some detractors disparagingly likening NAF aircraft to overripe mangoes that fall from trees at the slightest breeze.

Against this backdrop, security experts and public affairs analysts have called for more transparent investigations, improved maintenance, better training, stronger civil-military cooperation and a long-term strategy for developing Nigeria’s indigenous aerospace capabilities.

Speaking on the recurring mishaps, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Beacon Security and Intelligence Limited, Dr Kabir Adamu, described the recurrent loss of NAF aircraft as a national tragedy that extends beyond the substantial financial cost to taxpayers. More significantly, he said, these incidents represent the irreversible loss of highly trained and patriotic personnel whose expertise takes years and considerable financial resources to develop.

The crash of NAF 931 in Igbokoda on 5 October 2026 has, he noted, understandably reignited public debate about military aviation safety. However, he argued that addressing the crisis requires moving beyond speculation to examine the underlying systemic factors and develop evidence-based solutions.

According to Adamu, aviation disasters rarely result from a single point of failure. The Swiss Cheese Model of accident causation illustrates how incidents occur when multiple underlying vulnerabilities align.

He identified several factors that could contribute to recurring NAF mishaps. The first is operational tempo and environmental stress. The NAF operates across multiple theatres, from counter-insurgency operations in the North-East to maritime surveillance in the Niger Delta and internal security missions nationwide. Such demands increase flying hours, accelerate wear and tear, and heighten the risk of crew fatigue.

Operating in challenging weather conditions, including dense Harmattan haze and sudden tropical storms, also requires exceptional pilot proficiency and reliable instrument systems.

Adamu identified maintenance practices and supply-chain constraints as another concern. While cautioning against blanket accusations of poor maintenance, he observed that sustaining an ageing fleet in a challenging economic environment presents considerable difficulties.

Even when aircraft undergo major overseas maintenance, their continued airworthiness depends on local technical capacity and the availability of spare parts. He cited the crashed ATR-42, which, he said, had undergone maintenance in Germany before returning to Nigeria in late 2024, as an example of the importance of sustained maintenance beyond major servicing.

Delays in procuring genuine original equipment manufacturer (OEM) parts, he added, can sometimes result in workarounds or deferred maintenance, potentially compromising airworthiness over time.

Aircraft age is another consideration. Although older aircraft can remain safe with rigorous maintenance, many NAF platforms have reportedly been in service for 15 to 20 years or longer. As aircraft age, inspections become more frequent and expensive. Without a robust, adequately funded lifecycle-management plan, the risk of mechanical failure may increase.

Adamu also highlighted human factors and training gaps, noting that pilot decision-making, air traffic control and maintenance errors can contribute to aviation accidents. Although NAF pilots are highly skilled, he argued that recurrent training must evolve to address emerging operational challenges. Simulator training should adequately reproduce region-specific hazards, including sudden microbursts, instrument failures and spatial disorientation, to prepare pilots for critical situations.

To address these challenges and restore public confidence, Adamu called on the NAF and the Federal Government to adopt a proactive, transparent and systemic approach to aviation safety.

First, he advocated independent and transparent investigations, urging the NAF to strengthen its collaboration with the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) and aviation safety experts.

While acknowledging legitimate operational security concerns, he argued that declassified interim and final investigation reports should be made public. Transparency, he maintained, would promote accountability, dispel speculation and enable the wider aviation community to learn from previous incidents.

Second, he recommended comprehensive, independent safety and airworthiness audits covering the entire fleet, maintenance facilities and operational units. Such audits should examine not only aircraft condition but also spare-parts supply chains, maintenance engineers’ certification and compliance with technical manuals.

Third, he called for greater investment in simulator-based and recurrent training for aircrew and maintenance personnel. Pilots should undertake mandatory training in emergency procedures, navigation in adverse weather and crew resource management to reduce the risk of human error.

He also recommended a non-punitive, confidential safety-reporting system, or Just Culture, that would encourage pilots, engineers and ground crew to report near misses, minor technical faults and procedural violations without undue fear of disciplinary action. Identifying and correcting such problems early could prevent them from developing into serious accidents.

Furthermore, Adamu advocated stronger alignment between military aviation safety practices and the standards of the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Although military aviation has distinct operational demands, he argued that greater civilian regulatory input into safety reviews could strengthen oversight and improve standards.

He also called for accelerated fleet modernisation and comprehensive lifecycle planning. Government, he said, should develop a clear, adequately funded plan for the phased retirement of obsolete aircraft and their replacement with modern, reliable platforms. Continued reliance on ageing aircraft, he warned, could prove a false economy by increasing maintenance costs, downtime and the risk of further loss of life.

Adamu emphasised that the NAF operates in a demanding security environment and that its personnel deserve the highest possible standards of safety and support. Addressing systemic vulnerabilities, he said, should not be interpreted as an indictment of the service’s bravery or competence, but as a necessary step towards operational excellence. Through transparency, rigorous auditing and modern safety-management systems, Nigeria could honour fallen aviators by improving the prospects of their colleagues returning safely from every mission.

On his part, Head of the Department of Political Science at Benue State University, Makurdi, Professor Atah Pine, expressed concern over the persistent aviation mishaps involving military aircraft in Nigeria.

He argued that whenever an aviation accident occurs, the relevant authorities should promptly institute an investigation to establish its cause. Given the number of mishaps recorded over the years, he questioned how many investigation findings had been made available to the public.

Pine said the apparent lack of transparency made it difficult to draw empirically sound conclusions or develop evidence-based projections.

He also highlighted the importance of flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, commonly referred to collectively as black boxes, in establishing an aircraft’s performance and the circumstances leading up to an accident.

He questioned what these recorders had revealed about the incidents under scrutiny, observing that the public remained largely unable to access such information.

Pine called on the NAF authorities to conduct, as a matter of urgency, a comprehensive technical and mechanical audit of their aircraft and implement the necessary corrective measures to prevent a recurrence of accidents that had claimed numerous lives and caused profound trauma, pain and sorrow.

Also, former Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson, Ambassador Ogbole Amedu-Ode argued that the recurring aviation mishaps could be attributable to several factors, including inadequate funding, insufficient pilot training, poor maintenance practices and the procurement of used aircraft whose operational suitability might be compromised.

He maintained that addressing these challenges required adequate budgetary allocations, continuous personnel training, rigorous maintenance regimes and a shift towards acquiring new, fit-for-purpose aircraft.

Beyond immediate procurement requirements, Amedu-Ode called for a long-term national strategy to develop indigenous aerospace manufacturing capabilities. Nigeria, he noted, possesses relevant natural resources, including iron ore and aluminium, but requires sustained investment, technological advancement and the political will to translate these resources into industrial capacity.

He suggested that Nigeria could draw lessons from countries such as China, India, Brazil and Singapore to gradually develop its capacity to manufacture, maintain and sustain military aircraft. Such an approach, he argued, could improve flight safety, protect human lives, preserve valuable military assets and reduce long-term dependence on foreign suppliers.

Similarly, Chairman of the Guild of Public Affairs Analysts of Nigeria, Enugu State Chapter, Dr Ambrose Igboke, expressed concern over Nigeria’s numerous military aviation accidents, arguing that they raised serious questions about airspace management, operational safety and accountability.

He said the apparent disparity between civilian and military aviation safety warranted closer scrutiny, particularly regarding the sophistication of military navigational equipment and the extent of information-sharing between the military, the NCAA and other relevant agencies.

Igboke also emphasised the importance of training and capacity development, advocating stronger collaboration and personnel exchange programmes between the Ministry of Aviation and the military hierarchy. He welcomed the meeting between the Chief of the Air Staff and the Minister of Aviation as an initial step towards greater cooperation.

Accountability, he added, remained essential. He questioned what previous military aviation accident investigations had revealed about the causes of the incidents, including possible human error, mechanical failure or negligence, and whether anyone found culpable had faced disciplinary action, dismissal, prosecution or other sanctions.

He maintained that these questions required transparent, evidence-based answers if Nigeria was to strengthen aviation safety and prevent future tragedies.

Military aviation mishaps are not peculiar to Nigeria but remain a persistent hazard worldwide. A review of available records from October 2016 to October 2026 indicates that air forces in countries like the United States, Brazil, Egypt and Morocco have also experienced aircraft accidents and losses involving different aircraft types and operational circumstances.

The United States Air Force publishes mishap summaries and investigation reports, while Brazil maintains an established aviation accident investigation system through its Centre for Investigation and Prevention of Aeronautical Accidents (CENIPA). These examples demonstrate that aviation accidents remain a concern even among countries with extensive military aviation capabilities and formalised safety-investigation systems.

Nigeria’s experience should therefore be examined within the realities and inherent risks of military flying rather than portrayed as an exclusively Nigerian phenomenon. Military aviation involves complex training exercises, demanding operational missions, low-level flying, adverse weather, mechanical challenges and operations in environments where the margin for error can be limited. Such conditions expose military aircrews and aircraft to risks that cannot be entirely eliminated, even with rigorous maintenance and operational procedures.

Nevertheless, recognising the global hazards of military aviation should not diminish the need to investigate every mishap, establish its causes and implement measures to prevent recurrence. The crucial distinction lies between acknowledging that accidents occur across air forces worldwide and determining whether particular incidents could have been prevented.

Nigeria’s experience should consequently be assessed through verified accident investigation reports, casualty records, aircraft serviceability data and evidence of the implementation of safety recommendations. International comparisons must also account for differences in fleet size, flying hours, mission profiles and public disclosure practices, as raw accident totals alone cannot establish which air force operates more safely.

Ultimately, military aviation mishaps constitute a global operational risk requiring continuous vigilance, professional training, effective maintenance, rigorous investigation and institutional learning.

The objective should not be to portray Nigeria as uniquely susceptible to aircraft accidents, but to examine its experience within an informed international context while ensuring that every aircraft loss and every life lost contributes to improved aviation safety, greater accountability and the prevention of avoidable tragedies.

World.title: Oyebanji’s Industrialisation Blueprint for Ekiti’s Economic Transformation
World.content:
Governor Biodun Oyebanji of Ekiti State has unveiled his agenda to transform the State acclaimed as the ‘fountain of knowledge’ from a largely agrarian state to an industrial hub. Gbenga Sodeinde writes.

For years, the development story of Nigerian states has largely been measured by the roads constructed, bridges completed and public infrastructure delivered. But as fiscal pressures mount and states are compelled to build more productive economies, the real test of leadership is increasingly shifting from infrastructure delivery to wealth creation.

It is against this changing economic landscape that Governor Biodun Oyebanji is redefining the next phase of Ekiti’s development.

Having spent his first term laying the physical foundation for growth through road expansion, electricity projects, agricultural interventions and improved connectivity, Oyebanji says his second term will focus on converting those investments into industries, stronger businesses and sustainable economic opportunities.

In an interview, the governor unveiled an economic blueprint anchored on industrialisation, local processing of agricultural products, private-sector investment and support for small businesses, declaring that the state’s next major priority is to build an economy driven by productivity.

“Our next major focus, therefore, is industrialisation and support for small businesses. That is the only way we can deepen our shared prosperity agenda,” Oyebanji said.

The declaration marks a significant shift in the administration’s development strategy — from building the infrastructure required for growth to ensuring that those assets begin to generate jobs, expand enterprises and improve the livelihoods of Ekiti residents.

At the heart of the blueprint is the conviction that infrastructure, however essential, cannot by itself deliver prosperity. Roads, electricity connections, farm access routes, water systems and an upgraded airport must ultimately serve as platforms for production, investment and enterprise. For Oyebanji, the next phase of governance will therefore be judged not merely by the scale of public works completed, but by the economic activity those projects unlock.

During his first term, the administration constructed and rehabilitated roads, connected previously underserved communities to electricity, improved township and farm roads, and strengthened the foundations of agricultural production. By the end of the year, the governor said, the state would have completed close to 400 kilometres of roads. Those interventions, he argued, were necessary to create the conditions for a more productive economy.

The second-term agenda is designed to build upon that foundation. Oyebanji wants agricultural commodities produced in Ekiti to be processed within the state rather than exported in raw form, thereby creating additional value, expanding local supply chains and generating employment.

The objective is to move from production without sufficient value addition to an integrated economic system in which farmers, processors, manufacturers, transport operators and small businesses participate in a shared cycle of growth.

“Our farmers must also be able to produce at scale and have reliable off-takers who can purchase their produce and supply it to companies that will add value through processing,” he said.

That ambition is already reflected in the state’s emerging agro-industrial landscape. The Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone has attracted significant investment, with businesses committing billions of naira to agricultural production and processing. Companies such as Arog Agro-Allied and Agbeyewa Farms are part of this expanding ecosystem, while the latter’s large-scale cassava operation has been described as one of the biggest of its kind in the world.

The administration is also seeking to improve access to these investment corridors. The award of the Ayetoro-Iyemero Ekiti road project is intended to open up the area, facilitate the movement of goods and strengthen the connection between agricultural production zones and markets.

Ekiti’s selection by the African Development Bank as a Tier-2 state under the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone programme further reinforces the government’s strategy. Studies are being conducted on Itapaji Dam to assess the possibility of developing irrigation facilities, an intervention that could improve year-round farming, raise productivity and make the state more attractive to agro-processors.

Yet, the governor recognises that industrialisation cannot be achieved through agriculture alone. It requires a broader investment ecosystem supported by efficient institutions, predictable regulations, accessible land, reasonable taxation and reliable infrastructure.

To this end, the administration is reforming its investment promotion agency and establishing a one-stop shop for investors. The initiative is expected to simplify the process of obtaining approvals, accessing information and navigating government procedures. Land administration is also being reformed, while taxation is being streamlined to prevent excessive burdens on businesses and residents.

“Capital will flow to any place where it is treated well,” Oyebanji said, stressing that the responsibility of government is to create the conditions in which private investment can thrive.

The governor’s approach reflects a deliberate preference for enabling private enterprise rather than placing the state at the centre of industrial production. Government, he explained, is not necessarily expected to establish industries itself; its primary responsibility is to provide the infrastructure, security, policies and institutional support that encourage investors to commit capital and create jobs.

That philosophy extends to the transportation sector, where the administration is attempting to balance the need for affordable mobility with the survival of existing operators. Rather than displacing members of transport unions and other associations, the government plans to introduce fair competition through a pilot mass transit scheme.

If the pilot succeeds, more vehicles will be procured to expand the programme. But the governor believes that a lasting reduction in transport costs will require a transition away from petrol-dependent vehicles towards Compressed Natural Gas-powered buses, electric vehicles, tricycles and motorcycles.

Such a transition, however, will require more than the procurement of vehicles. It will demand conversion centres, refuelling stations, charging points and a supporting energy infrastructure capable of sustaining the new transport system. The administration is therefore engaging private companies to develop the necessary facilities and roll out cleaner, more affordable mobility options across the state.

The airport is another critical component of the economic blueprint. Oyebanji wants the facility to operate around the clock, rather than close at 6 p.m. or remain inaccessible to aircraft during adverse weather conditions. The installation of an Instrument Landing System is being assessed by a certification team, while contracts have been awarded for airport lighting infrastructure.

Once completed, the interventions are expected to enable night operations and improve the airport’s reliability. The commissioning of a private-sector fuel depot will further strengthen its commercial potential by allowing aircraft to refuel in Ekiti, making the facility more attractive to airlines and improving the viability of scheduled operations.

For the governor, these projects are not isolated infrastructure schemes. They are components of a wider economic strategy intended to connect Ekiti to regional markets, reduce logistical constraints and support the movement of people, goods and capital.

The same productivity-centred philosophy informs the administration’s plans for small businesses. Oyebanji identified welders, tailors, hairdressers, barbers and other small-scale entrepreneurs as essential participants in the state’s economic transformation. These businesses, he said, must have access to affordable financing if they are to expand, employ more people and contribute meaningfully to shared prosperity.

The challenge is to ensure that the benefits of industrialisation do not remain concentrated among large investors. A productive economy must also create opportunities for informal operators, women traders, artisans, farmers and young entrepreneurs. This is why the administration’s economic agenda is linked to its gender policy and its broader commitment to reducing discrimination and expanding women’s access to markets and enterprise opportunities.

Oyebanji also acknowledged that development cannot be sustained without effective urban planning and environmental management. The recent flooding in Ado-Ekiti, he said, was largely man-made, worsened by indiscriminate refuse disposal and the construction of buildings on waterways. The government has directed the Ministry of Environment to conduct a comprehensive inventory of structures obstructing waterways, with illegally constructed buildings facing removal.

The decision is politically sensitive, particularly where property owners claim to have obtained official approvals. But the governor insists that decisive action is necessary to prevent more severe flooding in the future. The administration intends to distinguish between buildings that received formal approval and those erected illegally, with compensation considered where applicable and unlawful structures removed.

Water supply remains another major challenge. Although Ekiti has four functioning dams and has benefited from World Bank intervention, the governor said the difficulties extend beyond the dams and pumping equipment. Ageing asbestos pipes, high energy costs, inadequate reticulation and consumer resistance to paying for water have all weakened the distribution system.

The administration has replaced pumps, procured generators and begun replacing obsolete pipes. It has also established water consumers’ committees to improve community participation and accountability. In the second term, the focus will be on rehabilitating the distribution network so that water pumped into reservoirs can reach households and businesses efficiently.

Taken together, these initiatives reveal an administration attempting to move Ekiti from a phase of foundational construction into one of economic activation. The roads, airport, dams, agricultural zones and electricity projects are being repositioned as instruments of production rather than ends in themselves.

The governor’s re-election, secured with 85.45 per cent of the votes cast, has given the administration a strong political mandate. But it has also raised expectations. The central question now is whether the infrastructure delivered during the first term can translate into factories, processing plants, stronger small businesses, lower transport costs, expanded agricultural value chains and more jobs.

Oyebanji’s answer is that the state’s future depends on productivity. His second-term agenda is therefore not simply a continuation of the first, but an attempt to convert public investment into private enterprise, agricultural output into industrial value and infrastructure into broad-based prosperity.

“We will do everything possible to ensure that our economy becomes more productive,” he said.

For Ekiti, the success of that promise will be measured not only by what government builds, but by what the people are able to produce, process, sell and earn from the economic foundations now being laid.

World.title: Ododo Tasks Kogi’s New LG Chairmen on Rural Security, Accountability
World.content:
Governor Ahmed Ododo of Kogi State has tasked the newly elected 21 Local Government Chairmen in the state on the need to prioritise rural security and ensure accountability.

Kogi State Governor, Alhaji Ahmed Usman Ododo, has charged the newly sworn-in chairmen of the 21 Local Government Areas of the State to strengthen rural security, ensure accountability in the management of public funds and prioritise grassroots development.

Ododo represented by state deputy governor, Comrade Joel Salifu, made this call recently during the swearing-in ceremony of the council chairmen at the Glass House, Government House, Lokoja.

The Governor urged the council chairmen to work closely with security agencies, traditional rulers and community leaders to protect lives and property, stressing that no community in the state would be abandoned to criminal activities.

He also called on them to prioritise rural roads, primary healthcare, basic education, environmental sanitation and programmes that create opportunities for youths and women.

Congratulating the chairmen on their election, Ododo thanked the people of Kogi State for their support for the All Progressives Congress (APC), which won all chairmanship and councillorship seats across the local government areas and two hundred and thirty-nine wards.

He described the victory as a call to greater service and urged the elected officials to justify the confidence reposed in them by delivering on their campaign promises.

The Governor expressed confidence in the state’s continued support for President Bola Tinubu and APC candidates ahead of the 2027 general and state Assembly elections, while commending the President for his leadership and commitment to development through his Renewed Hope Agenda.

Ododo further charged the chairmen to manage public funds transparently and responsibly, remain humble, accessible to the people and govern fairly without discrimination based on political differences.

The Governor wished the chairmen success in their tenure, while assuring them of the state’s government support for more development at the grassroots.

The swearing-in according to stakeholders is indeed the start of a new chapter in Local Government administration in the Confluence state, with a call on the chairmen to improve security, use public funds wisely and ensure government presence is felt at the grassroots.

World.title: Kano Promotes over 18,000 SUBEB Staff
World.content:
No fewer than 18,984 teaching and non teaching staff of Kano State Universal Basic Education Board were promoted between January and July, 2026.

Kano State Governor, Alhaji Abba Kabir Yusuf, has approved the implementation of promotions for 18,984 teaching and non-teaching staff of the State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB) for January and July 2026.

The approval followed a request submitted by the Executive Chairman of SUBEB, Yusuf Kabir, seeking the release of ₦235,116,339.09 for the implementation of the promotions across the 44 Local Government Education Authorities (LGEAs).

In the letter dated 2nd September 2026, SUBEB said the affected staff comprised eligible teaching and non-teaching personnel whose promotions for the January and July 2026 cycles had been processed, including the corresponding salary adjustment calculations.

The Board said timely implementation of promotions was essential to staff motivation, career development, capacity strengthening and improved service delivery within the basic education sector.

It noted that SUBEB, one of the largest public institutions in the state, has approximately 60,000 teaching and non-teaching personnel serving across the 44 LGEAs.

According to the Board, the administration inherited outstanding promotion backlogs, including arrears spanning seven years and another backlog of one-and-a-half years. It said Governor Yusuf had previously approved and ensured the implementation of the outstanding promotions.

SUBEB said the intervention had significantly boosted staff morale, restored confidence in the service and demonstrated the administration’s commitment to the welfare of public servants.

The Board explained that it had completed all necessary arrangements and processes for the January and July 2026 promotions, including staff eligibility verification and salary adjustment computations.

Governor Yusuf approved the request, which was ratified at recent State Executive Council paving the way for the release of the approved funds for the implementation of the promotions.
