World.title: Liberia: House Summons Health Authorities To Comprehensive Briefing On Liberia’s Preparedness, Response Measures Amid Latest Outbreak In Nigeria
World.content:
MONROVIA, October 22, 2026 — The House of Representatives has summoned Liberia’s health authorities to provide a comprehensive briefing on the country’s preparedness and response measures following reports of a confirmed Ebola case in Nigeria and an ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The House voted unanimously on Thursday to summon the Minister of Health, the Director General of the National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL), and other relevant health officials to appear before its plenary on Tuesday, October 27.



The decision followed a communication from Montserrado County Electoral District #16 Representative Dixon Seboe, who called on the Legislature to obtain detailed information about Liberia’s readiness to prevent and respond to a potential public health emergency.

Seboe’s request comes after the Ministry of Health issued a public notice directing health facilities, border entry points, public buildings and other institutions nationwide to strengthen screening procedures and enforce infection prevention and control measures.

While acknowledging the importance of the preventive measures, Seboe argued that the regional developments require a broader assessment of the country’s preparedness, including the availability of essential medical supplies, trained personnel and emergency response resources.

“Honorable Speaker, as representatives of the Liberian people, we have a constitutional and public responsibility to ensure that the appropriate authorities are taking all necessary measures to safeguard the health and well-being of our citizens,” Seboe stated in his communication.

The lawmaker wants the Minister of Health to brief the Legislature on the government’s overall Ebola preparedness strategy, emergency response arrangements and coordination with regional and international health authorities.

He also requested that the NPHIL Director General provide updates on disease surveillance systems and laboratory testing capacity, including the country’s ability to identify and confirm suspected Ebola cases promptly.

Additionally, Seboe called for representatives of the County Health Teams to explain the level of preparedness across Liberia’s 15 counties, particularly the availability of isolation facilities and other resources needed to manage suspected cases.

The communication further seeks clarification from border and port health authorities on screening procedures at the country’s points of entry and the protocols for handling travelers who exhibit suspected symptoms or report relevant exposure histories.

Emergency Funding, Public Awareness Under Scrutiny

Beyond surveillance and screening, Seboe wants health authorities to account for public awareness campaigns, infection prevention supplies, frontline health worker training and the resources available to enforce the Ministry of Health’s preventive directives.

He also called for information on measures to protect public schools, markets, government institutions, transportation facilities and densely populated communities, particularly in Montserrado County, where population movement and congestion could complicate efforts to contain an outbreak.

The lawmaker emphasized the need for transparency regarding the availability of emergency funding, medical equipment, trained personnel and logistical support.

“The briefing should clarify whether Liberia has adequate emergency funding, medical equipment, trained personnel, and logistical support to respond promptly to any suspected Ebola case, should one arise,” the communication stated.

Seboe maintained that his request was not intended to create public panic but to ensure that the government takes proactive steps to protect the population.

“Early preparation, accurate public information, and effective coordination among relevant institutions are essential to preventing a public health emergency,” he said.

He urged the House to treat the matter with urgency and direct the relevant authorities to provide a full account of the country’s preparedness.

Following the reading and deliberation of the communication, Margibi County Electoral District #2 Representative Ivar K. Jones moved that the health officials appear before the full plenary on Tuesday.

The motion was overwhelmingly approved by lawmakers.

Government Intensifies Preventive Measures

Before the House’s decision, the Ministry of Health had ordered heightened disease surveillance and stricter infection prevention measures at health facilities, border entry points and public institutions nationwide following reports of a confirmed Ebola case in Nigeria.

In a statement issued after the reports emerged, the Ministry said the directive took immediate effect and was intended to strengthen Liberia’s preparedness against the potential spread of Ebola and other infectious diseases.

The planned briefing is expected to give lawmakers an opportunity to assess the implementation of those measures and determine whether additional interventions are necessary to protect public health.

The health authorities had not yet appeared before the House as of Thursday, with their briefing scheduled for October 27.

World.title: Editorial: The Supreme Court Must Speak Clearly On Kolubah, and Soon
World.content:
Six months after the House of Representatives expelled Rep. Yekeh Kolubah while a Supreme Court stay order was pending, the full bench has heard his appeal and reserved its ruling. The case rests on a narrow question: whether the House was properly served with the order. But the answer will decide whether court orders bind Liberia’s Legislature, and whether due process protects elected officials. FrontPageAfrica urges the Court to rule promptly and plainly.

THE SUPREME COURT of Liberia heard arguments on Thursday in the appeal of Yekeh Kolubah, the Montserrado County District #10 lawmaker expelled from the House of Representatives in April. The Court then reserved its ruling. The Court has every right to take time to deliberate. But Liberia cannot afford a ruling that is late, narrow or vague. The case is about more than one outspoken legislator. It tests whether a court order means anything once it reaches the doors of the Capitol.

THE FACTS ARE simple and troubling. On April 16, 2026, Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba, presiding in Chambers, granted Mr. Kolubah’s petition for a writ of prohibition. He ordered the House leadership to stay all proceedings and summoned them to a conference on April 20. The next day the House voted to expel Mr. Kolubah. Forty-nine members signed the resolution. The House Clerk’s office said it had received no order from the Court. Yet the Court’s Marshal had delivered the writ to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk, where a receptionist and a computer operator received it.



IN MAY, JUSTICE Kaba dismissed Mr. Kolubah’s Bill of Information. He held that the House had not been lawfully served, because House Rule 26.5 names the Sergeant-at-Arms as the only officer authorized to accept court documents. Without proper service, he reasoned, the House could not be held in contempt. On Thursday, Mr. Kolubah’s lawyer, Cllr. Jonathan Massaquoi, argued that service on the Legislature is governed by the Civil Procedure Law, not by the House’s internal rules. He cited Section 3.38(9), which requires service on a government subdivision to be made on its chief executive. The Speaker’s office, he said, was the right place.

THIS IS THE first lapse the full bench must confront. A body’s internal rule cannot override the law of the land. If the House’s own rulebook decides who may receive a court order, the House effectively decides whether it has been served. Any institution that wants to escape judicial review would need only to keep its designated officer out of reach. No court in a constitutional democracy can accept that result.

THE SECOND LAPSE lies with the Court itself. The Marshal who delivered the writ is the Court’s own officer. If the service was defective, the defect began inside the Temple of Justice, not with the litigant. Yet Mr. Kolubah alone has paid the price, losing his seat while the procedural question was being argued. Justice should not depend on which desk a document happens to land on.

THE THIRD LAPSE concerns notice. The Court’s stay was public knowledge on Capitol Hill before the vote; Liberian newspapers reported it the same day. Justice Kaba correctly stated that contempt requires actual or constructive notice. The full bench should say plainly whether a legislature that reads of a stay order in the morning press, and proceeds anyway, can claim it did not know.

WE DO NOT defend Mr. Kolubah’s conduct. His remarks on the Liberia-Guinea border dispute angered many colleagues and citizens, and in 2021 he was suspended twice over his invective against then-President George Weah. Article 38 of the Constitution gives each House the power to discipline its members, including expulsion by a two-thirds vote of its entire membership. In a 73-member House, 49 votes is exactly that threshold. The House had the power to act. The question is whether it exercised that power lawfully, with due process, and while a court order was pending.

THE CONSTITUTION IS clear on due process. Article 20 forbids depriving any person of a right or privilege except after a hearing consistent with the Constitution and the law. Mr. Kolubah’s lawyers walked out of the committee hearing on April 15 after being denied a five-day extension and access to the evidence against him. That walkout may have been a tactic. But a committee that moves to expel an elected member within a week of the complaint, without giving his counsel time to see the evidence, invites serious constitutional doubt.

THE STAKES REACH far beyond District #10. Tens of thousands of voters have had no representative since April. If the expulsion stands on a technicality, every legislature in Liberia will learn that a stay order can be ignored if it is handed to the wrong clerk. If the Court instead voids the expulsion without addressing the House’s genuine constitutional powers, it risks a standoff between two branches of government. Neither outcome serves a country that has worked hard, since the end of its civil wars, to build institutions people trust.

LIBERIA’S DEMOCRACY HAS earned international respect, including through peaceful transfers of power. That record rests on a basic bargain: those in power obey the courts, even when the ruling is unwelcome. A House that can expel a member while a stay order sits in its own offices, and a Court that cannot say whether its orders were received, both weaken that bargain.

WE THEREFORE URGE the Supreme Court to rule promptly and to answer the questions directly. Who may lawfully receive service on behalf of the Legislature? Does the Civil Procedure Law govern, or the House rulebook? What is the legal effect of an act taken after a stay order was delivered, however imperfectly? And what process does the Constitution require before a member is expelled?

CLEAR ANSWERS WILL protect the next lawmaker, whatever party or district. They will also protect the House, by telling it exactly what the law requires. Silence or a narrow ruling would leave a dangerous precedent. Liberia needs the Court to be clear.

World.title: Govt. reaffirms continued support to visual artists
World.content:
Government has recognised the potential of the visual arts sector to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda through employment creation, entrepreneurship, tourism and cultural preservation.

Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts Permanent Secretary, Kangwa Chileshe, says visual arts provide an opportunity to showcase Zambia’s cultural heritage while generating income for artists and local communities.

Mr Chileshe notes that paintings, sculptures, crafts and photographs offer tourists authentic experiences of Zambian life and culture.

He says linking artists to galleries, hotels, lodges, airports and tourist sites would expand markets for their works, enrich visitors’ experiences and create economic opportunities.

The Permanent Secretary said this in Lusaka last evening during the official opening of the 62nd Independence Visual Arts Exhibition, held at the Showgrounds under the theme “Zambia at 62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future.”

Mr Chileshe said government remained committed to creating an enabling environment for Artists to develop their talents, access markets, protect their intellectual property and earn sustainable livelihoods.

He noted that the government, through the National Arts Council of Zambia, had continued to support artists and arts associations to participate in regional and international exhibitions and festivals, exposing Zambian art to wider audiences.

And, Mr Chileshe disclosed that renovation works at the Livingstone Art Gallery had commenced and once completed, it would provide Artists with a modern facility to exhibit and sell their works in the country’s tourist capital.

Meanwhile, Zambia National Visual Arts Council Chairman, Adrian Ngoma, disclosed that the Council has four galleries in selected provinces, with plans to expand its structures to all 10 provinces and develop functional art centres that would provide exhibition space, training, mentorship, research and entrepreneurship opportunities.

He called for increased investment in art Centres and galleries across the country to strengthen the sector and expand opportunities for artists.

Mr Ngoma stated that the Council would also explore collaboration with government’s youth internship programme to provide young people with practical experience in gallery management, art conservation, exhibition management, marketing and art education.

In a vote of thanks, former Zambia National Visual Arts Council Chairperson, Mulenga Chafilwa, called for greater investment in professional arts education and training.

Mr Chafilwa said many Zambian artists were self-taught and relied on sharing knowledge and experiences among themselves to develop their skills.

He welcomed government’s involvement in the arts sector and called for sustained support to ensure that Artists had access to appropriate facilities and programmes.

World.title: Zambia gets US$6.17M for railway maintenance
World.content:
Zambia has secured a US$6.1 million grant from Japan to support railway maintenance.

The grant announcement comes about twenty months after President Hakainde Hichilema’s official working visit to Japan in February 2025, where he met Japanese Prime Minister, Shigeru Ishiba and addressed the Zambia-Japan Business Forum in Tokyo.

Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson, Henry Kapata, says during that visit, the President engaged Japanese leaders and businesses on investment and economic cooperation.

Mr Kapata says the two countries also signed an investment agreement aimed at promoting and protecting investment.

He said the President’s programme included a train journey from Tokyo to Nagoya, offering a glimpse of Japan’s transport infrastructure and the role that efficient rail services play in moving people and supporting economic activity.

Mr Kapata has told ZANIS business news that the railway grant now provides an opportunity to examine how Zambia’s engagement with Japan fits into the country’s efforts to improve transport infrastructure, move goods more efficiently and support the production targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He says for farmers, manufacturers and mining companies, reliable rail transport can make a practical difference.

“It can help move bulk goods over long distances, reduce pressure on roads and connect production areas to markets,” said Mr Kapata.

Mr Kapata noted that the benefits will depend on where the funding is applied, the maintenance work it supports and how reliably the railway operates.

World.title: Mining companies urged to translate mineral wealth into tangible benefits
World.content:
Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary, Hapenga Kabeta, has urged mining companies in the country to ensure that mineral wealth translates into tangible and lasting benefits for Zambians.

Dr Kabeta says increased mineral production must be accompanied by local value addition, skills development, technology transfer and the growth of local enterprises.

He has advised that mining activities should also protect the environment and improve the welfare of citizens, noting that production targets would be meaningless if they resulted in environmental destruction and left communities without benefits.

The Permanent Secretary was speaking in Lusaka last evening when he officiated at the cultural night gala night held on the sidelines of the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

He said the Insaka also provides an opportunity for face-to-face engagements that can strengthen professional relationships, generate ideas and facilitate business deals.

Dr Kabeta encouraged participants to establish meaningful partnerships, share experiences and develop strategies that would help unlock Zambia’s mineral potential for the benefit of the people.

He said Zambia needs a productive, innovative, inclusive and responsible mining industry that attracts investment, creates decent jobs, supports local businesses and contributes to long-term economic transformation.

Dr Kabeta noted that the mining sector has continued to attract significant investments in various parts of the country, including the Copperbelt and North-Western Provinces which are contributing to national economic development.

Meanwhile, Dr Kabeta presented awards to organisations recognised for their participation and contribution to the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

Among the recipients were ZESCO, Konkola Copper Mines, First Quantum Minerals, Anglo American Corporation, Zanaco and Indo-Zambia Bank.

Passing a vote of thanks, Buterla Investment Limited Chief Executive Officer, Happy Mbulo, said the Grow Zambia Agenda can be achieved if mining firms apply themselves.

Mr Mbulo implored the private sector to work closely with government to fully realise their potential in enhancing the production of goods and services associated with the value chain system.

World.title: Mwense man jailed 12 months for theft
World.content:
The Mwense Magistrates court has sentenced a 34-year-old man of Mulundu village to 12 months concurrent imprisonment with hard labour for two counts of theft contrary to section 272 of the penal code Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

This is in a matter in which Simon Kunda masquerading as a traditional healer operating as Dr Mwiko is alleged to have obtained money amounting to K 1,500 belonging to Jacob Mwape and Ireen Chisha respectively.

This is after he claimed he would heal their sicknesses.

In the first count, Kunda is said to have Charged Mwape K 1000 on the pretext that he would give him treatment for his ailing feet.

In count two the now convict is alleged to have charged Chisha a K 500 as payment to treat her stomach pains.

The two complainants are said to have paid the money in full respectively after Kunda refused the 50 percent down payment claiming that the spirits being consulted demanded full payments before treatment could be given.

Testifying before Magistrate Fred Mwangala, the two complainants said that Kunda however vanished without offering the required services and was only arrested a few months after he was spotted in public.

In mitigation, Kunda prayed for the court’s leniency saying he was a poor man.

“Am a poor man so I ask the court to forgive me otherwise I have nothing more to say,” Kunda begged.

In sentencing, Magistrate Mwangala noted that the victims from whom the now convict had stolen the money were also not rich.

Magistrate Mwangala ruled that Kunda should be given a custodial sentence at a correctional facility for reformation.

Magistrate Mwangala handed Kunda eight months imprisonment on each count to run concurrently.

However, Magistrate Mwangala immediately increased the sentence to 12 months imprisonment after the convict warned the complainants as he stood down from the dock.

World.title: Lufuma calls on youths to engage in productive activities
World.content:
Kabompo East Member of Parliament (MP) Ambrose Lufuma has called on young people to engage in productive activities that will contribute to the attainment of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Lufuma says youths should be active participants in national development by becoming producers, innovators, entrepreneurs and job creators rather than relying on formal employment.

Contributing to the Motion of Thanks on the President’s address during the official opening of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly, Mr Lufuma, a former Defence Minister, also called for the upgrading of feeder roads leading to productive areas in Kabompo to gravel standard.

He said the government will continue creating opportunities for young people to acquire practical skills, establish businesses and participate in productive sectors such as agriculture and construction.

In his median speech to the House, the former minister of defense cited the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) grants, loans, empowerment programmes and National Service training as important interventions that can help empower young people.

Mr Lufuma stated that agriculture remains the mainstay of the constituency’s economy, with an estimated 95 percent of the population engaged in farming and related activities.

The MP called for improved access to farming inputs, extension services, appropriate technologies, irrigation, storage facilities, satellite depots and reliable markets to enhance agricultural production and food security.

Mr Lufuma has further urged the government to upgrade township roads in Kabompo to improve connectivity and facilitate economic activities.

Meanwhile, Nkombwa East MP Jairos Simbeye has called for a results-oriented public service, saying effective delivery of government programmes requires commitment, discipline and proper time management.

Mr Simbeye says public officers should focus on delivering tangible results rather than merely reporting for work.

He has commended the National Assembly for promoting professionalism and orderly service delivery, citing the conduct of security personnel and staff as an example of the standards that should be upheld across public institutions.

He stressed that all stakeholders must work together to support President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda and ensure the country achieves its development targets.

The MP cautioned against spreading misinformation about government programmes, particularly the school feeding programme, saying such conduct can discourage beneficiaries from accessing essential services.

On housing, Mr Simbeye encouraged residents to take advantage of land available in rural constituencies such as Nkombwa Constituency to support settlement and development, rather than concentrating on limited plots in urban areas.

He said efficient public service delivery at all levels is essential to restoring public confidence and ensuring that government policies and programmes benefit citizens.

He further called for unity of purpose among public officers and other stakeholders, saying collective efforts are necessary for Zambia to achieve its national development aspirations.

World.title: Government hails public support for energy diversification
World.content:
Government has commended the public for complementing its efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on hydropower.

Speaking during an interview with ZANIS, Ministry of Energy Principal Public Relations Officer, Bob Sianjalika, said the ministry has recorded an increase of Independence Power Producers and Independence Power Traders, which has increased the solar electricity generation.

Mr Sianjalika disclosed that the ministry is still receiving applications from individuals and groups showing interest in being in the Independence Power Producer chain, while others have power purchase agreements with ZESCO.

He further highlighted that the energy sector is now at 4,700 megawatts of collective generation across the country, giving them an assurance of meeting the target of 10,000 megawatts by 2026.

Mr Sianjalika added that about 2,600 megawatts of electricity is expected to be generated from thermal and solar plants alone, from the community.

He also disclosed that the government will be commissioning three solar power plants in three areas before the end of the year.

“We will be commissioning one in Shimabala generating 100 megawatts, one in Chipata generating 100 and the other one in Mumbwa with120 megawatts” he added.

Mr Sianjalika has described the current electricity generation state as comfortable if compared to the 2021 state.

He also revealed that the government intends to generate 1,000 megawatts of electricity before the end of the year 2026.

He has urged Zambians and foreign investors to invest in Zambia’s growing energy sector.

World.title: Police arrest suspect in Chasefu well poisoning
World.content:
Police have arrested a male suspect in the poisoning of a community well in Chasefu district, that affected about 38 people.

Yelemiya Zimba, 28, of Chalotwa Village of Chasefu District, was arrested immediately he was discharged from Lundazi District Hospital where he was being treated after ingesting the same suspected weed killer he had used to contaminate the community well.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba said that the suspect is expected to appear in court soon.

And all the 17 victims of the water poisoning have since been discharged.

Yelemiya Zimba, who stands charged with the offence of maliciously administering poisonous substances into drinking water with intent to harm innocent people, is one of the 17 victims that have been discharged.

“All the 17 victims who were admitted to Lundazi District Hospital have been treated and discharged today,” Mr Mweemba said.

He added that the other 21 people who also drank the same poisoned water within Chalotwa Village and complained of diarrhea and abdominal pains were treated at the local health facility within Chasefu district.

World.title: MoE staff urged to make cleanliness an everyday work culture
World.content:
Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, has implored the ministry staff to make cleanliness an everyday work culture rather than limiting it to national commemorations.

Ms Muneku says cleanliness should be embraced as a way of life rather than a temporary activity, stressing that everyone has a role to play in keeping the environment clean.

Speaking during a cleaning exercise at the Ministry’s premises in Lusaka today ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary, Ms Muneku emphasised that the ministry’s surroundings should remain clean and presentable at all times.

Ms Muneku urged the administration department to take the lead in maintaining high standards of cleanliness, stressing that staff must demonstrate their commitment through consistent action.

And Lusaka Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, called on members of the public to take responsibility for maintaining cleanliness around their premises and trading in designated market places.

Mr Mwewa expressed concern over the disposal of plastic waste into drainage systems, which he attributed to trading activities conducted in undesignated areas.

He said traders should operate from markets to promote proper waste management and ensure that business activities are conducted in appropriate environments.

Mr Mwewa further called for high standards of cleanliness along the road between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance, saying the area should be spotless.

He urged the public to support efforts to relocate traders to designated markets, emphasising that the initiative represents a permanent change in the way trading and environmental cleanliness are managed.

World.title: Senegal: General Strike Continues Amid Protests Against New Labour Laws
World.content:
Dakar — Senegal's labour unions have called for a 72-hour general strike, from October 21 to 23, 2026. The government disputes the legality of the strike, saying the notice filed by the unions doesn't comply with the procedures. This standoff comes amid ongoing tensions surrounding the reform of the Labor Code and the Social Security Code.

The confrontation between the government and the trade unions has entered a new phase. At the call of the Trade Union Front for the Defense of Labor (FSDT) and the mobilized trade union federations, workers are invited to observe three days of strike action to protest, in particular, against the conditions under which the new labor and social protection laws were adopted.

For several months, unions have been denouncing a process they deem insufficiently consultative. On July 10, the FSDT had already announced a general strike to express its opposition to the approach taken by the authorities. Despite this protest, the two texts were promulgated on September 3, 2026, under laws no. 2026-18 and no. 2026-19, before their publication in the Official Journal on September 18th.

A disagreement over the legality of the movement

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Faced with this new call for mobilization, the Ministry of Public Service, Labor, and Public Service Reform considers the strike order unlawful. According to information reported by PressAfrik, the administration contests the use of a single strike notice to cover the public, semi-public, and private sectors, which are subject to separate procedures.

In the private and semi-public sectors, the Labor Code stipulates that the dispute must be notified to the Labor and Social Security Inspector or the relevant Director General, as applicable. If no agreement is reached, or in the event of partial conciliation, a thirty-day notice period may then be given to the company's management.

For civil servants, the ministry reminds them that written notice must specify the reasons for and duration of the strike, with one month's notice given before the action begins. Local government employees, for their part, must notify the president of the departmental council or the mayor concerned of their strike notice.

The administration warns that failure to comply with these formalities may result in salary deductions for days not worked and disciplinary action. It also mentions potential consequences for the right to compensation and damages in the event of termination of the employment contract.

For more, read the original story in French.

World.title: Nigeria: Health Is Economic Infrastructure - Why Nigeria Must Invest in Health
World.content:
blog

Listen to this article 8 min The recently concluded World Health Summit in Berlin, themed "From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health", reinforced a key message: health spending is an investment, not just an expense. Yet Nigeria's 2026 Appropriation Bill proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health out of ₦58.47 trillion, about 4.2% of the budget. That is less than a third of the 15% target African governments agreed to in the 2001 Abuja Declaration.

Closing this gap requires recognising health as an investment in economic growth, much like roads and power. Nigeria's growth ambitions depend on people being healthy enough to participate in the economy. Health should therefore be treated as economic infrastructure in the country's development priorities and budget decisions.

What the evidence actually supports

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Egypt's experience illustrates the potential economic returns of health investment. At the summit session Funding the Future: Unlocking the Economic and Fiscal Returns of Health Innovation, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, described a $240 million early-detection programme reaching 60 million people, followed by affordable generic treatment. It was projected to save $7 billion by 2030, a 688% return.

However, these are projections, not a confirmed result. For Nigeria, achieving comparable gains would require screening capacity and reliable medicine supplies that are not yet available at the same scale. Martin Seychell, Deputy Director-General at DG INTPA at the European Commission, cautioned that better outcomes depend on how the money is spent.

"We should not make the mistake of simply gauging and assessing efforts simply on the basis of how much money we are investing in health budgets. Because we know, of course, if you underinvest, you will not get good outcomes. But it doesn't follow that if you just increase the health budgets without a clear strategy, you will get better outcomes."

Nigeria's clearest return is household income

One of the clearest benefits for Nigeria is the funds families could keep if healthcare were more affordable. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO, Amref Health Africa singled out Nigeria when discussing the high out-of-pocket health expenditure, noting that what people pay out of pocket is "ridiculously higher than the government spends."

People pay about 71.9% of current health expenditure out of pocket. An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5% of households faced catastrophic health spending, meaning health costs accounted for at least 10% of their household budget. These bills can force families to borrow, sell belongings or cut spending on food and education.

During the Strategic Health Economy session, Dr Ezekwesili recalled that evidence showing that malaria cost Africa about 2% of its GDP "changed the conversation" with ministers and described the disease as a "productivity tax on the economies." The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare estimates that malaria reduces Nigeria's GDP by more than $1.1 billion each year, while Nigeria accounts for 27% of global cases.

At the same session, Dr Satoshi Ezoe, Japan's Assistant Minister for Global Health, explained that Japan reached universal health coverage in 1961 while still recovering from the Second World War, and argued that "we laid the foundation by making UHC, which led to socioeconomic development."

Nigeria is one of the first eight countries in the UHC Knowledge Hub, a Japanese initiative with the World Health Organization and the World Bank that brings health and finance ministries together to plan for universal coverage. Successful coverage should mean fewer families are pushed into hardship by medical bills and fewer workdays lost, not enrolment figures alone.

Who captures the value?

The economic case for health investment extends to building local industries and creating employment opportunities. Yet Africa captures little of the value from the health products it uses, as Dr Obiageli Ezekwesili, founder and chief executive officer of Human Capital Africa, told the summit during the session The Strategic Health Economy:

"[Africa's] capacity in terms of... global manufacturing... it's less than 5%. Then you look at... competitiveness... how much value does Africa gain from the health value chain -- also insignificant...

Nigeria aims to increase local production of essential health products to 70% by 2030. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain is supported by tax and duty waivers on pharmaceutical inputs and about $2 billion in financing commitments.

However, packaging imported products locally is not the same as making them locally. Manufacturers still rely on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients to produce medicines, leaving them exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations and price volatility.

Local production also needs skilled workers, as does the wider health system. Nigeria has 95,456 registered doctors but only 60,551 with active practising licenses, while its 2024 National Policy on Health Workforce Migration requires wider implementation.

The role of policy in enabling health workers to deliver care also features in the summit session Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century, where Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO of Amref Health Africa, stressed its importance for community health workers.

Making investment accountable

Funding also must reach the services it is meant for. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Gitahi warned that prevention and vaccination budgets "are the first to be cut" when fiscal space tightens, because their results are less visible.

Nigeria shows the risk: in 2025, only ₦36 million of the ₦218 billion appropriated for federal health capital projects was released. For Nigeria, the value of health investment lies in the industries it builds and the workers it equips. Realising that value requires funding, procurement and regulation to support these goals.

Close 

The following steps could help put this into practice;

The Office of the Accountant-General and Budget Office should include health infrastructure in quarterly cash plans and publish how much funding is released.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and state schemes should automatically enrol eligible conditional cash transfer beneficiaries and publish whether enrolment reduces their out-of-pocket spending. In addition, the NHIA, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), and state governments could consider offering qualified Nigerian manufacturers multi-year purchasing agreements with clear standards for price, quality, and delivery. Reliable demand would make it easier for manufacturers to invest.

Incentives under the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) and NAFDAC approval pathways should reward verified local production, including making ingredients and meeting quality standards. Annual reporting should show which products are replacing imports.

Health belongs in Nigeria's growth strategy for the same reason ports and power do: the economy depends on it. That case must be reflected in funding released on time, stronger local production and affordable, quality care. Nigeria needs to spend more on health, use the funds strategically and measure whether people and the economy are better off.

World.title: South Africa: How Nurses Are Learning to Administer the New HIV Prevention Injection
World.content:
South Africa's rollout of lenacapavir, a six-monthly HIV prevention injection, requires nurses to learn, adapt and find ways to make it work for patients.

After 26 years in nursing, Sister Keitumetse "Tumi" Senokwane still had something new to learn about giving injections.

The six-monthly HIV-prevention jab, lenacapavir, often referred to as just LEN, presented a unique challenge.

"You know, lenacapavir is different. As much as I've got experience with injections, the needle size is different from the subcutaneous (beneath the skin) injections we are used to, and the solution is quite thick," says Senokwane. "Because we were not used to it, the practical training helped us to get used to it." She practised withdrawing the yellow liquid, using cooking oil as a stand-in.



That kind of preparation matters because lenacapavir for HIV prevention is being introduced at a time when South Africa still has a substantial need for effective HIV prevention options. The country had an estimated 140 000 new HIV infections in 2025. Modelling suggests that scaling up lenacapavir to 1.4 million to 2.1 million initiations a year by 2030 could avert an average of 32 200 to 51 700 infections annually.

But realising lenacapavir's potential will depend on more than getting the injection into clinics. It also requires nurses to administer it correctly, answer patients' questions, and adapt services to their needs.

Getting to grips with lenacapavir

Senokwane is a professional nurse and site manager at Maria Rantho Community Health Centre and Phedisong 1 Clinic in Tshwane, which are participating in the Wits RHI Len4PrEP study.

"LEN4PrEP is an implementation research study, so looking at how we can deliver the product in a real-world setting," says study investigator Dr Catherine Martin.

The researchers recruited 1 544 participants between November 2025 and June 2026, with follow-up continuing until June 2027. The study began several months before South Africa's national rollout of lenacapavir on 5 June 2026, when the injection was launched at 360 public health facilities across six provinces.

By 8 October, 76 922 people had initiated LEN nationally, including 36 733 in 133 facilities in Gauteng, according to health department spokesperson Foster Mohale.

For Senokwane and her colleagues, administering lenacapavir meant learning a new HIV prevention method.

Nurses first had to complete a compulsory Nurse-Initiated Management of Antiretroviral Therapy (NIMART) course, which provides a theoretical foundation for managing HIV and antiretroviral treatment. This was followed by practical training in preparing and administering LEN.

Training also covered eligibility, side effects, HIV testing and counselling, with videos and clinical mentorship providing additional support.

Mohale says feedback from early-rollout clinics, nurses and patients would help the department refine its training and guidelines.

At the study clinics, nurses also had to adapt the service to patients' needs and fit the new injection method into existing care.

The one-stop shop

The Department of Health's lenacapavir implementation guidelines emphasise counselling clients on their HIV prevention options and helping them choose a method that suits their needs.

At the study clinics, nurses incorporated LEN into existing sexual and reproductive health services, allowing clients to access HIV prevention alongside services such as family planning and STI screening and treatment during a single visit.

"You will get all services in one room like a one-stop shop," says Senokwane.

"Maybe you are here for lenacapavir, but we also check whether you are on a family planning method. If not, we will give you information and provide a family planning method for you, where we screen you for STIs, and then if you've got some infections, we also treat you," she says.

The LEN4PrEP study also used a mobile clinic to bring HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health services to young people in their communities.

"So many of our clients already know us. They know how we treat them and the quality of service we provide," she says.

Initial LEN consultations took longer as nurses explained the available prevention methods and how soon each would offer protection against HIV.

"We give you the information and explain how each method works, how long until it is effective. Participants would like to know when they are going to be protected from HIV if they take this specific method," says Senokwane.

At the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society's Long-Acting Antiretroviral Treatment Conference in Johannesburg in September, Wits RHI's Professor Saiqa Mullick, Director of Implementation Science, shared early findings from the LEN4PrEP study.

She reported that convenience was a major reason participants opted for the lenacapavir jab. They valued not having to take a daily pill or make frequent clinic visits, while the injection offered greater privacy for some. It also attracted people new to PrEP, alongside existing users seeking a method that better suited their lives.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, refers to antiretroviral medicines taken to prevent HIV infection. When used as prescribed, oral PrEP has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection from sex. For several years now, HIV prevention tablets have been widely available in South Africa's public healthcare system, although uptake has been somewhat muted with only around 350 000 people taking the tablets in mid-2025, according to estimates from Thembisa, the leading mathematical model of HIV in South Africa.

Of the 1 538 participants whose method choices were reported, 85.8% selected the lenacapavir shot, compared with 13.7% who selected the prevention pills and 0.5% who chose not to use PrEP.

"People want options that fit into their lives," Mullick told delegates.

Sticking the landing

Patients could also choose where in the body to receive the injections: the upper arm, buttocks, abdomen or thigh.

Among the 1 319 participants who started LEN, Mullick says approximately 50% of women preferred the buttocks, while about 51% of men preferred the upper arm. The ongoing study will explore both men and women's reasons for injection-site preferences.

For nurses, the challenge was to administer the injections correctly while making the process as efficient as possible.

Lenacapavir requires getting two injections during the same visit. Patients also need to take two lenacapavir tablets on the day of their first injections, followed by another two tablets 24 hours later. These tablets form part of the initiation dose before they continue with injections every six months.

Senokwane says a Wits RHI pharmacist taught her a way to withdraw the solution while keeping the vial upright, rather than turning it upside down.

"That was the best method for me because it worked faster," says Senokwane.

"So with that method, you pull up 1.5 ml of air into the syringe and inject the needle into the vial. [The syringe] draws at least one ml by itself, without assistance, which allows the nurse to multitask. And then you also save time because you are able to prepare two injections at the same time," she says.

But efficiency was only part of the learning curve. Because lenacapavir is a thick solution, it needs to be injected slowly.

"I wish I knew that you can't inject it fast," Senokwane said. The thick solution required a slower injection technique to reduce leakage.

Slow administration was included in nurses' initial training, but its importance in minimising leakage was reinforced as they gained practical experience and shared lessons with colleagues.

Dr Martin says that in the early stages of implementation, nurses consulted experts, including those involved in clinical trials, on how to manage leakage at the injection site.

"As local experience grew, they learnt to reassure participants that minor leakage could occur and to assess more substantial leakage to determine whether further follow-up was needed."

Answering patient concerns

Patients were also concerned about the side effects of lenacapavir.

Lumps or small nodules at the injection site are a common side effect of lenacapavir. In one clinical trial, which included 2 140 participants who received lenacapavir, roughly 64% developed subcutaneous nodules at the injection site.

"Most of the clients were curious about the nodules. They were worried about whether they would be able to continue with their normal activities, especially those who wanted to exercise," says Senokwane.

"They wanted to know how long the nodule would last and whether they would get another one when they came back for their second injection. Usually, by the time they came for their next injection, the nodule would have disappeared."

Others were worried about the pain.

"We advise them that if the nodule comes with pain, just use a warm or cold compress, or you can even use a painkiller," explains Senokwane.

Mullick says addressing these concerns and discussing them with clients in advance is part of making the injection work for patients in practice.

"This might seem something relatively small, but from an implementation perspective, it contributes considerably to the person receiving the product."

Close 

Making it work in real time

As nurses became more familiar with administering lenacapavir, the clinics also refined how they moved patients through the service, from the initial consultation to receiving the injection.

Patients first met a navigator who explained the available services. After registration, an HIV test and a check of their vital signs, they saw the research nurse.

The clinics later began using the waiting time more effectively, with navigators introducing patients to PrEP and other services before their consultations.

Initially, appointments could take about an hour and a half. As the clinics refined their workflow and nurses became more familiar with the process, Senokwane says visits took about an hour or less.

"Training manuals and guidelines provide all the theoretical knowledge and framework for delivering lenacapavir," Martin explains.

"But, that real-world experience gives you a little bit more insight into things that you can only learn by working with clients."

Each one teach one

Senokwane's experience eventually helped her become a mentor to other nurses.

"The mentorship was really very important. We've got support from our pharmacist, and then we've got support from our sub-investigator at site. So everyone needs to be mentored until you are really 100% sure that you can do it on your own," she says.

When non-research nurses started providing lenacapavir in June at the study sites, she went there to demonstrate the technique. Some nurses she had trained also helped their colleagues.

"They were always grateful that we really helped them. So they really appreciated it. The more you practice, the better you become," says Senokwane.

Lessons from the clinics also informed training. Videos demonstrating how to prepare and administer lenacapavir were produced by Wits RHI, alongside webinars. Martin says the videos would be incorporated into future training.

"It's always helpful to see something in practice. With a new product, although it can be explained theoretically, it is helpful to actually see a provider and a client interaction," she says.

World.title: Country star Jimmie Allen says he’s the ‘victim’ after $1.8M judgment in sexual assault lawsuit
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Jimmie Allen is maintaining his innocence and insisting he is the "victim" after a federal judge ordered the country star to pay nearly $1.8 million to a woman who accused him of sexual assault.

The 41-year-old singer faced two separate civil sexual assault and abuse lawsuits from two women in 2023. During an interview with Fox News Digital, Allen spoke candidly about the allegations that derailed his career, maintaining that his sexual encounters with both women who sued him were consensual while acknowledging that he was unfaithful to his then-wife, Alexis Gale.

When asked what he would say to his accusers today, Allen said he has forgiven both women but admitted that he struggled with being unable to publicly defend himself without being accused of blaming alleged victims.

JIMMIE ALLEN PUBLICLY APOLOGIZES TO ESTRANGED WIFE FOR ‘HUMILIATING HER’ WITH ‘AFFAIR’ AFTER SEX ABUSE LAWSUIT

"I wanted to just get on social media and call them liars and things like that," Allen said. "But it was interesting when I thought about it, someone said, 'No, well, you'll be a victim blamer and stuff like that.'"

"But I was like, 'I'm the victim here,'" he continued. "So they can say this about me, these horrible things about me and try to ruin and destroy everything that I worked my butt off for. But I can't say that they're lying."

In May 2023, the first woman, Jane Doe 1, who worked as the country singer's day-to-day manager, filed a lawsuit against Allen, in which she accused him of raping her in 2021 and subsequently sexually harassing her over the next 18 months.

JARED LETO RESPONDS TO SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS MADE BY MULTIPLE WOMEN IN EXPLOSIVE DOCUMENTARY

The second woman sued Allen in June 2023, accusing the "Big In A Small Town" singer of sexually assaulting her while she visited him at a Las Vegas hotel in the summer of 2022 while he was in Sin City for a bowling tournament. Jane Doe 2 claimed Allen had also recorded the encounter without her permission.

Allen denied both women's allegations and filed counterclaims against them in July 2023, accusing his former manager of defamation and other claims and accusing Jane Doe 2 of unlawfully taking his cellphone following their encounter.

In August 2025, Allen was found liable by default rather than following a trial in which a jury weighed the competing accounts.

The following June, a federal judge ordered Allen to pay Jane Doe 2 $1,790,541 in compensatory and punitive damages.

WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS HE'S THE ‘VICTIM’ AFTER SEXUAL ASSAULT ALELGATIONS UPENDED HIS LIFE

KATY PERRY UNDER POLICE INVESTIGATION OVER RUBY ROSE'S SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen said that he does not intend to simply accept the judgment.

"I'm pursuing options because I – me as a man and as a father and as the son and brother of real sexual assault victims – I cannot in good conscience do that," he said. "And that's why I feel like as a man and as a father it is my job to fight it and find and chase whatever other options I can."

Allen did not specify what legal action he intended to pursue. Fox News Digital reached out to his current attorney, Ted Anastasiou, for comment.

The default ruling followed a series of missed deadlines and court orders. According to court records, Allen and his touring company failed to meet discovery requirements, attend court-ordered mediation and obtain new counsel within deadlines set by the court.

Allen claimed that much of the breakdown was due to his former attorney, Alandis Brassel, becoming seriously ill while representing him. The singer told Fox News Digital that Brassel was a solo practitioner and claimed that he had difficulty reaching his lawyer while he was sick.

"I'm not in contact with the court. He is," Allen recalled. "So during that time, we missed a deadline."

Allen said Brassel later informed the court about his illness but claimed the judge "didn't care."

"So the judge dropped my countersuit and they awarded Jane Doe 2 default judgment because I missed the deadline," he said.

However, court records detail multiple missed deadlines and failures to comply with court orders.

The Grammy Award nominee acknowledged that there was at least one deadline during that period of time that he believed he could have met himself.

"I have no problem taking responsibility," Allen said. "I could have, you know, maybe done more. Absolutely."

"The other ones, I should have been more, I guess, involved with the court, but I've never been in a situation like this," he continued. "I didn't know even how to connect with the court. I didn't know if I could speak to the court without my lawyer because he was the one that was handling it."

Anastasiou later became Allen's legal representation. After the default ruling, Anastasiou similarly blamed Allen's "prior counsel's repeated failures to comply with discovery obligations and court orders" and said his client intended to seek to set aside the judgment.

"This ruling was not based on the merits of the allegations. Mr. Allen has consistently and unequivocally maintained his innocence, and he firmly denies these accusations," Anastasiou told People magazine in August 2025.

"As with earlier accusations brought on the same baseless grounds, this case is equally meritless," he continued. "The default judgment reflects the shortcomings of prior representation, not any wrongdoing by Mr. Allen. It is well-established that a client should not be penalized for the failures of their attorney, and Mr. Allen should not be deprived of his right to a fair defense."

Fox News Digital was unable to reach Brassel for comment.

WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS HE'S ‘PURSUING OPTIONS’ TO FIGHT $1.8M SEXUAL ASSAULT

According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe 2 met Allen on a flight to Nashville in May 2022 and the two remained in contact over the following months before meeting in Las Vegas.

FORMER MIT SCIENTIST WINS $6M DEFAMATION VERDICT AGAINST COLLEAGUE WHO ACCUSED HIM OF SEXUAL MISCONDUCT

Jane Doe 2 alleged that she willingly joined Allen in his hotel room and initially consented to having sex with him, but repeatedly told the singer that she was not on birth control and did not want him to ejaculate inside her. According to the complaint, Allen agreed but later disregarded her requests to stop and instead ejaculated inside her.

She also alleged that Allen secretly recorded their sexual encounter without her knowledge or consent. According to the lawsuit, Allen had asked her to remain on the hotel room's balcony after they arrived while he went inside, which she believed was because he was planning a surprise. Jane Doe 2 alleged that Allen instead used the opportunity to position his cellphone to later record them.

Jane Doe 2 alleged that after Allen fell asleep, she discovered the phone recording them, stopped the recording and deleted the video. According to the complaint, she was unable to permanently delete the footage without Allen's passcode and took the phone with her when she left the hotel room before later turning it over to police.

EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M

Allen disputed Jane Doe 2's account, maintaining that their encounter was consensual and that she knew she was being recorded. He said that they were together on the balcony when he explicitly told her he wanted to record and asked permission. While speaking with Fox News Digital, he described their alleged conversation regarding the recording.

"She said, ‘You were recording us without my permission.’ I said, ‘Oh, no, no.' I said, 'We were on the balcony.' And I have all this in texts that we were on the balcony. I told you, 'I'm recording, is it OK?.' And I don't ever hide my camera, ever. Ever. It's not my thing,'" he told Fox News Digital.

Allen has maintained since 2023 that Jane Doe consented to the recording.

The singer claimed to Fox News Digital that the recording depicts him "passing out."

"In the video, you can see me passing out," he claimed. "You can see me black out, like pass out.'"

Allen further claimed the recording shows Jane Doe 2 continuing to engage in sexual activity with him after he passed out, later getting dressed, returning to bed and rubbing his back before approaching the camera and turning it off.

WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS SEXUAL ASSAULT LAWSUIT ‘LITERALLY SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER DOCTOR'S DIRE WARNING

Elizabeth Fegan, an attorney who represented both Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2, blasted Allen's claims in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Mr. Allen's attempt to portray himself as the victim is as outrageous as it is offensive to the women who have come forward to report his sexual misconduct," Fegan said. "Two women have accused Mr. Allen of sexual abuse. Rather than accepting responsibility for his actions, he has repeatedly denied their accounts, sought to discredit them, and now attempts to rewrite the facts through the media, all while evading his financial obligations to the women who sought justice through the courts."

"Let there be no ambiguity: Jane Doe 2 never consented to being recorded," she continued. "Mr. Allen's continued insistence otherwise does not change her account or the Court's findings. Nor do his self-serving descriptions of selected portions of the recording establish consent to its creation. His attempt to shift attention to her behavior is yet another effort to blame the woman whose rights he violated."

JIMMIE ALLEN WELCOMES THIRD CHILD WITH ESTRANGED WIFE AMID SPLIT, SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS

"The real victim here is the woman whose privacy, bodily autonomy, and trust were violated and who has endured years of trauma and litigation seeking accountability," Fegan added. "Mr. Allen has had ample opportunity to tell his story in court. He chose not to do so. He should stop attacking the women who came forward and start taking responsibility for his conduct."

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen also addressed the allegations made by his former day-to-day manager, whose 2023 lawsuit first thrust the country singer into the scandal.

Jane Doe 1, who worked as Allen's day-to-day manager, accused the singer of repeatedly sexually harassing and assaulting her over an approximately 18-month period while she was employed by his management company.

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe 1 alleged that Allen first sexually assaulted her in March 2021 after a work trip to Los Angeles, where he was filming an appearance on "American Idol." She claimed that after having several drinks at a business dinner, she woke up naked in her hotel room with Allen beside her and had no memory of what happened after dinner. According to the complaint, she was bleeding and in pain and Allen insisted that she take Plan B.

Jane Doe 1 alleged that Allen continued to sexually harass and assault her afterward, including by touching her without her consent and forcing her to engage in sexual acts despite her objections. She claimed she repeatedly told Allen "no," pushed him away and tried to avoid being alone with him, but feared that resisting him could jeopardize her career because she was responsible for managing him.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen vehemently denied Jane Doe 1's allegations but acknowledged that the two had a sexual relationship, which he characterized as a consensual affair that continued on and off for approximately a year and a half.

"What I want people to understand about those allegations is one, they're not true," he claimed.

"I had an affair off and on for like a year and a half with my day-to-day manager," Allen said. "And It started, then we would cut it off, and it would start, and then we will cut it off. And it slowly became one of the things where I was like, I know what I was doing was wrong, but I was afraid to end it because I didn't really know exactly how to end without one, hurting her, right, and without hurting myself. Because it's one of those things where it's like you spend so much time, go, go go, go, go on the road. And, you know, we were around each other a lot. We were adults that made a decision."

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen accepted responsibility for having the extramarital relationship but denied Jane Doe 1's characterization of it as sexual abuse.

"If I would have never cheated on my wife, I wouldn't have been in that situation anyway," he said. "And that's the part that I take accountability for."

Allen and his former manager reached a settlement in 2024 in which they agreed to dismiss their respective claims against each other. Jane Doe 1's attorney said at the time that she continued to stand by her sexual assault allegations against Allen and had agreed to settle to avoid reliving the alleged abuse at trial.

While Allen maintained he never sexually assaulted either woman, he told Fox News Digital he does not consider himself blameless for the circumstances that led to the scandal.

"Did I cheat on my wife? Yes. Did I apologize to my wife? Yes. Did I owe my wife an apology? Absolutely," he said. "And I'm not going to put the blame on my life on those two individuals. Yes, they might've fabricated a story, but I still slept with them and I put myself in that position."

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen recalled the impact that the allegations had on his personal and professional life.

The singer said that he would tell his accusers that they "made life really hard for my kids."

Allen and Gale, who share daughters Naomi and Zara and son Cohen, initially separated and filed for divorce in April 2023, shortly before the first sexual assault lawsuit was filed against the singer. They simultaneously announced that Gale was pregnant with their third child, Cohen.

In a May 2023 Instagram post, Allen apologized to Gale for having an affair and acknowledged that his choices brought shame and humiliation to his family.

Gale gave birth to Cohen in September 2023 and the following month, Allen's representative said the divorce had not been completed and that the couple had decided to "work on things" and were still together.

The former couple's divorce was ultimately finalized in October 2024.

Allen told Fox News Digital that the "hardest conversation" that he had was with Gale. He admitted that he failed to even warn his then-wife before the first lawsuit became public.

"I handled that completely wrong," Allen said.

Allen said the fallout also affected his oldest son, Aadyn, whom he shares with a previous partner. He recalled struggling to explain why some of his son's friends stopped speaking to him or inviting him to parties after the allegations against his father became public.

The singer also recalled how his thriving career collapsed amid the scandal and worried about how he would continue providing for his children.

"Everything I've worked for is just gone," he said. "Record label gone, management gone, bookings gone, PR gone, endorsement deals gone."

He said that his mounting fears sent him into an increasingly dark place and eventually led him to contemplate taking his own life.

"Two years ago, I was riding around my truck at like three in the morning and I had my gun in my lap and I was trying to decide, do I want to live or not?" he told Fox News Digital.

Allen said he eventually sought help, turning to therapy and spending time in rehabilitation as he worked to get his mental health back on track.

He recalled that his struggles had begun well before the allegations became public. As Allen's career took off, the singer said he began taking pills to stay awake and others to keep himself in a good mood while trying to meet the demands of touring, his record label, radio, his family and fans.

Allen said that by 2021 and 2022, he felt like he was on a "train" going "a thousand miles an hour," knowing he needed to get off but unsure how.

"I would say in 2023, when that lawsuit came out, I felt like that was God derailing the train," he said. "One, it hurt because of what was being said about me. But at the same time, it literally saved my life."

"My doctor said if I had kept going, I'd have been dead in six months," Allen continued.

Allen told Fox News Digital that getting help also forced him to reconsider his relationship with music, which he admitted he had grown to hate at the height of his struggles.

However, Allen said that as he worked to rebuild his life, he also began rediscovering the love of music that he had lost.

Allen told Fox News Digital that while some relationships disappeared amid the controversy, he was surprised by the support he received from others in the entertainment industry.

"Dolly Parton being one of them," he said. "She called me and she told me she loves me. She said, ‘Jimmie, I know who you are.’ She said, ‘Try to just keep yourself surrounded by people that love you.’"

Allen recalled Jelly Roll, Darius Rucker, Kathie Lee Gifford and Kid Rock were among others who reached out to him.

Kid Rock's support eventually extended beyond words of encouragement. The "Freedom Was a Highway" singer recently collaborated with Kid Rock on his Christian album "Halfway to Jesus," marking another step in Allen's return to recording music.

Allen recalled Kid Rock telling him, "'As Christians, we're quick to ask for forgiveness but don't want to give it.'"

The musician is also working on several projects of his own, including Christian and gospel music as well as country and R&B material. He said his approach to his career has changed dramatically from the relentless pursuit of success that he described before the allegations surfaced.

"It's not about winning Grammys or CMAs or number one records," he said. "It's about doing what I love."

When asked whether he believes Nashville is ready to give him another chance, Allen explained being accepted back into the country music establishment was not his priority.

World.title: America's biggest buffet chain cracked the code to all-you-can-eat profits
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Customers at America's biggest buffet chain can pile their plates high with steak, shrimp and comfort food favorites, but behind the all-you-can-eat spread is a carefully calculated balancing act, according to a new report.

Golden Corral has developed a sophisticated system to keep the buffet model viable despite challenging economic conditions, The Wall Street Journal recently reported.

The chain, which has roughly 350 restaurants across the U.S., predominantly in the South and Southeast, offers about 150 different buffet items. What customers might not realize is that they are carefully arranged into "modules" that mix expensive and inexpensive foods, CEO Lance Trenary told the Journal.

AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS

Pricier items like meat and seafood are paired with lower-cost items like hush puppies and french fries. Meatloaf goes side-by-side with potatoes, gravy and green beans, for example.

"We have to be pretty creative in the way that we present our menu," Trenary told the Journal.

The chain also has to adapt to changes in the market.

RED LOBSTER'S 37-YEAR-OLD CEO BETTING ON NOSTALGIA, AI TO FUEL CHAIN'S COMEBACK AFTER BANKRUPTCY

As beef prices have shot up, Golden Corral added a bone-in fried pork chop as a cheaper alternative to sirloin. The pork chop costs the chain only about 40% of what the sirloin costs, so every customer who chooses pork instead of steak helps reduce Golden Corral's overall food costs.

Quality also matters more at a buffet, where customers can simply discard a poorly prepared dish and return for something else.

Golden Corral tries to prevent that by keeping food fresh, making about 80% of its buffet items in-house and preparing only what it expects customers to eat. The chain uses demand data to forecast needs in 15-minute increments rather than cooking large quantities in advance and leaving them under food warmers.

CLICK HERE TO 

But the careful approach doesn't mean it has been smooth sailing for Golden Corral.

"This has been a difficult year for us, don't get me wrong," Trenary said. "We are trying to at least tread water."

About 38 cents of every dollar Golden Corral brings in goes toward food, while the chain is trying to keep its dinner buffet priced below $20 at many locations.

Selling drinks separately helps bring in additional revenue, but rising food and other costs are making the all-you-can-eat model increasingly difficult to sustain.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Still, the promise of getting more food for a set price remains appealing to budget-conscious diners and other restaurant chains have leaned into that appeal, according to industry data.

Red Lobster, Applebee's and Olive Garden are among those offering different types of unlimited promotions.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Major chains rolled out about 150 such deals in the first half of 2026 — roughly four times the number offered in 2021, according to Technomic data.
