World.title: Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students
World.content:
Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students

toggle caption i Andri Tambunan for NPR

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

When Zyearre Amoah was a student at Sacramento State in 2023, there were times when he felt like the only Black student.

"There were African-American students on our campus," he recalls. But at a sprawling state university with more than 30,000 students, "it just felt like we had to look for each other."

Amoah graduated in 2024, just as his university was launching its Black Honors College, a school within a school with a special focus on Black history, life and culture. He's now a staff member at the BHC, as it's called, helping recruit students.

Sponsor Message

"Unfortunately I didn't have the luxury to be part of it as a student," he says, but the university's effort to elevate, and celebrate, the scholarship of Black students has changed how he perceives his alma mater.

"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," he says, laughing. "That is really helpful for everyone here. We're finding each other relatively easier. "

The initiative at Sacramento State, formally known as the California State University, Sacramento, began just months before the Trump administration began its widespread assault on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs on college campuses. In the last two years, dozens of colleges and universities have rolled back or eliminated such offerings to avoid accusations of racial discrimination that have led to loss of research funding and other sanctions.

"Historically, the campus struggled to create an environment of success" for Black students, says Luke Wood, Sac State's president, who helped create the BHC. "So we created an intervention that was designed to meet their needs while also serving any student who was interested in being part of it."

Wood sees this as a vital part of his, or any university's, mission. "I think that more institutions could be easily doing the same."

Sponsor Message

An 'elite, specialized experience'

There are more than 800 students currently enrolled in the BHC, and while the majority of them identify as Black, African, African-American or mixed race, Wood insists it's not exclusive and that it complies with federal and state laws.

"It's nondiscriminatory because you can be a white student, an Asian student or Latino and be in the Black Honors College," he says, "and we have non-Black students who apply who want to have an elite, specialized experience."

toggle caption i Andri Tambunan for NPR

All of the college's courses are taught from a Black studies perspective. A math class, for example, also includes stories of famous Black mathematicians.

Faculty are chosen based on their track record of educating Black students. Among the criteria are low withdrawal and failure numbers for those students.

Now in its third year, women make up a majority of the BHC's enrollment, according to the college's dean, Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe. That's the case on most U.S. campuses . She says one of her priorities is to change that. To do so, she plans to provide more male role models and mentors: not just to convince more men to enroll, but to support them when they do.

A climate of disappearing diversity programs

Following the Supreme Court decision in 2023 banning affirmative action , the Trump administration has launched civil rights investigations targeting programs that single out a specific race — such as a scholarship program for Black students or an office designed to celebrate multiculturalism.

In September, the Treasury Department proposed a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide help to students based on their race.

At President Trump's State of the Union address in February, he declared, "We ended D-E-I in America!"

Around the country, many students have felt increasingly isolated, and let down, as diversity programs have disappeared.

Sponsor Message

"I was pretty sad just at the fact that our university would comply with those federal guidelines," says Hayden O'Neill, a senior at the University of Michigan. She was part of a scholarship program that was shut down last year.

"It definitely feels disheartening," she says, "I don't feel as comfortable as I thought I would at a school like this."

O'Neill is one of the many students around the country who say that understanding their identity – especially as it relates to their race – is a high priority in college. And while O'Neill feels like she is losing some of that opportunity, students in the Black Honors College say they're being given that chance.

A strong sense of belonging

The bell above the door to the Black Honors College headquarters – housed on the first floor of Sac State's library – rings often:

A sophomore arrives to meet with an advisor. A first-year student has a question about tuition. Over in the corner, a professor has come to ready his notes before class. It's a hub, a home within a home.

On a recent day, one of the students in the office is Naomi Thrower, a junior majoring in Deaf Studies and American Sign Language.

She wanted to attend a historically black college, but California doesn't have any. So, she says, Sacramento State with its BHC felt like the closest alternative.

Growing up in the East Bay, she had what she calls a very multicultural experience, going to school with kids of all different races. While she gained a lot from that, she also felt she was missing a deep understanding of Black culture and identity.

"The kids used to bully me in middle school and say I was whitewashed," Thrower says. "So when it came time for college, I wanted to be surrounded by students who looked like me and also had that same academic drive."

Sponsor Message

She runs a natural hair business on campus as a side hustle, and says it has helped her develop a creative expression. "In high school, when I'd say I have to do my hair, my friends wouldn't understand it's an all day thing. They'd be like, 'Why does it take so long to wash and brush out your hair?'"

But when she made friends in the honors college, it seemed everyone understood. "Two of my friends helped me take down my hair. We detangled it, washed it. We were just listening to music and hanging out, and that was the community that I was longing for, just someone who understood."

She and others NPR talked with often quoted the saying, Ubuntu, which comes from South African philosophy. It describes an interconnected way of living, often translated as, "I am because we are."

Many students said this concept is central to their educational experience.

And at Sacramento State, Wood says, the efforts to build that identity and sense of community are paying off: Enrollment of Black students is up – and those students are doing better – with more of them re-enrolling, and graduating.

This story was produced with support from the Education Writers Association's Reporting Fellowship program.

World.title: With jet fuel prices near a record, holiday airfares soar higher
World.content:
With jet fuel prices near a record, holiday airfares soar higher

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

BALTIMORE — Herb and Latasha Williams flew from Dallas to Baltimore/Washington International Airport this week for a quick vacation to celebrate his birthday.

But their plane tickets cost hundreds of dollars more than they expected. And Latasha Williams is now wondering if they can afford to travel for the holidays.

"I kind of wanted to go somewhere warm. Florida, I'm thinking," she said.

Then she looked at airfares.

"Maybe next year. Maybe," she said with a laugh. "Fingers crossed."

Those planning to fly this holiday season, should be prepared to pay more than they did last year. Experts expect airfares for this holiday travel season will be the highest in years as airlines scramble to cover the rising cost of jet fuel, which is one of their biggest expenses.

Sponsor Message

The average price of jet fuel in the U.S. topped $4.75 per gallon this week, according to the tracking firm Argus. That's close to an all-time high, and almost twice what it was a year ago.

"Airfares right now are at what we see as a 10-year high because of the high cost of jet fuel," said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. "Airlines have to pass on these super high jet fuel prices in the form of higher fares to consumers."

Airfares for Thanksgiving are up about 30% compared to last year, according to Berg. Tickets for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20%.

But so far, Berg said, travelers seem willing to pay, at least for their big holiday trips.

"We're at the time of year where travel is really sticky. Even with higher prices, travelers are unlikely to make major changes to their traditional holiday home for the holiday trips," Berg said in an interview with NPR.

U.S. airlines say demand is holding steady even as fares have gone up. In an earnings call this month, Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said consumers have put up a "limited amount of resistance" and still view airfare as "reasonably affordable" even after fare increases.

Sponsor Message

"I think that's a very good sign for the future," Bastian said.

Some in the industry think fares will go even higher next year.

"You could see airfares rise next year in Europe. I think by 10, 15, maybe 20 percent," Michael O'Leary, CEO of the European low-cost carrier Ryanair, said this week in Belgium. "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months."

The picture may be slightly better in the U.S., which has more oil-producing and refining capacity than Europe. Still, higher fuel costs are hurting U.S. carriers, too.

"The airlines themselves are eating most of that cost," Chris Sununu, the head of Airlines For America, a trade group representing the big airlines, said in an interview this week with CNBC. "And some of it unfortunately has to be passed on to the customer and so you see that 20 to 30 percent increase as we go into the holidays."

Consumers are shopping around more in search of better deals, Berg said, and booking their tickets earlier to try to lock in reasonable prices.

"Usually I am shouting from the rooftops in the middle of October, 'Book your holiday travel by the end of this month, prices will not go down from here,'" Berg said. "But we actually saw an increase in customers booking holiday travel in September already."

At the airport in Baltimore, some travelers say they're priced out of flying for the holidays this year altogether.

"I'm gonna have to drive," said Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland. "I'm from Chicago originally, so I'm gonna drive. For me and my kids, just too much to get tickets."

But others said they're resigned to paying more for their holiday tickets. Mary Haller of Bethany Beach, Delaware is planning a trip to Europe.

"Literally I looked at the economy tickets two weeks ago and they have gone up," Haler said. "It was significant and I sort of had shell shock."

Sponsor Message

Still, Haller said she has little choice but to buy the tickets anyway.

"I feel bad for people who don't have the means to pay the extra money," she said.

World.title: After nearly 6 years, ex-Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi's son hears her voice
World.content:
After nearly 6 years, ex-Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi's son hears her voice

toggle caption i Myanmar President Spokesperson Office via AP

CHIANG MAI, Thailand — After nearly six years in detention, Aung San Suu Kyi's first words to her son were a question about his health.

"And then I said all the family was sending their love and asked after her health," said Kim Aris, who spoke by phone with his 81-year-old mother on Thursday, their first direct conversation since the 2021 military coup toppled the democratically elected Myanmar government she led.

The 20-minute call, which Aris believes the military monitored, offered a rare glimpse of how the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize laureate is being held. She was first sentenced in 2021, with consecutive trials through 2022 bringing her total sentence to 33 years on corruption and electoral fraud charges, widely condemned by the U.S., Western countries, and human rights groups as fabricated. The sentence was later reduced, leaving her with 18 years still to serve.

Sponsor Message

Little has been known about her condition since the coup, which triggered a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event data, a conflict monitoring organization. The U.N. says the conflict has displaced millions.

toggle caption i Myanmar President Spokesperson Office via AP

"My mother is actually alive and well," said Aris, a 49-year-old carpenter, who has campaigned for her release and sought to raise awareness of the crisis engulfing the Southeast Asian nation. He described the call to NPR in phone interview from London, where he lives. "Hearing her voice has reassured me."

Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed president, said on social media that Aris spoke with Suu Kyi by telephone through Myanmar's Embassy in London, and shared separate photographs of the two.

Until now, Aris said he had received almost no word from her — just a single censored letter three years ago and occasional second-hand scraps of information. From the call, he said he learned she is being held at "a residence" somewhere in the surroundings of Myanmar's capital, Naypyidaw. He also said he believes police and military personnel surround the building, which is "fenced off, with a scrubby, nondescript garden which I believe she is allowed to go out into."

Sponsor Message

"From what I can ascertain, she's basically being held in solitary confinement even if she's not in a prison cell," Aris said.

She was permitted to read books, he said, adding, "I don't think she gets any news. So no radio, no television, no newspapers."

Her health has long been a worry for the family. While she "sounded strong," Aris said, "she is still in a lot of pain because her hand is playing up." She told him she has tendonitis. "She said it is very painful, and at points she can't even use her hand." She also said she gets a health checkup every six months.

He believes food is cooked at the residence and sometimes delivered by her lawyers, though not directly to the premises. Aris said he hopes to send her care packages, and she had a request.

She would like "some healthy foods and some nice foods — something of a treat," he said. "She'd like it half and half so it wasn't too much of either."

toggle caption i Khin Maung Win/AP

Aris said he is thinking of including Ben's Cookies, a brand founded in Oxford, England, where she raised her two sons with her late husband, the British scholar Michael Aris, before leaving for Burma, now Myanmar, in 1988 to care for her ailing mother.

"And some chocolate wouldn't go amiss," he added.

Because the conversation was likely monitored by Myanmar's security forces, he said, "there's nothing we could talk about that's too sensitive," including Myanmar's civil war.

"We've had to deal with this for so many years on and off that we're pretty well-versed in how it works," he said, recalling her years of house arrest in her Yangon family home between 1989 and 2010. The regime back then would photograph parcels sent to her and "use that as propaganda," he said.

A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment.

Sponsor Message

Kim Aris believes Myanmar's generals are feeling international pressure as coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, who was installed as president after a military-engineered election in January, travels abroad seeking legitimacy.

"It's an indication that the military are wanting to present a better image of themselves, while actually giving very little," he said. "I hope that governments around the world won't be taken in. After all, they've used these same tactics for decades, and it's been proven time and time again that nothing comes of it."

As far as he knows, the call might be a one-off. He said his mother's situation "shines a light on what's going on in Burma, and reminds people this is happening to many others — and much worse."

"She believes she gives the people of Burma strength by being there with them, going through what they're going through," Aris said.

Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing remains under U.S. sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims that Washington has declared a genocide.

Based on interviews and social media posts, Suu Kyi remains a beloved figure for many inside Myanmar, though her international standing took a blow in 2019, when she appeared before the International Court of Justice to defend the country against those genocide allegations.

Since Min Aung Hlaing became president, the military has sharply escalated attacks on civilians, according to ACLED, even as regional governments step up diplomatic engagement.

An opposition figure, Nay Phone Latt, spokesperson for the exiled National Unity Government, told NPR in a recent interview he believes the regime "dare not release" Suu Kyi.

"If she's released, her strength will combine with the revolution — that's what Min Aung Hlaing fears," he added.

Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the non-profit International Crisis Group, said Suu Kyi's status is "potentially the most valuable card Min Aung Hlaing holds, but he is very reluctant to play it."

Sponsor Message

"The risk is that Aung San Suu Kyi becomes a bargaining chip, traded for concessions while airstrikes on civilian targets continue," Horsey said. "Her release is very unlikely. And while it would matter enormously to her family and to many people in Myanmar, it would not on its own end the war."

The State Department said the U.S. remains concerned about everyone it considers unjustly detained and continues to call for their release. It also urged the military to engage in "genuine dialogue with all opposition groups" to end the conflict.

In August, the department's Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs said in an online statement that it continued to call for Suu Kyi's "immediate and unconditional release."

World.title: Why Quebec's strategic reserve of maple syrup is running dry
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's roughly the size of 53 Olympic swimming pools, but the world's only strategic reserve of maple syrup — spread out across three Quebec warehouses — is running dry.

Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ), the group that represents nearly 13,500 maple syrup producers in the province and oversees the reserve, said its stockpile will be "completely depleted" by the end of February.

According to PPAQ president Luc Goulet, that's largely because demand for Canadian maple syrup has soared around the world, including in the United States — the $1.2-billion industry's largest export market.

There has been a "sharp rise in exports," Goulet said in an interview with Radio-Canada's Midi-Info radio program this week.

"We have major challenges with the strategic reserve, which needs to be replenished. But we also have the challenge of developing our sector" to meet increased demand, he said.

So what exactly is going on, and should breakfast lovers be worried? Here's what we know.

WATCH | Why people are choosing Canadian maple syrup over American: Why more people are choosing Canadian maple syrup — instead of American | Duration 2:18 A quintessential Canadian product is finding its way to more store shelves and breakfast tables around the world. Maple syrup producers say they're seeing a surge in demand amid Canada's trade war with the U.S. The CBC's Colin North reports.

First, how does the reserve work?

Quebec's maple syrup producers set up the reserve in 2000 to try to stabilize supplies and prices, said Maurice Doyon, a professor at Laval University in Quebec City who specializes in agri-food economics.

The province produces 90 per cent of Canada's maple syrup and more than 70 per cent of the world’s supply.

But the industry is heavily dependent on weather conditions: maple trees need regular springtime cycles of freezing and unfreezing to produce sap, which is transformed into syrup.

WATCH | Is your maple syrup real or fake?: Is your maple syrup real or fake? It’s not that hard to tell | Duration closed caption 3:58 An investigation by Radio-Canada’s Enquête program showed that fake maple syrup was being sold on Quebec grocery store shelves. Producers at one Quebec sugar shack tried both pure and bogus syrup and highlighted the differences.

Before the reserve existed, Quebec producers would have to lower prices when supplies outpaced demand. Conversely, prices would go up when demand exceeded supply after bad harvests.

"The idea was to manage that a bit better," Doyon told CBC.

A quota system was also put in place in the early 2000s to regulate production levels.

Today, the reserve can hold as many roughly 60 million kilograms, or 218,000 barrels, of maple syrup. "When there's a bad harvest, [they] can dip into that reserve to supply the market," Doyon said.

So did Quebec have a bad harvest?

No. This time, the reserve is running dry because Quebec's authorized maple syrup processors — who buy, bottle, process and market the sticky stuff — appear to have bought out what was there.

The reserve held 39.4 million pounds (around 18 million kilograms) of maple syrup in February, the PPAQ said.

In an email to CBC News, the organization said while it expects the reserve to be depleted by the end of February "once all volumes under contract have been delivered to buyers," the overall supply remains similar to what it was a year ago.

"Inventories have simply shifted from the strategic reserve to buyers' warehouses. We estimate that buyers' inventories have increased by more than 35 million pounds [about 15.8 million kilograms]."

Cans of maple syrup sit at the Bistro La dent Sucre sugar shack in St. Eustache, Que., on April 6, 2021. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

Why would processors buy from the reserve?

Doyon said processors don't have a strong incentive to dip into the reserve when it's full because they need to pay both for the syrup and to store what they don't immediately sell. But when the reserve is low, they are in competition with each other to secure their supply.

"It's initiated by the fact that the reserve is low," said Doyon, who likened buying up the reserve to taking out insurance.

"If disaster strikes — in other words, a bad harvest — they're going to be happy to have taken those precautions."

The Conseil de l'industrie de l'érable (CIE), which represents authorized processors in Quebec, said they "maintain inventories in their own warehouses to meet market needs throughout the year."

Asked how much maple syrup the processors have stored right now, the group told CBC it couldn't comment, citing confidential business practices.

"In a context where market growth is putting increased pressure on supply, our members must plan their needs flexibly to ensure business continuity and meet demand."

Why is there increased pressure on supply?

Both PPAQ and CIE say there has been a surge in global demand for maple syrup.

Canadian exports of maple products increased by 15.8 per cent in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to data provided by CIE. That followed a 9.3 per cent jump from 2023 to 2024.

Statistics Canada also said $844.2 million worth of Canadian maple products were exported last year — a 17.2 per cent increase from the previous year.

WATCH | Inside the Quebec maple syrup reserve: Inside the world’s only maple syrup reserve | Duration 2:09 CBC News goes inside the world’s only maple syrup reserve, a stash Quebec syrup producers recently tapped into because of growing global demand.

What's fuelling demand internationally?

PPAQ's Goulet pointed to several factors, including uncertainty linked to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs, which have not hit the maple industry yet, as well as success in promoting Canadian maple syrup abroad.

Sixty-five per cent of all Canadian exports in 2025 went to the U.S., the CIE said. The next largest market was Germany at seven per cent, followed by the U.K. at five per cent.

Growing demand for "natural sweeteners" also has been credited with making maple syrup more popular, according to experts.

Will Quebec run out of maple syrup?

The PPAQ says it's not time to panic.

It said the processors' inventories coupled with an increase in the number of taps being installed across Quebec mean "there are no concerns about market supply in 2027, even if the upcoming crop is not particularly strong."

"That said, we are hoping for an exceptional season so that we can replenish the reserve."

Barrels of pasteurized maple syrup are stored at a strategic reserve warehouse in Plessisville, Que., on March 6. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

But will 'an exceptional season' be possible?

We can't say for sure. Doyon said there are ultimately only two ways to get more maple syrup: get more sap out of the trees that are already tapped or tap more trees.

But both those things could be easier said than done, said Guillaume Moreau, another professor at Laval University who specializes in maple syrup production.

Tapping more trees is a challenge because maple syrup producers are competing with other interests — notably the hardwood lumber industry — to gain access to forests on public lands in Quebec.

Climate change also has created new challenges for producers, who have seen harvest periods gradually shift earlier in the year due to fluctuating temperatures, Moreau said.

"We're having trouble to know ahead of time whether it will be a bad year."

And with the reserve now sitting empty and climate change fuelling uncertainty, "we're ultimately at the mercy of that uncertainty," he told CBC.

World.title: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two people described the same financial scam to both the police and their banks over the past year. The only difference was where they lived — one in Canada, the other in the U.K.

And that determined what happened next.

Asif Mohammed lost $7,200 this spring and never got it all back. Meanwhile, Samantha Bradshaw was out £11,000 (nearly $21,000 Cdn) but her financial institution reimbursed the money within days.

That's because British banks are required by law to make most of their customers whole when money is lost to a scam, often returning the sum within days of making a claim. In contrast, Canadian banks have no such legal obligation, leaving scam victims here largely unprotected.

As CBC’s Marketplace found out, it also means British banks are incentivized to crack down on fraudsters in a way Canadian banks are not.

WATCH | Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace: Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace | Duration closed caption 2:01 David Common confronts a bank scammer who lures victims by pretending to be the fraud department at their financial institution.

'I've made a big mistake'

Toronto-based Mohammed was working on a major engineering project when he received a call that appeared to be coming from his bank, Tangerine.

The caller identified herself as a representative from Tangerine’s fraud investigations department and told him there had been multiple attempts to use his debit card at a Best Buy in Edmonton.

Mohammed explained the charges weren't his, and was told his card needed to be collected as evidence. The caller said Mohammed's case had been transferred to Toronto police, who sent a courier to his worksite. He handed over the debit card to this "courier" but says he didn't provide the PIN.

Minutes later, his wife, Salwa Sultana, texted him to say money had disappeared from the account — $1,200 to be exact.

"At that point, I realized that I've made a big mistake," Mohammed said.

The couple reported what happened to the real Tangerine but were told they would be on the hook for the losses.

WATCH | 'Real panic, real crying': U.K. victim recounts being scammed: 'Real panic, real crying': U.K. victim recounts being scammed | Duration closed caption 1:02 Samantha Bradshaw tells Marketplace's David Common about her experience as a victim of a bank impersonation scam.

Samantha Bradshaw received a near-identical call at her home in England’s East Midlands last fall that lasted four hours.

She was also told multiple cards had been compromised. A courier came to pick them up and scammers then used her cards to make purchases.

More worrying for Bradshaw, the scammers knew where she lived. She told Marketplace she called the police and the emergency operator instructed her to lock her doors.

"'Make sure everybody is safe,'" Bradshaw said she was told. "And then it was real panic, real crying, real horrible emotions coming through. My trust was completely gone."

Yet within days, Bradshaw’s bank called to tell her the entire loss was covered, under Britain’s reimbursement rules.

After months of pleading with Tangerine, Asif Mohammed and Salwa Sultana reached a settlement with the bank. While they aren’t able to tell CBC News about the details, it does not cover their entire loss.

Tangerine wouldn't comment on this particular case but said they use "fraud monitoring, security controls, client education… to identify and help prevent unusual account activity."

Multiple major police services across Canada have issued public warnings saying they would never send a courier to collect debit or credit cards.

Does reimbursement slow scams — or supercharge scammers?

Shifting the burden of responsibility from customer to bank is a recognition that financial institutions are better able to identify and stop scams, says Andrei Skorobogatov, a strategic advisor of Britain’s regulations.

Andrei Skorobogatov helped advise on the reimbursement rules in the U.K. and now works with the Global Anti-Scam Alliance. (Nelisha Vellani/CBC)

Skorobogatov, who works with the Global Anti-Scam Alliance, believes all countries have the responsibility to act.

"The public going about their day-to-day business will probably struggle to be able to detect [a scam] in a way that the bank with their highly sophisticated detection mechanisms are in a much better place to do," he said.

Britain’s third-largest bank agrees. Since the introduction of bank liability two years ago, Santander has introduced new measures to flag suspicious transactions and rapidly intervene when customers appear to be sending money to an unknown contact.

The new regulations have "pushed financial institutions," Chris Ainsley, head of fraud risk management at Santander, told Marketplace during a visit to the U.K. headquarters. "That's now a signal for us to take extra action to prevent more fraud and stop more at source."

Global anti-fraud groups track the multibillion-dollar scam industry, which has become extremely lucrative for individual fraudsters. One scammer, who identifies himself with the name "Cameron," told Marketplace he makes up to £5,000 ($9,400 Cdn) from each victim.

CBC Marketplace confronted this bank impersonation scammer about his role in stealing money from victims. (CBC)

He displayed no sympathy for those victims in a video call with Marketplace, in which he used a mask and sunglasses to conceal his face. He believes U.K. reimbursement rules mean that only the banks end up paying for his crimes.

In fact, banks recoup their losses through fees collected from all customers. Victims of these crimes may get their money back but often feel a deep loss of trust and embarrassment.

British banks are taking action to prevent scams. For instance, Santander uses machine learning to identify suspicious transactions, based on hundreds of thousands of past scams. The bank will message or call customers in real time, trying to "break the spell that the fraudsters put them under," Ainsley said.

The intervention on red-flagged transactions can sometimes delay legitimate transactions. But the vast majority of bank transfers in the U.K. still take less than 10 seconds, compared to multiple days in Canada.

If money is transferred to scammers, the British rules dictate that the sending bank and receiving banks are each responsible for half of the reimbursement to the customer who was scammed — except in cases of extreme negligence.

Will Canada follow Britain’s lead?

Marketplace asked Canada’s finance minister directly if he was considering forcing Canadian banks to reimburse scammed customers.

Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the government is working to better protect Canadians but didn’t commit to reimbursement. (Nelisha Vellani/CBC)

François-Philippe Champagne detailed a number of new efforts, including the introduction of Bill C-29, an act to establish the Financial Crimes Agency earlier this year, but stopped short of committing to liability for financial institutions.

"I would say we need to consult. There's many actors. There's the telecoms, there's the banks, there's other people in that ecosystem."

Champagne says specially trained federal officers have been deployed in an effort to arrest those responsible and prevent fraud in the first place.

"We put boots on the ground," he said. "I have officers who are embedded with the police force — for example, in Surrey, some regions in Ontario. And that has been the most effective thing because… it's about following the money."

World.title: Ontario private school under scrutiny for class video surveillance, making kids watch themselves 'misbehaving'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A former student of a London, Ont., private school and parents are concerned that children were under constant video surveillance in the classroom and asked to critique the footage with their peers.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) says it’s investigating the matter after receiving a complaint.

Lincoln Sandle, 11, attended Infinity School from August 2023 until January 2026, when he was in Grades 3 through 5.

He said a common classroom activity involved watching back videos of himself and classmates that were captured by multiple surveillance cameras throughout the school.

“The whole class was in one room, and we had a projector and we watched us with audio,” Lincoln said. “[We watched] how we were misbehaving and who needed the most help.

“People watching me is weird. I just don’t like people invading my privacy.”

WATCH | 11-year-old explains how surveillance cameras were used at his former school: Family describes how surveillance cameras were used in son's classroom | Duration closed caption 2:06 Lincoln Sandle, 11, explains how he and his classmates watched and critiqued surveillance camera footage from his private school in London, Ont. The school, Infinity School, is an affiliate of a U.S.-based network called Acton Academy. Its owners say cameras are a "tool" for learning and leadership. Lincoln's father, Greg Sandle, also shares his concerns about the use of cameras and how it can affect children's well-being.

Lincoln’s parents both gave CBC News permission to interview and photograph him for this story.

Infinity School focuses on hands-on and self-directed learning, according to its website.

It’s an affiliate of Acton Academy, a U.S.-based network of schools that emphasize Socratic discussions and project-based “quests,” its website explains. Each school is independently owned by “parent entrepreneurs,” who must follow a “shared learning design and high standards of excellence,” it says.

A map on the website shows nearly 300 Acton schools around the world, including nine in Canada.

Infinity School rents space in a church in London’s Wortley Village for its multi-grade classrooms and other facilities. Lincoln estimates there were up to 10 cameras around the school, including in classrooms, hallways, the gym and library.

Infinity School in London rents out a church building in the Wortley Village neighbourhood for its classes. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

“You couldn’t really talk about anything private with your friends,” Lincoln said. “It just cages us up.”

In a joint email statement to CBC News, the head of the Acton Academy Network, Jake Thompson, and Infinity School principal Eric Brown said cameras are meant to be a tool within the schools.

“At Acton, we trust young people with the responsibility for their own learning, and an important part of that learning is leadership,” Thompson said in a separate email. “Cameras give learners the ability to document, review and reflect on their leadership and learning experiences.”

Neither Thompson nor Brown responded to CBC's request for interviews.

Questions of consent

Lincoln’s father, Greg Sandle, said he didn’t know Infinity School had cameras when he first enrolled his two children, but started noticing them when he visited the school.

“I thought they were just for security … I didn’t believe that the cameras would be used for anything other than what I thought they were intended for, which was just safety of kids in the school,” Sandle said.

Greg Sandle says his family was not aware of how cameras were being used at Infinity School in London until he withdrew his children from classes there. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

He said he learned otherwise when the school's principal referred to camera footage in a December 2025 correspondence.

Some other parents told CBC News they also were also unaware of the cameras located inside the school until earlier this year, when conversations started within parent circles.

Thompson and Brown didn’t respond to CBC's questions about when and how parents were informed about the cameras, but said they are "openly discussed and visible to families."

What does the law say?

Public and private schools follow different privacy regulations laid out by different levels of government.

Ontario public schools are subject to the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, which is set out by Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario.

A spokesperson from the office said school boards must determine whether they have “lawful authority” to collect personal information, including surveillance footage. Consent is not required, though public notice is needed as part of the school’s “transparency obligations,” the spokesperson said.

The OPC oversees the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), which applies to organizations that collect, use and disclose personal information for commercial activities.

The Infinity School logo is shown inside the doorway to the private school at 120 Bruce St. in London. (Kendra Seguin/ CBC News)

PIPEDA may apply to private schools "if they engage in activities that are commercial in nature."

Infinity School is listed on the Ontario Business Registry as a corporation.

"PIPEDA provides that, unless certain exceptions apply, the knowledge and consent of the individual is required for the collection, use, or disclosure of their personal information," spokesperson Vito Pilieci said.

Pilieci declined to share the nature of the complaint about Infinity School, but said it is reaching out to the school to collect more information and determine next steps.

Who else can access student footage?

Sarah Starrs, another parent, said she remembers learning about cameras during an interview with the school before enrolling her then seven-year-old son in September 2024.

She recalled finding out that cameras would be used in the older students’ classrooms as a learning tool, but didn’t think it would be in her son’s mixed-age classroom for children as young as four years old.

Sarah Starrs sent her son to Infinity School in London from September 2024 to May 2026. She says she has questions about why there were cameras in his classroom and who had access to the footage. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

While searching through the school’s parent portal in February, Starrs said, she noticed a privacy policy document for the first time that outlined camera usage and livestreaming capabilities.

“I felt surprised and confused,” she said.

According to a July 2026 privacy policy on Infinity School’s website, Acton Academy requires all schools within its network to have cameras, which include livestream capabilities “for schoolwide inspection purposes only.”

However, parents say it’s unclear who has access to livestream footage and where they are located, given that Acton is based in the U.S.

CBC News requested this information from Thompson and Brown multiple times, but didn’t receive a direct answer.

"We regularly revisit our policies and are currently reviewing not just camera use, but our broader approach to privacy, to ensure we are best serving families across our campuses," they said.

Starrs said she continues to have questions about who has access to the livestream footage, which includes both images and audio of the children. She pulled her son out of Infinity School in May for unrelated reasons, but said the lack of transparency around cameras contributed to her decision to leave.

Impacts of surveilling children

Lincoln said the cameras at Infinity School made him feel stressed about going to class.

“I always tried to be the favourite person because then I wouldn’t have bad stuff happen to me, like people watching me."

Lincoln's parents withdrew both their children from the school in January following a series of unrelated challenges, said his father. That’s when Lincoln first told his family about the in-class footage reviews.

Lincoln says he's happier now that he's left Infinity School and started at a new school in London. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

“It was heartbreaking [to hear] because we wanted to do the best we could for the kids, and it makes us feel like it was the worst decision of our lives to put him in that situation,” Sandle said.

Alissa Centivany, co-director of the Starling Centre for Just Technologies & Just Societies and a professor at Western University, said she has concerns about camera surveillance in classrooms.

"Schools have a responsibility to student safety and well-being," Centivany said. "I think what we're seeing with the use of cameras in schools is that it's actually having the opposite effect, and it's diminishing schools' ability to carry out their legitimate and legal responsibilities."

She said surveillance cameras should be used only when it is authorized by law and if it's deemed necessary. For example, in a school setting, Centivany said, cameras could be justified when there is "illegal activity happening on school grounds or where there's been fights outside the school."

"How they were used as a way for school administrators and teachers to draw attention to classroom behaviour and use it as a teaching experience, to me, seems to not meet that second condition of being necessary.”

Lincoln started at a new school in September. He said there are no cameras on the premises.

“It makes me feel more open and able to share what I want with my friends,” he said.

World.title: Carney defends doing business with countries that don’t share Canada’s values
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government's approach to balancing human rights and trade on Friday, saying very few countries in the world can meet Canada's standards.

He made the remarks near the end of his trip to Turkey, where he signed a strategic partnership with the government of President Recep Erdogan, which has faced sustained criticism from human rights groups.

The complaints intensified this month when the Turkish government executed several high-profile operations to systematically silence opposition voices, suppress independent journalism, and restrict marginalized groups.

In the past Carney has said Canada is pursuing values-based realism in its approach, recognizing that not every partner will share all Canadian values.

"Engagement in those partnerships does not mean approval," Carney said Friday.

"There are very few countries in this world that have the standards of Canada."

A statement from the Prime Minister's Office said Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand raised the issue of human rights with her counterpart during meetings on Thursday.

Carney was asked by journalists on Friday whether he personally raised concerns with Erdogan during their separate meeting. The prime minister refused to be pinned down.

WATCH | Turkey is an 'exceptional partner,' PM says: Carney hails new trade, defence pact with 'exceptional partner' Turkey | Duration closed caption 2:07 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new strategic trade and defence partnership between Canada and Turkey, as Ottawa continues its drive to tighten relations with other middle powers and fellow NATO members.

"My approach on these issues is I have direct conversations with leaders," Carney said. "I find those conversations are more effective when they're direct and open and not then reported out in detail, but we have raised these issues."

Concern about the authoritarian reflexes of the Turkish government have partly overshadowed Carney's initiative to deepen trade ties.

The prime minister is looking to make Canada less dependent on the United States market and to diversify its trading markets. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific, but it has also included other states with questionable human rights records, including recently Saudi Arabia.

'Disappointed' by U.S. claims

Carney is holding a series of meetings with business leaders in Istanbul after the political talks in Ankara on Thursday.

One of the deals being pursued involves the possible sale of Canadian nuclear technology to Turkey as the Middle Eastern nation attempts to reach its climate goals.

Carney told reporters, following the signing of the strategic partnership, there were ‌now "good chances" for Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis to be picked as a partner to build the two power plants ⁠Turkey is planning.

Also Friday, Carney pushed back more forcefully against allegations of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a fact sheet on Thursday, officially accusing Canadian leaders of election meddling ahead of the Nov. 3 vote.

"There is no merit to these claims, so I'll call it out that way," Carney said. "I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions."

The prime minister went on to say Canada has a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States and lots of interaction with American companies, citizens and individuals.

"As a country Canada is very, very careful to not be seen to interfere in the democratic process," he said.

World.title: The haunting call of Canada's common loon is becoming less common amid widespread declines, study suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's a haunting sound synonymous with nightfall in the summer when an eerie calm spreads over glassy wetlands and cottage country lake surfaces across Canada.

But the trembling call of the common loon may be getting less common amid "substantial" North American declines, new research suggests — with Prairie and Atlantic populations suffering among the steepest losses.

"The most alarming thing is the extent of this decline," said Matthew Fuirst, an ecologist with Birds Canada and one of the authors of a study published Thursday in the journal FACETS.

Canada is home to 94 per cent of the global common loon population, with an estimated 254,000 breeding couples (half a million individuals) that migrate north to make the next generation every spring.

The iconic species, a minted representation of which many Canadians routinely carry around in their pockets and purses, has faced threats before — from DDT to lead-based fishing tackle and mercury poisoning.

WATCH | From the CBC archives: Lost loons (1971): From the CBC archives: Lost loons (1971) | Duration closed caption 3:33 Former CBC reporter Howard Sommerville explores how DDT threatened Canadian loon eggs in this 1971 story from the CBC archives.

Now, the latest team of nearly two dozen collaborators from Canada and the U.S. cite climate change among a list of possible drivers for declines in loon chicks.

The study analyzes loon breeding data from 3,421 lakes the past three or so decades, half of which came from thousands of volunteer observations as part of the long-running citizen science effort, the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey.

There were "significant declines" in how many chicks were observed in that time in a majority of regions.

The researchers looked at nearly 46,000 breeding loon pairs documented on given lakes where eggs or newborn chicks were recorded, but where no six-week-old chicks were recorded. This was the benchmark they defined as loon chick productivity rate.

The study suggests a 40 per cent average drop in loon chick productivity in 10 of 12 study areas — including in B.C. and Ontario — over the past three or so decades.

Loon chick productivity sank even more starkly by 65 per cent across Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba since the early 1990s. Meanwhile, Canada's East Coast saw a 74 per cent reduction, according to researchers.

Quebec and the state of Maine were the only regions where chick productivity seemed more or less stable.

A common loon range map that appeared in the new FACETS journal article documenting loon declines in North America. (FACETS journal)

The team notes that while the loon chick population isn't the only measure of how healthy or stable the population is, the long-term declines could "signal looming population declines" in the Prairies, Ontario, Atlantic Canada and in New York, Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

"This study design is very strong, and frankly, I consider the results that they are presenting here as being alarming," said Nicola Koper, dean of the faculty of environment at University of Northern British Columbia, who was not part of the study.

Koper is co-author of Best Places to Bird in the Prairies and she was professor of conservation biology for nearly two decades at the University of Manitoba before moving on to UNBC.

She said the losses are dramatic on their own, but the fact they've happened over only three decades is startling.

"Some [readers] will be 30 years old, and so if they think back to whether they feel like they saw more loons with babies when they were younger, the chances are that that's accurate, that they have themselves observed this change," said Koper.

Climate change behind declines

The research team says the cause of the declines may vary depending on the region and that unknown is something they're digging into now, said Fuirst.

But in all cases the losses are propelled by human activity.

"Human development and the development of shorelines, the environmental contaminants from climate change is another threat we're experiencing, " said Fuirst.

"As climate change influences weather patterns, the rain which is acidic makes the lake more acidic and thus reducing the amount of fish that are available for those loons."

A common loon baby rests on its parent's back in northwestern Ontario in July 2026. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

Warmer temperatures associated with climate change have also brought more rain and storm events to loon habitat.

That could be destroying low-lying loon nests or drowning eggs during flood events when waters rise or are disturbed from violent wave action, said Koper.

Recent research from the U.S. Midwest has also made a connection between poor loon health and lower water clarity, which can arise from sediment running into lakes as a result of more frequent rains.

That makes it harder for loons to see and hunt their minnow, crayfish and other prey in the water, said Fuirst.

"It's this domino effect of climate change basically down to water quality," he said.

The study pooled together Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba data into a single Prairie category because there wasn't enough data to analyze loon numbers confidently in each of those regions on their own.

Koper said that may be more a reflection of how many of the many lakes in the Prairies are inaccessible to volunteers or otherwise unpopulated.

Fuirst said anglers should opt for lead-free, less-toxic tackle options, boaters should avoid disturbing loons and cottagers should ensure shorelines remain as natural as possible.

"The everyday person can take several actions to help steward lakes and the loons that they rely on," he said.

Koper encourages people concerned by the findings to take action and get involved in citizen science projects like the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey and "advocate with ... politicians about the importance of climate change and how it's impacting our wildlife and our lives."

World.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 61-year-old Canadian woman living in the isolated U.S. town of Point Roberts, Wash., has died after refusing to seek medical care out of fears she would be detained or deported.

Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing, south of Tsawwassen, and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election.

The U.S. permanent resident was scheduled to appear at a deportation hearing before a federal immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman said Adamson called her on Thursday night asking to borrow a pair of crutches from local nonprofit Circle Of Care.

"I took them over and found her literally debilitated on the sofa, in very, very bad pain," Norman said.

"She told me that she had slipped and fallen on her right side … she was relying on the help of a few friends to come and help her get up and take her to the bathroom."

Norman, who was also a friend and neighbour of Adamson, said she urged the distressed woman to call paramedics or visit the local Point Roberts health-care clinic.

"And she said, 'No, no, I'm afraid if I go, I won't be able to come back. They'll keep me or they'll deport me.'"

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman says she urged Paige Adamson to call paramedics or visit the local health-care clinic. (CBC News)

Point Roberts is a U.S. pene-exclave at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country.

U.S. immigration lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson had mentioned not feeling well and needing to see a doctor. Residents of Point Roberts have to cross into Canada in order to get to other parts of Washington state or the U.S. and there was a risk she would be detained by ICE upon return to the U.S.

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years and crossed the Canadian border countless times. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"She was quite frankly scared about trying to drive up to Canada and come back in," Saunders said.

"There are no doctors where she lives. For all practical purposes, she was in detention," he said.

"I mentioned to her that I'd heard of people in the past maybe taking a boat or taking an airplane. But financially, I don't think she could afford it. She didn't have a lot of money."

Norman said she checked in on Adamson over the weekend, but her friend's condition had not improved.

"The next message that I got was on Monday, telling me to show up at her address," she said.

"She had died sometime in the hours previous."

In a statement, Whatcom County Sheriff public information officer Deb Slater said the death "appeared to be of natural causes."

Louise Trapp, operations manager with the medical examiner, said Adamson's body was in her office's care pending examination by a forensic pathologist.

'Absolute worst case outcome'

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years.

According to Saunders, her status meant she was legally entitled to leave and enter the country while awaiting deportation proceedings, but border officials had the right to detain her if they saw fit.

"Officers have the right to take you into detention and send you on a one-way trip to the Northwest Detention Centre down in Tacoma," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders says Paige Adamson had been missing appointments with her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., due to fears of being detained or deported trying to cross the border. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

"I asked her to speak to the Peace Arch port-of-entry. I believe she had called them but was given no guarantees on what would happen … I could understand her concerns."

As a U.S. resident, accessing health care in British Columbia was not an option. CBC News reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for comment but did not hear back before deadline.

Saunders said he couldn't believe it when he was advised of Adamson's death on Sunday.

"This is an absolute worst case outcome. Here's a lady with no prior immigration violations, no criminal convictions. She was about as squeaky clean as you could get," he said.



Adamson is survived by two sons, both residents of B.C.

World.title: Crime Stoppers had 'potentially one of the most harmful data breaches' Canada has seen. What's next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two days after an exclusive CBC investigation revealed the extent of the Crime Stoppers data hack in Canada, experts are now weighing the long-term implications of what could be among the country's most dangerous privacy failures.

"It strikes me as potentially one of the most harmful data breaches we've ever seen in Canada," said Michael Geist, a law professor at the University of Ottawa and the Canada Research Chair in Internet and E-commerce Law.

When it comes to the Canadian law, he says, both Crime Stoppers, the organization that collected the data, and Navigate360, the company it hired to manage it, could be held accountable.

"[How] Canadian privacy law functions is that the organization that collects the personal information is the one that's responsible," said Geist. "And even where they use third parties or subcontractors as part of what takes place, it's on them to ensure that no matter who gains access to the information, it has that appropriate level of protection."

However, enforcing those rules across borders — Navigate360 is U.S.-based — is notoriously difficult, he says, and the domestic penalties are weak.

"These kinds of incidents keep happening. There's a real urgency to addressing Canadian privacy law, which is woefully out of date," he said.

"And at the top of the list has been really weak enforcement."

Expert fears company doesn’t know leak's true scale

At the heart of the breach is Navigate360 and its tip management platform, P3. All Crime Stoppers chapters, including those in Canada and the U.S., relied on P3 to keep their data anonymous.

The information was stolen last March by a hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine, who stated they wanted to disprove the company's claim that its platform was "anonymous" and "secure." CBC News analyzed a copy of the hacked data and found that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed, along with tens of thousands of unredacted personal details.

CBC has reached out repeatedly to Navigate360 and shared the highlights of its investigation, but the company has not responded.

Adding to the controversy are accounts provided by the Toronto and Guelph Wellington Crime Stoppers chapters, where Navigate360 appeared to change its narrative about how much data had been stolen and what was affected.

According to a Wednesday statement from the Toronto chapter, Navigate360 initially told the organization that no Canadian data was taken, then said Toronto wasn't impacted, before finally revealing months later that years of Toronto data was compromised. Guelph Wellington shared a similar statement on Thursday.

Cybersecurity expert Ali Dehghantanha, who reviewed samples of the compromised data as part of CBC’s original investigation, said it was alarming that Navigate360's claims to Toronto Crime Stoppers appeared to change.

"They apparently received six different [accounts] in seven months from the vendor," he said, adding that this raises massive red flags about the company's ability to investigate the hack and fix the vulnerabilities that might have allowed it.

Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade, said he is also very surprised at how quickly Navigate360 seemed to have returned its system to an operational state following the hack.

WATCH | More about the investigation: Crime Stoppers hack exposes personal information of tens of thousands of Canadians | Duration closed caption 3:40 A massive data breach leaked 25 years worth of unredacted personal information from Crime Stoppers, compromising the identities of thousands of Canadian tipsters. The Toronto branch of Crime Stoppers has asked the public not to send in tips until the issue is resolved.

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it was told about the leak on March 18; a week later on March 25, Navigate360 told the organization that the system was "safe and fully operational."

"It doesn't seem that there was a full investigation there," Dehghantanha said, "that you could do and you could say, 'Oh, only these clients have been impacted.'"

Internal memo advises against calling privacy commissioner

Meanwhile, Geist says tipsters whose information has been leaked may be limited in their options for justice.

"In terms of actual compensation to the affected individuals, current privacy law doesn't really focus on that," he added. "You've got to look to other mechanisms like class actions if what you're looking for is actual compensation."

Beyond that, another avenue could be to launch a privacy commissioner investigation — but Geist warns that could take years, and any recommendations for the future would not be legally binding.

WATCH | Ont. police suspend tip lines: Multiple Ontario cities suspend Crime Stoppers tip lines over massive data hack | Duration closed caption 1:58 Toronto, Halton and Guelph are among the Ontario cities temporarily pausing Crime Stoppers tip programs after a CBC News investigation revealed a massive data breach exposed 1.5 million tips over the past 25 years to possible exploitation by hackers.

He noted that even if Canada's privacy commissioner investigates the matter, it can only issue a "non-binding finding" directing a company to fix bad practices — it cannot force a company to compensate victims.

Still, even with those limited powers, the privacy commissioner may have already been top of mind for the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) in the months following the hack, according to a copy of a June 18 internal memo obtained by CBC.

"We currently do not believe that you are required, nor should you contact the privacy commissioner in your region at this time," instructs CCSA president David Forster, saying his organization has "previously assessed that they [the commissioner] do not have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers."

Crime Stoppers is best known for its public appeals, often partnering with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

CBC has reached out to the CCSA for comment on the contents of the memo.

In a public statement on Thursday, Forster offered reassurance to the public: "Navigate360 has advised us that third-party cybersecurity experts investigated the breach, identified vulnerabilities and completed remediation."Those measures strengthen protections for current and future tips, he said.

However, he noted: "They cannot undo the exposure of information already taken, which remains a serious concern."

World.title: Meghan says U.K. police advised her of 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, said Friday she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's former home. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.

Meghan, also known as the Duchess of Sussex, issued the statement after the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that her half-brother found the images while clearing out the home of their father, Thomas Markle Sr., in the Philippines.

"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan said in a statement.

She also addressed the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service's Royal and Specialist Protection unit, which later shared its contents with her.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."

Brother reported father to police

Thomas Markle Sr., a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father. While some reports suggested she had shunned him in favour of her new royal status, Meghan said her decision to distance herself was intended to protect her children.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children," she said in her statement.

WATCH | Harry's uncle condemns 'appalling' attacks: Earl Spencer says ‘vicious’ treatment of Harry and Meghan not OK | Duration closed caption 0:52 Earl Spencer, the brother of the late Princess Diana, addresses the media’s treatment of Harry and Meghan, telling CBC Radio’s The Current host Matt Galloway that ‘vicious, personal’ attacks are never OK.

Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.

The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found "hundreds, if not thousands" of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father's former home in the Philippine city of Cebu when he was clearing out the property.

Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI in the U.S. earlier this year.

"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told the Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."

Meghan, an actress who starred in the television drama Suits, married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Relations with the rest of the Royal Family quickly deteriorated as the couple said palace staff had been insensitive to Meghan’s mental health and levelled charges of racism and media manipulation at other members of the family.

WATCH | Britons anticipate couple's return: Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K. | Duration 2:25 The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly returning to Britain this month – six years after they quit royal duties and relocated to the U.S. While details around the decision behind their shift are unknown, the British public has mixed feelings about the move.

After some time spent in British Columbia, the couple eventually settled in California. After six years there, they returned to the U.K. in September, and made their first joint appearance earlier this month in a series of charity events.

King Charles, Harry’s father, has made clear that the couple remain non-working members of the Royal Family, a status they accepted when they abandoned royal duties and moved to California.

World.title: Yotam Ottolenghi changed how a generation cooks. Now, he’s embracing a new simplicity
World.content:
Article content

Over his nearly three-decade culinary career, our relationship with food has become more complicated. Whether “proteinmaxxing” or the rise of GLP-1 drugs, it’s “much less instinctive than it used to be,” he adds. “We’ve completely stopped being the authorities of our own culinary journeys.” People shift from one diet to another thinking it’s the silver bullet. “Whilst, in actual fact, the answers are so complicated and are so related to us and what we like, and the notion of joy never comes into the equation.”

World.title: Bombs, food shortages and missing staff: ‘Wartime normality’ at Ukraine’s restaurants
World.content:
Article content

Stanislav Zavertailo, who runs the highly acclaimed Honey group of high-end patisseries and bakery cafes with his wife Anya, is one of the country’s most dynamic food entrepreneurs. At one of his sites in the historic centre of Kyiv recently, the cafe was still showcasing tempting displays of eclairs, intricately layered meringue cakes and filled pastries, but it was not as busy as usual. The surrounding streets were closed off by barriers, while a large armoured vehicle was parked a few yards away. A couple of weeks earlier, a Russian drone had slammed into the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service in the middle of the morning. The shock wave from the blast shattered the windows at the nearby Zavertailo cafe, scattering debris across the patio and inside the store. Most of the staff and customers had managed to scramble for shelter, although one woman who had been injured was taken to hospital.
