World.title: Who really writes the budget?
World.content:
Andy Burnham has promised Britain can “hope again”. But with inflation rising, borrowing costs soaring and trillions of pounds of national debt, how much room does Chancellor John Healey actually have to deliver in the budget on Oct. 28?

This week, Pat and Sascha speak to Treasury insiders to find out who really calls the shots when a Chancellor puts together a budget. First, they hear from Matt Pound, one of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ closest advisers, about the tough choices facing Healey, the dangers of leaks and U-turns, and why keeping the bond markets onside matters more than politicians might like to admit.

Then, Cameron Brown, who worked under both Kwasi Kwarteng and Jeremy Hunt, and Simon Finkelstein, who advised Hunt at the Treasury, reveal just how obsessed Westminster has become with the bond markets. And POLITICO’s Financial Services Editor Fiona Maxwell gives her predictions for what Healey might have in store on budget day.

CORRECTION: This podcast has been updated to correct the description of Simon Finkelstein’s role.

World.title: Explosion at coal mine in Turkey kills two, leaves one trapped
World.content:
An explosion at a coal mine in northwestern Turkey killed at least two people and injured five others, two of whom are in serious condition. One other miner remains trapped, local media reported on Friday.

 

The explosion at the mine in the town of Gelik was caused by a "firedamp," or flammable gas, local authorities said.

"Eight people were in the tunnel, seven were rescued. Unfortunately, two of our miners died after being taken to hospital," said Zonguldak governor Osman Hacibektasoglu.

Two of the rescued miners suffered burns and were in serious condition. One of the critically injured miners had been transferred to Ankara and preparations are under way to transfer the second miner.

"One of the miners is still inside the mine. We have made contact with him and are trying to get him out," the governor added.

The blast occurred at around 10 in the morning. After an emergency call, teams from the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), as well as medical and fire crews, were dispatched to the site.

According to local newspaper Pusula, the explosion took place at a private mine owned by Demir Madencilik. An investigation has been opened to determine the exact cause of the blast.

Mine accidents are not uncommon in Turkey. Earlier this month, five people were killed in a coal mine collapse in Soma, Manisa in western Turkey.

The independent monitoring group, Worker Health and Work Safety Assembly, or ISIG, reported that 1,267 miners were killed in workplace accidents between 2013 and 2025, mostly from incidents of cave-ins and suffocation.

World.title: World Culinary Awards: Which are the best airlines and airports for dining?
World.content:
It’s not just restaurants that were crowned at the 2026 World Culinary Awards – airlines, airports and airport lounges also picked up gongs for feeding hungry travellers.

 

Vietnam Airlines took the title of World’s Best Culinary Airline 2026, becoming the first Asian carrier to win the award. It beat fellow nominees including Emirates, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Air France, Cathay Pacific, and Turkish Airlines.

Other aviation sector winners included London’s Heathrow Airport, Turkish Airlines' international lounges, and Clubrooms at Gatwick South Terminal.

What’s on the menu with Vietnam Airlines?

Designed to “promote Vietnamese cuisine” to international travellers, the carrier’s in-flight menus are adapted to the seasons and routes, so that “each flight gives passengers a different culinary experience”.

Economy class cuisine is marked by its “signature dish” – the crispy, layered croissant served for breakfast. Lunches and dinners feature rice and spaghetti dishes with an accompanying sauce, a dessert and bread roll.

In addition to Vietnamese cuisine, business class travellers are treated to dishes from around the world, depending on their destination. On flights to South Korea, mixed fried rice, or bibimbap, makes an appearance on the menu, alongside other dishes like ginseng chicken soup (samgyetang) and black bean noodles (jajangmyeon).

While on trips to Europe, expect to dine on French, German and British cuisine. Further, business class travellers to European, Australian and American destinations can pre-order their meals.

The world’s best airport for dining

London Heathrow was crowned the World’s Best for Airport Dining 2026, outranking Dubai International, Hamad International Airport in Qatar, Hong Kong International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, Paris Aéroport, and Singapore Changi Airport.

Across Heathrow’s four terminals, passengers can choose from a range of casual, café and international dining concepts.

Heathrow also offers what it describes as “dining in style”, where the likes of Terminal 2’s Le Café Louis Vuitton features. Guests can choose from sweet treats, such as the hazelnut flower dessert, a morsel of hazelnut ganache, tender praline and fleur de sel, which sports the brand’s iconic monogram flower.

While in Terminal 5, celebrity chef Gordan Ramsay’s Plane Food Market serves up all-day breakfast, pizza, sushi, noodles and traditional British favourite, fish and chips.

The world’s best airline lounge for dining

Turkish Airlines' International Lounges were awarded the World's Best Airline Lounge for Dining. Other nominees included Air France’s La Première First Class Lounge in Paris-Charles de Gaulle, Etihad Airways’ First Class Lounge and Spa at Zayed International Airport, and Lufthansa’s First Class Lounge at Frankfurt Airport.

Qatar Airways’ Al Safwa First Class Lounge at Hamad International Airport, SWISS’ First Class Lounge at Zürich Airport, Thai Airways’ Royal Orchid Prestige Lounge at Suvarnabhumi Airport, and Virgin Atlantic’s Clubhouse at London Heathrow Airport were also nominated.

At Turkish Airlines’ international lounges, in locations such as Edinburgh International Airport, guests can dine on Turkish and world cuisine, with hot and cold offerings at the buffet.

The world's best airport lounge for dining

Clubrooms at Gatwick South Terminal was awarded the World’s Best Airport Lounge for Dining 2026.

Other nominees included Blue Sky Premier Lounge in Terminal 1C at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Indonesia, Plaza Premium First Hong Kong, Plaza Premium Lounge in Terminal 3 at Dubai International, SkyTeam Lounge at Sydney Airport in Australia, and the Star Alliance Lounge at Los Angeles International Airport.

Gatwick's Clubrooms offers menus that are seasonally updated with a range of hot and cold dishes to choose from, alongside light bites and nibbles. For breakfast, eggs benedict and Belgian waffles feature on the menu.

While for evening dining, chicken Caesar salad, gochujang chicken thigh bowl and Moroccan nut roast with green beans in lemon olive oil are just some of the menu items.

World.title: First Russian diesel shipment is heading to US under Trump-Putin deal
World.content:
A tanker carrying Russian diesel is en route to New York after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Moscow in early October, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.

 

The Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes loaded about 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel, roughly 300,000 barrels, at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk.

The tanker is signalling New York as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of 7 November, according to Kpler. That would be four days after the US midterm elections.

Separate shipping data from LSEG also put the cargo at 40,000 tonnes.

If delivered as indicated, it would be the first Russian diesel or gasoil cargo shipped to the United States tracked by Kpler since July 2023, and the first diesel shipment from Primorsk to New York since January 2022.

The buyer and seller were not immediately known.

On Wednesday, Russian news agencies quoted Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees energy policy, as saying the first shipment of Russian diesel bound for the United States would depart the following day. He said more shipments would follow as Russian and US companies worked out contracts for the deliveries.

On 9 October, Trump announced an agreement between Washington and Moscow for the delivery of Russian diesel to the US and global markets, temporarily easing US sanctions on Russian diesel. Russia also agreed to lift its own ban on diesel exports.

Trump said Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tonnes, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.

The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm elections. It drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies, including members of Trump's Republican Party.

The move also comes after Russian diesel exports had shifted mainly to Brazil, Turkey and African countries following the EU’s embargo on Russian petroleum products in February 2023.

World.title: From education to cancer care: Global summit calls for better support for children
World.content:
With 412 million children living in extreme poverty, a global summit in Uzbekistan has called for greater investment in children's healthcare, education and protection, alongside closer coordination between services that often operate separately.

 

This was at the core of the Samarkand Declaration, adopted on Thursday at the end of a two-day gathering attended by representatives from more than 100 countries.

The declaration calls for stronger social protection systems, nationally determined targets and regular reporting on the quality and effectiveness of services for children.

According to UNICEF, two-thirds of the child-related UN Sustainable Development Goal indicators it monitors are off track, raising concerns about progress towards the 2030 targets.

Why access to services is not enough

Providing access to essential services does not necessarily guarantee children receive the care and support they need, summit participants said.

"We should invest not sector by sector, but we should complement each other and this will give a better result for the children," UNICEF Regional Director Édouard Beigbeder told Euronews.

Beigbeder also highlighted the importance of investing in social workers and healthcare professionals, rather than focusing exclusively on infrastructure.

Uzbekistan's First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva, who received the WHO Director-General's Award 2026 for her contribution to childhood cancer care, also called for closer cooperation between services.

Uzbekistan’s First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva honoured for contributions to global health Centre for the Production of Content of Mass Media

"Let us integrate medical, social and psychological support so that parents do not have to go from one institution to another in search of assistance," she told the summit.

Turkey's First Lady Emine Erdoğan questioned whether conventional indicators adequately reflect children's experiences.

"However, going to school does not always mean receiving a quality education, not being hungry does not mean being properly nourished, and not being subjected to violence does not mean being loved and valued," she said.

Protecting children from violence means services need to work together, particularly when victims require medical treatment, psychological support, social assistance and legal protection.

Global Head of Child Protection at Save the Children International Rebecca Smith told Euronews that children face violence at home, in conflict zones and increasingly online.

She stressed the importance of ensuring that survivors can seek support without facing stigma.

Uzbekistan presents its approach to integrated care

Uzbekistan used the summit to show how different services can be brought together to support children and families.

“Because for a parent, a child is not the future. A child is the present,” Shahnoza Mirziyoyeva, First Deputy Director of Uzbekistan's Social Protection Agency, told the summit.

Shahnoza Mirziyoyeva, First Deputy Director of Uzbekistan's Social Protection Agency Centre for the Production of Content of Mass Media

In an address to participants, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasised that children's wellbeing should be measured by their quality of life today, not their future economic contribution.

According to figures presented by Mirziyoyev, preschool enrolment has increased from 27.7% to 78%, while the number of inclusive schools has risen fivefold over the past two years.

Visiting First Ladies also attended the opening of the new Imkon rehabilitation centre in Samarkand, which combines preschool education with medical, psychological and educational support for children with disabilities.

First Ladies attended the opening of the new Imkon rehabilitation centre Social media page of the First Lady of the Kyrgyz Republic

The facility can accommodate 150 children and provide outpatient rehabilitation services to up to 100 children aged three to 18 each month.

Lebanon's First Lady Nehmat Aoun, who visited the centre, told Euronews that countries should learn from one another's experiences to improve children's education, care and protection.

Childhood cancer exposes global inequalities

The importance of coordinated healthcare becomes particularly evident in childhood cancer, where a child's chances of survival differ dramatically depending on where they live.

A parallel international congress in Samarkand examined inequalities in early diagnosis, specialist treatment and access to essential medicines.

According to the World Health Organization, around 400,000 children and adolescents develop cancer worldwide each year. High-income countries cure more than 80%, compared with fewer than 30% in many low- and middle-income countries.

The exhibition’s “Kemacha” section presents integrated support for children with oncological and haematological conditions and primary immunodeficiencies Euronews

Carlos Rodriguez-Galindo, Executive Vice President of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, told Euronews that delayed or missed diagnoses are among the main obstacles.

"The only way to address childhood cancer is by a comprehensive package," he said.

Such an approach requires earlier diagnosis, specialist care, reliable access to medicines and continued support for children and families.

The WHO has set a global target of at least 60% survival for children with cancer by 2030.

The congress also announced the creation of a Global Network to support children with serious and life-threatening illnesses, including cancer.

Imkon rehabilitation centre Euronews

Bringing together first ladies and spouses of heads of state, the initiative aims to strengthen international partnerships and improve access to care.

Uzbekistan's first lady will chair the network for two years. Mirziyoyeva also proposed an international mechanism to improve children's access to essential medicines.

An exhibition titled "The World Through a Child's Eyes" presented initiatives connecting healthcare, education, social protection and family support.

World.title: Suspect arrested after 1 killed and several injured in a shooting in Paris suburb
World.content:
A man opened fire from a vehicle on a public road in Trappes and La Verrière, in the Yvelines department, around 25 to 30 kilometres south-west of Paris.

 

At least one person was killed and four others were wounded, a police source said.

The suspect was quickly arrested by police in Coignières, the same source said. The incident is reported to have taken place at around 10.30 a.m.

The man was arrested in nearby Coignieres after opening fire in Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere around 10:30 am, police said. Local authorities said they are assessing the toll which could change.

“Very serious events have just taken place in Trappes,” French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu wrote on X. The prime minister said that “all the resources of the security forces and the judicial authorities are fully mobilised.” He added that “the national anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office has announced it is monitoring the situation.”

“I offer my sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of the person who died, and my full support to the other victims,” the mayor of Trappes wrote on Instagram. “An investigation is under way to determine the exact circumstances of these events and the motives of the gunman,” he added, saying the town will set up a psychological support unit in the coming hours.

This is a developing story, which will be updated by our journalists when more information becomes available.

World.title: Gaza: Moment Israeli airstrike hits building in Nuseirat caught on camera
World.content:
Dramatic footage captured the moment the building was struck, with a powerful explosion lighting up the night sky. Flames spread through the wreckage as Palestinian residents gathered nearby and rescue teams rushed to extinguish the fire.

 

Other images showed people carrying a wounded person away from the scene. No deaths were reported following the strike, although the extent of the injuries was not immediately clear.

By Friday morning, residents were picking through the rubble of destroyed homes, searching for belongings and assessing the damage. Men and women collected possessions from the ruins, while bags of food supplies lay scattered among the debris. Children were seen walking across the roof of a damaged building as families surveyed what remained of their homes.

The aftermath footage showed piles of broken concrete and shattered structures across the affected area. The strike left residents confronting extensive destruction in Nuseirat, with rescue workers and local families dealing with the immediate consequences of the attack.

World.title: Starlink restrictions not lifted in Ukraine despite Trump's claims, defence officials say
World.content:
Restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade version, Starshield, have not been fully lifted along Ukraine's front lines, Ukrainian defence officials said on Friday, despite US President Donald Trump's claim that Elon Musk had removed them.

 

Officials monitoring the systems said they continued to record instances of terminals losing connectivity when travelling at speeds of 161 kilometres per hour.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy known by his call sign Flash, confirmed that the restrictions remained in place.

"We are currently seeing no indication that the Starlink restrictions have been lifted," he wrote on Facebook on Friday.

"There are isolated cases when Starlink can operate at speeds slightly above the limit, but this is probably due to SpaceX's algorithms or particular conditions of use, rather than the restrictions being removed."

The statements follow a report by The Wall Street Journal that Trump called Musk on 21 October to request that he lift the restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications service.

Following the call, American and Ukrainian officials reported improvements in connectivity, although some cautioned that full functionality had not been restored.

Trump subsequently claimed that Musk had removed the speed restrictions but declined to confirm whether he had personally contacted the billionaire.

The disruption began without warning on 14 October, when Starshield terminals used by Ukrainian forces started losing connectivity as they approached speeds of around 160 kilometres per hour.

The unexpected restrictions disrupted military operations, including mid-range strike drone missions and the use of interceptor drones deployed to defend Ukrainian cities against Russian aerial attacks.

More than a week later, responsibility for the decision remains publicly disputed. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had ordered the restrictions, while other accounts pointed to possible White House involvement. Trump has denied ordering the move, and neither SpaceX nor the US administration has publicly accepted responsibility.

The episode has exposed Ukraine's heavy dependence on Starlink, a critical component of its battlefield communications, drone operations and air defence, and the risks of relying on a satellite network controlled by a foreign provider.

Ukraine moves to reduce its dependence on Starlink

Ukraine is meanwhile seeking to develop its own satellite communications capabilities, in a move that could eventually reduce its reliance on SpaceX.

On Thursday, Ukraine's Defence Ministry signed a letter of intent with Finnish technology companies ICEYE and Nokia to explore cooperation on developing a sovereign satellite communications system.

Zelenskyy announced the agreement during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's visit to Kyiv, describing it as "important for our defence and for the resilience of Ukraine".

The proposed systems would give participating countries ownership and control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals, reducing their exposure to decisions taken by foreign governments or commercial providers.

"Ukraine needs secure, sovereign, and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," said ICEYE chief executive Rafal Modrzewski.

Mikko Hautala, chairman of Nokia Defense, echoed that message, saying the partnership would give Ukraine "control over the connectivity it depends on".

The agreement, however, remains at an early stage, leaving Ukraine reliant on Starlink for critical battlefield communications in the meantime.

World.title: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny
World.content:
Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria crossed paths at Uganda's main airport as conflicting accounts cloud the source of one infection.

The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.

Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.

Uganda insists it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.

Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.

The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers, or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes?



The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.

Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?

Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an imported Ebola case in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.

"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.

The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.

Pate said the patient was stable and that health officials had identified 44 contacts, including healthcare workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.

But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.

Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.

Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account

Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.

"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.

But on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.

"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.

The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.

Ebola cases have now been detected in four African countries: DR Congo, ​Uganda, Kenya ‌and Nigeria Image: Afolabi Sotunde/AP Photo/picture alliance

On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.

The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.

Uganda maintains it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.

Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation

In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.

Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.

But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.

According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.

"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth told the newspaper.

The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.

Being an untraced contact does not mean he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.

Can border screening stop Ebola?

Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.

Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.

Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ebola symptoms typically develop between 2 and 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.

Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.

The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.

Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry, while Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.

The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.

Anxiety grows in Nigeria

In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.

Others fear Nigeria's healthcare system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.

Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and that contact tracing is continuing.

What remains unanswered?

Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.

But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3, and where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?

Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.

Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.

For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.

The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Serbia: Hope, tension and apprehension as voters prepare to elect new parliament
World.content:
After two years of protests, Serbia faces a pivotal election on Sunday, with a student-led challenge to Aleksandar Vucic's lengthy rule. Allegations of electoral irregularities and fears of a post-election crisis abound.

A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years.

The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination.

"We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd.

"People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List.

Students emerge as agents of change

After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power.

Three is the number of the Student List on the ballot paper Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance

For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign.

"These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote."

The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure.

In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics.

SNS presents itself as a guarantor of continuity

Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally.

'They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements,' Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters on Thursday Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos.

The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests.

"They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements."

Rising tension

The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies.

It's not just students who support the Student List. The red hand became a symbol of the student protest movement in November 2024 Image: Uros Arsic/REUTERS

By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners.

CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters.

Allegations of links to criminal networks

In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks.

Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government.

But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome.

He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports.

Concerns about irregularities

There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process.

The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters.

Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative.

Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party.

DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party.

What could come after the election?

Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety.

For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night.

The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result.

Supporters cheered Aleksandar Vucic and the ruling SNS party at a rally this week Image: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW

"But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally.

The EU's reaction could be crucial

Whatever happens, the European Union's response could be crucial.

"I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW.

An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012.

Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo, a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box.

But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris
World.content:
French police have arrested a suspect after gunshots were fired in a town in the suburbs of Paris on Friday. Police are investigating a possible racist motivation.

One person was killed and four others were injured when gunshots were fired from a vehicle in a town outside Paris on Friday, local authorities have confirmed.

The shooting occurred in Trappes, about 20 kilometers (13 miles) west of the French capital, close to Versailles, and a suspect was arrested in the neighboring town of Coignieres and has been taken into police custody.

Mayor: 'Miracle' that more were not killed

"An individual fired shots from his vehicle at multiple people along his route," the mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, wrote on social media.

He later told French broadcaster BFM TV that one of the locations at which shots were fired was a playground. "It is a miracle that there were not more victims," he said.

Rabeh said the person killed was of African origin, while one of those critically wounded was of North African origin.

The shooter allegedly opened fire from a vehicle, shooting indiscriminately Image: AFP

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon."

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the incident "very serious" and said that "all available resources of the security forces and judicial authorities have been fully mobilized."

He added that France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (Pnat) is monitoring the situation.

The Pnat itself said it had opened an investigation into "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed on the basis of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion."

France shooting: what else do we know?

The potential motive for the shooting was not immediately clear but it came as France braces for yet another day of protests against the high costs of living on Saturday, with major museums in Paris and other major cities closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence.

"We are not talking about ​a nice protest," Interior Minister Nunez told reporters, announcing the deployment of 70,000 security personnel. "We are ​ready ⁠tomorrow to be extremely firm ⁠and ​not tolerate anything."

France: Why students are taking to the streets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

France has also seen a spate of Islamist terrorist attacks in recent years and, although the number of incidents has fallen, authorities have warned that risks remain.

The town of Trappes has experienced its own share of tension, with a local teacher reporting receiving threats after saying that the state did not do enough to protect Samuel Paty, a teacher in another Paris suburb who was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.

There was no immediate suggestion that Friday's shooting was linked either to the current protests or Islamist terrorism.

World.title: Sri Lanka: Death of iconic elephant raises habitat concerns
World.content:
The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human-elephant conflict in rural communities. The island country sees a high number of deadly encounters.

The recent death of an iconic male elephant in Sri Lanka has raised concerns over ongoing contact between humans and the giant animals, whose habitats have been greatly reduced.

The elephant known as "Kavantissa" had been considered to be the tallest living male elephant in the Sri Lanka. Thought to be around 45 years old and measuring roughly 3.3 meters tall (11 feet), he roamed Sri Lanka's northwest near the village of Galgamuwa, and was widely admired for his majestic stature.

In late September, villagers noticed the 5.5 ton-tusker (5,500 kg) was limping, and a closer look reveled a gunshot wound on his right leg. Despite the intervention of veterinary surgeons, the elephant died on October 16.

Sri Lanka records the highest number of elephant deaths annually and the second highest number of human deaths globally from violent interactions between elephants and humans, which usually happen when crop raiding elephants encroach on farmlands.

According to official statistics, since 2019, an average of 370 elephants and 125 humans have died in human-elephant conflict incidents each year.

The situation affects the natural habitats of elephants and the livelihoods of rural communities.

Home to about 10% of the global Asian elephant population and occupying about 2% of their total natural range, Sri Lanka has the highest density of Asian elephants in the world.

The Sri Lankan elephant is an endangered subspecies in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, and protected under Sri Lankan law, with punishment by fines and jail terms for wildlife-related offences.

Some villages use electric fences to keep elephants away from crops and people Image: Ravi Corea

A shrinking habitat for elephants

During the past few decades, forest cover in Sri Lanka has shrunk as the population has grown.

Statistics show the rural population of Sri Lanka increased from 8.25 million in 1960 to 17.8 million in 2020.

Agriculture remains the primary source of income for these rural communities. As a result, the land is cleared for agricultural activities.

According to Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) statistics, in 2024, an estimated 7,451 wild elephants were recorded in Sri Lanka. About 70% of these wild elephants live outside protected areas.

Research shows elephants have a massive daily dietary requirement of about 150 kilograms (330 lbs.) of green matter, which drives them into farmland.

"Driven primarily by habitat loss, agricultural expansion, fragmentation of elephant corridors, and increasing competition for land and resources, human-elephant conflict continues to cause hundreds of elephant deaths and more than 100 human fatalities annually," said Ravi Corea, President of Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society, a Sri Lankan non-profit conservation organization.

The conservationist told DW that rural communities are severely affected, and the agricultural losses caused by elephants can threaten a family's primary source of food and income.

"This distinguishes human-elephant conflict from many human-wildlife conflicts in economically developed countries, where wildlife encounters, although sometimes serious, generally do not threaten household subsistence to the same extent," he said.

Indian villages deter wild elephants with lemon trees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Elephants and humans clash

"Despite the efforts by the government to mitigate HEC, the numbers are rising demonstrating the continuing severity of the crisis," Corea added.

Elephants are shot, poisoned, or killed by improvised explosives hidden in food and train collisions, experts say.

In view of the escalation of human-elephant conflict, the Sri Lankan government in 2020 drafted a national action plan to mitigate the problem.

"The 2020 Action Plan provides a valuable foundation for reducing human–elephant conflict, but its recommendations must be strengthened through a comprehensive national conservation strategy with enforceable habitat protection at its core," Corea said.

"The ultimate measure of success must be not merely a reduction in human–elephant conflict, but the permanent protection of ecologically connected habitats, the survival of viable wild elephant populations and the ability of people and elephants to coexist sustainably for generations to come," he added.

Community-level initiatives protect people and elephants

Meanwhile, community-based programs by non-government organizations have proven effective and sustainable. These initiatives are complemented by elephant monitoring, scientific research, habitat assessments, community education, and the development of locally appropriate deterrents, Corea said

"Our flagship initiative Project Orange Elephant in Sri Lanka's Wasgamuwa region promotes the cultivation of citrus which elephants do not like to eat as a trophic deterrence. This reduces crop raiding while generating alternative income for farmers," Corea added, pointing to things like electric fencing protecting settlements and agricultural lands while encouraging local responsibility.

Elephants do not like the taste of citrus fruits Image: Ravi Corea

Another issue is confrontations on elephant corridors, that in some cases have discouraged children from walking to school.

Elephant corridors are designated strips of land that connect larger forest and habitat patches, allowing elephants to move safely between them for food, water, breeding, and seasonal migration.

To address this, the "EleFriendly" bus service in Wasgamuwa, provides safe transportation for schoolchildren through elephant corridors and has reduced dangerous human-elephant encounters along its original route by over 90%.

A bus takes students to school in order to avoid elephant paths Image: Ravi Corea

"An ethically just solution must protect human lives, livelihoods, and elephant populations simultaneously, said Kamal Shashendra, a Sri Lanka-based environmental ethics researcher.

He told DW that this required scientifically informed land-use planning, protection of elephant corridors, appropriate community-based fencing, effective early-warning systems, and fair compensation for affected families.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Greece joins countries putting age-limits on social media, banning access for kids under 15
World.content:
Greece has passed legislation banning social media access for children under 15. New rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027, and are designed to protect children's mental health.

A bill to "ban the use of online social media services by minors" was passed by a majority vote of the Greek parliament Thursday and will go into effect on January 1, 2027.

The New Democracy party was the only bloc in parliament to support the measure; while opposition parties SYRIZA, Greek Solution, KKE, Niki and Freedom Course voted against it, and PASOK abstained.

Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou called the step, "necessary, effective, proportionate and EU-law-compliant," according to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, adding that social media platforms would have until the first of the year to, "determine whether the accounts they host and the services they provide are intended for adults or not."

Pointing to similar age limits on alcohol and tobacco sales to minors, Papastergiou said lawmakers had no time to wait for Brussels to pass "the perfect European law," saying, "let's send the message that the problem of uncontrolled internet use — which leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health — cannot continue."

Why does Greece want to introduce social media age limits?

The move to put legal age limits on social media use began last year in Australia, with numerous countries around the world swiftly following suit.

Greece is one of seven EU countries seeking to introduce standards for age-verification on social media, which proponents argue will curb the "endless scrolling" that deprives kids of sleep, destroys their attention span and ability to concentrate and keeps them from playing outdoors and spending time with their friends.

Papastergiou defended the use of an app known as "Kid's Wallet" as a means to that end, saying that it had been established according to codes and technical specifications set by the EU.

The minister was emphatic that the app, "does not provide any personal data whatsoever about children or users, other than whether they are over or under 15 years of age — not even their date of birth."

"We owe our children their childhood," said Papastergiou. "That is what we are doing today. We have a duty to protect them. Given the current challenges, the social media bill delivers what society has been waiting for."

World.title: Germany news: Wadephul says 'threat of famine' due to ongoing wars
World.content:
Published 10/23/2026 Published October 23, 2026 Wadephul warns shipping disruptions could lead to famine

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that continuing disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea could potentially lead to famine in the global south.

"We're all feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping lanes, whether at the gas station or in the supermarket," he said ahead of a meeting with fellow foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday. "But elsewhere, there is a threat of famine when fertilizers don't arrive in the places where they are essential for basic production."

Wadephul was referring not only to the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi threats to the Bab al-Mandab strait, but also to Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea as part of Moscow's ongoing war against Ukraine, one of the world's leading producers of wheat.

"This effects the poorest people in the world whose basic provisions are especially dependent on wheat, as well as our partners such as Turkey, the biggest wheat processing country in the world," he said.

"Together, we want to send a signal: we will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias [in Yemen] holding global trade hostage," Wadephul continued.

"The indiscriminatory attacks on free shipping and on neighboring countries must stop. For people across the region who are suffering from hunger, who no longer feel safe in their own homes, the continuing insecurity is not acceptable."

World.title: Israel preparing 'full closure' of West Bank, Netanyahu says
World.content:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel is shutting down the occupied West Bank after having prevented a "major attack."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the Israeli government was preparing to close down the occupied West Bank after gunmen attacked Israeli soldiers on Friday morning.

Netanyahu said Israeli military prevented a "major attack" after soldiers killed two gunmen in a firefight at a checkpoint near the West Bank city of Hebron.

What do we know about the shooting in the West Bank?

At least five people were wounded in the attack, several critically.

"I commend our heroic fighters, who acted resolutely and prevented a major terrorist attack, and wish our wounded a speedy recovery," Netanyahu said in a statement.

He added that he had instructed the military to "impose a cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire West Bank starting today."

The Israeli operation comes a week before Israel heads into an election next week, the first since the October 7 Hamas attacks.

Settler violence has been on the rise in the West Bank and dozens of Palestinians have been killed in the territorysince the start of the year.

How much power do Israeli settlers have over West Bank policy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the Israeli military say about the shooting in the West Bank?

Earlier, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had prevented a "terror attack against Israeli civilians" and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun.

The IDF did not say who the attack was targeting and gave no details on the two dead alleged attackers or those injured in the shooting.

The military has set up roadblocks and closures in and around Palestinian towns in the area.

FM Bezalel Smotrich calls for military action in West Bank 'exactly like in Gaza'

The far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a military campaign in the West Bank, "exactly like in Gaza," in response to Friday's incident.

"There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon," Smotrich said, using the Israeli term for the West Bank.

He went on to say he had called for the demolition of buildings near the site of Friday's shooting.

"Following the attack, I have ordered the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site," he said.

"The order will be carried out within the next hour and will take place throughout the afternoon hours."

Smotrich, himself a settler in the West Bank, leads the Religious Zionism party. He is widely known for championing ultranationalist and inflammatory policies and has previously made similar calls for "war" in the West Bank.

Israeli elections take place next week: What to know

The Israeli election on October 27 is widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, who has been criticized by opponents for failing to prevent the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.

Polls indicate that the elections will be a close race between the pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs.

Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite international attention on Gaza and the West Bank, there is little difference between the two blocs regarding Israel's treatment of Palestinians.

Just days ago, masked Israeli settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and journalists in the West Bank as they accompanied Palestinians for the start of the annual olive harvest.

The IDF condemned the acts of violence and opened a rare investigation into the settlers. Both Israel's occupation and the settlements, which are dotted throughout the territory, are illegal under international law.

World.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North again
World.content:
South Korea is attempting to mutually determine the land border with North Korea amid military incidents and escalating tensions.

South Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday proposed military talks with North Korea in an attempt to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels.

The ministry said it had proposed talks last November to resolve differences over the line, and reduce the risk of accidental deaths, but Pyongyang had not responded.

Why is South Korea proposing talks with the north?

The latest proposal, announced by Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy Kim Hong-cheol, follows a landmine blast in the demiliterized zone (DMZ) in September that injured three South Korean soldiers.

North Korean troops have been building tactical roads, fences and been laying mines in the DMZ in the recent years. South Korea's Kim said the North's troops have repeatedly crossed the line in the process.

Seoul's military also concluded that North Korea had buried mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) which caused the recent blast. Pyongyang has rejected those findings.

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Avoiding future incidents on the Korean peninsula

Miliatry tensions between the two Koreas has been escalating. Just days ago, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong announced that Pyongyang had moved new troops into "firing position" along the border.

She later said the North would also place loudspeakers on standby along the border, a repeated move of aggression aimed at harassing South Korean soldiers and villages along the border.

Jin Yong-sung, chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, also ordered the military to "respond with firm resolve" should North Korea use Seoul's actions as a pretext for aggressive action.

It is difficult to predict "what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed," the South's Defense Ministry said on Friday, adding that they hoped for a positive response from their rival neighbor.

It also proposed the option of "three-way talks involving the United Nations Command would also be possible."
