World.title: EDF intel chief: Russia greatly exaggerating its military success in Ukraine
World.content:
Russia continued to exaggerate its battlefield gains in Ukraine and launch large-scale attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure over the past week, while reports also emerged of potentially hostile Russian satellite activity in space.

"Russia's leadership is consistently trying to portray developments in the war in Ukraine in a far more favorable light than they actually are. During a visit to a reserve command post of Russia's joint force grouping on October 16, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Russia had captured 310 settlements and 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year," Ants Kiviselg, head of the Estonian Defense Forces Intelligence Center, said at his weekly press conference.

Kiviselg said Army Gen. Valery Gerasimov had reported to Putin that Russian forces had captured 92 settlements and 1,800 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September alone and were advancing along a broad front. According to Gerasimov, Russia had also begun "launching massive strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers and the energy and transport infrastructure supporting their operations."

"There is no objective evidence to substantiate the Russian leadership's claims of advances on the front and the Ukrainian General Staff has refuted Gen. Gerasimov's claims in detail," Kiviselg said.

The intelligence chief noted that during a meeting with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, Putin continued to portray the fighting in Ukraine as an unstoppable Russian offensive along all major axes. "Witkoff presented President Putin with peace proposals from Ukraine and European countries, which Russian presidential aide [Yuri] Ushakov said 'did not contain much that was useful,'" Kiviselg said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced his willingness to freeze the war along the current line of contact, effectively establishing a ceasefire. Moscow, however, reiterated its longstanding position that Russia is interested only in peace on its own terms, not a ceasefire.

According to Kiviselg, Russia's inaccurate portrayal of the location of the line of contact could become one of the points of contention in establishing a ceasefire — should the issue even arise.

Russia continues its attempts to push Ukraine back and break its resistance through information, diplomatic and military measures. Moscow's persistent efforts to shape perceptions of the situation on the front to suit its interests fall within the realm of cognitive warfare, through which Russia seeks to influence attitudes and decision-making processes to achieve its objectives.

Number of civilian casualties in Ukraine greater than in previous years

An average of 240 combat engagements took place along the front each day, an increase from the previous week.

The most intense fighting took place along the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes in Donetsk Oblast, followed by the Huliaipole axis in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and the Southern Slobozhanshchyna axis in Kharkiv Oblast. Ukrainian counterattacks were concentrated primarily in Kharkiv Oblast and along the Oleksandrivka axis in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.

Russia suffered an average of 1,900 military personnel losses per day. Russian forces lost more than 2,000 personnel on three separate days, while total weekly losses exceeded 10,000 for the eighth consecutive week.

Russian long-range strikes hit Ukraine's energy infrastructure, commercial and industrial facilities, transportation infrastructure and residential buildings over the past week. According to the United Nations, the increase in strikes against civilian targets led to an 85 percent rise in civilian casualties in September compared with the same month last year. This trend has continued into October and the UN estimates that civilian casualties in Ukraine this year will significantly exceed levels recorded in previous years.

Russia attacked targets in nearly every Ukrainian oblast, causing power outages in at least half of them. Since July 16, Russia has carried out more than 2,100 attacks against Ukraine's energy infrastructure and continues its efforts to create a humanitarian catastrophe in the country to force it into submission.

"To ensure the stability and resilience of its energy system, Ukraine needs assistance in the form of both the necessary equipment and air defense systems," Kiviselg said.

Between October 12 and 18, Ukrainian energy workers restored electricity to 1.7 million customers in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, as well as in Donetsk, Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.

Despite increasingly frequent Russian attacks, Ukraine's state-owned oil and gas company Naftogaz has accumulated its largest gas reserves for winter in six years. Reserves in underground storage facilities total 16 billion cubic meters, the highest level since 2020.

Ukrainian long-range strikes hit Russian fuel infrastructure facilities in the St. Petersburg area, Ryazan and Tambov oblasts and the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug. Ukraine also attacked a data center near St. Petersburg, a drone factory in Rostov Oblast, a military airfield in Voronezh Oblast and other military targets in occupied territories and areas near the border.

Russia's hybrid efforts in space

Over the past week, information about Russian hybrid activities in space came to light.

Russia's military satellite Kosmos 2612 reportedly came dangerously close to ICEYE-X36, a U.S.-registered satellite owned by a subsidiary of Finnish company ICEYE. According to various estimates, the distance between the two satellites may have ranged from a few meters to several hundred meters, but in any case was below the safe separation distance.

Russia launched the Kosmos 2609-2614 satellites into orbit in April this year and the Kosmos 2609 satellite had previously passed within 2.5 kilometers of ICEYE-X36. Kosmos 2612 began approaching ICEYE-X36 in late September.

"Ukraine has been using data from ICEYE's radar-equipped satellites in its war against Russia since 2022 and the Russian satellite's activities may have been intended to disrupt ICEYE-X36's operations, gather intelligence or send a message to Western countries that their satellites are not protected in space," Kiviselg said.

World.title: Estonia supports postponing methane requirements
World.content:
The government endorsed a European Commission proposal at its meeting to postpone certain verification and reporting requirements under the EU Methane Regulation by one year.

The additional time will help avoid a situation in which implementing the new requirements limits fuel suppliers' options and increases price pressures on the European energy market, the government's press service said.

"This is also what businesses have been calling for. Reducing methane emissions is important, but the requirements must be feasible in practice. The additional time will help companies and producers get the necessary systems up and running and reduce the risk of fewer suppliers on the European market and growing price pressures," Minister of Energy and the Environment Erkki Keldo said.

The change primarily affects companies that import fuels into the European Union from non-EU countries and are required to submit data and evidence on methane emissions generated during their production. If producers are not ready to provide this information by the deadline, the range of supplies eligible for the European market could shrink, even if the fuel itself is available.

Estonia's gas supply depends on the regional market and international deliveries. As a result, supply disruptions on the European market could also affect the availability and price of gas for Estonian consumers. Estonia believes these risks must be taken into account when implementing the Methane Regulation and that companies must be given sufficient time to comply with the requirements.

The additional year will allow companies, producers in non-EU countries and authorities in EU member states to prepare the necessary monitoring, reporting and verification systems. Estonia supports reducing methane emissions but considers it important that the requirements be feasible in practice and not impose disproportionate administrative burdens or costs.

The proposal does not suspend the Methane Regulation or represent a retreat from its environmental objectives, the press service said. The European Commission's proposal changes only the deadlines for certain obligations, not their substance. Other requirements for reducing methane emissions and reporting information will remain in force.

World.title: Foreign ministry top official to run for prime minister in 2027 election
World.content:
The top official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Jonatan Vseviov, has said he will resign on Thursday to run in next spring's national election for the opposition Social Democratic Party (SDE). He hopes to be the party's prime ministerial candidate.

Vseviov is currently in his second term as the ministry's secretary general and is Estonia's former ambassador to Washington. Previously, he was secretary general at the Ministry of Defense.

Vseviov will submit his resignation on Thursday and will leave his post on November 1.

"I have devoted my entire life so far to protecting and developing Estonia as a diplomat and civil servant. I have had the honor of leading dedicated teams with whom we have shaped Estonia's foreign and defense policy and implemented many of the decisions that have brought us to where we are today," Vseviov said.

"Today, however, I see that protecting Estonia and moving it forward requires more than what I can do as a civil servant. That is why I have decided to leave the civil service, join the Social Democrats and run in the upcoming elections," he said.

SDE Chairman Lauri Läänemets said Estonia's security and its position in the international arena require strong leadership.

Jonatan Vseviov Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"Jonatan Vseviov knows Estonia's security and foreign policy inside out and has extensive international experience. He has shaped Estonia's defense policy, led the Ministry of Defense, represented Estonia as ambassador in Washington and headed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Läänemets said.

Vseviov took office as secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 2021. Before that, he had served as Estonia's ambassador to the United States since August 2018.

From 2008 to 2018, Vseviov worked at the Ministry of Defense, eventually becoming its secretary general.

Before being appointed secretary general in January 2016, Vseviov served as deputy secretary general for defense planning, acting deputy secretary general for defense policy and director of the policy planning department.

Vseviov graduated from the University of Tartu with a degree in political science and earned a master's degree with honors in security studies from Georgetown University.

From 1999 to 2005, Vseviov was a member of the Reform Party.

Vseviov to run for prime minister

Läänemets said the party reached an agreement with Vseviov in the summer. The deal included Vseviov becoming the SDE's candidate for prime minister. At the time, the media was linking the secretary general to a possible presidential bid.

Läänemets said at a press conference on Thursday morning that he will propose at a board meeting on November 1 that Vseviov stand as the party's prime ministerial candidate.

Läänemets told ERR the process began around a year ago, when he started thinking about how the party could achieve the best possible result in the 2027 Riigikogu elections.

Asked whether the agreement also included the position of candidate for prime minister, Läänemets said it did.

Jonatan Vseviov and Lauri Läänemets at the press conference. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The idea didn't start with me saying, 'Come into politics.' As secretary general, he attended government meetings when I was a minister, and you could see common ground developing from there. Ultimately, it was a process of growing closer on both sides."

Läänemets added that security determines a great deal in Estonia today and that, given Vseviov's experience and knowledge, he would make a very good next prime minister of Estonia.

"We came to the conclusion that we cannot move forward the way [Reform Prime Minister Kristen] Michal is doing things now. Or the way [Isamaa Chairman Urmas] Reinsalu would do them. And I'm not even going to talk about [Center's Mihhail] Kõlvart. Can anyone imagine Kõlvart negotiating with Russia on behalf of Ukraine?" the chairman said.

Vseviov said: "I will now first seek a mandate from the Social Democratic Party — specifically from the Social Democratic Party, because I see in this team the potential to be a responsible and forward-looking force at Estonia's helm. And if the party grants me that mandate, I will seek a mandate from the Estonian people."

Läänemets said he will continue as leader of the party and will also run in the elections.

'We are capable of more and deserve better'

Both men said Estonia must be able to assert itself more on the international stage and participate in various discussions concerning security.

"We must understand that the surest guarantee of our freedom is that it is also valuable to other like-minded countries. Our freedom must be valuable to others, and then others will value our freedom. For our freedom to be valuable to others, we need courage, sharpness of mind, intellectual reach and political reach as well, to bring Estonia back into Europe's political core. In doing so, we must understand that those who remain silent go unnoticed, so we must not remain silent. But those who rant are not listened to, so we must not rant either," Vseviov said.

"I feel that today we are desperately lacking both intellectual reach and the courage to assert ourselves," he added.

Vseviov said Estonia needs radical progress to survive, and that the Reform Party no longer offers this.

"If I believed that Estonia's current political leadership was up to the task, I would continue working as a civil servant and would not be standing here before you today. I am absolutely convinced that with the current leadership, we are incapable of sailing through this storm, and I believe that the team beside me and behind me is the team that today offers Estonia intelligent but also forward-looking policies," he said.

"Some want to tell us that we should be satisfied that the economy is no longer shrinking and that the war has not yet reached Estonia. My message is that we are capable of more and deserve better," he said.

Läänemets was more specific in his criticism of the government, saying that it should have responded immediately to the arson attack on defense industry company Milrem's production facility and made greater efforts to secure a seat at the table in discussions concerning Ukraine's security.

"As for Ukraine and the negotiations or conditions being imposed on Ukraine, the president of Finland and the Norwegian head of state are holding meetings, the Americans are going there, and I ask whether Estonia has even tried to have a say in this at the level of its national leadership, to get involved. Certain things are beyond the reach of civil servants; there are limits to what officials can do. But when such agreements are being made in one place or another and we are not invited, does that mean we should not at least try to have a say? We could start listing examples, both close to home and farther afield, where Kristen Michal simply takes the opportunity to do nothing," Läänemets said.

Vseviov said his decision to enter politics has absolutely nothing to do with the fact that he was nominated as a presidential candidate.

Minister: Not a surprise to me

Margus Tsahkna. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said Vseviov's move did not come as a surprise to him.

"For several years, I have encouraged senior civil servants to enter politics. And I am glad that some of them are doing so. Because there is a big difference between developing policies as a civil servant and literally putting your own skin in the game. Taking a mandate and assuming responsibility as a politician. So in that sense, it was not a surprise to me. Jonatan Vseviov informed me yesterday that he would be running in the elections with the Social Democrats," Tsahkna told ERR.

The minister did not want to comment on Vseviov joining the SDE, adding it is up to him to explain his ideological choices.

Tsahkna said he had not forced Vseviov to resign.

"But I didn't try to keep him either. We discussed it, and it was his own suggestion that these things are incompatible if you have decided to enter politics and are moving into the active campaign phase while simultaneously serving as secretary general. Although, yes, there is no legal requirement whatsoever for a person to leave their position. But it was his own wish, and as of November 1, Jonatan Vseviov will no longer be secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," he said.

Tsahkna said there are no criteria for the next secretary general to come from within the ministry.

"But clearly, this person must not only understand foreign policy theoretically and be an expert, but also know how foreign and security policy is handled in Estonia and who is involved. It is certainly difficult to separate defense policy from foreign policy, because today they are very closely intertwined. So this person must be capable of working with everyone: the Riigikogu, the president, coordinating our own ministry, the Ministry of Defense, and also think tanks. And communicating with international partners. That is also extremely important," the minister said.

Reform: Vseviov took offense when we didn't make him defense minister

According to Reform Party Secretary-General Kristo Enn Vaga, the Reform Party held extensive talks with Jonatan Vseviov both when it was looking for a presidential candidate and when it needed to find a new defense minister following Hanno Pevkur's resignation.

"When we were looking for a defense minister, we sounded out whether he would be willing to talk to us if we were to give him a call. The response was positive," Vaga told Äripäev.

The Reform Party ultimately chose former Estonian Defense Forces commander Martin Herem, which Vaga said was the right decision for Estonia's defense policy.

"That certainly left him [Jonatan Vseviov] feeling somewhat resentful toward us because we didn't choose him after all. I suppose that may have been the deciding factor in why he went with the Social Democrats," Vaga said.

According to Vaga, the Reform Party also courted Vseviov over the summer when it was still looking for a presidential candidate and Vseviov was one of the leading contenders. This is why Vaga finds Social Democratic Party leader Lauri Läänemets' claim that Vseviov had already decided to join the Social Democrats in the summer questionable.

This story was updated to add comments from Margus Tsahkna, Jonatan Vseviov, Lauri Läänemets and Kristo Enn Vaga.

World.title: Investigation finds no deliberate activity aimed against Estonia in Auvere drone incident
World.content:
The Prosecutor's Office has closed its investigation into a drone that struck a smokestack at the Auvere Power Plant because it was unable to establish the exact circumstances of the incident.

"Because the drone was so extensively destroyed in the collision and explosion, it was not possible to reliably determine its origin from the remaining fragments," State Prosecutor Gardi Anderson said.

According to Anderson, the Prosecutor's Office carried out all possible and reasonable investigative procedures to establish the circumstances of the incident, but the evidence gathered does not allow the investigation to continue effectively or anyone to be held responsible.

"If new information or evidence emerges that could help establish the circumstances of the incident more precisely, we can reopen the investigation," Anderson added.

The Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS/KAPO) said the information gathered during the investigation did not indicate that the drone's entry into the Auvere Power Plant grounds was a deliberate act directed against Estonia.

"As long as Russia continues its aggression against Ukraine, we can expect to see more incidents like this. Drones are weapons of war and if one is found, people should keep their distance to protect themselves and others and report the discovery," ISS Deputy Director General Andres Ratassepp emphasized.

At 3:43 a.m. on March 25 this year, a drone struck a smokestack at the Auvere Power Plant near the Russian border, causing an explosion. The smokestack was damaged, but no one was injured and the incident did not affect the operation of the electricity system.

Criminal proceedings were launched to investigate the incident on suspicion of causing an explosion.

During the investigation, authorities examined, among other possibilities, whether the drone could have been a Ukrainian drone that had veered off course. To investigate this possibility, they consulted Ukrainian experts and commissioned a forensic examination. However, the information gathered did not establish the drone's origin.

World.title: Defense minister: Estonia not entering the drone warfare era completely barehanded
World.content:
Defense Minister Martin Herem says the threat from Russia will increase dramatically once its war in Ukraine ends, making it essential for Estonia to accelerate defense preparations, strengthen air defenses and ensure the public understands the risks and how to respond.

Before taking office, you told journalists that, as defense minister, you considered it important for the government to formulate an updated threat assessment that would guide all sectors and the entire civil service. How has that gone during your first few weeks in office? Have there been any obstacles?

There have been no obstacles. I can't say that I've formulated it precisely in the government or that it's been put down on paper anywhere, but I have done so at the Ministry of Defense. The assessment is that the threat from Russia will increase dramatically from the moment it stops using its current resources in Ukraine. After that, I would say, the threat to us will increase dramatically.

The Defense Ministry's former secretary general, Kaimo Kuusk, gave an interview to Õhtuleht that was published Saturday. He said that you cited a very different perception of the threat as the reason why it was impossible to continue working with him. Describe the ways in which your perception of the threat differs from that of the ministry's previous senior leadership.

I don't want to turn this into some kind of competition and I wouldn't want to describe anything as impossible. But one example concerning the speed of action is this: If the Russian threat exists and will increase at some point and we don't actually know when that increase will begin — whether it's the day after tomorrow or a year from now — then we should be asking when organizations and institutions providing vital services need to know what threats they would face in wartime and what measures they can take to reduce or mitigate those threats.

Or other similar questions, all related to the threat assessment: When should these things be known? When, for example, should Estonian construction companies have an overview of the obstacles and fortifications that Estonian military personnel need along the eastern border? When should they be informed and what is their role? Or when should everyone in Estonia know what their role would be in wartime?

In my view, they could know that today. They could have known it yesterday. I'm trying to make sure they find out over the course of next year.

Before March, even before the end of this government's term?

Some of it before March, yes, but the effects of certain measures will certainly extend throughout next year.

Can you point to anything else you have done fundamentally differently during your first few weeks in office compared with how the defense sector was previously managed?

I can't really point to anything that's entirely new. It's very important not to dismantle things that have been done well in the past and a great many things have been done well. So I'm not competing to come up with new initiatives.

What I've been examining is Estonia's overall preparedness at sea, against threats from the air and against threats coming overland from the east. I've made some preparations and drawn up plans in these areas and presented them to the Ministry of Defense. The ministry has reviewed them, improved them and made some changes and we'll proceed on the basis of that plan.

This isn't some personal management style of mine. It's simply the Ministry of Defense carrying out its responsibilities in response to the threat environment.

A public opinion monitoring survey commissioned by the Government Office and published in late September shows that the share of Estonian residents concerned about the possibility of war breaking out in Estonia or elsewhere in Europe has increased by three percentage points. Sixty-seven percent of residents are now concerned about this. What should be done about that concern?

That concern isn't necessarily a bad thing. It simply reflects the picture we see when we look east. The problem arises when those people who are worried don't have solutions. The Ministry of Defense is certainly one of the institutions that must explain those solutions and, of course, provide them. That's the most important task.

When people talk about fear of war, both I and psychologists believe that what we're seeing in the media coming out of Ukraine inevitably creates fear. People's imaginations and their knowledge of warfare amplify that fear and then things can get completely out of hand.

The sensible approach is for the state to explain what the threats are and what solutions exist to address them. Research tells us that this should reduce anxiety.

Minister of Defense Martin Herem. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

There are actually people who consider you someone who stokes fears of war. Some public figures have expressed that view on social media in response, for example, to the public lectures you gave at the University of Tartu this fall. Among other things, you've shown maps illustrating how far different types of drones launched from across the Russian-Estonian border can fly or how far Russian glide bombs can travel, showing that the city of Tartu, for example, falls within their range. What purpose does publicly visualizing Russia's capabilities on a map of Estonia in such detail serve? Some people believe it fuels fear and that you therefore shouldn't do it. What do you see as its purpose?

Very much the same purpose as the images we see on cigarette packages. They're all unpleasant images, but they're not scaremongering and they're not false.

I've visualized these threats and possible scenarios, thereby explaining to people what a military conflict might look like. The aim isn't simply to make people understand the threat, but also to show what measures can be taken to reduce or mitigate it.

I know that about a year ago, when Ukrainian drones entered our airspace, people in the Tallinn area assumed that the drones capable of reaching Tallinn were small FPV drones. There was even talk of using fishing nets to catch them.

That's wrong, because those types of drones are extremely unlikely to reach us. Instead, what can reach us are large drones measuring two or three meters, which you can't catch with a fishing net.

That's precisely why these threats and their solutions need to be visualized, so people in different regions understand what threats they may face at different times.

I would emphasize that this is purely about education, not scaremongering of any kind.

Have you also received a different kind of feedback on your lectures and visual materials? I'm thinking specifically of people who previously had no connection to the defense sector and have now gained access to this information through your public lectures.

The feedback I've received, to the extent that people have provided it, has been mostly positive.

There has been some criticism that I would describe as politically motivated, but I believe that stems more from whom those people see me as representing — a Reform Party minister in the current government.

That criticism also needs to be taken into account and those people need things explained to them several times as well.

I've had some success on social media, too. We exchange five or six posts and eventually the person says they understand what's going on.

A teacher has to be patient. That's how students become knowledgeable.

At what pace is Estonia's defense capability improving? Are the weapons systems and ammunition purchased with increased defense spending now arriving and to what extent? And to what extent are we actually developing new capabilities?

The overall military picture isn't bad. A great deal of ammunition and military equipment that is very important for our defense will be delivered to Estonia this year, next year and the year after that.

Last year, the Ministry of Defense completed almost 100 percent of its planned procurements. We'll see how things go this year and next.

So the picture is good in that respect. Where we really need to catch up is in society as a whole.

Again, this isn't about frightening people. It's about explaining the threats, preparing to address them and, in part, taking physical measures as we're already seeing along the eastern border, for example.

Will any of the funds allocated in this year's defense budget go unspent and if so, how much? For example, because ammunition cannot be delivered due to the U.S.-Iran conflict or some other reason?

I can't say today. My prediction is that it will be a very small proportion.

At present, there's no indication that any procurements will fail to go ahead because of the U.S.-Iran war or anything else.

All our procurements are proceeding and I don't see any major risks here.

There are some things that will probably be pushed into next year, but they'll be completed next year.

For years, you've advocated the approach that if war breaks out, we shouldn't be chasing arrows but should instead target and hunt down the archer. That's the rationale behind our purchase of HIMARS systems from the United States. However, we haven't received the long-range HIMARS ammunition from the U.S. that would allow us to fire at targets up to 300 kilometers away and hit the archers on Russian territory — those who are firing at us. What are the prospects? When will we receive the long-range ammunition?

The shortage of ATACMS missiles is, of course, very bad. There's no need to make excuses for it. It is bad and I can't say when they'll arrive.

However, we do have the ammunition with a range of 70 kilometers. Everything that was included in our original contract has now arrived in Estonia.

The launchers for the Korean system (K239 Chunmoo — ed.) will arrive next year. Hopefully, the ammunition will also arrive next year, but more likely at the beginning of the following year.

In addition, various types of ammunition with ranges well beyond 50 kilometers, approaching 100 kilometers, will arrive this year and next. That includes both artillery ammunition and loitering munitions, which are large, winged drones.

HIMARS. Source: Kermo Pastarus

What does that mean in practical terms? Now that we have ammunition with a range of 70 kilometers, does that mean the Russians can't fire at us from Pskov, Pechory or Ivangorod because they know they'll immediately be destroyed? That they'll have to move farther away?

They can still fire, but we have weapons that pose a threat to them.

War doesn't work in such a way that having a particular weapon solves everything. No, it's much more complicated than that.

But the adversary has to take into account that we can now strike targets as far as 100 kilometers away.

We've also had anti-ship missiles with ranges exceeding 200 kilometers for quite some time.

A few days ago, the Ukrainians used their Neptune anti-ship missile to destroy Su-34 aircraft at a distance of about 300 kilometers. There's now some debate over whether they destroyed four or six.

So we actually have a weapon of that kind. Of course, it's not the most sensible weapon for destroying aircraft on the ground, but at some point it could prove useful.

Let's suppose Russia's objective isn't to seize a large area of territory but to drive a wedge between NATO allies — a scenario that has been widely discussed. Russia launches what it calls a limited military operation, for example, taking control of Narva in a surprise attack and sending drones against infrastructure targets in Estonia. I am concerned about whether NATO allies and particularly the United States under President Trump would allow Estonia to use long-range HIMARS ammunition to strike targets inside Russia in such a situation. Would the U.S. share the necessary intelligence with us or would it cut off that intelligence and say this is actually just a small conflict and that it won't allow strikes against Russia?

There are several things I want to emphasize here.

First, such a scenario is highly unlikely to unfold before the war in Ukraine comes to some kind of halt. Until then, Russia remains tied down.

Would the United States prohibit us from using certain ammunition? There's nothing like that in the contracts and I haven't seen any indication of it in my current conversations with U.S. military personnel.

Could certain intelligence channels be shut down on Trump's orders? That's difficult to predict today.

Unlike Ukraine, however, we are a NATO member and I don't think it makes sense to panic about that now.

But the fact is that we need to develop the relevant capabilities ourselves anyway and that's what we're doing.

Estonia is currently drafting its next 10-year national defense development plan and as a new defense minister with a fresh perspective, you now have an opportunity to influence its priorities. Which areas need a change in policy compared with the approach taken so far?

In military terms, it's still the commander of the Estonian Defense Forces who leads and develops the armed forces. The defense minister's job is to shape and improve the operating environment and resources.

If we're talking about the defense minister's responsibilities, then first, together with our allies, we need to establish a clear understanding of the Baltic Sea situation, one that the public also understands: We must maintain control of the Baltic Sea's maritime connections at all times.

Those connections must not disappear in a crisis or war and we must ensure that together with our allies.

The second task, which is more domestic in nature, concerns society's preparedness. That requires discussions with other ministries.

Martin Herem. Source: Arp Müller/ERR

Again, the defense minister and ministry officials shouldn't be seen as people coming in to defend the 5 percent defense spending target and talk about war. Instead, there should be a clear explanation of the threats and the Ministry of Defense should also offer concrete solutions.

Third, the minister must certainly do everything possible with landowners, various government agencies and businesses to accelerate construction of the defensive zone.

Whatever we don't build now must be planned, agreed upon and capable of being completed within a sufficiently short period.

I'd like to ask about a few specific areas. Will you proceed with the plan launched under the previous defense minister to purchase four new vessels for the Estonian Navy over four years — two for operations near the coast and two for operations farther offshore?

Under the previous defense minister, that plan had already been changed to a single type of vessel. We're working on it now.

Again, together with our allies, we need to examine what solutions will allow us to maintain control of those sea routes.

But the fact is that the navy needs vessels.

We need vessels, whether crewed or uncrewed, for mine hunting, mine laying, maintaining a presence at sea and carrying out peacetime duties.

Whether that's maritime search and rescue or oil spill response, for example, vessels are definitely needed for those tasks.

Although my background is in the infantry, I also don't see all of these being some kind of 10-meter uncrewed systems.

We definitely need larger vessels as well, several dozen meters long, with crews on board.

The question is what additional military functions they'll perform. That's something we're still working out.

How do you respond to criticism that it might be more cost-effective to invest in maritime drones and coastal defense systems and purchase a large number of small, fast boats that would be harder for the enemy to neutralize in a conflict than, say, four ships?

It's very difficult to conduct mine hunting along sea routes — in plain language, several dozen kilometers from the coast — using a small, fast boat.

If we want to lay naval mines, we need to do it quickly, which means the vessel must be able to carry a large number of mines. By a large number, I mean 20 or more.

You can't do that with a small, fast boat either.

Small, fast boats aren't suitable for oil spill response.

And if we want to maintain a presence at sea and, when necessary, deploy a team from a vessel to board a suspicious ship, a very small boat isn't suitable for that either.

So we can't carry out our missions at sea if all we have are, for example, 12-meter vessels or boats. It's simply not possible.

As for shore-based sensors and effectors — missiles and other uncrewed systems, for example — that's all absolutely right. Of course we need to develop those capabilities.

But none of that eliminates the need for certain types of vessels.

If someone thinks that's sheer stupidity, then all the countries around the Baltic Sea must be complete fools because they're building ships too.

A minehunter at sea. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

What changes do you envision in Estonia's approach to drone warfare specifically?

The Defense Forces is actually moving in the right direction.

What we probably need to explain to society as well is that we shouldn't talk about "drone warfare." Drones perform specific functions within combat operations.

Drones can replace certain reconnaissance equipment and sensors and gather information.

Drones can take on some of the roles of artillery, mortars and anti-tank weapons. But they don't replace those systems entirely; they supplement them.

Drones can carry out transportation tasks and they also have a role in air defense.

So we should look at drones in terms of the functions they perform, rather than simply saying we need drones.

That's exactly the direction the Defense Forces are moving in, step by step: conducting experiments, learning from Ukraine and making procurements.

Do we need to make any major changes? More in our understanding of what we need drones for.

The term "drone" covers a very broad range of systems, from an aircraft with a wingspan of three or four meters that can fly 1,000 kilometers to a drone that flies just 10 kilometers to conduct reconnaissance.

Those are very different things.

As I understand it, people's concern right now is more about the scenarios you've described: If hundreds or thousands of these drones suddenly started coming toward us, would we have the capability to shoot them down or not?

In some areas, our counter-drone capability is quite similar to what Ukraine had a year ago.

If we look at our air defense weapons — whether shoulder-fired missiles, heavy machine guns or anti-aircraft guns — we already have all of those.

In Ukraine, 12.7-millimeter machine guns are being used effectively today.

Whether they're remotely operated with computer assistance or simply mounted in the back of a truck is a separate question.

We have all of those weapons.

Many of them still need to be adapted and we need to practice using them, but hopefully we'll have time to do that.

So we're not completely defenseless.

And finally, as recently as 2023, people in both Ukraine and Estonia were saying that electronic warfare systems were needed to counter small drones and that nothing else would work.

EDF conscripts manning a ZU-23 anti-aircraft cannon. Source: EDF/Joonatan Jõgiaas

Today, drones are being shot out of the sky in Ukraine with small arms.

Our conscripts have been practicing shooting drones out of the sky with their own Rahe assault rifles for two years now, if I'm not mistaken.

So the situation isn't quite as bad as it might seem, but we still have a great deal to develop.

Is it even possible to defend Narva against a drone attack or will the state simply announce that it isn't? That if it becomes clear things are going badly and war is approaching, those who want to save themselves in Narva will have to evacuate?

Narva is very similar to Kherson where people talk about a "human safari" in which drones hunt people. And they really do hunt people!

But tens of thousands of people still live there.

It's dangerous, but the city remains under Ukrainian control and ordinary civilian life continues there as well.

I've driven through the city myself, although faster than usual and choosing my routes carefully, but no drone attacked me, for example.

I believe Narva can be defended in much the same way as Kherson.

In interviews with privately owned media outlets, you've spoken about the need to improve air defense, a mobile application for the public and the possible acquisition of small fighter jets, such as the Czech L-39, of which Estonia already has two as training aircraft. Could you explain to the public broadcaster what problem we would solve by acquiring these fighter jets?

First, the air raid warning system.

We need to bring our nationwide air raid warning system up to the level that exists in Ukraine.

Otherwise, to put it simply, if we declare an air raid alert across northern Estonia during wartime, production accounting for 75 percent of GDP would simply grind to a halt.

And if Russia starts playing games with us by triggering such alerts before a war, we'll go bankrupt pretty quickly.

That's why we need a system that allows businesses to decide for themselves whether a particular threat is actually heading in their direction.

As for the L-39 or other light jet fighters, aircraft of this kind are currently destroying more than half of the long-range drones and jet-powered drones flying in Ukrainian airspace.

A Czech-built Aero L-39 Albatros trainer jet in Air Force service. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

And this appears to be the most cost-effective approach.

When I talk about fighter jets, I don't mean F-35s or F-16s. I mean the jet aircraft we already operate today, which we could probably arm and use against those same drones.

At present, ours aren't armed.

How much would a modernized version of an aircraft such as the L-39 cost, equipped with radar and weapons suitable for engaging aerial targets? How many would we need, where would we find the necessary pilots and how quickly could we theoretically acquire such a capability?

I really can't say at the moment.

As for pilot training, in terms of simply flying the aircraft, we could get quite a few planes into the air immediately. We have the pilots.

But it's all much more complicated than that.

The aircraft would need to be integrated with ground-based air defense.

That means assigning aircraft their own areas of operation and ground-based air defense systems their own areas, so they don't end up engaging one another.

What tactics the aircraft would use, how they would be directed from the ground against these drones and at what altitudes they would operate — all of that requires separate training and planning, as well as the development of operational concepts.

That will take time.

At the same time, I don't think this is something we couldn't accomplish within the next four years, either in terms of time or financial resources.

Are we talking about something on the order of five aircraft or 50?

If the choice is between five and 50, then closer to five.

And the price of an aircraft is around €20 million, I believe?

I really can't tell you the price of an aircraft today.

But modern air defense systems are also quite expensive. The cost of shoulder-fired missiles — just the missiles themselves — has already risen to several hundred thousand euros each.

So the ammunition used by those aircraft would undoubtedly be cheaper.

Will the updated 10-year national defense development plan provide an answer to that question?

The updated development plan was actually submitted to the Government Office back in the spring and I can't say when it will receive approval at the national level this fall. That's beyond my control.

It's been the work of the Defense Forces.

The commander of the Defense Forces has made additional proposals, including these same light fighter jets.

We'll review those carefully.

And I see no reason why, even if the 10-year development plan is approved, we shouldn't make changes to it as the threats from Russia evolve, technology develops and our understanding of how to use that technology changes.

The 10-year development plan is more about showing us what resources we have available, how much we'll need to spend maintaining equipment and capabilities we've already acquired and developed, how much we can devote to developing new capabilities and how we can maneuver within those limits without locking ourselves into particular choices.

There's also an ongoing debate about developing one or more ballistic missile defense bubbles. Figures of €1 billion or even €2 billion have been mentioned, but in reality, such a bubble would protect only a very small part of Estonia's territory, just a few percent. Is that a sensible investment or could we achieve better results by spending that money on other defense capabilities? Will the development plan answer that question?

At present, the development plan's answer is that we'll begin developing that capability.

But you're right. For that kind of money, we'd be able to protect Tallinn, Paldiski and Tartu against ballistic missiles. That's it.

And the protected areas would be roughly the size of those cities.

When Ukraine was facing large numbers of ballistic missiles, it intercepted around 30 percent of them.

If I apply that picture to Estonia, then even after acquiring such a defensive capability — a ballistic missile defense system — we would still be unable to protect 80 percent of Estonia's airspace.

Presentation of the U.S. Patriot air defense system in Estonia. Source: EDF / mil.ee

And the fact is that ballistic missiles wouldn't be fired only at Tallinn.

There's a very strong political and public expectation for this capability, but I think a somewhat mistaken impression has developed that if we have a long-range air defense system whose missiles can hit targets 120 kilometers away, then a couple of launchers will cover all of Estonia.

That's true when we're talking about air defense against aircraft and helicopters.

Against ballistic missiles, those coverage circles become very, very small.

What developments are planned for the Baltic Defense Line? Could you explain what changes are expected, for example, in Setomaa Municipality near the Estonian-Russian control line, beyond the anti-vehicle ditches that have already been dug there on local initiative?

First, we need to continue developing what the Defense Forces want to do and what the state and the Setomaa Union have already done.

Second, we need to give businesses a clear understanding of what's expected of them.

To do that, we need to build some examples, some demonstration sections, whether they're dug-in positions, obstacles or drone protection in the form of so-called net tunnels.

We need to do this to understand how to build them, what resources they require and how well they withstand the weather and different seasons.

So we might see a trial section of anti-drone netting installed over a road somewhere in Setomaa?

The current plan is to build such a trial section in both northeastern and southeastern Estonia.

'Dragon's teeth' on the Baltic Defense Line in Estonia's southeastern Setomaa region. Source: Leevi Lillemäe/ERR

And finally, a political question. Martin Herem, when will you decide whether to join the Reform Party and whether to run in the March elections? There have already been hints after all. You appear in one of the Reform Party's campaign videos.

Yes, I had absolutely no objection to appearing in a Reform Party , supporting the Reform Party and, at the same time, using the Reform Party as a platform for developing national defense.

Unlike the others, I appeared in the video wearing a green shirt.

But as for whether I'll be on the party's candidate list, I'll leave that question open for now, following the example of other politicians who aren't in a hurry to make such decisions or at least to announce them.

How much time do you have to make that decision?

I have exactly until the candidate lists are finalized.

And when will that happen, as far as you know?

I don't know off the top of my head right now. But I have time.

--

World.title: Ukraine says two soldiers died after arrested girl sent Russian poison
World.content:
Kyiv – Ukrainian police said Friday they had detained a 17-year-old girl suspected of helping Russia’s security services to poison Ukrainian soldiers and that two had died.

Ukraine and Russia have throughout their war since 2022 accused each other of recruiting minors for sabotage acts including poisoning.

The girl, who was not named, is suspected of having packaged deadly drugs and sending them to Ukrainian soldiers she contacted by Telegram, said a police statement.

She was arrested by police in Zhytomyr, west of Kyiv, after allegedly following instructions from a Russian handler in exchange for at least 5,000 hryvnias ($111), they said.

After receiving packages with “free drugs”, the soldiers were “instructed to take them on camera”, the statement said.

“The recipients did not know that the capsules contained a lethal dose of methadone,” it said, adding that “two soldiers died from poisoning in the Zhytomyr region.”

Police said they had identified other recipients of the packages, which “prevented four more murders” across the country.

“The young woman was notified that she is suspected of aiding and abetting the premeditated murder of two people as part of a prior conspiracy,” the police statement said.

She was also suspected of “shipping drugs and psychotropic substances for the purpose of distribution”, it said, adding that she faced up to 15 years in jail if found guilty.

Police cautioned that Russia aims “to kill our people and destabilise the situation within the country”.

“Do not accept medication or other substances, as well as food or drinks of dubious origin, from people you do not know well,” police cautioned.

Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian authorities say they have opened thousands of investigations into collaboration with the enemy, and frequently arrest individuals accused of working for Moscow.

In 2023, Ukraine accused Russia of poisoning the wife of Kyrylo Budanov, who was then head of Ukraine’s military intelligence and is now a presidential advisor.

World.title: Volvo Cars shares plunge on losses, job cuts
World.content:
Stockholm – Shares in Swedish carmaker Volvo Cars plunged Friday after it said US tariffs and strong competition from local brands in China pushed it into a third-quarter loss.

The company also said it would cut about 2,500 jobs worldwide.

Volvo Cars, controlled by Chinese group Geely, reported revenue of 66.9 billion kronor ($6.7 billion) for the third quarter, down nearly 23 percent from the same period last year.

It swung to a net loss of 5.7 billion kronor for the quarter from a net profit of 4.5 billion kronor a year earlier.

Shortly after 0800 GMT, Volvo Cars shares were down almost 30 percent.

“We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change,” chief executive Hakan Samuelsson said in a statement.

In response, the company announced a new five-billion-kronor savings plan it said would lead to about 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and 500 more globally, “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The company, which had bet heavily on electric vehicles, said the removal of consumer incentives for EVs in the United States under President Donald Trump had also hit its margins.

In 2024, Volvo Cars dropped a plan to transition to exclusively EV sales by the end of the decade.

“We are convinced that we have the right long-term strategy addressing these challenges,” Samuelsson said.

“However, in the short term, with severely challenged volumes, we need to reinforce our turnaround plan with additional decisive actions, lowering our break-even point and improving cash flows to make us more resilient.”

Struggling along with other European auto companies in the face of a difficult global landscape, Volvo Cars last year announced an 18-billion-kronor cost-cutting plan.

The company said in September that Samuelsson would resign when his contract ends, with Skoda Auto CEO Klaus Zellmer set to replace him “no later” than October next year.

World.title: France braces for new protests as Macron seeks to restore order
World.content:
Paris – France was on Friday bracing for a weekend of new protests after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, as President Emmanuel Macron sought to reclaim the initiative and restore order.

Macron, who on Thursday announced that only union demonstrations would be authorised this weekend, was to hold a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and also meet security forces.

He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked a movement that has broadened nationwide into a show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.

The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.

Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.

Macron is due to announce “additional decisions” after hosting the meeting of his defence council, on top of the limited curfews already announced, his office said.

At the meeting with students, “we will present our demands to him — which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system,” Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP.

Pierre Sourzat, who heads the organisation Les Lyceens (The High School Students), was sceptical: “He’ll listen to us, pretend he’s understood us, and then nothing will come of it.”

Macron’s government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.

In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.

On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, accusing “ultra-left” groups of having sought to “bring down the republic” last weekend.

– ‘Police have a responsibility’ –

Demonstrations in Marseille in the south and Lyon in the southeast have been banned at the weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.

Marseille authorities however reversed a decision to halt all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.

Some 20 percent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.

“In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.

The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government’s debt pile also troubling investors.

A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.

It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 percent of the vote.

World.title: Kering shares tumble as Gucci fails to reassure investors
World.content:
Paris – Kering shares were down more than 10 percent in Paris Friday after the French luxury group published results that failed to reassure investors about a turnaround at its key Gucci brand.

At 0730 GMT, Kering shares were down 10.8 percent at 190.40 euros, their lowest since June 2025. The market’s CAC40 index was down 0.3 percent.

Kering reported late Thursday that third-quarter sales were flat at 3.34 billion euros ($3.75 billion).

Sales at Gucci, by far the group’s largest single brand, fell by four percent to 1.29 billion euros, worse than the three-percent decline registered in the second quarter.

“Gucci has not shown convincing signs of stabilisation,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note.

Italy-based Gucci is key to Kering’s fortunes, but has been in freefall since 2023 as the brand lost its luxury cachet.

World.title: West Bank attack wounds 5 as Israel PM cancels events
World.content:
Hebron – An attack in the occupied West Bank wounded at least five Israelis on Friday and touched off a shootout that ended with two suspected Palestinian assailants dead, prompting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cancel political events days ahead of elections.

An AFP journalist who witnessed the firefight saw two Palestinian men in casual attire and armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city of Hebron.

The journalist reported that Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers, their two lifeless bodies on the ground next to a petrol station as Israeli troops patrolled in all directions.

The Israeli military said soldiers had rushed to the Judea Junction area, also known as the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint, after the early-morning shooting attack.

“IDF (Israel Defense Forces) soldiers eliminated two terrorists and continue searches in the area,” it said in a statement.

The initial shooting wounded five people, two of whom were in critical condition, said Magen David Adom, Israel’s emergency medical rescue service.

The Magen David Adom said one of the victims was a man in his 20s in “very serious condition” with gunshot wounds.

Netanyahu, running for a new term in elections on Tuesday, called for all political meetings to be cancelled Friday due to the attack.

Israeli National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir, who has been rising in the polls, called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be dismantled because of the attack.

“The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarized, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” he said in a statement.

No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian government in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was connected to Friday’s attack.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, praised the response by troops.

“Like all Israelis, I pray for the complete and quick recovery of the injured,” he said.

The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters, and days ahead of Israeli elections.

According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

World.title: South Korea proposes holding border talks with North
World.content:
Seoul – South Korea proposed on Friday military talks with North Korea to “mutually confirm the precise location” of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, after an explosion in the DMZ further strained relations.

Tensions between the two Koreas have soared since the South last month blamed the blast inside the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating the countries on landmines laid by the North, an accusation it has fiercely rejected.

The South Korean defence ministry “formally proposes holding military talks with North Korea to mutually confirm the precise location of the land Military Demarcation Line (MDL) and discuss ways to restore military communication lines and prevent accidental clashes in border areas,” Kim Hong-cheol, deputy defense minister for policy, told reporters Friday.

The proposal comes just days after Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, announced that Pyongyang had moved new troop units into “firing position” along the border.

Seoul’s defence ministry said Friday it was difficult to predict “what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed”.

The ministry said that “three-way talks involving the United Nations Command would also be possible”.

“Specific dates and locations could be discussed through Panmunjom,” said Kim, referencing the symbolic truce village where troops from both Koreas stand face-to-face.

He added they hoped for “a positive response from North Korea”.

The South Korean defence ministry also noted that talks proposed last year with the North did not get a response from Pyongyang.

– Grave situation –

Seoul’s military on Tuesday accused Pyongyang of attempting to shift the blame for escalating military tensions, while confirming the use of loudspeakers and warning shots as “legitimate defensive measures to prevent North Korean troops from crossing the MDL and to drive back troops that have crossed it”.

Jin Yong-sung, chairman of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, also ordered the military to “respond with firm resolve” should North Korea use Seoul’s actions as a pretext for aggressive action.

Pyongyang has rejected claims it was behind the explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers inside the DMZ and mockingly dismissed calls for an apology.

The country on Monday called the situation along the border “grave”, saying it was considering deploying additional “tactical strike means” to the area.

On Thursday, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border “within days” and had put unspecified “new counter means” on alert.

South Korea’s foreign ministry also said Thursday it planned to send a letter to the president of the UN Security Council later in the day over the landmine incident, which it called a “clear violation of the armistice agreement”.

President Lee Jae Myung has called for the North to return to dialogue, an overture Kim Yo Jong later slammed as “the climax of the farce”.

World.title: Asian football endorses Infantino re-election as FIFA president
World.content:
Tokyo – The head of the Asian Football Confederation on Friday said the region supported Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president following fierce criticism of his aborted World Cup selloff plan.

The 56-year-old Swiss was present at a Tokyo meeting of the AFC when president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa gave his unequivocal backing.

The AFC in August had joined UEFA (Europe) and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) in condemning Infantino over his plan to open FIFA’s premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino has faced calls to quit and has lost the support of many associations in his bid to be re-elected to a fourth and final term.

“I think that we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as FIFA president,” said Sheikh Salman, in a significant boost to Infantino’s prospects.

“I think you’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent.

“I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear.”

Hinting at previous discord, Sheikh Salman told the AFC Extraordinary Congress and Infantino: “Gianni, yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past.

“But let’s not relate the two things together. We need to move forward… football is strongest when we work together.”

Infantino, who apologised last week for the failed project, has headed FIFA since 2016 and is running for re-election in March.

The deadline for submitting candidacies is November 18.

No heavyweight candidate has put themselves forward to run against him so far, despite outspoken condemnation especially from Europe.

Many leading European national associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino over controversies including his relationship with US President Donald Trump.

World.title: Rooney calls United squad ‘selfish babies’ after Fernandes criticism
World.content:
Manchester – Manchester United great Wayne Rooney has labelled the current squad “babies” and “selfish” after a humiliating Champions League capitulation and post-match criticism by Bruno Fernandes of manager Michael Carrick.

Carrick’s men are 13th in the Premier League ahead of Sunday’s visit by Bournemouth and could drop into the bottom three if results go against them this weekend.

With the club beset by infighting and off to their worst domestic league start for decades, Carrick was left clinging to his job after the 4-1 defeat at Como on Wednesday.

Deepening the sense of crisis, the captain Fernandes afterwards took aim at his manager’s tactics, saying United had to be more “brave”.

Defender Lisandro Martinez last week criticised the club’s board for not investing enough in the transfer market.

Rooney, United’s all-time leading goalscorer, said he was in “shock” and “disbelief” at the Como display.

A friend and ex-teammate of Carrick, former striker Rooney pointed the finger at the players.

“When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart,” Rooney told The United Stand podcast on Thursday.

“That was the start. We’ve seen it now with Bruno and you’re going to see it with more players because these players, they don’t want to take responsibility.

“You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.”

He added: “These players, they’re selfish. They don’t care about their team-mates, don’t care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

“If they’re not getting what’s right for them, they’re like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves.”

World.title: 'Always respected': Uttarakhand CM Dhami calls Daler Mehndi days after on-stage row
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

on Friday spoke with singer Daler Mehndi over the phone, days after a controversy erupted over a cabinet minister reprimanding the singer on stage during an event.

According to the CMO, Dhami inquired about Mehndi's well-being and told the artiste that Uttarakhand upholds the rich tradition of 'Atithi Devo Bhava'.

"Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami spoke with singer Daler Mehndi over the phone to inquire about his well-being. During the conversation, the chief minister also discussed the events of the past few days. The chief minister stated that Devbhoomi Uttarakhand upholds the rich tradition of 'Atithi Devo Bhava'," the Uttarakhand chief minister's office said.

"He emphasised that folk culture, warm hospitality, and a spirit of harmony form the distinct identity of Devbhoomi, where art, culture, and artists have always been welcomed and respected," it added.

The controversy erupted after Uttarakhand minister Subodh Uniyal went on stage and expressed displeasure while Mehndi was performing at the Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair, a cultural event organised by the Uttarakhand government at Narendra Nagar in the New Tehri area on Sunday night.

The minister, however, defended his decision to reprimand Mehndi on stage, saying the artiste should not have performed if he was unwell.





"Daler Mehndi, being a big name, was invited to the Kunjapuri Fair. But during the performance, it became apparent that he was only lip-syncing and not singing. I, being a local representative and also associated with the organising committee, felt the pressure from people who wanted this to be questioned," Uniyal said.

"Mehndi was not able to speak or walk. At that point, I thought he was under the influence of some substance.

I don't know what, because a medical examination was not conducted," he added.

Meanwhile, several people from the entertainment industry, including actor Anupam Kher, stand-up comedian Vir Das and singers Shaan, Palash Sen, Gurdas Maan and Alisha Chinai, came out in support of Mehndi. They said the artiste, who has been singing for three decades, was unwell, did not drink and should have been treated with greater respect.

World.title: ‘Murder of democracy’: Raj Thackeray targets BJP over ‘Rs 500 crore payment’ audio clip
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

(MNS) chief

on Friday accused the

of "murdering" democracy by allegedly exerting pressure on the media and using religious polarisation to divert public attention. The barb came after an audio clip triggered a political row over claims of a Rs 500 crore payment to Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange.

In a post on X, Thackeray said the 29-minute recording, which has gone viral in Maharashtra, allegedly featured BJP office-bearers, a senior Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) functionary and social media influencers discussing political strategies, media pressure and ways to divert attention from sensitive issues by fuelling religious polarisation.

âThe chief minister has tried to buy time by saying heâs called for a forensic report on the audio clip, making a show of justice,â Thackeray said, referring to Maharashtra chief minister

Devendra Fadnavis

's announcement of a forensic examination.

âBut if you actually listen to the conversation in this, youâll realize itâs nothing short of a murder and rape of democracy itself!â he added.

Thackeray said the alleged Rs 500 crore payment mentioned in the recording required an explanation but argued that the broader allegations about attempts to influence the media and public discourse also deserved scrutiny. He urged Fadnavis to investigate the conversations allegedly captured in the clip, rather than limiting the inquiry to verifying the recording's authenticity.





The controversy erupted after Jarange released a portion of the recording on Thursday, alleging a conspiracy to silence him and weaken his agitation for Maratha reservation. In one segment, a woman allegedly claims that Rs 500 crore had been delivered to Jarange through Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Shinde, son of deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde.

The recording also purportedly contains discussions about Jarange's growing political influence ahead of the 2024 Maharashtra assembly elections and strategies to counter his agitation in the Marathwada region.

Shiv Sena leaders have also sought an investigation, while BJP leaders have questioned the recording's authenticity and the timing of its release. World.title: 'Movement will continue': Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das appear before SEM
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka and

appeared before the special executive magistrate on Friday.

After appearing before the magistrate, Ranka said the movement would continue whether the CJP leaders were in jail or outside.

"There was a verification process for our sureties. Everything went well, and we have been given a new date sometime in the third week of November," Ranka said.

âThe movement will continue. We are not leaders; we are custodians of this platform that the people of this country have given us, and we are just trying to do our best. The movement will continue whether we are in jail or outside. We have learnt a lot about ourselves and how the regime operates.

We will, of course, change and evolve as necessary,â he added.

The development follows their release from judicial custody after a special executive magistrate court accepted their personal and surety bonds and recorded their written undertakings to maintain peace and abide by the law.

SEM Ritu Raj directed Ranka and Das to furnish personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the enquiry. They were also directed to appear on every hearing date and comply with the conditions laid down in their bonds and undertakings.





In their written undertakings, the two leaders pledged not to breach peace or disturb public tranquillity. They also promised not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law. Any future protests, they said, would be held within the constitutional framework.

âFurther judicial custody does not appear to be necessary at this stage, particularly after written undertakings before this Court,â the SEM court observed while ordering their release.
