World.title: When fear and loathing tip the scales
World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor When fear and loathing tip the scales Jordan Baker October 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Most Australian MPs’ paths to parliament are via well-honed political structures. From youth branch to staffer to elected office, perhaps via a union or a private firm run by party powerbrokers. This has, rightly, prompted community concerns that MPs are too deeply entrenched in their political bubble to have much experience of life outside it. Helen Haines came to parliament armed with decades of expertise in healthcare, as well as a deep understanding of and love for regional Australia. Alex Ellinghausen Helen Haines is not that kind of politician. She grew up on a dairy farm in Victoria, and became a nurse and midwife. Few professions are more exposed to the challenges faced by ordinary families than frontline health workers. One can only imagine the joys and agonies Helen saw daily while working with women and babies, and the empathy and patience she needed to guide them through. She came to parliament armed with decades of expertise in healthcare, as well as a deep understanding of and love for regional Australia. As an independent, she was free of the baggage of party affiliations, and able to develop her own positions on issues. She did so thoughtfully and bravely. Australia could do with more politicians with the life experience, rigour and integrity of Helen Haines. But after Monday’s attack, women who might be thinking of following in her footsteps would be forgiven for deciding that the cost of entering public life is too high.



We’ve heard myriad stories this week about skyrocketing threats to the safety of Australia’s politicians, and women seem to be disproportionately targeted. NSW National Party MP Nichole Overall was targeted by a nasty, threatening meme. Alex Ellinghausen On the eve of the attack on Helen Haines, someone posted a meme to a NSW National Party MP Nichole Overall’s social media page saying, “not enough politicians are afraid for their lives right now and I think that’s a problem.” On Wednesday afternoon, a man was charged for making threats and swinging nunchucks outside West Australian MP Hannah Beazley’s office. After calling for a return to civility, Governor-General Sam Mostyn was abused on her social media account. Public life is hard enough. Politicians have always had to deal with political ruthlessness, job insecurity and public criticism, and it’s worse for women (including Queen Victoria, as Julia Baird wrote today). But if you add this relatively new element of living in fear, the scales tip heavily against giving it a try. A Women for Election survey of women who have been elected or are running for office found 90 per cent have experienced online abuse. Fifty per cent are questioning whether they would run again, or should have run in the first place.



There are no simple solutions. More civility from our political classes might improve the tone from the top, but the barometer of what’s acceptable has shifted so significantly in Australia and overseas – the mockery of Jacqui Lambie’s vaginal prolapse in a One Nation video is just one example – that change would need a level of multilateral agreement that we have yet to see, despite Monday’s shocking attack. Jacqui Lambie was mocked by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson over her personal health issues. Alex Ellinghausen Even if politicians lifted their tone, the malaise runs deep. I remember a time when we could disagree. Now, however, there are many who interpret a different opinion as a personal insult, and respond to this perceived insult with not only explosive fury, but also threats of – and sometimes actual – violence. To these people, the offence comes not from the nature of the opinion expressed, but from the fact it was expressed at all. Law enforcement bosses have repeatedly warned about the real-life impact of violent words, and how an environment with increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation have made violence seem permissible. And this is happening in an era in which we have less and less in common as a society, and live within our own algorithms, which keep reinforcing our worldview. Perhaps Australians are losing their tolerance of opposing views because they have less exposure to them. As Waleed Aly wrote today, “focusing on [how politicians respond to these crises of violence] can be a form of self-exoneration, as though citizens are not participants in our political culture … yes, it matters how we speak to one another. But maybe the problem is we’re too obsessed with speaking. It might matter even more how well we listen.”



The Sydney Morning Herald supports plans to allow Australians to opt out of algorithms, because we should be allowed the choice. Any insistence that we stay in these vortices against our will is its own limitation of freedom. Related Article Haines attack Haines pursues a political experiment – that decent people can disagree. Has this attack changed that? The Herald will also continue to publish a range of views on topics, because we believe our readers are broad-minded, educated adults who are able to weigh perspectives and make their own decisions. We also believe democracy is stronger for having an informed voting public. We know some readers disagree with some of the opinions we publish or express, but we also know you have the intellectual bandwidth to consider those views anyway, and make your own decisions. We welcome your thoughtful feedback when you disagree. Our thoughts are with Helen Haines and her family. Monday’s attack was a dark day for our democracy. Hopefully, Australia responds by focusing on the myriad factors that contributed to it, and making an effort to address them. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: ‘No information, no nothing’: The surprise move to phase out this type of school
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaSchools ‘No information, no nothing’: The surprise move to phase out this type of school Bridie Smith and Jackson Graham October 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Schools in Melbourne’s west are facing a shake-up as part of a government restructure that has blindsided teaching staff and prompted fears of job losses. Under the plan, announced by Point Cook MP Mathew Hilakari on Friday, schools in his electorate that serve year 10 to 12 students will become secondary schools spanning years 7 to 12. Under the plan, Alamanda College in Point Cook could have a primary and a secondary campus. Luis Enrique Ascui The change means the prep to year 9 feeder schools will become dedicated primary schools. Hilakari said every school in his electorate would transition within the decade, and the new system would prevent students who attended some primary schools from having to move schools twice during their time at secondary school.



“The community raised this issue in the time I’ve been in parliament,” he said. “And their main question is: why P-9s and why here?” However, Victorian Association of State Secondary Principals president Belinda Hudak said the announcement had followed a lull in consultation. “There had been some initial conversations, and then it went quiet for a while, and then suddenly it came to an outcome,” she said of the announcement. “Our preferred process is always that school communities and principals are part of final decisions.”



Hudak said it was vital that future changes be made in a staged manner and in consultation with the community. The change will start with Homestead Senior Secondary College in Point Cook, which will transition from a year 10 to 12 school to a year 7 to 12 school by 2028. Saltwater P-9 College, which shares a campus with Homestead, will become a dedicated primary school within three to five years. Like many schools in the city’s inner west, Saltwater P-9 College has recorded rapid growth. It opened in 2019 with 580 students and by last year it had 2199 students. Hilakari said some P-9 schools had already expressed a preference to become standard primary schools in the near future, but acknowledged there would be some locals hesitant about the change. “Every transition is going to have some challenges, and we are up for working through that with the community,” he said. “While we’ve got some indicative timings on it all, we’re open to a conversation with each school.”



A staff member at one of the schools, speaking anonymously to protect his employment, said staff had been blindsided by the announcement, which had prompted fears of “massive job losses”. Related Article Education ‘Bursting at the seams’: The schools that can’t keep up with student growth “This is the biggest change to schools in years with absolutely no evidence for change apart from a bogus survey,” he said. He said impacted schools had been left with more questions than answers. “There has been no information, no budget. No nothing. Just a ‘this is what we are doing’,” he said. Hilakari said the Department of Education would work closely with schools, including teachers, who “we could do with more [of] if anything”.



In emails to staff on Friday, seen by this masthead, principals said the change was designed to ensure consistency across Melbourne’s western metropolitan area. Principals at the affected schools met their leadership teams on Friday morning after emailing news of the changes to staff. Alamanda K-9 College principal Lynette Jobson said that while details were still to be finalised, it could mean that the single campus school of 3335 students could end up with a primary and a secondary campus. “Everyone has received the news, and we understand what it is about,” she said. “It’s five years away for us, so we have time to digest it.” Enrolments at the Point Cook school have grown by more than 300 per cent since it opened in 2013. However, Jobson said the school had not reached its capacity of 3700 students.



Point Cook Senior Secondary College, which has more than 770 students in years 10 to 12, is expected to become a year 7 to 12 school within three to five years. Melbourne’s western growth corridors are facing a school enrolment surge , driven by rapid population growth in local government areas such as Wyndham, Melton and Hume. Opposition education spokesman Brad Rowswell said locals shouldn’t have uncertainty about schools just weeks out from the state election. “Victorian parents and students in Melbourne’s west have every right to be confused and disappointed in the Victorian Labor government,” he said. A government spokesperson said that no schools would close and that the consultation process was ongoing.

From pools to spas to ponds to water views, being around water can be calming and relaxing, and research suggests it helps relieve stress and improve sleep and focus. Beyond the personal benefits, water features can also attract wildlife, create an aesthetic focal point, and add value when it comes time to sell. Here are five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy. 26 Mary Street, Longueville, NSW



Designed to be surrounded by water, three-bedroom home “Four Waters” truly lives up to its name. The gas- and solar-heated swimming pool is the centrepiece, with an internal bridge spanning the pool and connecting the home’s two wings. Complementing this are the spa, koi pond, and wide river views from the elevated aspect. Other highlights include curved glass, clerestory windows, polished timber parquetry floors, and a location within walking distance of Longueville Wharf and Lane Cove. 41 Crammond Avenue, Bundeena NSW



It may be on the Bundeena waterfront, but this newly built property has been inspired by the Bahamas. Given its position, the views are spectacular. The north-facing position offers 180-degree panoramas across Bundeena and Port Hacking to the Royal National Park, Manly and Cronulla. Private stairs lead directly to a sandy beach and picturesque rock pool, or you can walk the 500 metres (approximately) to Horderns Beach. The property also features a sunken spa and waterfront terraces including a cantilevered deck that appears to float above the water.



33 Bradleys Head Road, Mosman NSW This Federation residence is positioned on a corner block with landscaped gardens, an east-facing terrace and a saltwater pool. It features period details including sculpted arches, leadlight glazing, pressed-metal ceilings and marble fireplaces, while upstairs there are harbour views. The kitchen has been updated with refined stone, Miele appliances and a walk-in pantry.



The property is located close to Clifton Gardens Reserve, Bradleys Head, Mosman Village and Taronga Zoo Wharf. 9 Fowler Crescent, South Coogee NSW Designed in 1966 by renowned Sydney architect Hedley Carr, this is the first home built on one of South Coogee’s most coveted family streets, Fowler Crescent. Set on an elevated position, it showcases indoor-outdoor living through floor-to-ceiling glazing and ocean views.



The home features natural materials including restored Tasmanian oak floors, original parquetry, Roman clay walls and travertine rosso. Outside, the original kidney-shaped solar-heated pool is surrounded by established gardens. 35 Bishops Avenue, Randwick NSW This Californian bungalow welcomes you with its original double-fronted 1920s frontage and a water feature.



At the rear, floor-to-ceiling windows look out onto the landscaped garden, entertainer’s deck, lush lawn and heated mosaic-tiled pool. Bifold doors open from the open-plan living, dining and kitchen to an outdoor bar and al fresco with an auto roof and a nearby underground 600-bottle cellar. There is also an outdoor shower in which to wash off before heading inside. The home’s interiors have been updated for modern living, including a kitchen with a waterfall island, a top-floor parents’ retreat with a study, and burnished concrete floors in the entryway. The location, just a short walk from Clovelly Beach and Bronte, is also a notable feature.

A court order to pay $10 in damages hasn’t wiped the smile off Rebel Wilson’s face as she emerged victorious in a bitter legal spat with her latest film’s co-producers. The Pitch Perfect star directed, co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US. Loading Filmed on a $22 million budget, The Deb made just $335,000 at the local box office and is yet to screen outside Oceania. Wilson’s co-producers allege that shortfall could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.



The Bridesmaids star claimed in July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money, and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star. Related Article Updated

Defamation ‘Grateful’ Rebel Wilson thanks judge after defamation case thrown out The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could buy it from them. On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden awarded the trio a mere $10 in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons in the NSW Supreme Court. Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.



Peden awarded her $359,000 plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgement. Wilson took to Instagram to welcome the victory with a photo of herself in a graduation gown holding a degree from the University of NSW. “This girl never knew how much she was going to need that law degree!!” she wrote. “I spoke up because I believed there were serious concerns that needed to be raised on my film The Deb.



“Defending myself has come at an enormous personal, emotional, and financial cost. But I’m proud I stood my ground – for myself and for others I was trying to protect.” Wilson said she struggled to remain positive throughout the proceedings and thanked her family and followers for their support. Rebel Wilson outside the Federal Court in Sydney in May. Dominic Lorrimer It’s the second victory for Wilson after she was cleared of defaming her debut film’s star, Charlotte MacInnes, earlier this year following a fiery Federal Court hearing. MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.



The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together. MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ms Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023. That decision is under appeal. AAP Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Millions have watched Livi’s struggle online. It’s taken a heartbreaking turn
World.content:
NationalNSWCancer Millions have watched Livi’s struggle online. It’s taken a heartbreaking turn Jack Gramenz October 23, 2026 — 7:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Byron Bay teen documenting his treatment for a rare and aggressive brain tumour has taken a heartbreaking turn as his family reveal he cannot walk or talk as he undergoes treatment in the United States. Olivier “Livi” Eddington, 17, was diagnosed earlier this year after he started getting headaches. He has been participating in a clinical trial in the hope it will give him a chance to beat the condition. Loading Livi has been chronicling his journey on TikTok, posting video updates which garnered millions of views as he participates in the CAR T-cell trial at the University of North Carolina, home to the Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Centre. “These experimental treatments involve re-engineering cells from the patient’s immune system to recognise and direct the attack against the patient’s cancer,” the centre says.



The cells are collected and sent to a lab where genetic information is added, along with “chimeric antigen receptors” – a type of synthetic protein. Hundreds of CAR T-cell clinical trials have taken place around the world, the majority of them focused on blood cancers such as leukemia, but some have also focused on solid tumours and other conditions. Despite some encouraging signs, Livi has also experienced multiple seizures, spending time in an induced coma and in intensive care. Livi’s family say he will now undergo radiation treatment amid an “extremely serious” situation. An online fundraiser has raised more than $148,000 to support Olivier “Livi” Eddington’s treatment costs in the US. “Unfortunately, Olivier’s condition has continued to deteriorate, and things are really not looking good right now,” the Eddington family revealed through an online fundraiser this week.



“He is now unable to walk, talk, roll over in bed by himself, or even drink water properly. “The simplest things that we all take for granted have become incredibly difficult for him. “It is absolutely heartbreaking watching someone so young, strong, and full of life go through this. “He is only 17 years old and has already fought harder than anyone should ever have to.” The fundraiser has so far raised more than $148,000 towards its $160,000 goal to help cover treatment costs in the US. Any remaining funds will be donated to brain cancer research.



A community fundraiser at Byron Bay High School also raised more than $35,000 earlier this month. Eddington has been sharing his cancer journey online, garnering millions of views. TikTok/@livi.eddington “Our small town has truly come together to support one of its own, and we are so grateful for everyone’s generosity and care – it really means a lot,” the school said. “We have a few bald staff members around our school today – they’ve shaved their heads in support of Livi and to show him he’s not alone in this fight.” Livi’s father, Blake, told NBN News earlier in October the teen started having headaches in January, before a tumour was found during a brain scan. He was diagnosed with a high-grade glioma, a fast-growing and aggressive, cancerous tumour.



The rare tumours are primarily diagnosed in adolescents and young adults, according to a review of research published in a Nature partner journal in 2025. Livi has been documenting his treatment online. “I’m 16 years old with brain cancer, and this is what I did today,” he says in the first video in a series on “beating brain cancer”, which has had more than four million views. “I sat in hospital all day, felt pretty shit, it’s affected me heaps.” A few days after the first video, Livi was in a medically induced coma after a series of seizures as his 17th birthday approached.



He returned on camera for day eight of his journey. “Sorry about yesterday, sorry I didn’t post, I’ve been unwell,” he said. “Had a seizure and was in a coma for a few days but I’m now way better,” he said. On the fundraising page Livi says surfing was his “whole life” and it “honestly sucks” that he can’t surf at the moment, but hopes he will again one day. “My balance is cooked and my brain doesn’t work the way it used to … but getting back in the water is one of the things keeping me going.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio and city planner Carlos Moreno had positive things to say about Melbourne, but both agreed that Federation Square needs a makeover.

Having attended the opening session of the Melbourne Assembly at the square, I can only agree that it is looking tired and forsaken – there are few open cafes or restaurants and the aluminium cladding is looking weathered and cheap. As a gateway to the city the Taxi pub building remains a nondescript disappointment and access to the river is obstructed.

That’s not to say it isn’t a marvellous asset for the city – where it works, it works well. But it shouldn’t be regarded as set in stone (or aluminium) – it should be thought of as a work in progress adapting to the city’s needs. We should heed the advice of our objective visitors and take the opportunity to make Federation Square the world-beating icon it could be.

Bruce King, Malvern East The health benefits of tree canopy

Heatwaves kill more Australians than bushfires, floods and storms combined, yet we are sleepwalking into a scorching El Nino summer (“Experts sound health alarm over hot summer”, 22/10). Trees are one of our best defences, cooling streets and homes, and the Victorian government’s 500,000 new trees across Melbourne are welcome. But every development that bulldozes established trees undoes that work, and our overall tree canopy keeps shrinking.

Protect the trees we have. Build homes with light-coloured roofs that reflect heat, and add proper cooling. Open cool refuges for those most at risk. And make sure our hospitals are ready for the surge. Heat is a silent killer, and we need to start talking about it.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Labor’s housing narrative is troubling

The narrative surrounding the demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers is deeply troubling, particularly given the gusto with which the Labor government has pursued this policy. The article “Hundreds of market rate rentals but no public housing” (17/9) highlights the contradiction at the heart of this issue. Labor has shifted substantially from its historical position on the left towards a political centre increasingly shaped by the imperatives of capitalism, at the expense of public housing, welfare and education. These are fundamental responsibilities of a government that previously claimed to represent working people.

Travelling regularly through the CBD, I see growing numbers of people experiencing homelessness. At a time of escalating housing insecurity, the demolition of public housing raises serious questions about our collective priorities and the kind of society we are prepared to accept. I can no longer vote for a party whose policies appear so far removed from the social values it once represented. While the Greens do not align with all my views, they at least offer a clear commitment to addressing many of these concerns.

Rozalind Drummond, North Carlton



THE FORUM The right priority

The Snowy Hydro upgrade is now estimated to cost up to $25billion (″⁣Huge setback as Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b″⁣, 23/10). For this investment, the country gets an important power generation facility that has very little ongoing environmental impact, and will operate for 100 years.

The estimated cost of the AUKUS deal is $368 billion, a figure that will probably increase dramatically. For this spend our country becomes a potential nuclear target, and gets an arguably 20th-century military deterrent, which will be obsolete before it is paid for. I know which investment seems good value to me.

Mike Francis, Fitzroy Words matter

ASIO boss Mike Burgess has repeatedly conveyed concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse.

It starts in parliament with the normalisation of extreme rhetoric in parliamentary debate, or what passes for debate today. Question time especially is characterised more by point scoring, personal insults and mindless character assassination than by any genuine attempt to debate policy. Many (most) politicians today appear to have lost the capacity to debate, reliant on dot points and staying on message. Genuine intellectual engagement rarely happens.

Democracy worldwide is under threat and Australia is no exception. ″⁣Words matter,″⁣ says Burgess. It’s time our parliamentarians acknowledge this and resolve to ″⁣debate with respect and disagree with restraint″⁣.

Difference and diversity are our future.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Error of his ways

After the release of jailed American Stephen Hubbard, according to Donald Trump, “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia.” (″⁣Russia releases retired US teacher″⁣, 23/10).

Of course, this ignored the removal of sanctions on Russia and the purchase of diesel to bolster Russia’s war machine. This is nothing, according to Trump – but the rest of the world knows otherwise.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Touch of madness

How amazing that it is only recently that the risk from touch screens in cars is receiving the attention it deserves (“Experts hit alarm button on touchscreens risk”, 23/10). I have been arguing for years that they are a dangerous distraction to driving. There should be no need for studies and data gathering on the topic as anyone who has driven a modern car knows how distracting touch screens are.

We are banned from using mobile phones while driving for good reasons, but in many ways screens are a worse distraction. Any function that is accessed while in motion should be operated via a button or a dial. The reasons car makers prefer screens is that are much cheaper to design and install and they look modern. Virtually every car designed this century comes with a dangerously distracting touch screen.

It’s time to go back to the days of common sense car designs or ahead to driverless cars.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne



Cuts are coming

The public finance guru ″⁣who did the numbers for Kennett and Andrews″⁣ is canvassing ″⁣belt tightening″⁣ (″⁣State heading for big bill″⁣, 23/10). As a former public servant who barely survived Kennett’s mayhem, I can only read that as meaning one thing for public servants, and that’s voluntary and involuntary retrenchments.

I expect the first action of a Liberal/One Nation government will be to establish an ″⁣audit committee″⁣, which will announce that the finances are ″⁣much worse than we thought″⁣.

David Fry, Windsor Tax the rich

Dear Premier Carroll, please do not sell any more assets owned by Victorians. The proposed sale of the vegetable market will just add a profit margin, add to inflation and continue the reckless and destructive neo-liberal policies that have reduced Australia – and the world – to their current parlous conditions. Tax the rich, not the poor.

Ian Porter, Kensington Offshore operations

Many of us, myself included, assume that most companies providing services to Australians are Australian. I recently had a billing issue with my energy provider. Imagine my surprise to learn that the person trouble-shooting my issue was based in South Africa and that the company providing my energy was Chinese-owned.

Ewa Haire, Moonee Ponds Don’t cut taxes

It is disingenuous (Letters, 22/10) to interpret Ross Gittins’ opinion piece (21/10) that a 15 per cent GST will do nothing to balance the budget as a criticism of excessive government spending. It is quite clear that the reason the Grattan plan would not assist budgetary repair is that it recommends (unnecessarily in my view) that the largest share of revenue gain from an increased GST should go to tax cuts, not to government spending on income support for lower-income households as your correspondent implies.

As other correspondents have explained recently, Australia, by international standards, is a low-tax country. Further reducing taxes will not address the budget deficit and will handicap the ability to supply the education, healthcare, aged care and housing services that the electorate wants and needs.

Terry Burke, Cape Paterson Living with the cuckoos

Reports that Starlink has degraded the service provided to the Ukraine military such that they are less likely to intercept Russian drones should be a wake-up shout to the Australian government and military.

What is being done to reduce any reliance that we have on Starlink for our defence? Anyone who thinks that this could not happen to us because of treaties or that our ″⁣friends″⁣ would never do that to us is living in cloud cuckoo land.

David Robertson, Wheatsheaf



Don’t raise rates

Is the Reserve Bank part of the solution to our current woes or is it part of the problem? If the economy falls into recession, many will think the bank has failed the community. Increasing interest rates to high levels has many adverse effects, including increased unemployment, and an even larger intergenerational gap between young and old in so many areas. Also, increased disenchantment in these uncertain times can result in a downward pressure on innovation and productivity.

A 2 per cent to 3 per cent inflation rate would, of course, be good to have but is it really feasible in times like these?

I would suggest that interest rates should now be regarded as at a peak. Further increases will add to frustration and anger. Overseas, that has led to upheavals in democracies, which we want to avoid here.

John Kent, Mornington No taste

Pauline Hanson said the video about Jacquie Lambie’s vaginal prolapse ″⁣wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been″⁣. Would she please explain how you can tastefully mock or trivialise someone’s vaginal prolapse?

Angela O’Connor, Glen Iris Sage advice

At a wedding in 1968, which I can still clearly see, the minister at the altar meets the gaze of the young couple after declaring them “man and wife”.

Looking at them over the top of his glasses, he kindly says he has three words of advice for them: “Watch. Your. Words”.

This is now a long time ago, but his advice could continue to be heeded and spread to all humanity. Words, said and written, are powerful and they truly matter especially in these troubled times.

Helen Clements, Mount Waverley Behave, you’re not MPs

When my year 10 students were acting up I would say (rather forcefully) to them, “Behave yourselves! Where do you think you are, parliament?“

Mary Rice, Greensborough Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING Foreign affairs

David Shoebridge says the Greens do not support giving military aid to Ukraine. That puts him in the same bracket as Donald Trump.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully An ″⁣entente cordiale″⁣ between Russia and the US based on lies, deception and self-interest where the betrayal of allies barely gets a mention. Donald Trump will go down in history, just not in the way he imagines.

Claude Miller, Castlemaine Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian″⁣. Did I miss something, US special envoy Steve Witkoff?

David West, Essendon Furthermore

Faced with a choice between a Labor frying pan and Coalition or One Nation fire at the state election next month, voters might be wise to stick with the frying pan (“Voters signal end for Labor”, 22/10).

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills



To your letters correspondent (PM, act on gambling, 22/10) I’d say: Don’t bet on it.

Marlene Krelle, Surrey Hills With the predicted El Nino drought, we won’t need Pauline Hanson to drain the swamp (″⁣Experts sound health alarm over hot summer″⁣, 22/10).

Alan Boltman, Blackburn South I was shocked to see a photo of the data centre in West Footscray dwarfing the adjacent residential houses. How was planning permission ever given? Buildings of this size should be in paddocks far away. And do we really need them?

Alec Dean, Soldiers Hill The person trapped in their flooded car (“ABC reporter saves man as car sinks”, 23/10) was lucky. All vehicles should be designed with a way of opening a window manually from the inside. I carry a brick under the seat.

Graham Patterson, Briar Hill In what profession can you fail all your major KPIs, yet still receive your maximum salary? The Australian men’s first XI.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Finally

After the horror of the past week I rejoined The Cloud Appreciation Society. I urge readers to look to the skies and ground themselves.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove

World.title: With Leichhardt Oval out of action, Tigers in talks to take home game to New Zealand
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 With Leichhardt Oval out of action, Tigers in talks to take home game to New Zealand Christian Nicolussi October 23, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. As Leichhardt Oval undergoes a much-needed $40m revamp, the Wests Tigers are exploring the possibility of taking a home game to the deep south of New Zealand next year. Sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly confirmed the Tigers have been deep in discussion with Dunedin officials about playing a “home game” at Forsyth Barr Stadium. Benji Marshall is sure to prove popular in Dunedin. Jamie Brown/SMH Canterbury and the New Zealand Warriors played an NRL game at the same venue, which includes a glass roof, in 2017. The sources confirmed the Tigers had originally been approached about playing a game in Christchurch, which would help promote the region and its push to be included as the NRL’s 20th team.



There was even talk about playing the game against the Warriors in the middle of June when Origin II takes over the Warriors’ Auckland backyard for the first time. The idea was for travelling Australian fans to spend a few extra days on local soil to take in a club game. The Tigers fielded similar interest from stadium officials in Hamilton, then Wellington, before Dunedin put together a strong proposal in the last fortnight. The club was not commenting when approached for comment, while representatives at Forsyth Barr Stadium did not return calls. The sources confirmed the stadium was also in talks with two powerhouse out-of-Sydney NRL clubs playing a pre-season trial in late February. A refurbished Leichhardt, which includes a new northern grandstand, and significant improvements to the main western grandstand, will be ready for the Tigers at the start of the 2028 season – but the club is now working through its potential venues for next year.



Campbelltown, the club’s other spiritual base in south-western Sydney, will host up to six games before it gets its own renovation in 2028. Parramatta’s CommBank Stadium is expected to host as many four games, even though fans have shown a reluctance to embrace the home of their bitter western Sydney rivals Parramatta, while the Tigers enter the final year of taking a “home” game to Suncorp Stadium for Magic Round. The Bulldogs played at Forsyth Barr Stadium in Dunedin in 2017. Teaukura Moetaua They will be the away team when they meet Melbourne in Las Vegas. Regional NSW, especially Mudgee, has been prepared to pay decent money for clubs to take NRL games to their towns, but the appetite from the other side of the Tasman is growing, especially with the interest in the Southern Orcas – not to mention the excitement and success of the Warriors.



Related Article NRL 2026 The contract clause that shows how serious Cody Walker is about steering Souths to a title Tigers coach Benji Marshall remains hugely popular with New Zealand sports fans on both islands. The Tigers on Thursday confirmed gun back-rower Samuela Fainu had inked a two-year extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029. New recruit Tyson Frizell is playing with Tonga, but with his involvement in Newcastle’s grand final campaign, and the fact he is a veteran player, which means he is entitled to extra leave, the forward will only have a few weeks of pre-season training before returning to Vegas for a second straight year.

World.title: ‘No information, no nothing’: The surprise move to phase out this type of school
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaSchools ‘No information, no nothing’: The surprise move to phase out this type of school Bridie Smith and Jackson Graham October 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Schools in Melbourne’s west are facing a shake-up as part of a government restructure that has blindsided teaching staff and prompted fears of job losses. Under the plan, announced by Point Cook MP Mathew Hilakari on Friday, schools in his electorate that serve year 10 to 12 students will become secondary schools spanning years 7 to 12. Under the plan, Alamanda College in Point Cook could have a primary and a secondary campus. Luis Enrique Ascui The change means the prep to year 9 feeder schools will become dedicated primary schools. Hilakari said every school in his electorate would transition within the decade, and the new system would prevent students who attended some primary schools from having to move schools twice during their time at secondary school.



“The community raised this issue in the time I’ve been in parliament,” he said. “And their main question is: why P-9s and why here?” However, Victorian Association of State Secondary Principals president Belinda Hudak said the announcement had followed a lull in consultation. “There had been some initial conversations, and then it went quiet for a while, and then suddenly it came to an outcome,” she said of the announcement. “Our preferred process is always that school communities and principals are part of final decisions.”



Hudak said it was vital that future changes be made in a staged manner and in consultation with the community. The change will start with Homestead Senior Secondary College in Point Cook, which will transition from a year 10 to 12 school to a year 7 to 12 school by 2028. Saltwater P-9 College, which shares a campus with Homestead, will become a dedicated primary school within three to five years. Like many schools in the city’s inner west, Saltwater P-9 College has recorded rapid growth. It opened in 2019 with 580 students and by last year it had 2199 students. Hilakari said some P-9 schools had already expressed a preference to become standard primary schools in the near future, but acknowledged there would be some locals hesitant about the change. “Every transition is going to have some challenges, and we are up for working through that with the community,” he said. “While we’ve got some indicative timings on it all, we’re open to a conversation with each school.”



A staff member at one of the schools, speaking anonymously to protect his employment, said staff had been blindsided by the announcement, which had prompted fears of “massive job losses”. Related Article Education ‘Bursting at the seams’: The schools that can’t keep up with student growth “This is the biggest change to schools in years with absolutely no evidence for change apart from a bogus survey,” he said. He said impacted schools had been left with more questions than answers. “There has been no information, no budget. No nothing. Just a ‘this is what we are doing’,” he said. Hilakari said the Department of Education would work closely with schools, including teachers, who “we could do with more [of] if anything”.



In emails to staff on Friday, seen by this masthead, principals said the change was designed to ensure consistency across Melbourne’s western metropolitan area. Principals at the affected schools met their leadership teams on Friday morning after emailing news of the changes to staff. Alamanda K-9 College principal Lynette Jobson said that while details were still to be finalised, it could mean that the single campus school of 3335 students could end up with a primary and a secondary campus. “Everyone has received the news, and we understand what it is about,” she said. “It’s five years away for us, so we have time to digest it.” Enrolments at the Point Cook school have grown by more than 300 per cent since it opened in 2013. However, Jobson said the school had not reached its capacity of 3700 students.



Point Cook Senior Secondary College, which has more than 770 students in years 10 to 12, is expected to become a year 7 to 12 school within three to five years. Melbourne’s western growth corridors are facing a school enrolment surge , driven by rapid population growth in local government areas such as Wyndham, Melton and Hume. Opposition education spokesman Brad Rowswell said locals shouldn’t have uncertainty about schools just weeks out from the state election. “Victorian parents and students in Melbourne’s west have every right to be confused and disappointed in the Victorian Labor government,” he said. A government spokesperson said that no schools would close and that the consultation process was ongoing.

World.title: Five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy Shona Hendley October 23, 2026 — 7:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. From pools to spas to ponds to water views, being around water can be calming and relaxing, and research suggests it helps relieve stress and improve sleep and focus. Beyond the personal benefits, water features can also attract wildlife, create an aesthetic focal point, and add value when it comes time to sell. Here are five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy. 26 Mary Street, Longueville, NSW



Designed to be surrounded by water, three-bedroom home “Four Waters” truly lives up to its name. The gas- and solar-heated swimming pool is the centrepiece, with an internal bridge spanning the pool and connecting the home’s two wings. Complementing this are the spa, koi pond, and wide river views from the elevated aspect. Other highlights include curved glass, clerestory windows, polished timber parquetry floors, and a location within walking distance of Longueville Wharf and Lane Cove. 41 Crammond Avenue, Bundeena NSW



It may be on the Bundeena waterfront, but this newly built property has been inspired by the Bahamas. Given its position, the views are spectacular. The north-facing position offers 180-degree panoramas across Bundeena and Port Hacking to the Royal National Park, Manly and Cronulla. Private stairs lead directly to a sandy beach and picturesque rock pool, or you can walk the 500 metres (approximately) to Horderns Beach. The property also features a sunken spa and waterfront terraces including a cantilevered deck that appears to float above the water.



33 Bradleys Head Road, Mosman NSW This Federation residence is positioned on a corner block with landscaped gardens, an east-facing terrace and a saltwater pool. It features period details including sculpted arches, leadlight glazing, pressed-metal ceilings and marble fireplaces, while upstairs there are harbour views. The kitchen has been updated with refined stone, Miele appliances and a walk-in pantry.



The property is located close to Clifton Gardens Reserve, Bradleys Head, Mosman Village and Taronga Zoo Wharf. 9 Fowler Crescent, South Coogee NSW Designed in 1966 by renowned Sydney architect Hedley Carr, this is the first home built on one of South Coogee’s most coveted family streets, Fowler Crescent. Set on an elevated position, it showcases indoor-outdoor living through floor-to-ceiling glazing and ocean views.



The home features natural materials including restored Tasmanian oak floors, original parquetry, Roman clay walls and travertine rosso. Outside, the original kidney-shaped solar-heated pool is surrounded by established gardens. 35 Bishops Avenue, Randwick NSW This Californian bungalow welcomes you with its original double-fronted 1920s frontage and a water feature.



At the rear, floor-to-ceiling windows look out onto the landscaped garden, entertainer’s deck, lush lawn and heated mosaic-tiled pool. Bifold doors open from the open-plan living, dining and kitchen to an outdoor bar and al fresco with an auto roof and a nearby underground 600-bottle cellar. There is also an outdoor shower in which to wash off before heading inside. The home’s interiors have been updated for modern living, including a kitchen with a waterfall island, a top-floor parents’ retreat with a study, and burnished concrete floors in the entryway. The location, just a short walk from Clovelly Beach and Bronte, is also a notable feature.

A court order to pay $10 in damages hasn’t wiped the smile off Rebel Wilson’s face as she emerged victorious in a bitter legal spat with her latest film’s co-producers. The Pitch Perfect star directed, co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US. Loading Filmed on a $22 million budget, The Deb made just $335,000 at the local box office and is yet to screen outside Oceania. Wilson’s co-producers allege that shortfall could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.



The Bridesmaids star claimed in July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money, and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star. Related Article Updated

Defamation ‘Grateful’ Rebel Wilson thanks judge after defamation case thrown out The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could buy it from them. On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden awarded the trio a mere $10 in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons in the NSW Supreme Court. Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.



Peden awarded her $359,000 plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgement. Wilson took to Instagram to welcome the victory with a photo of herself in a graduation gown holding a degree from the University of NSW. “This girl never knew how much she was going to need that law degree!!” she wrote. “I spoke up because I believed there were serious concerns that needed to be raised on my film The Deb.



“Defending myself has come at an enormous personal, emotional, and financial cost. But I’m proud I stood my ground – for myself and for others I was trying to protect.” Wilson said she struggled to remain positive throughout the proceedings and thanked her family and followers for their support. Rebel Wilson outside the Federal Court in Sydney in May. Dominic Lorrimer It’s the second victory for Wilson after she was cleared of defaming her debut film’s star, Charlotte MacInnes, earlier this year following a fiery Federal Court hearing. MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.



The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together. MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ms Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023. That decision is under appeal. AAP Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Millions have watched Livi’s struggle online. It’s taken a heartbreaking turn
World.content:
NationalNSWCancer Millions have watched Livi’s struggle online. It’s taken a heartbreaking turn Jack Gramenz October 23, 2026 — 7:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Byron Bay teen documenting his treatment for a rare and aggressive brain tumour has taken a heartbreaking turn as his family reveal he cannot walk or talk as he undergoes treatment in the United States. Olivier “Livi” Eddington, 17, was diagnosed earlier this year after he started getting headaches. He has been participating in a clinical trial in the hope it will give him a chance to beat the condition. Loading Livi has been chronicling his journey on TikTok, posting video updates which garnered millions of views as he participates in the CAR T-cell trial at the University of North Carolina, home to the Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Centre. “These experimental treatments involve re-engineering cells from the patient’s immune system to recognise and direct the attack against the patient’s cancer,” the centre says.



The cells are collected and sent to a lab where genetic information is added, along with “chimeric antigen receptors” – a type of synthetic protein. Hundreds of CAR T-cell clinical trials have taken place around the world, the majority of them focused on blood cancers such as leukemia, but some have also focused on solid tumours and other conditions. Despite some encouraging signs, Livi has also experienced multiple seizures, spending time in an induced coma and in intensive care. Livi’s family say he will now undergo radiation treatment amid an “extremely serious” situation. An online fundraiser has raised more than $148,000 to support Olivier “Livi” Eddington’s treatment costs in the US. “Unfortunately, Olivier’s condition has continued to deteriorate, and things are really not looking good right now,” the Eddington family revealed through an online fundraiser this week.



“He is now unable to walk, talk, roll over in bed by himself, or even drink water properly. “The simplest things that we all take for granted have become incredibly difficult for him. “It is absolutely heartbreaking watching someone so young, strong, and full of life go through this. “He is only 17 years old and has already fought harder than anyone should ever have to.” The fundraiser has so far raised more than $148,000 towards its $160,000 goal to help cover treatment costs in the US. Any remaining funds will be donated to brain cancer research.



A community fundraiser at Byron Bay High School also raised more than $35,000 earlier this month. Eddington has been sharing his cancer journey online, garnering millions of views. TikTok/@livi.eddington “Our small town has truly come together to support one of its own, and we are so grateful for everyone’s generosity and care – it really means a lot,” the school said. “We have a few bald staff members around our school today – they’ve shaved their heads in support of Livi and to show him he’s not alone in this fight.” Livi’s father, Blake, told NBN News earlier in October the teen started having headaches in January, before a tumour was found during a brain scan. He was diagnosed with a high-grade glioma, a fast-growing and aggressive, cancerous tumour.



The rare tumours are primarily diagnosed in adolescents and young adults, according to a review of research published in a Nature partner journal in 2025. Livi has been documenting his treatment online. “I’m 16 years old with brain cancer, and this is what I did today,” he says in the first video in a series on “beating brain cancer”, which has had more than four million views. “I sat in hospital all day, felt pretty shit, it’s affected me heaps.” A few days after the first video, Livi was in a medically induced coma after a series of seizures as his 17th birthday approached.



He returned on camera for day eight of his journey. “Sorry about yesterday, sorry I didn’t post, I’ve been unwell,” he said. “Had a seizure and was in a coma for a few days but I’m now way better,” he said. On the fundraising page Livi says surfing was his “whole life” and it “honestly sucks” that he can’t surf at the moment, but hopes he will again one day. “My balance is cooked and my brain doesn’t work the way it used to … but getting back in the water is one of the things keeping me going.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Chief of Defence resigns over 'inappropriate relationship'
World.content:
The Chief of Defence Air Marshal Tony Davies has resigned over questions of integrity, Defence Minister Paul Goldsmith says.

The issues make his role no longer tenable and it has been referred to the Inspector General of Defence.

"Air Marshal Tony Davies has informed me that he'll be resigning from his position as Chief of Defence Force, effective immediately.

"The reasons regarding his decision relate to integrity matters, that he did not previously disclose. We both agree his position is no longer tenable.

"I will be recommending to the Governor-General that she accepts Mr Davies' resignation."

In a statement, Davies said the matters involve an "inappropriate relationship".

"The resignation is for personal reasons, and results from errors of judgement made by me in the past, for which I am taking responsibility. The errors of judgement were contrary to the values of the Defence Force.

"These matters revolved around an inappropriate relationship I had when in a position of unit command, and I regret not disclosing this when I had the opportunity to do so."

The Defence Force said arrangements were underway to transition responsibilities to the vice chief of Defence Force, Rear Admiral Mat Williams, who will serve as acting chief of Defence Force.

Former Defence Minister Ron Mark, who is standing for New Zealand First again this election, said the circumstances surrounding the resignation needed to be thoroughly investigated - including what was known about the matter and when.

Mark said the resignation pointed to a possible failure of Defence Force processes.

World.title: Fetū Samoa thrash Wales in 14-try World Cup romp
World.content:
Fetū Samoa sprung back from their first-up loss to Australia last weekend to claim their first win at the Rugby League World Cup, thrashing Wales 76-0 in Sydney on Friday night.

They created history in the process, recording their highest win at a world cup.

A dominant first half set the pace for the Samoans, who ran in seven tries in the first 35-minute spell to lead 40-0.

That was topped off by an almost faultless goal-kicking by playmaker Pauline Piliae-Rasabale, who kicked six out of the seven conversion attempts she took.

In the end, the Samoans had piled on 14 tries to nil, 10 of which were converted.

Captain Evania Isa'ako said post-match the team played well and deserved the win.

"Really proud of the effort the girls put in tonight," she said.

"All our debutants that debut at this world cup, really proud of them.

"They really put their best foot forward."

Player of the match Amber Hall said they had worked hard after the loss to Australia.

"I guess after last week we worked pretty hard to get here today and the girls put it on and how good.

"It's been pretty good; we had talked about all the women that had come before us."

Having been unable to score a single point against the Jillaroos in round one last weekend, the Samoan women turned on the firepower in the first 10 minutes of Friday's clash.

Two early mistakes ruled by the referee meant Samoa did not complete their first two sets.

But once Laikha Clarke crashed through to score close to the left post after a good Samoa attack in the seventh minute, the floodgates opened.

Piliae-Rasabale kicked the conversion and Fetū Samoa were up 6-0.

Wales tried to piece moves together but it was ruthless from the Samoans who just kept applying the pressure, showing power and strength from their forwards and an entertaining backline that ran the ball at every chance.

Samoan forwards Annetta Nu'uausala, Mary-Jane Taito, Laikha Clarke, Leilani Wilson, Ivana Lolesio and Tavarna Papalii kept the ball tight and ran through the Welsh defensive line, setting up play deep inside their opponents' half.

One such move in the 12th minute saw Piliae-Rasabale feed Tyra Ekepati, who stepped in and out before diving over the line in the right corner for the team's second try.

Then it was Destiny Mino Sinapati's turn two minutes later before Ekepati got her second for the night.

Amber Hall of the Sydney Roosters, playing her third World Cup, burst her way through after coming off the bench, to score Samoa's fifth try, before the 2026 NRL-W Rookie of the Year, Newcastle Knights' Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, dotted down for her try in the 31st minute.

Hall was the provider again in the last seconds of the first half, running through the Welsh defensive line, before setting up Ivana Lolesio for the team's seventh try, as Samoa led 40-0 at the breather.

Dominance continues

The second half saw Wales getting some possession early, trying to get some territorial gain.

But Samoa's defence stood out, keeping Wales in their own half.

They went straight back to where they left off in the first half, with captain Isa'ako, a former World Cup winner with Australia, picking up the ball and diving over the line to claim her try.

Hall was at it again a few minutes later with another strong run through, before she offloaded to Monica Tagoai, who stepped in and dived over to score Samoa's ninth try.

The try of the match would have been Sinpati's second, after she had collected the kick from Wales near Samoa's tryline before running through from one end of the field to the other to score.

Then it was Taulelei-Siala's turn to claim her second for the night, after Nu'uausala ran through the defense and offloaded.

Eighteen-year-old Freedom Crichton Ropati scored her first try for Samoa with 11 minutes to play after she finished off another Samoan attack.

That was followed by 19-year-old Ekepati, who finished off another exciting Samoa move, before Tavarna Papali'i sent the Weslh defence the wrong way with her dummy and ran over to score her team's final for the night.

Samoa dominated the run metres, recording 2,136m against Wales' 596m.

World.title: Fire and Emergency New Zealand chief executive Kerry Gregory resigns
World.content:
The chief executive of Fire and Emergency New Zealand has resigned.

Kerry Gregory's resignation was announced by Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) board chairperson Raveen Jaduram on Friday afternoon.

Jaduram said Gregory had resigned "effective immediately" from his role.

"Mr Gregory says that, in the light of of the Minister of Internal Affairs' recent public statement that she did not have confidence in him, it has become untenable for him to remain in his role.

"The Board wishes to acknowledge and thank Mr Gregory for his 36 years of dedicated service, including a very lengthy period as an operational firefighter, and wishes him well for the future."

Darry Purdy would remain as acting chief executive and Megan Stiffler as national commander.

Friday's announcement came after RNZ lodged enquiries about Gregory's employment status earlier this week.

Minister of Internal Affairs Brooke van Velden, said she was advised of the resignation by the board on Friday afternoon.

"I expect the Board to manage the leadership transition appropriately and ensure the organisation remains focused on delivering for firefighters and communities."

Before Gregory's resignation he had been on extended leave for more than a month.

FENZ declined to say whether Gregory was on paid or unpaid leave.

The New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union said Gregory's resignation should be the catalyst for massive and sweeping change for FENZ.

The union's national secretary Wattie Watson said Gregory's position was untenable.

NZ Professional Firefighters Union nation secretary Wattie Watson. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"This is incredible it took more than a month to happen quite frankly. I think there needs to be a proper full investigation. Those that have been enabling him to undertake the damaging policies and in his words vision that he had also need to come under strong scrutiny," she said.

Watson said Fire and Emergency was in a "dire situation".

"This should herald in wide sweeping changes. In the very least the board now needs to stop the changes that he was pushing through including the restructure, including the attacks on emergency response," she said.

"We would welcome the opportunity to meet with them to reset not only the bargaining but where this organisation needs to head."

Van Velden publicly withdrew her confidence in Gregory on September 17, accusing him of withholding significant information from her for a year.

She described his conduct as a "serious breach of trust", saying he failed to notify her despite being advised that he should.

Van Velden subsequently told RNZ's Morning Report that Fire and Emergency had been breaching the law governing levy collections.

The agency confirmed a "historical" matter relating to the administration of its levy scheme had been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

World.title: Wellington social housing sale: Living there 'changed my life' councillor says
World.content:
A Wellington councillor says living in a block of social houses at the centre of a controversial sale changed the course of his life.

Labour's Paekawakawa/Southern Ward councillor Nureddin Abdurahman said Kāinga Ora's decision to sell the sites on 6,8,4 Nuku Street in Strathmore was personal for him, after he and his family lived in one of the units between 2010 and 2019.

"It was crucial because I had nothing.

"It changed my life."

Having arrived in New Zealand from Ethiopia in 2008 to join his wife who had a refugee background, Abdurahman said he was driving taxis at night and studying during the day at Victoria University when he lived in the Strathmore flats.

He said he couldn't afford to rent on the private market at the time, and it gave him the chance to "navigate through and get to my potential".

"I had my kids there, so it gave me an opportunity to spend more on food instead of going to the private market."

Nureddin Abdurahman in social housing at Nuku Street, where he lived with his family between 2010 and 2019. RNZ / Supplied

Abdurahman said he contested the idea that people got trapped in social housing, and that it had helped him gain a higher tertiary education with a master's degree, going onto his career in national and local politics.

He said he forged strong friends there, recounting a former neighbour called Chris who he had shared food and money with when times were tight, and who had tracked him down during Covid, asking if his family had enough to get by.

"Those people are my family."

He was among 11 Labour/Green members of Wellington City Council, including Mayor Andrew Little and Deputy mayor Ben McNulty, who signed a letter to the minister and associate minister of housing Chris Bishop and Tama Potaka, as well as Kāinga Ora chief executive Tracey Taylor.

"Why [is Kāinga Ora] selling when there are hundreds of people sleeping on our streets? For me it doesn't make sense," Abdurahman said.

Protest signs erected by Strathmore Housing Action on the Nuku Street public housing blocks. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But not all city councillors agree on the issue.

Wharangi/Onslow-Western Ward councillor Diane Calvert said she did not sign the open letter, because she wanted the council to focus on its own housing portfolio.

The council needed to make sure it could meet its own commitments under the Deed of Grant with government, she said.

"We have tenants living in our own substandard housing and I think our efforts are better directed to ensuring council housing upgrades occur as quickly as possible and at a minimum cost to ratepayers."

The council had recently reached an agreement with Kainga Ora regarding a scaled back development in Arlington Street in Mount Cook, she said.

Housing minister Chris Bishop has declined to comment on the sale, saying it was "an operational decision for Kāinga Ora".

The deadline sale - which was for 21 October - sparked community and political backlash - including from Wellington City Mission, Downtown Community Ministry, Pōneke Public Housing Futures, Strathmore Housing Action. Residents protested and sat in at the site earlier this week.

RNZ earlier walked inside the properties, where mould flaked from the ceilings, paint was peeling, and puddles of rainwater collected on the floor.

Fences have been erected around the Nuku Street social housing complex since the sit-in event RNZ / Supplied

On Friday, fences had been put up outside the blocks.

Kāinga Ora regional director for Greater Wellington Sarah Willson said earlier this week the agency had no plans to review the sale at Nuku Street.

"We understand the strength of feeling in the Strathmore community about the Nuku Street site and recognise how important public housing is to Wellington," Willson said.

Willson had earlier said that developing the site into social housing was not financially viable, but that other buyers may see potential in it.

She said a scaled back plan for 37 homes on the nearby Ngatiapa Street would still go ahead, and that any money from Nuku Street would go back into the homes.

Willson would not reveal how many offers the site had, saying that could jeaopardise the sale process, and saying the next step in the sale process could take several weeks.

World.title: Police and Oranga Tamariki launch joint investigation into tutor
World.content:
Police and Oranga Tamariki are jointly investigating a community-based tutor.

They said the person has previously taught at a number of schools and community organisations in the Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions.

Detective Inspector Kevin McNaughton said the two agencies have been working with schools and the Ministry of Education to identify children who may have had contact with the tutor.

They have also been meeting with affected families to explain the process of the investigation.

"Our focus is on ensuring that enquiries are conducted thoroughly, professionally and with the wellbeing of children at the centre of the process."

McNaughton said police and Oranga Tamariki have begun meeting with affected families to explain the investigative process.

"Parents and caregivers are being asked not to question their children about the matter or undertake their own enquiries. We appreciate that parents naturally want answers and reassurance. However, conversations of this nature are best undertaken by trained professionals to ensure children's wellbeing is protected and information obtained is as reliable as possible.

"Police emphasise that being contacted as part of the investigation does not mean that any particular child has been harmed."

McNaughton said the investigation has involved extensive engagement with schools, providers and community organisations, all of which have been cooperative and supportive of police enquiries.

When contacted by RNZ the Ministry of Education said, "We're working with police, Oranga Tamariki and schools to support families who are being contacted as part of this process while enquiries continue. Because this is an active investigation, we can't comment on the specifics of the case."

Anyone with information should contact the police by calling 105, or via 105 online, referencing file number 260919/1953.

World.title: Explainer: The 10 biggest questions New Zealand has about the election
World.content:
Explainer: With about two weeks until we decide who the next government will be, New Zealanders still have questions.

A lot of them.

As the election enters the home stretch and early voting is about to begin, we take a look at the most frequent questions being asked.

After a dive into some analytics, we found 10 of the most common NZ election questions being asked out there in cyberspace on Google, Copilot and ChatGPT - and the answers.

When is Election Day?

Saturday, 7 November... coming your way before you know it.

What is an election?

There are no stupid questions here.

An election is how we choose our government, and we'll be deciding if the current National-led coalition will get a second term or if the opposition led by Labour will form the next government.

We'll elect 120 members of Parliament (and possibly more, if you start getting into overhangs, which are a whole thing you can read about here).

How can I enrol?

It's easy and it's free, and if you haven't done it yet, time is running out.

In case you missed it, the rules this year have changed and there will be NO enrolling in the early voting period or on election day.

That means, if you haven't enrolled by midnight on Sunday, 25 October, you're out of luck.

How to enrol to vote: Visit the Electoral Commission website and put in your details.

"This weekend, we'll be at events around the country to help people enrol or check their details. You can also drop off an enrolment form at one of our hubs. Locations and hours are available on vote.nz," Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne told RNZ.

Youth enrolment rates for those aged 18-24 are particularly bad this year, so if you're in that demographic and on the fence, you're almost out of time before Sunday night's deadline.

Early voting begins on Monday. Samuel Rillstone/RNZ

When does voting start?

You can find your local voting place details here. You can also call the Electoral Commission on 0800 36 76 56 to find a polling place.

Votes will be taken at a total of 2638 locations during the voting period.

Early voting then continues right until election day, Saturday, 7 November, when places will be open from 9am to 7pm.

Pool / STUFF LTD

How does MMP work?

'Mixed Member Proportional' is New Zealand's system that allows you to vote for both local electorate candidates and also whatever party you support.

Read RNZ's full explainer here on just how MMP works and what it means for how our election results will be determined.

What are the main parties' policies and how do they differ?

There have been a flood of announcements by all the parties in the last several weeks and it's impossible to keep up.

If you want to know the positions on cost of living, climate change, health, AI or a heap of other topics, we'd suggest a good place to start is RNZ's handy-dandy policy guide, which gathers up information the parties have announced.

You can also find more about party positions on their official websites.

Each local electorate has different candidates. RNZ / Nik Dirga

Who are my candidates?

First, you need to know what electorate you're in. If you're not sure, you can check that through the Electoral Commission website.

Once you know your electorate, you can then find out who the candidates are for both general and Māori electorates through the government's website.

Who should I vote for?

Look, we can't make these decisions for you, but a good place to start gathering information is a nonpartisan websites like Policy.nz to see what your local electorate candidates are saying about themselves. You can look up the candidate info for every electorate there.

And for broader party policies, RNZ's guide as linked above and the individual party websites are good places to go as well.

How to vote in the NZ election from overseas?

Overseas voting began this week and will end at 7pm on election day. Overseas voters who are enrolled can download their voting papers from the Electoral Commission website, fill them out and then upload them.

There are also overseas voting places available - check here to find out if there's one near you.

Labour party leader Chris Hipkins and National party leader Christopher Luxon are battling for votes, but their party votes are declining in polls.

Who is most likely to win?

It's really too close to call. It's been a tight race, but polls generally suggest National and Labour's support is cratering, while parties like the Greens and NZ First are surging, and Opportunity remains the wild card.

At this point, it's pretty hard to predict who could lead the next government.

RNZ-Reid Research's most recent polling, released 6 October, had National at 25.9 percent support and Labour at 30.8 percent, with the Greens at 14.8 percent, New Zealand First at 10.6 percent, ACT at 9 percent and hopeful newcomers to Parliament - Opportunity - at 5.5 percent, while Te Pāti Māori sits at 2 percent in the party vote.

Other polling has had similar results, with National and Labour practically tied, when you start factoring in the margin of error. The New Zealand Herald's most recent average of polls showed a near-tie between the two major parties.

World.title: Kerrin Leoni breaks silence on resignation, says whānau turned into 'political weapon'
World.content:
Kerrin Leoni says she quit as a Labour candidate to stop the controversy surrounding her association with the Mongrel Mob being used as a "political weapon" to help National win the election.

In her first public comments since resigning, Leoni said the intense focus on her whānau had become "increasingly difficult".

"I can handle the media scrutiny. I can handle the National Party attacking me. That comes with being in politics," she wrote on Facebook on Friday afternoon.

"What has become increasingly difficult is the intense focus on my whānau and community."

Leoni resigned as Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate on Friday morning, after footage emerged of her campaigning alongside Mongrel Mob members at an event in early October.

The video showed the former Auckland councillor encouraging those present to enrol to vote and change the government. A separate photograph showed her posing with people wearing Mongrel Mob regalia and making gang-related hand gestures.

Audio player for " Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni resigns over gang campaigning " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2101807%2Fkerrin-leoni-breaks-silence-on-resignation-says-whanau-turned-into-political-weapon

Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni resigns over gang campaigning Nine To Noon Download MP3 4m

Leoni said a "whānau function", attended by mokopuna, kaumātua, gang members and non-gang members had been turned into a "political weapon", used for political gain and media clicks.

"Is this really the kind of New Zealand we want to live in? Is this really the behaviour we want to model to our tamariki and mokopuna? Is this really how desperate some political leaders have become to cling onto power?"

She said she had always tried to show her family members other opportunities in the hope they would choose a different path.

"I cannot change who my whānau are or who I grew up with, nor would I ever turn my back on them."

Leoni said she was proud to have represented Labour and stood by her apology to Labour leader Chris Hipkins: "I want everyone to know that I am okay. I will be back."

Earlier on Friday, Hipkins told reporters Leoni had displayed "very very bad judgement" and had paid a "very high price" for that.

Both Hipkins and Leoni had earlier condemned Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs for visiting a gang pad this campaign.

Despite Leoni's resignation, electoral law states that she will still appear on the ballot as a Labour candidate because nominations have already closed.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407256721112

'What's good for the goose is good for the gangster'

National and ACT were both quick to seize on the past day's developments, arguing they had revealed Labour's true colours.

National leader Christopher Luxon said the "chaotic situation" proved Labour could not be trusted when it came to law and order.

"The Mongrel Mob clearly want them to be elected to power, because they know that they're soft on crime," he said.

"Even their candidates think that's okay to hang out with gang members and pal around. We don't think it is."

Luxon said National was not open to engaging with gangs in any capacity: "I am not tolerant of gangs at all. I have no time for gangs."

He rejected Hipkins' claim that there was a racist element to the response: "It's a crime issue... not a race issue."

National leader Christopher Luxon said the "chaotic situation" proved Labour could not be trusted when it came to law and order. RNZ / Lillian Hanly

ACT leader David Seymour also came prepared to his daily media conference with a string of one-liners. He said the saga showed that the Labour did not truly believe that gangs were bad.
