"[Leoni] has revealed that what's good for the goose is good for the gangster," he said.

"You've got a real possibility that the Labour Party is being funded by P money, and I don't mean the artist from the 1990s."

Hipkins earlier said he had been assured that the function was not a fundraiser.

NZ First leader Winston Peters struck a different tone from his coalition partners, saying his party would not be "gloating" or "salivating over somebody else's misery".

"I'm trying to focus on the issues of those who are still on the ballot, not those who are not."

Peters stressed NZ First was "utterly opposed" to gangs and had no sympathy for the argument that they were the "victim of colonisation".

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi accused the political right of exploiting the controversy. RNZ / Rachel Moore

'A sad day for Māori'

In a separate social media post, senior Māori Labour MP Willie Jackson said the loss of Leoni as a candidate was a "real shame" but she "sadly made the wrong call".

"I want to congratulate Kerrin for her courage," he wrote. "She did not want to get in the way of us trying to get rid of this rotten government, and she knew the Nats would come after her if she stayed a candidate."

Te Pāti Māori defended Leoni, with co-leader Rawiri Waititi describing her resignation as "a sad day for Māori".

"Our whānau do not stop being our whānau because they wear a patch, and our responsibility to them does not disappear because someone finds their presence politically inconvenient."

Waititi accused the political right of exploiting the controversy to divide parties seeking to replace the government.

"The right benefits every time we turn on each other, and we will not give them that victory."

He urged voters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to Labour or the Greens.

"We can disagree on how this has been handled without losing sight of what unites us. Our people cannot afford another three years of this Government."

Green co-leader Chloe Swarbrick declined to weigh in on the saga, saying she was focused on the issues that matter: "Most people are kind of sick and tired of this one."

Former Māori Party co-leader and minister Te Ururoa Flavell said Leoni's resignation was inevitable because she was not honest with Labour leadership.

"Saying one thing and doing another was probably the biggest sin," he told RNZ's Checkpoint. "Mr Hipkins probably didn't have too many choices on the back of that."

Flavell said meeting people from all walks of life, including gang members, was part of an MP's job.

"To put a line in the sand and say you cannot go and talk to somebody about voting, for goodness sake, seems way out of order."

He said politicians from both major parties had met gang members before, including former prime minister Rob Muldoon.

Flavell said it was sad to see Leoni and Te Pāti Māori MPs Oriini Kaipara and Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke "hammered" for their interactions with gangs.

World.title: Sexual abuse survivor feels unable to move on as quest for compensation and apology stalls
World.content:
Audio player for " Abuse survivor fights for compensation after more than 50 years " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2106468%2Fsexual-abuse-survivor-feels-unable-to-move-on-as-quest-for-compensation-and-apology-stalls

Abuse survivor fights for compensation after more than 50 years Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Warning: This story is about sexual abuse

Sexual abuse survivor forced to deal with school where it happened frustrated over lack of progress in compensation and apology bid

Top human rights lawyers says her firm has to turn away people seeking redress from their old schools for abuse because of the volume of claims

Officials are looking into gaps in redress system, including people abused at schools

A survivor of sexual abuse at a high school more than 50 years ago is feeling frustrated and unable to move on as his quest for compensation and a meaningful apology stalls.

The man is required to deal directly with the school where the abuse happened and says he's getting nowhere.

This is all part of a redress system that a top human rights lawyer said is full of holes, although officials said they're working on improvements for survivors, including those who suffered abuse in schools.

'Affected day to day'

The man, who RNZ is calling Simon, is now aged in his mid-60s, and has spent five decades dealing with what happened to him as young teen.

"I'd just turned 13 and in the first term of the first year at Tauranga Boys' College I was groomed by one of my teachers. That continued for some time. It's something I've had to live with," Simon said.

"I've felt that it's affected me both in relationships with people and also in my formative years in trying to be able to learn and get work. I found that I didn't do very well at school, and those sorts of issues have continued through my working life."

Simon said the police approached him about eight years ago about the teacher who abused him, and he was interviewed. The teacher was now out of the country and officers didn't know where he was.

"There were times in my life where it wasn't much of a problem at all. It kind of came up and I thought about it - probably in more recent times when I hear stories of other people's sexual abuse, particularly the stories of those from Dilworth.

"There's also dealing with post-traumatic stress. Those things affect me day to day - looking at photos or even just hearing or seeing the word 'Tauranga'."

Frustration mounts as years roll on

Four years ago Simon decided to seek compensation and an apology so, as is required for survivors of abuse at high school before 1989, when New Zealand's schooling system was restructured, he approached Tauranga Boys' College.

The man has made a sensitive claim with ACC and receives counselling. But he is unhappy there is no clear process for survivors in his situation, where dealing with different schools means there are inconsistencies in how matters are resolved.

If the abuse had happened at a state primary or specialist school before 1989, or a state school that was now closed, he could have sought redress though State Redress NZ, relating to the Ministry of Education.

An Ombudsman's ruling this year found the different experiences for claimants was unreasonable.

A spokesperson from the office of Erica Stanford, the minister in charge of the response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into abuse in state and faith-based care, said that in January Cabinet "agreed to a phased approach on considering options for supporting survivors that are currently outside the scope of the state redress system".

"This includes survivors of abuse in care of non-government and faith-based organisations, and some school settings. Further advice is expected to be delivered in 2027.

"As part of this work, the Ministry of Education is leading the development of advice on possible options to support survivors of abuse in education settings who cannot currently access the Ministry of Education sensitive claims process."

The ministry confirmed: "This work includes consideration of claims that currently sit with school boards."

While that happens, however, Simon said he felt isolated in negotiating with his old school.

"I wrote to the school exactly four years ago to this month. They initially were not responsive or receptive to looking at any form of redress. We've gone through a process of them trying to verify all the facts, which I can understand.

"We have moved forward over those four years, but getting an apology and a way forward to redress has been a particularly hard thing to get."

Tauranga Boys' College principal Andrew Turner said it was in ongoing correspondence with Simon's lawyer, seeking a resolution.

"As this matter is highly sensitive and we are still working through a resolution, it is not appropriate for us to comment. The College is open and remains open to finding an appropriate resolution to [Simon's] claim."

It did not answer general questions about whether it had a process for redress claims, or if it was dealing with others.

Simon said the school offered had an apology, but he didn't think was adequate for reasons that included it being made in a letter discussing legal matters with his lawyer.

He said the school had also recently suggested that because the teacher was employed by the then-Department of Education Simon should lodge a claim with the ministry, taking him back to square one.

Law firm sees flood of survivors of abuse at schools seeking compensation

Lawyer Sonja Cooper. (File photo) RNZ / Aaron Smale

Top human rights lawyer Sonja Cooper said the education sector was a gaping hole in the redress system that people such as Simon could fall through.

"You might be lucky. You might have gone to a school that has an established redress process - it knows what it's doing and it knows how to help survivors through a process, and it has a process and it will pay redress.

"Most schools don't have any process. They're kind of shocked when these allegations come to them because, obviously, some of them can be very historical."

Her law firm, Cooper Legal, had even had to turn away people in similar situations to Simon because it couldn't deal with the volume of abuse claims, where survivors had to deal directly with schools.

"We've been flooded with Board of Trustee claims in the last year or so, and I think we've reached that point where we're saturated and we just can't deal with them all. We know there is a large cohort of survivors out there who suffered abuse in schools who want to have their claims dealt with."

Cooper said change was needed, but she wouldn't advocate that all survivors of abuse in education having to go through the ministry process because it demanded a high standard of proof and moved at a "glacial" speed.

"We are getting offers now for clients who came to us at least 10 years ago, and their claims have been sitting with the Ministry of Education for eight or nine years."

She said people getting nowhere when dealing directly with their old schools could consider complaining to the Human Rights Commission, depending on when the abuse happened, or the Teaching Council.

The ministry said it had 770 claims for redress being assessed through its process. It had settled 255 since 2010.

While he waited for an outcome for his claim, Simon said he felt like he was trapped between two locked doors, without keys to get through and move on.

"It wears me down. I've had to engage a lawyer to be able to fight the battle as well. It doesn't do my mental health any good trying to deal with a [school] board who have been resistant all the way along."

World.title: How the Western Bulldogs engineered a return to AFLW finals
World.content:
It's a story that's been told countless times. The Western Bulldogs hit rock bottom in 2023, opted to undertake a review into their program, and made wholesale change. Since then, they've made steady improvement, but that hasn't been without some rocky moments along the way.

Now, the Bulldogs are locked into finals for the first time since 2022 and present as a genuine threat in the post-season, rather than simply making up the numbers.

And while their off-field changes have been immense, and an easy starting point when it comes to analysing their improvement, what has happened on field is even more interesting.

Rock bottom

The Bulldogs finished 2023 as wooden spooners, winning one game from 10 rounds of footy just a year after reaching its second ever final. Across that season they gave up control in-game easily, and relied heavily on a small handful of players to carry the load.

This required a personnel change to start the improvement spike. A new head coach, head of footy and list manager were certainly key to the shift, but change on field was also essential.

From the playing list that reached a final in 2022 just 12 players remain, and while the club has largely focused on careful draft selections, it has also engaged in trades to add experience on top of the youth.

Listed in 2022 S7 Added since Elle Bennetts Deanna Berry Ellie Blackburn Alice Edmonds Jess Fitzgerald Elisabeth Georgostathis Isabella Grant Britney Gutknecht Sarah Hartwig Isabelle Pritchard Rylie Wilcox

Heidi Woodley Lauren Ahrens (trade) Brooke Barwick (draft) Mizuki Brothwell (draft) Cleo Buttifant (draft) Mikala Cann (trade) Dom Carruthers (draft) Ellie Gavalas (trade) Maggie Gorham (free agent) Elaine Grigg (draft) Keeley Hardingham (draft) Kaylee Kimber (replacement) Vaomua Laloifi (trade) Emma McDonald (draft) Analea McKee (trade) Charlie O'Connor Moreira (draft) Sarah Poustie (draft) Jasmyn Smith (trade) Lou Stephenson (trade) Amaia Wain (draft)

This list build has happened quietly. There are no boom recruits among the incoming trades, no premiership players or All-Australians in the mix as other clubs have targeted, but they have been specific choices to work toward the game plan.

Mikala Cann has been one of those players. Little more than a role player at Collingwood, albeit a very good one, Cann has been exactly the kind of midfielder/forward required at the Dogs to elevate the team as a whole.

The stat changing Geelong in 2026 When Geelong made the move to bring Mick Stinear to the cattery, it made a bigger difference to their 2026 season than any player movement could.

Outside of this, the club's capacity to improve some down-and-out senior players has also been important.

Mua Laloifi has emerged on the other side of an ACL injury in close to her best career form, offering important intercepting strength behind the ball, and Ellie Gavalas has spent a couple of years in the wilderness but now adds some leadership and ground-level speed in the forward half.

And the draftees have been carefully selected. Although some choices haven't quite come on in the way the club would have hoped — every club has been burned by a speculative pick here or there — others have been the ideal slow burn.

Emma McDonald and Elaine Grigg were arguably the Dogs' biggest-name draftees across this period, but others like Cleo Buttifant and Dom Carruthers have complemented the growth of the list.

The Bulldogs are becoming a team that is clearly greater than simply the sum of its parts. The puzzle as a whole works well together.

Build defence

The traditional route for a club's rebuild is to start with defence, then add attack, and that's exactly the direction the Bulldogs went once Tam Hyett was appointed coach in 2024.

They were coming off a base that was easy to win the ball against, easy to maintain momentum against, and ultimately far too easy to score against.

Taking back control

Avg disposals conceded Avg uncontested possessions conceded Avg disposal efficiency conceded (%) Avg marks conceded 2026 236.4 120.6 61.8 51.2 2025 241.1 124.9 62.0 44.4 2024 241.9 128.5 63.0 50.2 2023 269.4 155.9 66.6 56.2

Finding that defensive mindset isn't simply about establishing a strong backline, rather as the numbers above suggest, it is about making the game scrappy at times to prevent the opposition from clean access at the footy.

No longer are the Bulldogs walkovers around the footy, or easy to maintain possession against around the ground. When a team plays the Bulldogs, they are to expect a battle around the contest and pressure on the outside.

This, then, leant into tightening up on the scoreboard.

Becoming harder to score against

Avg points against Avg I50s conceded Avg marks I50 conceded Avg shots per I50 conceded (%) Avg shots on goal conceded 2026 32.3 32.5 7.7 36.9 12.0 2025 32.1 28.1 4.8 38.6 10.8 2024 41.9 31.5 7.4 43.1 13.6 2023 59.5 37.5 11.3 52.3 19.6

To get here they played some admittedly ugly footy (everyone remembers that 2024 game against the Bombers), but the first step in the plan has been the foundation upon which everything else has been built. And although some of those numbers have swung slightly back up (specifically inside 50s and marks inside 50 conceded), this has been a result of now working to find the balance between defence and attack.

Learn to attack

In Hyett's first year at the helm, the Bulldogs had their worst year in attack since the AFLW began, averaging just 26.5 points per game. Things seemed bleak and the end of the tunnel felt a long way away. But steadily, on top of that tightening defence, they have also found their own confidence to attack.

As with the defensive tightening, the first part is establishing more control through the middle of the ground, then the next layer is engaging those forwards close to goal to actually get scores on the board.

Winning the footy

Avg handballs Avg kick rate (%) Avg uncontested possessions 2026 120.3 55.5 148.4 2025 99.8 59.6 122.8 2024 70.7 64.4 95.2 2023 93.1 61.8 135.3

Getting their hands on the footy has been a key part to winning back control throughout games, but part of that has also been a shift in how they want to use the ball.

Instead of dump kicking the ball long to escape danger or opting for long down-the-line kicks to a contest where they can compete again, the Dogs are now establishing a clear handball game; moving neatly from layers around the contest via hand and looking for the running handball receive option to add speed on the ball.

That outside ball has been a huge growth area as they develop more confidence in their game style, and for the first time since 2022 the club is averaging a positive uncontested possession differential.

Kicking a winning score

Avg points for Avg I50s Avg shots on goal Avg shots per I50 (%) 2026 45.5 32.9 14.8 20.1 2025 40.6 34.3 14.6 16.1 2024 26.5 27.0 9.3 13.5 2023 32.0 27.4 10.8 16.4

A whole new forward line has been built, with Sarah Hartwig becoming the club's all-time leading goalkicker back in round nine, and Emma McDonald posting the most goals of any Dog in 2025, her debut season.

It has been a calm, steady club-wide build that has flown under the radar in the context of the wild swings that occur in the AFLW, but it has been done for the long haul.

And in a fortnight, the Dogs will get a chance to show their wares in finals, and are a good chance of winning their first final since their flag in 2018.

World.title: Man United legend lashes current players for behaving 'like babies'
World.content:
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney has labelled the club's current players selfish, lashing them for behaving "like babies" after captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the coaching staff's tactics following their Champions League thrashing by Como.

Fernandes said United failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding in the second minute, as Thursday morning's 4-1 loss intensified scrutiny of manager Michael Carrick.

United's collapse at Como left them staring at another damaging result, with only a stoppage-time goal from Joshua Zirkzee reducing the margin of defeat.

Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss Bruno Fernandes takes aim at Michael Carrick as Manchester United's horrible start to the season goes from bad to worse in the Champions League.

The criticism follows signs of growing frustration within the squad. Earlier this month, defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy after a 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, saying he expected greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast on Thursday.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno, and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

Wayne Rooney (right) was a long-time teammate of current United boss Michael Carrick (left). (Getty Images)

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their teammates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Carrick, a former United midfielder who played alongside Rooney at Old Trafford, was appointed on an interim basis following Ruben Amorim's dismissal in January before earning a contract through 2028 after overseeing a dramatic improvement in results.

Carrick is under growing pressure with United winless in seven matches across all competitions. They are 20th in the Champions League standings and 13th in the Premier League.

Reuters

World.title: Trump calls LeBron 'total disgrace' over perceived anthem disrespect
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warm-ups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia's season opener on Wednesday AEDT.

"I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video.

"LeBron James should apologise to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"

James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at New York's Madison Square Garden.

James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.

Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.

James offered a short response to Trump's comments when questioned, declaring it was a "slow news day in the office".

Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers' need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.

"I think that goes right in with other outside noise we've already had," Nurse said before Friday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers.

"I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they've had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding."

AP

World.title: Awkward questions linger as creaky Australia receives South African hiding
World.content:
That Australia slowly folded and lost the Gqeberha Test by an innings and 31 runs late on day five was hardly surprising in light of its batting calamities of 24 hours earlier. That Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen ran through the tail to finish things off even less so.

But it remains startling to consider the reversal of fortunes this quite disastrous loss represented for Australia. On day two, they were 1-0 up in the series, had South Africa on the ropes at 5-97, on a greenish pitch, and fancied a rout of their own.

Bavuma hides from Smith catch as Boland outdoes batters in loss Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test.

Instead, in a game that lost 145 overs to rain and associated delays, the annihilation took place in reverse and a series some considered Australia's stepping stone to more difficult engagements ahead is now set for an enticing decider. For Australia, the task ahead is now daunting on multiple levels — not just to find form and the right combination of players to defeat an ascendant and cohesive opponent, but how to do so in Cape Town, with all the extra heat that will entail.

First the few positives. Travis Head, whose role as opener will continue to be endlessly scrutinised, laboured unselfishly for five hours to make 121. Nightwatchman Scott Boland, who was Australia's best all-round performer of the game, absorbed 187 deliveries for his rearguard 40.

Scott Boland's vigil at the crease on day five was one of the few positives for Australia. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The negatives? Australia's next-best batsman was Mother Nature, who wiped out the first session of play and briefly raised hopes that Australia would force a draw. It didn't, for neither did Boland's patient hand inspire his better credentialed batting partners to hang around and save the day.

It is pointless to analyse the tail. Most culpable this time was Steve Smith, who in his short and strange stay at the crease was given a reprieve by Proteas keeper Ryan Rickelton but failed to make South Africa pay, falling soon after to an objectionably unserious dismissal in a game that was, from Australia's perspective, a little too full of them.

Australia was 5-219 at the time of this pivot point, not entirely written off. Rabada had just taken the second new ball. Boland, batting steadily, had just driven him to the long-off boundary with a beautifully straight bat. Smith? Convention be damned. Rabada sent down a length ball on a fourth-stump line. Smith, for reasons known only to him, decided he should launch over the fence at deep mid-wicket. Instead he skied it and Matthew Breetzke juggled a catch. Therein lay the death of the contest.

Steve Smith's nightmare shot in the second session opened the door to a South African win. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Much has been made of Marnus Labuschagne's battle against his cricketing mortality, but Smith is now a fairly pressing problem too. For a long time, he has been Australia's Mr Dependable — not simply a better batsmen than younger alternatives, but an undroppable ornament, encouraged to play how he likes, to bat where he wants and indulge his obsessions however he sees fit.

Yet that greatness is suddenly fading fast, the numbers dwindling, Smith's insularity intensifying into less pardonable distractions. It is hard to shake the feeling that he and Labuschagne's overall effect on Australia's flaky batting group is a net negative on a psychological level as much as a statistical one.

A subtle but remarkable insight into this dynamic — ignored at the time — was glimpsed during the Bangladesh series in August, when Cameron Green used a post-match interview to explain the genesis of his own breakthrough first Test century on home soil.

South Africa has the momentum going into the final Test, something that seemed inconceivable two days into this match. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

"I was able to go back to Shield cricket … kind of a good little reminder about how I want to go about it," Green told ABC Sport at the time. "I think when you're playing in a pretty good Australian Test team, you bat behind some pretty good players in front of you and I think I probably got caught up in how they go about it. So, I think the beautiful thing about going back to state cricket is to remind myself how I want to go about it."

In other words, Australia's most gifted player of the generation to come was admitting that in order to get himself firing as a middle-order batsmen in this Test side, first he had to get himself far away from the influence of his teammates.

Green, of course, will be pushing his case for selection in Cape Town after injury ruled him out of the first two Tests. Should he be declared fit, the Beau Webster dilemma need not be as emotive as Australian coach Andrew McDonald made it in his press conference on day four.

Beau Webster (right) is likely to make way for Cam Green for the series finale, provided Green is fit to play. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

But it is puzzling to consider the reasoning for even selecting Webster in this match, in which he was never likely to bowl many of his seamers in an attack featuring four frontline quicks, was not asked for his off-spin, nor deemed top-six material with the bat.

McDonald was right to say the issue is not as straightforward as armchair selectors would have it. Like Mitch Marsh before him, Webster is clearly a much-loved team man. Over the English summer just gone, Warwickshire teammate Sam Hain spoke with genuine emotion of the mutual respect and pride Webster had created from the minute he arrived. Warwickshire duly won the championship trophy. But Webster's numbers told a less compelling story: 403 runs at 33, 12 wickets at 40. At Test level, same goes.

The most sensible scenario at the top of the order is that Nic Maddinson, a walking wicket against Rabada, will drop out and Matt Renshaw slide up. Cooper Connolly, who at ODI level recently justified the hype around him, must surely be in line to enter a team crying out for fresh blood.

Australia selector George Bailey's refusal to infuse the Test side with youth is providing diminishing results. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Looking beyond this result and this series, one wonders whether Australian cricket can find a clarity of purpose and be as ruthless as it needs to be to avoid toppling over a cliff when Smith, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are finally gone.

On that note, here is a quote to consider, from Australia's chairman of selectors: "Part of our charter is obviously to provide for the future," he said. "We are very aware that some of these blokes are getting on in age, and that's why it's very, very important for them to continue to perform."

Unfortunately, that was not George Bailey referring to this current Australian team, average age 34, which in Durban was the oldest XI since the 1920s and the first in Test history to not feature a single player under the age of 30.

No, it was Trevor Hohns, late in 2000, referring to arguably Australia's greatest combination ever. Its average age? Erm, 30.

Time, perhaps, for a new charter.

World.title: England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
World.content:
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.

Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.

Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.

The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.

Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.

He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.

The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.

Harry Brook's record-breaking double-century was ultimately in vain as Sri Lanka chased down the target of 430 with a ball to spare. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.

"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.

"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.

"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."

Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.

Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.

Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.

England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
World.content:
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.

Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.

Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.

Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.

At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.

They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.

Inspiring young fans has been at the forefront of Emily Chancellor's mind. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson)

"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.

"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.

"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.

"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].

"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."

Tight bond

After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.

The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.

A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.

Emily Chancellor captained the Wallaroos in 2025. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.

She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".

"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.

"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."

'Limitless' future

The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Emily Chancellor made her Test debut against New Zealand in 2018. (Getty Images)

Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.

"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.

"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.

"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."

Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.

The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.

"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

World.title: Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outdoes batters
World.content:
Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Head passes 100 but can't go on

Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.

And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.

It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.

But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.

Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.

2. Boland shows batters how it's done

By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.

But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.

Boland found the middle of the bat more often than not during his heroic vigil. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.

He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.

But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.

3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away

It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.

The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.

Bavuma couldn't watch as Breetzke took a dramatic juggling catch. (Fox Cricket)

It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.

But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.

Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.

Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.

4. Mulder does damage after tea

With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.

But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.

And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.

First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.

At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.

There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...

5. South Africa beats descending gloom

All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.

With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.

Clouds were gathering ominously with the Proteas in search of their final two wickets. (Fox Cricket)

Two wickets were needed.

Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.

And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.

But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.

Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.

The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

World.title: Cummins admits Australia 'long way from our best' as South Africa levels series
World.content:
Australia has fallen to defeat by an innings and 31 runs against South Africa in the second Test at St George's Park in Gqeberha.

Brave innings from Travis Head (121) and night watchman Scott Boland (40) were not enough for Australia, as the Proteas levelled the series at 1-1.

"We were a long way away from our best," Pat Cummins said at the presentation.

"Across the board just not enough of us contributed.

"Ideally we'd be scoring more runs. The pitch was pretty good out there."

The two teams will now head to Newlands in Cape Town for the final Test on Tuesday with the series on the line.

The hosts came into the final day needing just six wickets for victory, but were made to wait to get on the field after the first session was washed out by rain.

The persistent drizzle, interspersed by heavier squalls, may have given Australia hope that they may be able to orchestrate a great escape.

Even once play eventually resumed, every over that Head and Boland successfully negotiated raised hopes even further.

Head's 13th Test century was the first by an Australian batter in a follow-on innings since the 1980s and added to the pressure South Africa must have been feeling, with Anrich Nortje's injury leaving the Proteas a bowler down.

"I thought there was some good fight today," Cummins said.

"Scotty Boland and Trav [Head] both played their roles really well, but it was a fair way to come back from and it wasn't quite enough."

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Once Head chopped on to Wiaan Mulder just before the second new ball was due, the writing may have been on the wall.

Steve Smith, batting at seven after being hampered by a sore neck on day four, initially looked sprightly, before he top edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer to Matthew Breetzke when on 3.

Boland's brave, 166-ball vigil came to an end soon after, a brilliant off cutter from Mulder taking the top of his off stump.

Pat Cummins followed in the same way for just 4 to leave South Africa just two wickets from victory.

Still, Australia had hope as clouds gathered and threatened yet more rain to rescue an unlikely draw.

But then Rabada returned, bowling Mitch Starc for 11, before Marco Jansen extracted an edge from Josh Hazlewood for a duck.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Tech.title: Startup equips genetically enhanced dogs with Palmer Luckey’s military tech
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new Texas-based defense startup has a plan to improve military and police dogs in the US: it’s going to genetically modify them and equip them with Anduril’s military technology. Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm, co-founder of Colossal Biosciences (the company that says it’s trying to resurrect extinct animals), and it’s already secured $200 million in funding from investors.

Warhound plans to use Colossal’s work in genetics, cloning, and animal biology to “produce healthier dogs with characteristics suited to demanding missions,” with Anduril then equipping them with its “advanced cybernetic Augments.” That includes eye and ear protection and EagleEye military technology to provide the dogs and their handlers with “greater awareness and protection in the field.”

“Man’s best friend deserves man’s best tech,” Luckey said in the press announcement. Bloomberg reports that despite having helped with the company’s conception, Luckey has no equity or ongoing role in Warhound.

The goal is to reduce dependency on Europe, where 80 percent of US military dogs are currently sourced, and improve the success rate of training the animals for specialist work. According to the startup’s press release, less than half of the dogs procured from overseas are typically deemed fit for service following the current three-year acquisition-and-training pipeline.

In a statement to TechCrunch, Lamm said Colossal is looking to enhance the animals by editing their genes to remove problems like poor eyesight and cancer likelihood, while adding new genes to improve performance “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot.” High-performance working dog breeds like the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd are the base of their studies, but the plan is to create “a new type of dog.”

These dogs don’t exist yet, but when (or if) they do, Warhound says they’ll be deployed for elite working roles in US military forces, emergency first response teams, and law enforcement. The American Humane Society will help to guide the company and certify its training programs. Marine veteran and intelligence specialist David Spirk has been named as Warhound’s CEO, and said the company’s goal is simple: “healthier dogs, better-prepared teams, and more service members and first responders coming home safely.”

Tech.title: No, the iPhone Duo isn’t a small phone
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When we published our review of the iPhone Duo, I got a lot of hopeful questions from my fellow Mini fans who took note of the cover screen’s Mini-ish 5.4-inch size. “Is this… a small phone that turns into a tablet?” they asked. And I’m sorry to be the bearer of bad news, but no. The Duo is not the small phone we’ve been looking for.

I wish it was. I like a small phone. I own an iPhone 13 Mini that I refuse to surrender, even though it barely lasts a full day.

But the Duo is thick and heavy. You will feel its weight every time you read an email, scroll Instagram, or put it in your pocket. It is a dense phone, and after a week with the Duo, my 13 Mini feels almost comically light. Like, can this be a real phone? Surely not.

Thanks to its wider format, the Duo gives you a bigger keyboard compared to the Mini.

The Duo’s front panel is also quite a bit wider than the 13 Mini — 84.1mm compared to 64.2mm — which makes it much harder to reach your thumb all the way across like you can with the Mini. The Duo tries to compensate for this by putting controls on the right side, which helps a bit. As reported by Wired, Apple is also planning to add its reachability feature to the Duo later this year to help out in those moments. But inevitably there’s something I need to tap that’s out of one-handed reach on the Duo, and the illusion of using a small phone is gone. On the other hand, you get a much larger onscreen keyboard with the Duo; the Mini’s feels cramped by comparison.

It comes down to this: Liking a small phone isn’t the same thing as liking a small screen. Sure, all things being equal, a big screen is nicer for a lot of stuff. But I’ll put up with a tiny screen to enjoy the benefits of a phone so small I can forget it’s in my pocket. It’s a tradeoff. The iPhone Duo offers a different set of tradeoffs. Put up with the small screen on the outside, and you’ll be rewarded with a really big screen whenever you need it. And that small screen is attached to a big, heavy phone.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The iPhone Duo is harder to operate one-handed.

This sounds like I hated using the Duo, but I didn’t. I just had to calibrate my expectations. I think you’ll be disappointed by the Duo if you expect a small phone that expands into an iPad Mini. But if you go in expecting a small-screen experience you can tolerate in order to get a much bigger screen whenever you want, you’ll have the right idea about the Duo.

Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

Tech.title: Etsy is cracking down on AI slop listings
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Etsy is announcing stricter rules about how AI can be used in listings to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform. In a post, the company says that “many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content” and that sellers are “concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways,” spurring the new policies and restrictions.

Under the new policies, every listing must include “at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background,” and all photos must “accurately represent the item a buyer will receive.” The photos that aren’t the first one can be edited with software or AI-powered tools, as long as “the final result remains an accurate representation of the physical product.” The company shared a few examples to demonstrate the type of misleading images that are prohibited, including the cat stuffed animal at the top of this post.

Image: Etsy

While uploading images for a listing, if Etsy detects that any may be AI-generated, the platform will show a pop-up where you can note if an image was made with AI or not, as shown in a video. If a buyer reports that what they receive is “materially different” from a listing, a seller may be responsible for a refund.

For sellers who offer “functional guides,” which include patterns, recipes, or instructions,” Etsy says that the information in those products “must be your own work, not generated by AI.” Sellers will have to show an “actual result” made from a guide. The company also says that listings made by bots are no longer allowed.

Selling AI-generated art is still allowed on the platform, but a seller must disclose that it was made with AI, Etsy says.

Tech.title: Spotify says yes, it is busting people for using Family Plan sharing too widely
Tech.content:
This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base.

As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.

Tech.title: The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication’s Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028.

My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It’s DOA.

My second thought: Microsoft knows people won’t pay that much. It couldn’t possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. “I wouldn’t release it at all,” former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said.

My third thought: Didn’t Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won’t pay that much?

Did Fortune get it wrong?

I don’t think Fortune’s insiders are the problem here. With today’s incredibly overpriced RAM and storage, it wouldn’t be surprising if it cost over a thousand dollars to build, package, distribute, and sell “the largest technical leap you will have ever seen in a hardware generation,” as former Xbox president Sarah Bond called the next Xbox back in 2024.

But there are at least five ways the report could be correct without making you pay all that money at once. I just don’t think you’re going to like most of them.

Subsidies: Microsoft could pay to give you a discount

The least-likely possibility is the one Fortune suggests itself. Let’s look at the original quote, bolding mine:

[…] the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.

Historically, Microsoft has subsidized the Xbox. Microsoft sold boxes at a loss right out of the gate, making its profits when you buy games and Xbox Game Pass subscriptions instead of on the hardware alone. That’s not our speculation — it’s exactly what Microsoft told The Verge in 2021. In 2023, we learned that Microsoft may have spent $1.5 billion to make sure it could sell the Xbox Series X and S at $499 and $299 respectively, instead of what they actually cost.

But Microsoft has suggested that it’s done with hardware subsidies. “Going forward, this cannot continue,” wrote Sharma in her “Xbox reset” memo, referring to the $20 billion in content, platform, and hardware subsidies Microsoft made over the past five years.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that idea on the Hard Fork podcast: “No one can accuse Microsoft of not having invested for the last 25 years, and now we have to turn this into a sustainable business.”

It isn’t just new management that’s hinting at no more subsidies: Bond primed the pump for a $1,000 box when she called Helix “a very premium, very high-end curated experience” late last year, comparing it to gaming PCs like the $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld.

Perhaps Microsoft has changed its mind since then. “We are working very hard to rethink everything that we can about Helix,” Ball said in June, referring to affordability. “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan,” Sharma said in February (though not about affordability specifically).

But subsidies would be a tremendous risk if the Helix still plays PC games in addition to Xbox ones. Valve’s Steam is by far the dominant PC gaming platform — so PC gamers who buy a Helix won’t help Microsoft recoup its money.

Subscription: “Get it free with 36 months of Xbox Game Pass and qualifying trade-in”

There’s another way Microsoft could subsidize a $1,200 Xbox.

Today, AT&T will give you a $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro for $0* — if you lock yourself into 36 months of AT&T phone service that costs $100 or more per month and trade in a recent phone, too.

Microsoft could do the same with a new, pricier tier of its Xbox Game Pass game subscription service, effectively bundling the games with the console and making you slowly pay for both at the same time. Perhaps you’ll have the option to buy an “unlocked” Xbox for full price, but it won’t be the norm.

To make it happen directly, Microsoft would need a pricier new tier of Xbox Game Pass, which wouldn’t necessarily align with the company’s recent moves. Sharma actually cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate to $22.99 a month in April, writing that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players,” while removing Call of Duty games and unlimited access to Xbox Cloud Gaming from the deal.

I don’t know if it would work. People feel naked leaving the house without phone service. They might not feel the same about games. Subscription fatigue is real. But if it worked, Microsoft’s moat would be stronger than ever. You’ll be more likely to play the games you’ve already paid for and are committed to keep paying for. Many would get sucked into a profitable upgrade cycle, just like they do with phones, since they can buy the next Xbox for “$0” as soon as it comes out.

Cellphone subsidies have been around nearly as long as pricey phones: The 1994 IBM Simon, arguably the first smartphone, eventually cost half its $1,100 price tag if you signed a contract with BellSouth. My first phone, a Kyocera QCP-6035 with a built-in PalmPilot, was subsidized when it arrived in 2001. So it’s not exactly a “radical new business model,” but it would be new for game consoles.

Rental: Maybe most people won’t own a Helix themselves

It’s also possible that Microsoft simply doesn’t plan to sell a console to the masses anymore — it can sell an $1,800 Xbox to those who can afford “video game ownership” and try to hook everyone else on the Netflix model.

After all, the “K-shaped economy” and RAMageddon have already made gaming PCs and existing game consoles into luxury goods. Society’s wealthier individuals seem perfectly happy to pay inflated prices for the few consoles Sony and Microsoft still pump out.

“I can tell you definitively, demand for our console exceeds supply. We are putting them in as many stores as possible, we are producing them as quickly as possible. There is a severe limitation to how quickly we can do that,” Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball told The Game Business in June, blaming RAM shortages.

But Microsoft has another way of giving less affluent people access to “next-gen” Xbox power. It can rent you one. The company just launched pay-as-you-go cloud gaming starting at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud gaming (50 hours for $11.99).

Maybe all of Microsoft’s recent talk about affordability isn’t about the masses owning a next-gen console. Maybe it’s about finding an affordable way for people to “play Xbox” without owning the games at all.

The next gen is the current gen

After Fortune’s report, some of the very first reactions I saw boiled down to this: “I’m out. Forget next gen, I’m going to stick with my existing Xbox/PlayStation/Switch.”

That’ll be the reality for many people if the Xbox costs over a thousand bucks. But if the RAM shortage continues — if Microsoft knows it’ll sell every Xbox it can make to wealthy individuals because it can’t make a lot — it’s not necessarily a huge risk to sell it sky-high on day one.

Perhaps the Xbox Helix will be an early adopter console, the same way the iPhone Duo is an early adopter phone, the same way the Steam Frame is an early adopter headset. These products are selling out instantly despite their high price tags, leaving many would-be buyers in the cold. They’re shipping messy and unfinished, but that’s okay because early adopters want to come along for the ride.

Microsoft knows the same is true of some Xbox buyers, because it helped ship an unfinished $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld even before the RAM crisis, and the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 follow-up is already sold out.

But if Microsoft splits the Xbox audience into “have” and “have-not,” it means the next generation won’t truly arrive. Game developers won’t spend all their effort targeting a console people can’t buy. The next Xbox won’t be any more necessary than a PS5 Pro if you already own a PS5. In industry lingo, the Helix would be a “mid-cycle refresh” instead of true next gen.

I wouldn’t hate that, though, and neither would many video game execs. They’ve long complained that the pace of technology has ballooned the cost of building a video game to unsustainable levels, leading to today’s world where too many development teams are cut to the bone right after their games ship.

Former PlayStation and Xbox execs like Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden, and Mike Ybarra have argued that the next gen isn’t necessary.

“Stick with PS5 Pro/Series X until prices normalize. The capabilities of those boxes are both fine for 99% of the audience. No one is screaming ‘I need a more powerful console’ right now,” Ybarra tweeted on October 20th.

“I think [Sony and Nintendo] should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because I think people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2,” Yoshida told me on The Vergecast.

“I think we’ve plateaued on the tech, frankly,” Layden told GamesIndustry.biz in 2025. (He’s said similar before and since.) “Make it cheaper and simpler. Let’s do that instead. And let’s find a way to have more hardware companies participate.”

Microsoft and its chip partner AMD have already taken one step to help extend the current generation — AMD’s performance-enhancing FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series S and X, which should make it easier for both to deliver crisp 4K images to your TV.

Pay what you can afford

Even if Microsoft ships a $1,800 console, the company’s been clear it won’t be the only Xbox you can buy. Sharma has publicly said that Helix will be a “family of devices,” which has been broadly interpreted to mean that Microsoft will let PC industry partners like Asus sell their own “Xbox” as well.

If the reporting pans out, that wouldn’t just be a cobranded Xbox Ally handheld that runs Windows — Asus could make a console-shaped box that runs a Windows-based Xbox OS, too.

Some of those partners could offer more affordable, less powerful Xboxes than Microsoft’s own flagship box, perhaps with less storage and memory. Microsoft, too, might have creative solutions for storage, like how the company shipped the Xbox 360 with different-size hard drives, or none at all, to make it more affordable. “We will have to empower customers to have very flexible storage offerings,” Sharma said in June.

Or you could buy another Xbox that’s likely going to continue to count as part of Microsoft’s “family”: the existing Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.

This can all work because games don’t need to target a single console anymore; they haven’t needed to for a long time. An Xbox One game runs on an Xbox One X and an Xbox Series S and an Xbox Series X because they’re all effectively AMD-powered Windows PCs, just with different amounts of performance on tap. The Xbox Helix is a powerful extension of the same continuum. The same is true of PlayStation 4, PS4 Pro, PS5, PS5 Pro, and presumably PS6, minus the Windows part.

Perhaps a particular piece of hardware will stand out as the one developers should target as the baseline for “it looks and runs great on Xbox,” the same way the Steam Deck handheld became a baseline for PC game developers starting in 2022. Maybe, like the Steam Deck and the Nintendo Switch, it’ll help reset our expectations of what a top-shelf game needs to look like.

At this rate, I wouldn’t be surprised if the existing Xbox Series S will be the one. But it could also be Microsoft’s own next handheld Xbox. Fortune’s insiders say it’s coming holiday 2027.

Tech.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.

Previous Next







1 / 5 An image generated by Canva Craft. Image: Canva

The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.

Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.

Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

Tech.title: PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low.

Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes.

Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”
