Tech.title: Beyond the Review: Inside the Onyx RCR 80V
Tech.content:
Joseph Maldonado

The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York City, I’m more interested in what it’s like to live with.

The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?

My impression is that Onyx is trying to build a compact electric motorbike with BMX-inspired maneuverability and modern electronics, while leaving owners room to customize it and keep it running. Riding the RCR and talking with founder Tim Seward helped me understand that approach. Whether it holds up over years of ownership is a question a few hundred miles can’t answer.

More from CNET

Joseph Kaminski

Onyx RCR 80V GeekBox

Manufacturer figures below are advertised specifications, not independently measured performance results. Prices checked Oct. 14, 2026.

Specification Onyx RCR 80V Starting price $4,699 Street / $4,899 Dual Sport Motor Rear hub; advertised 8kW nominal Battery Removable 80V, 45Ah / 3.6kWh Claimed top speed 65–75 mph, depending on configuration; advertised for off-road use Claimed maximum range 140 miles; current table associates this with Cruise Tune Eco at 15 mph Claimed acceleration 0–30 mph in 1.7 seconds Ride modes tested Eco, Normal, Sport and Hyper Wheels 17-inch tubeless Brakes Hydraulic discs with 220mm rotors Display TFT touchscreen Phone integration Apple CarPlay / Android Auto Other features Reverse, cruise control, regenerative braking, turn signals and alarm/key fob Advertised ready-to-ride weight Approximately 155 pounds

Sources: Onyx model and pricing overview⁠, RCR product page⁠, RCR feature page⁠ and Onyx’s brake and wheel description⁠.

Joseph Maldonado

Street, Dual Sport and getting it home

The Street and Dual Sport share the advertised motor and battery ratings. Their clearest hardware differences are the tires and fenders: Street has 4-inch street tires with optional fenders; Dual Sport has 4.5-inch tires with a more aggressive tread and fenders included. See the Onyx model comparison⁠

Neither arrives like a lightweight bicycle. The RCR is a heavy freight delivery that still needs final assembly, and I wouldn’t recommend unpacking it alone. At roughly 155 pounds ready to ride, it also demands some thought about storage before you order.

I live in a three-flight walk-up. That matters more to my daily experience than another few miles per hour at the top end.

Yes, the RCR has pedals. I doubt many people are spending nearly $5,000 because they’re looking forward to using them.

Joseph Maldonado

Small bike, serious performance

I’m 6 feet tall, around 260 pounds and usually carrying a backpack. The RCR has had no trouble moving me around.

Most of my riding has been between 15 and 35 mph, with plenty of time in Normal. I haven’t often felt the need for more. What I appreciate is the reserve power for acceleration and hills, rather than having to ask the bike for everything just to carry a heavier rider.

Seward made a similar point when we talked about the RCR’s development around San Francisco. Steep hills help explain why usable power matters beyond a top-speed claim.

His background also helps explain the bike. An industrial designer whose portfolio includes projects for Sonos and Bird, Seward founded Onyx to bring classic motorbike character to an electric machine. ⁠

He described a combination of motorcycle performance and BMX-style maneuverability. I grew up racing BMX, and I can relate to that influence. The RCR’s compact dimensions make it easy to move around underneath me and maneuver in tighter spaces. Its size is part of its appeal, although the weight is a reminder that this is a very different machine from a BMX bike.

“It’s like a blank canvas that you can customize… It’s not a BMX at all, but it definitely has some influence from when I was a kid,” says Seward.

Joseph Maldonado

The throttle changes the experience

With this much power, how it arrives matters.

On my test bike, Eco and Normal feel smoother and more forgiving. Sport and Hyper respond more immediately to wrist movement. Switching modes changes more than the available speed; it changes how carefully I need to feed in the throttle.

I like having that choice. Sometimes I want an easy cruise. Other times, I appreciate a quicker response. A gentler mode doesn’t eliminate the need for careful throttle control, but it makes the bike’s delivery better suited to how I want to ride.

These impressions apply to the software on my test bike. They aren’t a comparison of Onyx’s newer Cruise and Thrill tunes.

What I can say about range

I haven’t completed a controlled range test, so I don’t have a measured full-charge figure to give you.

What I do have is several hundred miles of use without range anxiety. On one ride from around 151st Street in Harlem to East 26th Street, the display showed a drop of about nine percentage points. My ride took me through Central Park, so we’re looking at about 9 miles. After longer outings through Queens and Brooklyn, I’ve returned with roughly 60% to 70% of the indicated charge remaining.

My much lighter teenage son also rode the RCR on an outing through those boroughs. I recall the indicated charge dropping by 17%, although that wasn’t a controlled comparison with my own riding.

One thing that continues to impress me about the Onyx RCR 80V is just how quiet its motor is. There’s none of that high-pitched whining or wheezing you sometimes hear from electric motors. Power delivery is equally impressive, remaining smooth and consistent whether I’m accelerating from a standstill or riding at higher speeds. I’ve also noticed how much the route itself can affect battery consumption. On a recent commute from 151st Street to East 26th Street, I took a different route instead of traveling entirely through Central Park and used just 6% of the battery compared with 9% on a previous ride. It’s a good reminder that real-world range isn’t simply about distance. Terrain, elevation changes, traffic, speed and riding conditions all influence how efficiently the bike uses energy.

Joseph Maldonado

Those readings describe what I saw on the display. They don’t establish that each percentage point equals a mile, or that the bike will travel 100 miles on a charge. Without recorded distances, consistent conditions and a fuller discharge test, that would be an extrapolation.

Rider weight, speed, acceleration and terrain all matter. My conclusion is narrower: the battery has comfortably covered the rides I’ve taken. Someone spending more time at high speed should expect a different experience.

Onyx itself recommends watching battery voltage for a better indication of remaining charge and range. That’s another reason to treat my percentage readings as observations rather than precision measurements. See ONYX battery guidance⁠

Joseph Maldonado

Comfortable suspension, with limits at the seat

The RCR fits me surprisingly well, and the suspension has done a good job taking the edge off New York’s potholes and broken pavement.

The seat is comfortable with good cushioning for shorter rides. After about 90 minutes, though, I start shifting around. The suspension helps with the road underneath me, but it doesn’t eliminate the discomfort that builds during a longer ride. That also could be due to my size; I’m far from a lightweight.

The brakes have also felt consistently strong. After a few hundred miles, lever travel still feels close to how it did at the start, and I haven’t noticed a meaningful decline in stopping performance. That’s a riding impression, not a measured stopping-distance or brake-wear test.

Cruise control and reverse were pleasant surprises

Cruise control sounded like a minor convenience until I used it. On the inclines I’ve encountered with it engaged, the RCR has held the selected speed even with my weight aboard. That has been a more useful demonstration of its available power than a top-speed run.

Discovering that it could also reverse was another pleasant surprise. On a machine this heavy, powered reverse is a feature I’m glad to have. Onyx documents both functions in its advanced controls guide.

Joseph Maldonado

CarPlay is a favorite feature — and a frustration

I didn’t expect to care this much about CarPlay. Having navigation and audio controls on the built-in display means I can leave my phone put away.

My main complaint is what happens to the motorbike’s own information. While using CarPlay, especially during a call, I want speed and battery status to remain easy to see. On my test bike, they aren’t presented as conveniently as I’d like.

Onyx told me it intends to address the display issue through a software update.

Navigation brings up another issue. I’d like routing that better reflects the vehicle I’m riding. Because it uses CarPlay, it offers driving directions. However, I would like the option to choose a different route if I choose to.

“Having Android Auto and CarPlay in the bike makes me want to ride more… Part of the new update will show stats like battery level and mode on the side while using it,” says Seward, who is also Onyx’s chief design officer.

Joseph Maldonado

Signals, lights and wet pavement

The turn signals sit close to the body, with less protruding hardware to catch on something. I like that design, but in sunny settings, the signals may not be as visible.

They don’t self-cancel. The display indicators help, but I’d prefer automatic cancellation to discovering I’ve announced a left turn for the last 20 blocks (minor complaint). The Bluetooth connection indicator is another small, useful display detail.

The headlight has worked well for the nighttime riding I’ve done. The halo running light and main beam give the bike a distinctive look, with high beam available when needed.

Joseph Maldonado

I’ve also ridden in the rain and on wet pavement without noticing handling problems. That’s limited experience, not a comprehensive wet-weather test. The more immediate issue is spray, as my bike doesn’t have the optional fenders installed, and New York street water gets everywhere.

Fenders are high on my list before doing more wet-weather riding.

Tubeless tires and everyday maintenance

The tubeless setup matters to me because removing a motorized rear wheel to deal with a flat tube can become a project. I’d rather avoid that extra complication where possible.

Tubeless doesn’t mean puncture-proof, and I wouldn’t assume any roadside plug is a permanent repair suitable for motorcycle speeds. But it’s a great go-to when in a pinch. Not having to remove the wheel to make it to your destination is clutch.

“These are basically motorcycle wheels and tires, so if you get a nail, you can patch or plug it without taking the wheel off and replacing the whole tube,” says Seward.



Joseph Kaminski

Forget the fob and the bike stays put

I’ve kept the RCR in storage at my partner’s apartment because she has an elevator. I sometimes forget to leave the key fob with it, which works well until I arrive without the fob.

That experience made phone or NFC access more appealing. Seward told me Onyx is developing app-based diagnostics, firmware updates and service support, and we discussed possible phone access. I’d welcome it, along with integrated tracking or movement alerts.

For now, I keep an AirTag hidden in the bike. I’ve also found the rear-wheel locking behavior reassuring when the bike is secured, although that isn’t a substitute for a physical lock.

Onyx already links a Superpower BMS app for battery monitoring. That should be distinguished from the broader app and unlocking features we discussed; I haven’t established that those proposed functions are available. See the Onyx product page

Joseph Maldonado

⁠

The pedals don’t settle the legal question

I think of the RCR as a compact electric motorcycle. That description doesn’t, by itself, establish whether a particular example can be registered for road use. But it can be insured.

New York’s legal definition of an electric-assist bicycle includes a motor below 750 watts and specified assistance-speed limits. The RCR’s advertised power and performance exceed those limits. Buyers shouldn’t assume that pedals or a lower-speed setting make it a legal e-bike. See New York DMV definitions⁠

I haven’t verified New York registration eligibility for this exact model and configuration. That needs to be resolved with the DMV and the manufacturer before it can be presented as a straightforward street-legal commuting option. Bicycle lanes and walking routes should not be assumed available to it.

Joseph Maldonado

Beyond the ride: A conversation with Tim Seward

Seward’s explanation of Onyx starts with the products he no longer wanted to design. During our conversation, he described working on consumer electronics for brands including Sonos, HP and Samsung, only to watch products become disposable shortly after reaching the market. His experiences with furniture and old gas-powered mopeds suggested a different approach.

The following excerpts are edited for length and clarity from the interview transcript. Questions have been shortened, and the discussion has been reordered by topic. Future features are plans described during the interview, not confirmation that they are available today.

Joseph Maldonado

Question: Is there anything about your background or the bike that people might not know?

Seward: Before Onyx, I was a big consumer-electronics designer. I worked on Sonos, HP, Samsung, and all sorts of products you would see at Best Buy. While I liked that job, I didn’t like that people were throwing away their products.

When I was customizing gas-powered mopeds, I realized I was working on vehicles 30 to 50 years old. Who knows how many hands it went through until it got to me? I was like, I need to make products like this. I need to make products that, even if Onyx dies tomorrow, the products will live on. I didn’t want to continue to create landfill.

Joseph Maldonado

Question: If an owner keeps this bike for five years, what can they realistically expect for battery health?

Seward: With our extra layer of health protections, we are confident our battery pack will show only a 10% degradation in 10 years. So, at the five-year mark, you won’t even notice much of a difference, if any, in performance.

(That’s an ambitious prediction. Seward’s response didn’t include the testing, charging habits or usage conditions behind it, so I wouldn’t treat it as a guaranteed outcome or a warranty. It does give me something specific to follow up on as the bike ages.)

Question: How committed is Onyx to supporting owners with replacement parts years down the road?

Seward: We strive to offer hard-to-find parts even for discontinued products that are 5 to 6 years old. Also, our newest model, the RCR 80V, uses many parts that are compatible with aftermarket upgrades, so you can modify or maintain it for decades to come.

(That gets to one of my biggest questions about an expensive electric vehicle: What happens when something breaks after the model is no longer current? Aftermarket compatibility could help keep the RCR running, although it isn’t a guarantee that every component will remain available.)

Joseph Maldonado

Question: What sets Onyx apart from the growing number of electric motorcycle companies?

Seward: We are not just building a bike. We are building a community of riders who support each other across the globe.

(That connects with how I found my way to Onyx. I met John Angel while testing another bike, and he kept encouraging me to try an RCR. Before I spoke with the company, another rider had already shared his experience and got me interested.

The community side matters most when it becomes useful: Someone helping you understand a feature, troubleshoot a problem or figure out a modification. That’s the kind of owner involvement I’d like to see continue as Onyx grows.

Onyx also brings its community together through events like Onyx Week, where owners and enthusiasts participate in organized rides, meet members of the Onyx team, exchange ideas, and connect with other riders. Events have been organized in Los Angeles and New York, giving owners an opportunity to experience the community beyond online discussions and social media.)

Joseph Maldonado

What stays with me

The RCR has more power than I usually need and has covered my outings without battery anxiety. CarPlay and cruise control have become features I actually value. The seat can become less comfortable on longer rides, and the display should show the current speed and battery level while on a call.

Talking with Seward gave me a clearer understanding of the decisions behind those experiences. Customer feedback helped shape the 80V, while his experience with disposable electronics explains why he wants owners to keep these bikes running.

It’s nice to hear a company talk about making something you can keep for years instead of pushing you to buy a new model every year. That intention still has to be backed by replacement parts, documentation and service. Onyx’s published guidance says it doesn’t repair, refurbish or rebalance batteries, so long-term battery support remains an important question. See Onyx’s battery support policy⁠

For me, that’s what makes this worth looking at beyond the review — understanding why the RCR was built this way, how owners influence what comes next and whether the support can live up to the design. Would I recommend getting one? Heck yeah!

Tech.title: A New Bird-Recognizing Feeder Under $100 Launches for Beginner Bird-Watchers
Tech.content:
Birdbuddy released its latest line of smart bird feeders equipped with cameras that can detect birds by species on Thursday, and it’s never been a better time to start birdwatching at your home. The reason is a new model called the Birdbuddy Nook, which starts at $99 and offers its AI features for free with no subscription needed.



Most of the smart bird feeders we’ve tested, including past Birdbuddy models, cost around $200 or more. The particularly affordable Nook includes a 2K-resolution camera with both portrait and landscape orientations, plus a 3.8-cup birdseed container. It wakes up via motion but can keep recording for longer periods of time when there’s lots of activity. All the alerts and species recognition features happen on your phone, via the Birdbuddy app.

More from CNET

The Nook comes in both a standard model for $99 and a model with a solar panel built into the roof for $159. I’ve tested many solar-powered security cameras, and these small panels really do help keep wireless batteries charged for long periods. Since the Nook’s battery is only rated for around a month, and the bird-feeder battery looks a bit more complicated to charge up, I highly recommend the solar model.

Along with the Nook, the company is releasing a Birdbuddy Home mode for $219, which is similar, except it has a larger 6-cup capacity and a wraparound bar for more perching space.

Where should you put the Nook?

The Nook holds nearly four cups of food. Birdbuddy

Feeders should be placed within 4 feet to 10 feet of shrubs or trees, which is close enough for birds to feel safe from predators, while still being far enough to deter squirrels, according to Mary Mack Gray, Birdbuddy’s in-house ornithologist, who told CNET the best placement options. “If using a pole, a height of 5 to 6 feet off the ground is ideal. Nook is designed for compact spaces like patios, balconies and small yards.”

If you’re worried about squirrels messing up your view or getting in the way, Gray suggests using safflower seeds and suet, which squirrels tend to ignore, and avoid feed like corn or peanuts that squirrels love.

How does the bird recognition feature work?

AI trained on birds has seen success in identifying species. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

Birdbuddy uses AI that has been trained on bird species visits to feeders, so it can analyze shape, color, markings and other aspects to pull up a match if one is available. The camera needs a couple of moments to wake up and take a snapshot, as well as a Wi-Fi connection, so you don’t want to put the feeder out too far from your router.

Once a bird lands on the feeder, the feeder will send a snapshot to algorithms for analysis and return an identified species or label it as currently unknown. Birdbuddy doesn’t say if it’s all local AI or if processing is done in the cloud.

CNET’s previous birdwatching reviewer noted that, aside from an occasional misstep, the bird recognition was quite good and even self-corrected itself. That sounds like a handy package for someone who wants to get to know birds in the area while paying the minimum amount.

Tech.title: Will Meta’s $25 Billion Court Loss Change Its Ways? (Spoiler: Probably Not)
Tech.content:
Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty on Wednesday when a judge in New Mexico found the company had misled users about data privacy practices. The decision marks one of the steepest corporate payouts ever levied against a technology company.

Under the ruling, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and other platforms and services, was ordered to pay the fee for misleading social media consumers about their data privacy in a case dating back to Cambridge Analytica’s privacy violations involving the 2016 presidential election. The ruling against Meta imposed civil penalties for violating New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act after a jury trial found Facebook liable for nearly 44 million violations of that law.

Meta could appeal the verdict; it was unsuccessful in its filings to cap its penalties at $3.45 billion. It could have been worse for the company. Some estimates had suggested it could have been hit with $219 billion in penalties.

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

“A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

Meta previously paid $725 million to users to settle a lawsuit over Cambridge Analytica, a high-profile scandal in which a British consulting firm working with the Donald Trump presidential campaign was given access to Facebook user data. That data purchase is credited with helping sway the 2016 election results.

Just two months ago, the company settled with multiple US states to the tune of up to $18 billion for intentionally designing its social media platforms to be addictive and harmful to children and teens. Before that, Meta had especially bad luck in a previous New Mexico case, with orders to pay $375 million in March, then another $567 million in August over failures to warn the public about the dangers its social media platforms, including Instagram, pose to children.

Unbowed and unbothered?

But, surprisingly, Meta’s gigantic payouts (never mind its mountain of legal fees) haven’t turned one of the world’s largest tech companies into a meek player in social media or in news cycles.

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg testifies in July for a New Mexico data privacy case. New Mexico Attorney General's Office

Almost weekly, the company is taken to task for privacy-related overreach, most recently over its Muse agentic AI platform and its hit hardware product, Meta Glasses.

Just this week, the company suspended a feature for sharing Muse conversations after researchers found that the links it generated could be accessed by people who weren’t meant to receive them.

Meta has also been fending off cycles of outrage over whether it will add potentially intrusive facial-recognition features to software in its smart glasses. In September, reports surfaced that Meta is at least partially acknowledging the backlash by working on models that don’t include cameras. But those would be in addition to all of the versions of Meta Glasses that still carry them.

Assuming the verdict in New Mexico stands, Meta may pay a large penalty. But it’s unlikely that the case will directly impact its newer business ventures other than serving as a lesson on how not to treat user data on Facebook. The New Mexico case still hasn’t determined what changes, if any, Meta will need to make to comply with the state’s privacy laws and whether that will be a bigger hit to the company than a $25 billion payout.

“What changes a company is a court order that dictates how the product has to work, with someone independent checking,” said Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, a data security software and technology company.

For Meta’s newer technologies, including AI and AI-assisted hardware, the ruling would have little impact.

“Settlements written for 2018 don’t cover those devices,” Stokes said.

Will Facebook users get a cut of $25 billion?

Meta could continue to pay out billions of dollars in additional cases involving privacy and the effects of its platform design on younger users. Cases are pending in Washington, DC, Florida and Texas, among other places, covering issues such as more Cambridge Analytica fallout and WhatsApp privacy.

For this new verdict, users shouldn’t expect another payout; the money will go to New Mexico’s public school fund.

The sum may sound huge, and in education, it could go a long way, but Stokes said it won’t destroy Meta’s business.

“Meta’s stock went up the day the judgment went down,” he said. “That tells you how the market sees a fine on its own.”

Still, a judgment against the company that could lead to even more litigation can’t be good for Meta. It’s not alone. Many other tech companies, from Google to OpenAI to Snap, are facing similar lawsuits over how they collect or use data.

“The question in every case is the same: Do a company’s privacy and safety promises match how the product works?” Stokes said. “Any company making those promises should expect to be tested on them.”

Tech.title: Hugging Face Announces AI Model to ‘Chat’ With DNA
Tech.content:
A new AI model can connect DNA to human language, enabling scientists to interact with genetic code in new ways. Hugging Face announced the Carbon-X model on Thursday as the latest and most powerful in the company’s Carbon family, a group of AI models built to analyze DNA.

“Carbon-X allows researchers to ‘chat with DNA’ for the first time: They can provide a sequence and ask questions about it in natural language,” Hugging Face research scientist Lewis Tunstall told CNET via email.

The word “chat” doesn’t mean talking to your genome but rather using an AI as a conversational interface, allowing users to paste in a DNA sequence, ask a question in plain English and receive back an interpretation, prediction or explanation — like a chatbot for DNA analysis.

More from CNET

The most popular chatbots, such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, are cloud-based models that don’t run on your computer. The processing happens remotely, and you get the results back. But if you’re working on confidential or proprietary research that you haven’t yet published, you might not want to share it with an AI company. “Researchers need models they can study, adapt and run with sensitive or unpublished sequences on their own hardware,” said Tunstall.

One of the nice things about smaller, specialized AI models like Carbon-X is that it can run without using someone else’s computer. Hugging Face says the model can also work in tandem with other AI agents.

DNAgents

To be clear, Carbon-X is not a lab machine, so it can’t physically sequence DNA. It can look at DNA, such as a DNA sequence in a text file, and you can ask questions about it. Tunstall said Carbon-X’s strongest area is the model’s ability to predict mutation effects and complete DNA sequences.

“Carbon-X is particularly strong at helping researchers investigate genetic variation, for example, predicting whether a change in a DNA sequence is likely to be harmful,” Tunstall said.

He also said that it can give another AI model access to a DNA specialist when it needs to extract information.

However, the model does have limitations, according to the company’s blog post. Carbon-X can mess up sequencing operations through miscounts, and it can also hallucinate, which means the model just makes up information. Hugging Face noted that the model may invent the identity or function of a sequence when a user does not provide sufficient information in the prompt.

The quality of Carbon-X’s output also tends to degrade when users ask the model to produce particularly long DNA sequences, according to the company.

Lightning fast

In September, Nvidia announced it would buy Hugging Face for a little under $13 billion. At the time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the company a “vibrant home for the open model developer community.” Open models are AI models in which some aspects of how they were trained are publicly available.

The release of Carbon-X comes just weeks after OpenAI models began solving longstanding mathematics problems. The AI lab drew widespread backlash from academic researchers after its proprietary models solved several long-standing problems without consulting scientists or showing what work went into solving them.

But Carbon-X is an open model, so AI-savvy biologists can at least peek under the model’s proverbial hood and glimpse how it runs.

“We think researchers also need open alternatives whose capabilities, limitations and risks they can examine independently,” Tunstall said. “By releasing Carbon-X and its training recipe openly, we enable the wider scientific community to test where it works, identify where it fails and help improve it.”

Tech.title: TextNow’s $150 Yello Phone Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
Tech.content:
Low-cost carrier TextNow launched its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized 2024 edition of the Moto G Play that costs $150 and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments. It’s a simple 4G-only Android phone with a 6.5-inch display, but TextNow makes a number of software changes to restrict most access to the internet.

The phone doesn’t include Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts. TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 50-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2024 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. Its 5,000-mAh battery should easily get through a day or two of use, and its IP52 certification should keep it resistant to light splashes of water. The phone has a limited amount of storage at 64GB, but that might work out fine considering the deliberate constraints placed on this device.

It’s worth noting that Motorola is only providing security support to this older model of the Moto G Play through 2027, but TextNow’s website says that its Yello software will continue to be built upon as the carrier gets user feedback. Since Motorola’s official support period for this phone is almost over, it will be important for TextNow’s Yello software to step in as it builds up features for this phone for kids.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same sapphire blue that’s on every 2024 Moto G Play.

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited that Yello was using a different edition of the Moto G Play. TextNow clarified the model after Yello’s announcement, and the story has been updated accordingly.

Tech.title: Anthropic Introduces Claude Duet: A New Agentic AI App for Professionals
Tech.content:
Anthropic is dropping yet another AI product into our laps: Claude Duet, a dedicated app for professionals and business owners to handle tasks they would otherwise have to do manually. While agentic AI isn’t new, this app caters to a group that likely needs those capabilities most. Anthropic has always targeted the professional sector, and Duet, while specific, feels very on-brand for the company.

Claude Duet is designed around Opus 5.5, and the app is aimed at streamlining your daily operations. Not unlike Claude itself, Duet allows you to connect with the software you use for your work, and will continuously look for things that need your attention. This means you can connect your Gmail, calendar, Slack and thousands of other work and productivity apps.

Like other agentic tools, Duet is a proactive assistant that will help you prioritize things that it deems are most important and worthy of your attention first. The “proactive” part of Duet is that you don’t always have to prompt it to do something for the future; it’ll assess and assemble what you need to know by looking through your work apps. It’ll also do the opposite, and tell you when things can wait for later so you can focus on higher-priority tasks.

More from CNET

Anthropic says that Claude Duet prioritizes your privacy. As much as an AI tool can, at least. There are specialized safety protocols and measures to make sure sensitive information doesn’t go out into the world unless you want it to. Duet will automatically reject highly sensitive information, like credit card numbers, ID information and more. With other sensitive information, like health and finance information, Duet will ask before it sends anything out.

Duet is currently available in a research preview, but only for the Pro or Max subscription plans. You can join the waitlist now.

Tech.title: FTC Imposter Scam Threatens to Unplug Your Phone Number
Tech.content:
The scam du jour sounds like a real brain twister. According to a Federal Trade Commission alert issued Thursday about the newest imposter scam, fraudsters pretending to be from the FTC are calling to “warn” you that your phone number is being used to commit scams in another country and that if you don’t reply to them ASAP you run the risk of your phone getting deactivated.

And it sounds like a pretty intricate hoax. According to the alert, the caller will transfer you to a phony police officer and provide a search query to find the (fake) phone number to file a “report,” and if you call, more scammers pick up. And once you’ve handed over your personal information, they’ll tell you you have to travel to the relevant country to resolve it, unless you fork over a “security deposit.”

This is just one of the latest in the raft of scams we face daily, and frequently fall for. I know the recents list on my phone is mostly pages and pages of suspected-spam-labeled calls.

More from CNET

Just picking up provides scammers with the knowledge that your phone number is active and that you may be more likely to fall for the next step down a fraud’s path. Answering adds value to your personal information and a link to it all in its own.

I think scams like these rely on a series of adrenaline-fueled responses — the little spikes you get when you hear the phone ring, then see the ID (it’s the government!) and, if you pick up, the succession of scary warnings. Ignoring unexpected calls from strangers gives you time to think rationally about claims, if they leave a voicemail, and if they don’t, that’s telling as well.

In this case, it could start with the realization that it’s truly unlikely the FTC would be contacting individuals about this, especially before issuing a public statement that there’s a problem.
